Falsification fraud in insurance markets: Algorithms, auditing, and nitpicking
abstract: Abstract This paper studies falsification fraud, where a policy holder suffers a real loss that is excluded from coverage but reports it as covered. Without commitment to costly auditing, equilibrium features positive auditing and falsification, and contracts may exhibit either under‐ or overinsurance. We study two claims‐handling tools: pre‐audit screening and post‐audit payment reductions (“nitpicking”). Under CARA preferences, a sufficiently sensitive screening algorithm concentrates audits on flagged claims and lowers falsification, premiums, and equilibrium coverage; when sensitivity is low, these effects reverse. Nitpicking strengthens audit incentives by reducing payments on audited insurable claims, but its role diminishes as screening improves, implying substitution between the two tools. The welfare comparison between screening and no screening extends to general preferences, as does the weak welfare gain from allowing nitpicking. Numerical exercises under IARA and DARA preferences yield the same qualitative equilibrium patterns.

title: International cooperation and the challenges of financial, environmental and social sustainability: a centre-periphery model
abstract: This paper focuses on the role of international cooperation in shaping a sustainable growth path from a social, economic and environmental standpoint. It builds on the post-Keynesian and Structuralist traditions to include the impact of this cooperation in easing the external constraint on growth and accelerating the international diffusion of green technologies. It also highlights the potential of international Keynesian coordination as a pathway toward sustainable development. Within the conceptual framework of Ecological Macroeconomics, the paper addresses the “sustainability trilemma” faced by a peripheral small open economy and outlines a baseline scenario marked by a triple crisis arising from unsustainable debt burdens, environmental degradation, and widening social vulnerability and inequalities. In addition, the paper explores potential policy scenarios for financial, social, and environmental sustainability in the periphery, while underscoring the rise of both national and international tensions in the process of ecological transformation by discussing emerging policy proposals that link debt relief to green investment and sustainable development commitments.

title: Generative AI and the Evolution of Mortgage Underwriting: Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities
abstract: Abstract Mortgage underwriting is entering a new phase of technological change as general-purpose generative AI tools begin to appear in mortgage origination workflows. We develop an audit framework to evaluate how large language models process mortgage applications. Using real HMDA applications, we experimentally manipulate borrower race, race proxies, and credit quality, and prompt leading commercial LLMs to make approval and pricing recommendations. LLMs recommend more denials and higher interest rates for Black applicants than otherwise identical white applicants, with disparities largest for riskier loans and persisting when race is signaled through names or locations. A simple instruction to avoid bias substantially reduces disparities when race is explicit, partially reduces the name-based pricing gap, and does little against the geographic pricing gap. In matched HMDA–Freddie Mac data, race-blind LLM recommendations correlate with actual lender pricing and subsequent delinquency, though the delinquency association operates largely through observed credit scores. The results show how AI auditing can inform mortgage underwriting governance before general-purpose models become more deeply embedded in origination workflows.

When Green Incentives Backfire: ESG‐Linked Compensation, Dual Accountability, and Corporate Greenwashing
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether executive pay that responds to ESG performance is associated with corporate greenwashing. Using 8634 firm‐year observations for 1286 Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2012 to 2022, we measure greenwashing as the gap between Bloomberg ESG disclosure scores and Huazheng ESG performance scores. We estimate fixed‐effect models and check robustness with dynamic system GMM, propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and instrumental variable estimation. ESG pay sensitivity is positively associated with greenwashing. Dual accountability, where pay relates to both financial and ESG performance, is negatively associated with greenwashing. Female directors are associated with a weaker link between ESG pay sensitivity and greenwashing only when critical mass is accompanied by relatively higher female director pay, with this pattern appearing around the 40th percentile in an exploratory analysis. The associations appear stronger among small and less profitable firms, although most group differences are modest. Because contract‐level ESG targets are not observed and unobserved firm orientation may play a role, we interpret the results as associations rather than causal effects. The findings suggest that how pay is structured and who oversees it matter for whether ESG‐responsive pay is accompanied by symbolic reporting.

title: Measuring Product Value Preservation Under Extended Producer Responsibility: A Strategic Framework for Circular Business Practices
abstract: ABSTRACT Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) has become a central policy instrument for improving environmental performance, yet its implementation remains largely focused on end‐of‐life (EOL) waste management, with limited attention to how firms strategically preserve product value during use. This paper develops a product‐level framework to assess how original equipment manufacturers operationalize value preservation within their environmental strategy under EPR. Building on a systematic review of academic literature, policy instruments, standards, and industry practices, the study identifies and consolidates observable, manufacturer‐controlled attributes that enable product longevity, repair, upgrade, and responsible lifecycle management. The resulting framework comprises six strategic dimensions and 18 measurable criteria covering product design, documentation and information, spare parts and support, digital and software continuity, user empowerment, and EOL guidance. These dimensions are operationalized through the Extended Producer Responsibility–Value Preservation Index (EPR–VPI), which enables consistent assessment and comparison across products. The framework is applied to three illustrative cases: a mechanical appliance, a smartphone product line across generations, and a printer product family. The results show that the EPR–VPI captures both temporal improvements and intra‐family variation in value‐preservation strategies, while revealing that the balance between EOL measures and upstream design and support provision differs across product contexts. The printer family and the first smartphone generation emphasize EOL guidance over spare‐parts support, whereas later smartphone generations show strong parts and repair provision, and the non‐digital appliance shows the reverse pattern. By reframing EPR from a reactive waste management obligation to a proactive business strategy for value preservation, this study contributes a practical measurement tool for researchers, policymakers, and managers seeking to align product design and support decisions with circular economy and environmental performance objectives.

title: Beyond Patents: External R&D Conditions, Organisational Capabilities, and Technical Efficiency in Agri‐Food Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether the external R&D environment is associated with the technical efficiency of agri‐food firms and whether this relationship differs between patenting and non‐patenting enterprises. Using 1668 observations for 243 firms over 2004–2021, including 27 patenting and 216 non‐patenting firms, with substantially broader coverage from 2012 onwards, the analysis applies conditional data envelopment analysis (DEA), complemented by firm fixed‐effects regressions and a Simar–Wilson bootstrapped truncated regression. Comparing conditional and unconditional frontiers shows that external R&D conditions alter firms' positions relative to the production frontier. The preferred fixed‐effects specification finds no robust differential association by patenting status after controlling for persistent firm heterogeneity and year shocks. The complementary Simar–Wilson analysis suggests a stronger association among non‐patenting firms and no significant association among patenting firms, consistent with a possible compensatory role of external R&D conditions. These associations are non‐causal and highlight the organisational relevance of external knowledge and innovation ecosystems.

title: Green Entrepreneurship as a Catalyst for Local Environmental Management in South Africa: Opportunities, Barriers, and Policy Implications
abstract: ABSTRACT Building on the question of how environmental management can be addressed at the local level, the transition from a linear “take–make–dispose” model to a circular economy ( CE ) has become central to sustainable development, particularly in emerging economies facing intertwined environmental and socioeconomic challenges. In South Africa, high unemployment, energy security, and escalating waste generation intensify the urgency for systemic restructuring. This study examines green entrepreneurship (GE) as a catalyst for CE development within environmental management, focusing on Limpopo Province as a contextually rich case of resource potential and developmental vulnerability. Using a qualitative design grounded in thematic analysis, data were collected from 40 green entrepreneurs and 10 policymakers across recycling, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, green manufacturing, and governance sectors. Findings reveal a layered circular ecosystem comprising downstream resource recovery (recycling and waste management), midstream production transformation (renewable energy and regenerative agriculture), and upstream systemic enablers (consultancy and ecodesign services). These activities represent distinct circular business model innovations through which firms create environmental value by recovering resources, extending product life cycles, substituting fossil‐based inputs, and redesigning production processes. Findings indicate that green entrepreneurs implement a range of CE practices, including resource recovery, renewable‐energy provision, composting, and environmentally oriented manufacturing. Participants reported that these activities contributed to waste reduction, resource efficiency, and environmental sustainability. However, these reported outcomes reflect participant experiences and perceptions rather than independently verified environmental performance measures. However, scaling remains constrained by limited access to finance, high upfront technology costs related to waste management infrastructure, technical skills shortages, policy fragmentation, and weak institutional coordination. The study argues that GE is not peripheral but central to South Africa's circular transition. It concludes that strengthening green finance mechanisms, technical capacity development, gender‐inclusive support systems, coherent policy integration, and value chain coordination is essential for unlocking sustainable investment growth. By situating entrepreneurial agency within provincial socioeconomic realities, the paper contributes to debates on implementing CE in the Global South.

title: Organising Project-to-Operations Transition: A Processual Model of Discursive–Material Boundary Work
Workplace gender discrimination: key insights, emerging trends, and future research directions
abstract: Workplace gender discrimination has been extensively examined across disciplines, yet its evolving research landscape remains fragmented. This study applies Structural Topic Modelling (STM) to 1,091 peer-reviewed articles published between 1975 and 2024, identifying six major themes: wage gaps, performance evaluation bias, work-family conflict, unequal working conditions, professional inequality, and structural masculinity. Temporal analysis reveals a shift from concerns about pay and promotion towards broader discussions of identity, mental health, intersectionality, and inclusivity. Integrating these findings with related literature, the study develops the Inclusive Impact Matrix, a conceptual framework connecting workplace culture, formal policies, and everyday organisational practices to outcomes including reduced stereotyping, equitable career advancement, work-life balance, professional support, and employee well-being. The matrix illustrates how cultural, policy-based, and practice-based mechanisms can jointly address distinct dimensions of gender inequality, emphasising their alignment rather than isolated interventions. The study contributes by synthesising fragmented research streams and identifying intersectionality and women’s self-neglect under sustained workplace and care-related pressures as areas warranting further investigation. It offers organisational leaders, HR practitioners, and policymakers an evidence-informed framework for advancing workplace equity and inclusion.

title: Autism and personality testing: Improving reactions and mitigating adverse impact risk in hiring contexts
abstract: Abstract This study examined applicant reactions, mean score differences and measurement invariance for autistic (ASD) and non‐autistic individuals, focusing on the role of work ‘contextualization’ of personality assessment content as a way to potentially minimize negative testing outcomes. Respondents completed general and work‐contextualized personality tests under applicant‐like conditions. ASD respondents rated personality tests less favourably than non‐ASD respondents, particularly for invasiveness and perceived predictive validity, but group differences were small. Contextualization improved reactions for both groups. However, personality scores increased from general to contextualized test conditions for non‐ASD respondents, whereas scores did not significantly increase for ASD respondents. Thus, contextualization widened score gaps between groups, particularly for socially oriented traits. Furthermore, the contextualized test exhibited evidence of measurement bias. Findings suggest that contextualization has some benefits for ASD respondents but also unintended consequences. Thus, contextualization should be implemented cautiously, and tests should be validated to ensure equitable selection outcomes.

Cultivating Team Psychological Safety: A Model Rooted in Conservation of Resources Theory
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine team psychological safety (TPS), the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk‐taking, in its function as a resource caravan passageway. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, we develop a multilevel process model explaining how individual initiative, team interaction, and organizational conditions cultivate and sustain this shared climate, and how it shapes resource protection, investment, and acquisition. Our theoretical model comprises three stages: Cultivation, in which TPS is established, maintained, and nourished; Bloom, in which TPS supports participation, engagement, and sustained performance; and Harvest, in which these processes generate opportunities for resource acquisition across levels. We advance psychological safety research by specifying mechanisms connecting its development and consequences across levels and extend COR theory by explaining how resource caravan passageways are cultivated and renewed.

title: ‘The More We Could Be Involved in Stuff, the More Effective It'd Be’: The Need for More Employer Involvement in Active Labour Market Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT While internationally, interest has grown in employer engagement with active labour market policy (ALMP), their involvement in policy development has been limited—especially in liberal market economies, which lack the institutional frameworks and traditions of social partnership observed elsewhere. Applying a social dialogue lens to interviews with 124 employers, policymakers and other social actors in the UK context, we consider its potential expressive and instrumental functions, and the extent to which facilitating conditions exist to enable it. As in‐work poverty and poor job quality present key intractable challenges for policymakers at national and local levels, we present a revival in social dialogue in ALM policymaking as a critical factor for preventing institutional failure and unlocking innovative policy solutions, especially where supporting people to access and progress in ‘good work’ is a policy priority.

title: Developmental pathways of online grooming victimisation: Understanding adolescent vulnerability
abstract: Abstract Background: Adolescents increasingly engage with digital environments as a central part of their daily lives. While digital environments offer valuable opportunities, they also expose young users to risks, such as online grooming, a manipulative process in which adults build deceptive relationships with minors for sexual exploitation. Recent policy debates in Europe have reignited concern over the need to regulate adolescents’ Internet use, especially given their developmental vulnerabilities.Objective: This study aimed to identify psychological, behavioural, relational, and contextual factors associated with online grooming victimisation in adolescents and to explore how these vulnerabilities vary across developmental stages, informing prevention strategies.Participants and Setting: Data were collected from 240 Portuguese adolescents aged 12–19 in schools in Porto, Portugal.Methods: A quantitative cross-sectional design was used. Online grooming victimisation was coded as a dichotomous outcome based on reported grooming-related experiences. Individual, relational, behavioural, and prior victimisation factors were analysed. Descriptive analyses, group comparisons, and binary logistic regression models were conducted for the overall sample and separately by developmental group.Results: Three predictors of online grooming victimisation emerged: risky online behaviours (OR = 1.21; p < .001), gender (OR = 2.49; p = .012), and previous (cyber)bullying victimisation (OR = 2.21; p = .012). Age-stratified models showed developmentally contingent vulnerability: early adolescence involved behavioural exposure, prior (cyber)bullying experiences, and gendered vulnerability, whereas in later adolescence, risk was associated with risky online behaviours. Conclusions: Prevention should adopt age-sensitive approaches that address behavioural exposure, prior victimisation, and gendered vulnerability.

Reporting Recommendations to Promote Data Quality and Transparency in Online Sexuality Research
abstract: Many aspects of human sexuality—including sexual dreams, fantasies, and solo or partnered sexual behaviors—are often private, difficult or impossible to observe with current technologies, and/or unethical for researchers to observe. As such, human sexuality research often uses self-report methods such as surveys or interviews. Historically, surveys and interviews were conducted in person (e.g., surveys distributed in classrooms or at community events; face-to-face interviews) and/or by telephone or postal mail (Richters et al., 2003 ; Santelli et al., 2000 ). As examples, the National Health and Social Life Survey in the United States (Laumann et al., 2000 ) and the first four waves of the British National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal; Wellings et al., 2001 ) used probability sampling to first identify eligible individuals to invite into their studies followed by face-to-face interviews for data collection. The first two waves of the Australian Study of Health and Relationships, conducted in 2001–2002 and 2012–2013, also used probability sampling, specifically random digit dialing and computer-assisted interviewing techniques (de Visser et al., 2014 ; Richters et al., 2003 ). Data collection in person or by telephone or postal mail meant researchers could have high confidence that the respondents were real people and, depending on the study, part of the target population (e.g., recruiting for interviews at a sexual and reproductive health clinic for a study on sexual and reproductive health care).

Mapping Multiple Pesticides in Vegetables from Major Producing Areas across China: Coexposure Risk Assessment and Risk Prioritization
abstract: Abstract The application of various pesticides to ensure vegetable yields may result in the occurrence of pesticide residues as mixtures. However, information regarding the dietary exposure assessment and risk prioritization of multipesticides in vegetables remains limited. Here, we employed a suspect screening strategy to examine the occurrence of pesticides in 205 samples of cowpea, leek, and celery collected from markets and fields across 11 major producing provinces in China. Totally, 38 pesticides were identified, including 22 in cowpea, 25 in leek, and 23 in celery. Of these, the mean total concentrations of pesticides (∑Pesticides) were 163 ng/g, 96.3 ng/g, and 301 ng/g in cowpea, leek, and celery, respectively. Notably, fungicides and insecticides contributed to >90% of ∑Pesticides, reflecting their extensive use in these vegetables. Exposure to pesticide mixtures was estimated to pose greater health risks than those of single exposure. Additionally, risk prioritization identified six high-priority pesticides (lufenuron, difenoconazole, λ-cyhalothrin, azoxystrobin, procymidone, and propiconazole; ToxPi score >0.5) using the ToxPi framework. The predicted strong binding affinities (<−7.0 kcal/mol) for 61.5% of the protein–pesticide complexes toward neurotoxic and endocrine-disrupting targets suggested potential molecular-level interactions linked to toxicological concerns of the identified pesticides. These results underscore the potential health concerns associated with coexposure to multiple pesticides in vegetables.

Voyage-level energy management of wind-assisted ships with controllable pitch propellers under realistic metocean conditions
abstract: Wind-assisted propulsion introduces route-dependent renewable wind energy into ship propulsion, but its fuel-saving benefit depends on the coupled response of sail thrust, propeller loading, and engine efficiency under realistic metocean condition. This study develops a voyage-level energy management framework for wind-assisted ships equipped with controllable pitch propellers. The rigid wing sail orientation and propeller pitch setting are treated as coordinated operating variables, and a semi-empirical four-degree-of-freedom integrated ship energy performance model is combined with Bayesian optimization to minimize fuel consumption. Reynolds number-dependent sail aerodynamics and pitch-dependent controllable pitch propeller characteristics are integrated to represent wind-assisted thrust and propulsion system flexibility. Ten real-world voyages of a Kamsarmax bulk carrier are used to evaluate route-dependent energy saving performance. Propulsion-only optimization reduces fuel consumption by 0.50%–1.77%, sail-only optimization by 2.19%–9.23%, and joint sail–propulsion optimization by 3.17%–9.88%. The results show that wind-assisted thrust changes net propeller loading and engine operating points, making coordinated sail–propulsion energy management essential for realizing voyage-level fuel and emission reductions.

Thermodynamic analysis of a distributed trigeneration system driven by tandem steam screw expanders
abstract: Screw expanders (SEs) exhibit attractive cost-effectiveness at low power outputs and favorable off-design performance, making them promising candidates for distributed trigeneration systems. However, few studies have addressed the thermodynamic performance of SE-based trigeneration systems across diverse modes. This paper investigates a trigeneration steam Rankine cycle system employing tandem SEs, and evaluates the technical feasibility and application suitability of four series-connected layout schemes. The layout with an alternator sandwiched between two SEs shows particular advantages for trigeneration implementation. Five operating modes are formulated to satisfy variable consumer demands for cooling, heating and power, namely sole-power-generation (SPG), two combined-heating-and-power (CHP) modes and two combined-cooling-and-power (CCP) modes. CHP1 and CCP1 activate only the high-pressure-stage SE, whereas SPG, CHP2, and CCP2 operate with both SEs in service. Calculation results indicate that the 7+8 built-in volume ratio ( ) combination yields a peak thermal efficiency of 22.12% under SPG mode at an evaporation temperature of 250 °C. Critical cross-mode trade-offs between power-generation efficiency and thermal/cooling output are observed. Notably, only the 2+3 and 2+4 combinations are capable of fulfilling the constraint requirements of all five modes. Under representative mode-duration fraction scenarios, the system achieves a maximum energy utilization ratio of 81.51% and a weighted-average exergy efficiency up to 71.45 %. This work provides design references for multi-mode distributed solar-driven trigeneration systems based on tandem SEs.

When does post-demolition vacancy become persistent, and how much vacant land remains? Nationwide evidence from South Korea
abstract: Vacant-land inventories show where parcels remain vacant, but not how long they have remained without built reuse after demolition. Using nationwide administrative histories of 435,702 demolished parcels in South Korea (2005–2024), we link demolition dates to subsequent occupancy approvals and estimate Kaplan–Meier still-vacant curves. We identify when these curves enter a sustained period of slow decline, yielding two measures: stabilization time (ST), when the slowdown begins, and stabilization survival (SS), the share remaining without registered built reuse at that point. Under the main three-year persistence criterion, the pooled national curve reaches this phase 1055 days after demolition, with an estimated still-vacant share of 56.4%. Among parcels without observed registered built reuse at the end of 2024, 29% had elapsed durations shorter than this benchmark. Across 1148 neighborhoods, similar ST values can correspond to different SS values, and vice versa. Neighborhood and municipal conditions are more systematically associated with SS than with ST. These findings show that the timing of slowing reuse and the amount of vacancy remaining capture different aspects of post-demolition change.

title: A climate of countering extremism? Exploring the enrolment of climate activism into UK counter-extremism policy discourses
abstract: Climate activists are increasingly branded as ‘extremists’, ‘terrorists’, and ‘zealots’ by political actors hostile to decarbonisation, including the enrolment of climate activism into preventing/countering violent extremism (P/CVE) policies. Drawing inspiration from political geographic theorisations of territory ( Elden, 2010 ) and security ( Amoore, 2013 ), I conceptualise (counter-)extremism as a political technology which partially functions through the construction of spectrums (calculative discursive tools which take the form of an ‘array’ of possible positions). The paper draws on a discourse-historical analysis (DHA) and semi-structured interviews with activists based in the UK. I contend that two spectrums are constructed, each of which works according to a spatial logic: the first is an ideological spectrum, which positions climate activists as part of an extreme ‘far left’; and second is a spectrum of political practices which proximises physical violence to climate activists. I conclude with reflections on the implications of counter-extremism for climate activism, particularly in the context of the increasing repression of climate (and other) activists worldwide.

Carbon emissions regulation, input-output networks, and firm dynamics: The case of a low-carbon-zone pilot in China
abstract: Abstract Input-output linkages among sectors and firms are largely overlooked when assessing regulatory policies. Using a carbon emissions regulation in China as an example, we find that the regulation facilitates the transition to green technologies and reduces entry and carbon emissions in the regulated sectors with large carbon emissions. We also find unintended spillovers via the input-output network, resulting in more entry and innovation in the downstream sectors; and less entry and innovation in the upstream sectors. These facts can be rationalized by a firm-dynamics model with input-output linkages. The results of quantitative exercises are substantially different when taking input-output linkages into account.

Illiberal gateways and hubs: Chinese push and European pull in Hungary and Serbia
abstract: In this article, we examine how Chinese economic engagement positioned Hungary and Serbia within US–China network competition from 2013 to 2025. Drawing on the network-centrality thesis, we apply a push–pull framework across infrastructure, digital technology, production and finance. On the push side, Chinese firms sought markets, production sites and natural resources, channelled domestic overcapacity outward and internationalised the renminbi. On the pull side, illiberal governance was a key factor, since weak legal and societal constraints reduced entry friction. Because a gateway controls the institutional access point to a larger regulated space while a hub concentrates flows, the two positions emerged bidirectionally, as third countries adapted to great-power competition and China selected partners that fitted its expansion logic. Hungary became a gateway, where tariff-jumping access to the Single Market, tax breaks and lax regulation met Chinese demand for cost-effective production. At the same time, Serbia became a hub, where sovereign-guaranteed borrowing and resource endowments offered sites beyond EU oversight. Most European states became neither, and illiberal government is what distinguished those that did. The gateway–hub distinction therefore illuminates how third countries position themselves under great-power competition.

title: Traceability as a Quality Cue: How Consumers Respond to Product‐Level Information
abstract: ABSTRACT Food supply chains have become longer, more fragmented and less visible to the people at the end of them, leaving consumers unable to verify the safety, provenance and ethical credentials of what they buy and firms unable to demonstrate them credibly. Against this background of growing supply chain complexity and consumer uncertainty, we examine whether traceability information functions as a quality cue in meat consumption and how it influences purchase intentions. Focusing on electronic identification (eID)‐enabled lamb traceability in Australia, we employ a multi‐study, mixed‐method design. Study 1 ( n = 10) explores consumer perceptions through in‐depth interviews. Study 2a conducts a pilot, whereas Study 2b uses a Facebook A/B field experiment to test behavioural responses in a natural setting. Study 3 ( n = 402) applies an online experiment to test a moderated mediation model. Qualitative findings show generally favourable attitudes, linking traceability to quality, safety and assurance. Whereas the field experiment shows no significant behavioural effect, the controlled experiment demonstrates that traceability increases purchase intention via perceived product quality, with stronger effects for highly involved consumers. Findings suggest that traceability can serve as a strategic, institutionally verified quality signal but that its effectiveness is conditional on consumer involvement and communication context. For firms and policymakers, this suggests that the consumer‐facing returns on traceability investment depend not only on verifying information but also on how that verified information is communicated at the point of choice.

title: Women on Boards and Interagency ESG Rating Dispersion: The Moderating Roles of Board Age and Size in S&P 500 Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between women on corporate boards and the consistency of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) evaluations across rating agencies, while recognizing that ESG rating divergence also reflects methodological heterogeneity across rating agencies. Although prior research has predominantly focused on ESG disclosure scores from individual raters, divergence in ESG scores across agencies for the same firm, referred to as interagency ESG rating dispersion, represents a critical challenge for stakeholders seeking reliable sustainability assessments. This study extends existing literature by analyzing firm‐level governance mechanisms as determinants of such a rating misalignment. Employing panel data from S&P 500 firms for the period 2015–2022, the analysis investigates how board gender composition is associated with interagency ESG dispersion between Bloomberg and Refinitiv, and how board size and average age moderate this association. The study draws on upper echelons theory and the attention‐based view to interpret the mechanisms through which board characteristics are related to the coherence of ESG signals communicated to external stakeholders. The findings indicate that greater representation of women on boards is associated with lower ESG rating dispersion, consistent with greater interpretive convergence across agencies evaluating firms' sustainability‐related disclosures. However, larger boards and boards with older members attenuate this effect. Notably, the moderation by board age runs contrary to conventional assumptions, suggesting that boards with older directors may constrain the alignment of ESG evaluations. This study contributes to ESG and corporate governance literature by emphasizing firm‐level determinants of rating coherence and the conditions under which board composition affects the interpretability of sustainability information.

title: A framework for deploying the customer success function in organizations

Roadway safety during active wildfires: A machine-learning analysis of crash occurrence and injury severity
abstract: Wildfires create rapidly changing conditions for roadway operations and safety, yet how wildfire-related conditions relate to crash occurrence and injury severity remains insufficiently understood. Using data from 10 California wildfires between 2020 and 2025, this study examines crash occurrence at the roadway segment-day level and injury severity at the crash level through two separate machine-learning analyses. Across the two analyses, predictors included fire advancement toward roadway segments, fire-risk context, smoke exposure, historical Public Safety Power Shutoff exposure, and distance to the active fire perimeter, alongside conventional roadway, land-use, weather, traffic-exposure, and temporal characteristics. The severity analysis additionally incorporated driver, vehicle, and collision attributes. Five tree-based classifiers were evaluated using cross-validation, and predictor contributions were examined using complementary feature-importance measures and SHAP. Fire advancement toward roadway segments emerged as the strongest crash-occurrence predictor across all importance measures, while fire-risk context and smoke exposure also contributed to model predictions. In contrast, injury severity was characterized primarily by collision, vehicle-safety, driver, roadway, and built-environment factors, with collision type and airbag deployment among the strongest contributors. Most wildfire-related variables ranked below the leading crash-specific predictors in the severity model. Together, these findings highlight distinct predictor structures for crash occurrence and conditional injury severity, supporting their separate assessment when examining roadway safety during active wildfires.

Temperature-Dependent Decay of Infectivity of Infectious Salmon Anemia Virus (ISAV) in Raw Seawater
abstract: Abstract Infectious salmon anemia virus (ISAV) is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA, orthomyxovirus, distantly related to influenza viruses. ISAV poses a significant threat to global salmon aquaculture and wild fish and is a notifiable disease according to the World Organization for Animal Health. Understanding virus persistence in seawater under different environmental conditions is critical for biosecurity and disease mitigation. In this study, the persistence of ISAV infectivity was studied in raw seawater at five temperatures. Cell-culture propagated ISAV was incubated in raw seawater at 4, 7, 10, 13, and 17 °C for defined time periods. The persisting ISAV infectivity was then determined using an in vivo salmon fry challenge model, based on the assumption that the resulting infection prevalence correlates with the number of infectious ISAV virions present during the bath challenge. The results showed a clear temperature-dependence in infectivity persistence, with higher temperatures leading to faster decay of infectivity. The experimental data were used to estimate ISAV infectivity half-lives that were incorporated into a dispersal model to simulate the spread of infectious ISAV at different seawater temperatures. The modeling showed that the average potential exposure distance to infectious ISAV decreased approximately 40% when seawater temperature increased from 4 to 17 °C.

title: Experimental study on the coordinated control of the indoor thermal environment and photovoltaic power generation by the EAHE-PV/T system combined with heat source and fan
Hybrid Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning for Vehicle-to-Grid Operation with Distributed Energy Resources Considering Transformer Thermal Loading
Digitalisation, Eco‐Innovation and SME Internationalisation: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT This study integrates the digitalisation and dynamic capabilities literature to examine the relationship between digitalisation, eco‐innovation and internationalisation in small and medium‐sized enterprises (SME). Using data obtained from 300 SME owner‐managers operating in the United Kingdom, the findings suggest that digitalisation positively impacts eco‐innovation and consequently the nature of internationalisation activities. In addition, there is a moderating effect of internationalisation experience on the relationship between eco‐innovation and internationalisation. These findings highlight the pivotal role of eco‐innovation, digitalisation and international experience in enabling SMEs to thrive in international markets. Furthermore, the study offers empirical evidence of how SMEs dynamically develop digital resources, and internationalisation is an outcome of building such capabilities. The implications for practice and future research avenues are examined.

title: Capabilities Over Stakeholder Pressure: How Sustainable Learning and Green Dynamic Capabilities Drive Corporate Sustainability Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT With the growing emphasis on sustainable development, corporate sustainability performance (CSP) has become an important indicator of organisations' environmental, social and governance commitments. This study examines the effects of sustainable learning capabilities (SLC) and green dynamic capabilities (GDC) on CSP, focusing on the mediating role of GDC in the SLC–CSP relationship and the moderating role of stakeholder pressure (SP). The proposed model was empirically tested using data collected from organisations in Brunei Darussalam and analysed using SmartPLS. The results reveal that both SLC and GDC have significant positive effects on CSP, whereas SLC also positively influences GDC. Furthermore, GDC partially mediates the relationship between SLC and CSP, suggesting that sustainability‐oriented learning contributes to improved sustainability performance both directly and through the development of green dynamic capabilities. However, SP does not significantly moderate the SLC–CSP relationship, indicating that its moderating effect was not supported in the study context. Drawing on the resource‐based view (RBV) and institutional theory, this study advances understanding of how organisational capabilities contribute to CSP. The findings also offer practical implications for managers seeking to integrate sustainability‐oriented learning and green dynamic capabilities into organisational strategies to strengthen long‐term sustainability performance.

title: Translating Scope 3 Carbon Accounting Into Climate Disclosure in Maritime‐Port Ecosystems: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Maritime‐port ecosystems pose distinctive challenges for credible Scope 3 carbon accounting and climate disclosure because emissions, data and responsibilities are distributed across organizational boundaries. This study systematically reviews 114 peer‐reviewed journal articles (84 from Scopus database and 30 supplementary studies identified through Google Scholar), combining bibliometric mapping with qualitative content analysis. The synthesis identifies three interconnected research areas: Scope 3 accounting and boundary‐setting; climate disclosure and accountability; and digital infrastructures and traceability. While existing research prioritizes emissions measurement, monitoring and decarbonization, less attention has been paid to disclosure credibility and distributed accountability. Addressing this gap, this study conceptualizes the transition from Scope 3 accounting to climate disclosure as a governance‐dependent translation process shaped by boundary‐setting and commensuration, data governance, verification and assurance and responsibility allocation. This study proposes a theory‐informed framework and a Theory, Context, Characteristics and Methodology (TCCM)–based agenda for future empirical research in fragmented value‐chain ecosystems.

title: Rethinking Paradoxical Tensions in the Transition Toward Circular Business Practices: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT As central actors in the transition toward a circular economy, firms face multiple tensions when implementing circular business practices, often resulting in paradoxical situations. Although paradox scholars increasingly call for a systems perspective to capture the full complexity of wicked problems, the extent to which systems thinking informs research on paradoxes in firms' transition toward circular business practices remains unclear. We address this gap through a systematic literature review of 42 peer‐reviewed articles published between 2018 and 2025 and indexed in Scopus and Web of Science. We examine the implicit assumptions underlying the reviewed studies, drawing on the three core elements of systems: hierarchy, interconnections, and emergence. To structure the analysis, we classify paradoxical tensions across four analytical levels—macro, interorganizational, organizational, and individual. Based on recurring patterns in the literature, our review identifies four implicit assumptions that constrain a more systemic understanding of paradoxes in firms' circular transition: (1) Paradoxes largely exist in isolation from one another and (2) remain stable over time, (3) within the organizational level, strategy is the key element shaping paradoxes, and (4) individual actors, and their perceptions and experiences of paradoxes, play a limited role in shaping firms' circular transition. We contribute to the literature on organizational paradoxes and circular transitions by revealing these underlying implicit assumptions and showing how they limit the adoption of systems thinking. In response, we develop four alternative perspectives that provide directions for refining and advancing paradox research on firms' circular transition to better account for their systemic complexity.

title: Exploring frontline ambidexterity in robot restaurants: balancing efficiency, human touch and cultural variations
abstract: Purpose This study sought to explore frontline ambidexterity dimensions in robot restaurants, theoretically grounded in the employee–robot–customer service triad and cross-cultural differences between Japan and the USA. Design/methodology/approach The study utilized a mixed-methods qualitative–quantitative observational methodology. It adopted a triangulated approach, comprising three main stages: (1) identification of frontline ambidexterity dimensions, (2) exploration of frontline ambidexterity emergent themes in Japanese and USA service triad and (3) analysis of cross-cultural quantitative patterns of frontline ambidexterity dimensions. Findings Via the multi-stage observational research design, the study identifies four distinct dimensions of frontline ambidexterity: parallel, facilitation, intervention and synergy. These dimensions demonstrate that frontline ambidexterity operates through multiple behavioral mechanisms through which employees balance robot-enabled efficiency and human touch within the service triad. The findings further demonstrate that ambidexterity manifests differently across Japan and USA cultural contexts, with statistically significant differences observed for parallel and synergy behaviors. Practical implications This research offers actionable insights for restaurant managers, HR professionals and service robot designers on how to tailor effective and culturally sensitive robot design, implementation strategies and training programs. Originality/value This study is the first to develop a multidimensional framework of frontline ambidexterity within the employee-robot-customer service triad. The cross-cultural comparison between Japan and the USA further offers a forward-looking perspective on how technological advancement reshapes triadic service dynamics as robotic services evolve from novelty (USA) toward normalization (Japan). Methodologically, this study is among the first to employ a mixed qualitative–quantitative observational approach to examine real-world employee–robot–customer interactions, thereby addressing limitations of prior perception-based studies that could not capture the robot as an active linkage in triadic service encounters.

title: Two limericks about ethics
The metrics of silence: I call it slow undoing
abstract: The metrics of silence: I call it slow undoing Weight of silenceIn corridors lined with intellectual minds, and polished profiles on LinkedIn and X, I tread softly, measuring every word.Each syllable feels like a spark that might ignite the fragile peace of academic air.Ideas, once birds, now perch in my throat, their wings folded, trembling, afraid to soar too far from consensus.I see the cancelled, paused mid-sentence, their names whispered like warnings over coffee breaks in conferences.Freedom of thought wears a delicate mask, a smile stitched from fear and survival.I sip my coffee, nod at the proper moments, while my unspoken truths dissolve like sugar in silence.

title: AAAJ Literature and Insights Feminine dilemmas of a Global South academic

One Meeting That Should Not Be an Email: Manager–Direct Report One‐on‐One Meetings and Employee Engagement
abstract: ABSTRACT Building and maintaining an engaged workforce is a priority for organizations worldwide. While the antecedents and benefits of an engaged workforce are well documented, organizations continue to struggle to keep employees engaged. These ongoing difficulties point to the need for alternative, practical ways to foster engagement at work. To this end, we examine whether workplace meetings, specifically one‐on‐one (1:1) meetings between managers and direct reports, can foster engagement. Grounded in job demands and resources (JD‐R) theory, self‐determination theory (SDT) and Kahn's engagement theory, we hypothesized that 1:1 meeting quantity and quality promote engagement by satisfying employees' basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. We tested a moderated mediation model using two time‐separated online surveys ( N = 303). Results indicated that meeting quality, reflected in a managers' task‐ and relations‐oriented behaviors in 1:1 s, was more consistently associated with engagement than meeting quantity. These relationships remained after accounting for managers' use of the same behaviors outside 1:1 meetings, suggesting that 1:1 meetings provide a unique and meaningful context for individualized, synchronous support. Overall, the results identify 1:1 meetings as a practical tool managers can use to promote direct reports' engagement and advance both meeting science and engagement literature.

title: From missing traffic states to crash detection: Evaluating low-rank imputation under heterogeneous missingness
Longitudinal associations between maltreatment, bullying victimization and externalizing problems in children and adolescents: Evidence from Brazilian High Risk Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Empirical observations consistently demonstrate heightened levels of trauma and bullying victimization among children and adolescents with conduct problems. However, most of this evidence is generated in high-income countries and little is known about the development of conduct problems in low- and middle-income countries, which are characterized by elevated risks of threat and deprivation. Methods: To explore conduct problems development in a high-risk setting, we used data from 2,511 children and young people (aged 6 - 23 years) enrolled in the Brazilian High Risk Cohort Study. Caregiver reports were used to assess developmental risk factors and conduct problems across three waves of data collection. A Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model was applied. Results: Both trauma at T1 (β = .08, SE = .22, p = .024) and bullying victimization at T1 (β = .08, SE = .12, p = .016) predicted conduct problems at T2. Gender disparities were also observed: while males showed a consistent increase in conduct problems at T3 following trauma exposure at T2 (β = .14, SE = .46, p = .031), females demonstrated a decrease (β = -.26, SE = .65, p = .003). Conclusions: Our study highlights longitudinal associations between trauma, bullying victimisation and conduct problems, with differences across genders. These findings emphasize the need for a stronger focus on child and adolescent mental health problems in Brazil, particularly targeting males, as well as in other low- and middle-income countries more generally. Moreover, collaborative research with carefully coordinated methods is essential to identify global and context-specific mechanisms involved in the development of conduct problems.

title: Negotiating Competing Expectations—Chiefs and Mineral Governance in Ghana
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines what shapes chiefs' discretionary decision‐making and how they exercise authority within hybrid governance arrangements, focusing on Ghana's artisanal and small‐scale mining (ASM) sector. Existing scholarship recognizes that traditional authorities can strengthen or undermine state governance but offers limited explanations for variation in their practices. Drawing on interviews with chiefs, miners, and state officials, the paper develops a discretionary governance framework that integrates hybrid governance, access theory, and discretion. It argues that overlapping customary and statutory authority creates a discretionary space for chiefs to navigate competing expectations. Chiefs exercise this discretion through diverse governance practices, including restricting access to mining sites, mobilizing communities, and collaborating with state institutions, as well as facilitating access to land, negotiating informal payments, and shielding unauthorised miners from enforcement. These practices can reinforce, negotiate, circumvent, or undermine formal mining regulation. The paper advances debates on traditional authority and hybrid governance while challenging assumptions that constitutionally empowering chiefs necessarily strengthens mineral governance.

The Search for Parental Leave and the Early-Career Gender Wage Gap
abstract: Gender differences in preferences for parental leave contribute to the early-career growth in the gender wage gap among highly educated millennial Americans. Estimating a hedonic job-search model, I show that, while both men and women experience wage growth by entering firms offering better pay and benefits, the wage gap increases as women accept lower wages upon receiving job offers from employers providing parental leave. The wage-gap growth could decline by 60% if preferences for paid parental leave did not differ by gender. It could also decline if mandating and subsidizing the provision of paid leave muted workers’ leave-wage trade-off.

title: Getting Teachers Back to Study: Input-Based Teacher Incentives and Student Achievement
abstract: Rewarding teachers on the basis of student performance is a growing trend in educational policy. This paper estimates the effects of a policy that ties payments with teachers’ pedagogical skills instead. We study a large-scale reform in Chile that introduced financial incentives tied to a teacher evaluation system. Using a unique administrative data set of over 500, 000 student-teacher-year matches, we estimate the effect of the policy on student performance exploiting the program’s gradual roll-out through a differences-in-differences analysis. We document precise, null effects of the policy on student math and language standardized test scores. Estimating a structural model of teacher skills and student performance, we show that by making incentives more homogeneous across the distribution of teacher characteristics policymakers can improve the policy’s effects on student performance and overall welfare.

title: A new equilibrium: COVID-19 lockdowns and WFH persistence
abstract: This paper documents a robust link between COVID-19 lockdowns and the uptake and persistence of working from home (WFH) practices. Exploiting rich longitudinal data, we use a difference-in-differences strategy to compare office workers in three heavily locked-down Australian states to similar workers in less affected states. Locked-down workers sustain 43% higher WFH levels through 2023  0.5 days per week  with a monotonic doseresponse relationship. Persistence is driven by adjustments on both sides of the labor market: employers downsize office space and open remote/hybrid positions, while employees relocate away from city centers and invest in home offices and technology.

Structural Empirical Analysis of Vacancy Referrals with Imperfect Monitoring and the Strategic Use of Sickness Absence
abstract: This paper provides a structural analysis of the role of job vacancy referrals (VRs) by public employment agencies in the job search behavior of unemployed individuals, incorporating institutional features of the monitoring of search behavior by the agencies. Notably, rejections of VRs may lead to sanctions (temporary benefits reductions) while workers may report sick to avoid those. We estimate models using German administrative data from social security records linked with caseworker recorded data on VRs, sick reporting and sanctions. The analysis highlights the influence of aspects of the health care system on unemployment durations. We estimate that for around 25% of unemployed workers, removing the channel that enables strategic sick reporting reduces the mean unemployment duration by 4 days.

title: Living for the lineage: Ancestral beliefs and the spiritual foundations of fertility in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Conventional demographic models systematically overestimate fertility decline in sub-Saharan Africa. This paper proposes a complementary explanation grounded in a prevalent but understudied belief system: ancestors influence the living and seek the continuation of their lineage. In this worldview, having children becomes a moral and collective duty, rooted in the spiritual responsibility to ensure the survival of the lineage. Drawing on first-hand data, novel ethnographic information, and historical and contemporary surveys, I document a strong and quantitatively large positive relationship between ancestral beliefs and fertility across contexts and time periods. A simple model in which children are a public good for the lineage rationalizes the patterns observed in the data: the fertility effect of ancestral beliefs is concentrated in patrilineal societies, and a specific form of free-riding emerges among siblings whose children continue the same family line. • Beliefs in ancestral spirits raise fertility across sub-Saharan Africa. • Shown in Benin, the DR Congo, 19 countries today, and global folklore records. • Having children is a collective duty to the lineage, not a private choice. • Effects concentrate in patrilineal societies, where sons continue the line. • Free-riding appears among siblings whose children continue the same line.

title: Comment on “Slackness, Openness, and the Anatomy of Cash Transfer Multipliers” by Minki Kim and Mitchell VanVuren

Emotional State and Market Activity: Cause or Consequence?
abstract: Abstract Many observers have asserted that there is a correlation between traders’ emotional states and asset market behaviour, with Joviality associated with high prices and Fear with low prices. In this paper, we conduct a laboratory experiment to examine the direction of causality in this relationship. The results show that moods, induced by videos, shown in virtual reality, do not influence market prices. However, there is a strong relationship between market activity and subsequent emotional states, suggesting that the correlation between emotional state and market activity is driven by the influence of market activity on emotional state, not the other way around.

title: Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence From China's College Expansion
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how human capital shapes both the level and direction of automation. We develop an endogenous Schumpeterian growth model in which skilled labor is allocated across production, horizontal automation of new tasks, and vertical upgrading of existing automated tasks. A positive skilled‐labor shock reallocates labor toward R&D and accelerates automation along both margins. Using China's 1999 college enrollment expansion as a natural experiment, we find that firms in skill‐intensive industries increased robot adoption significantly more after the reform, with a stronger effect on the horizontal than the vertical margin.

An Investigation of Market Invariance for the Tokyo Stock Exchange
abstract: ABSTRACT We test the invariance‐of‐bet hypothesis from Kyle and Obizhaeva (2016) for the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE). The pooled regression coefficients of the logarithm of the number of trades on the logarithm of the product of volume and volatility range from 0.663 to 0.665, close to the theoretical value of two‐thirds predicted by the invariance‐of‐bet hypothesis. Using the TSE as a relatively clean benchmark, we further examine when the empirical two‐thirds relation deviates from its theoretical prediction. We find that deviations become more pronounced during extreme market conditions, for stocks facing more binding tick‐size constraints, and around the market open and close. Our results also suggest that measurement errors in transaction data can contribute to deviations from the two‐thirds relation.

title: Misperceiving the roots of inequality: Cross-country evidence from Europe
Solution method of a macroeconomic model with rational expectations
Pro-poor land reforms, education and fertility: international evidence, 1820-2010
abstract: Abstract Land reforms are often assumed to promote economic development in unequal societies. However, supportive cross-country evidence remains limited, largely because major land reforms are rare events that provide insufficient identifying variation in small samples. Drawing on a global dataset of major land reforms over the period 1820–2010, we provide evidence that pro-poor land reforms promote economic development by increasing school enrollment and reducing fertility, whereas non-pro-poor land reforms do not. We further show that these empirical patterns are consistent with the relaxation of credit constraints among poor households and the weakening of the political power of the landed elites, which together facilitate greater human capital investment and demographic transition. Event-study analyses, semi-parametric difference-in-differences estimations, two-way fixed effects, instrumental variable estimates, and placebo tests collectively suggest that the results are not driven by endogeneity.

title: Resource nationalism and economic outcomes: evidence from national policy interventions
The effect of being a poll worker on democratic attitudes in a post-conflict society: evidence from an experiment in Colombia
abstract: This paper examines how citizens’ direct participation in democratic processes boosts attitudes toward democratic practices. Focusing on compulsory poll working, we argue that citizens selected to work at polling stations on Election Day gain additional information about democratic procedures, and that this shapes their attitudes toward electoral integrity and democracy. We test our claims by leveraging a pre-registered large-scale experiment from the 2023 Colombian regional elections. Based on a unique survey dataset of over 25,000 poll workers matched with a sample of ordinary citizens, we identify a positive and robust causal effect of electoral task management on attitudes toward electoral integrity and democracy that operates mainly via a theory-based mechanism, but also via a practice-based mechanism. Moreover, we discover that this treatment effect is smaller in municipalities heavily affected by political violence during previous civil conflict.

title: Economic dynamics of flood damage: The roles of private capital, public capital, and financial accelerator
Disparities in climate risk-mitigation and recreation services in Grenoble (France)
abstract: Summary Urban green spaces provide cultural and climate risk-mitigation ecosystem services (ES) critical for the well-being of urban residents. Yet these benefits are not equally shared across social groups, and environmental segregation - i.e., the spatial separation of population groups between areas of contrasted environmental quality - is common. For instance, environmental justice studies have shown that green space acreage and quality are typically lower in low-income neighbourhoods. However, more detailed assessments integrating a range of ES and the diverse needs of multiple groups are needed to effectively inform equitable urban planning. Here, we combine socio-demographic spatial data with ES modelling to assess social disparities in the distribution of three ES - heatwave mitigation, flood regulation, and urban recreation - in the Grenoble metropolitan area, France. Our results show that low-income households generally benefit from lower climate risk mitigation, but from equal or slightly greater urban recreation opportunities. We also identify mismatches between ES supply and demand from vulnerable groups, which are particularly acute in disadvantaged neighborhoods. These findings highlight the importance of integrating social needs and vulnerabilities into urban greening strategies. Policies that move beyond generic measures of green space provision and explicitly consider multiple ES can help ensure that urban green infrastructure delivers fair and effective benefits across diverse communities.

title: A post-growth deal for Italy: Exploring the coalition-building potential of non-reformist reforms
abstract: Challenging green growth narratives, degrowth argues that achieving ecological sustainability in high-income countries requires a democratically planned and socially just downscaling of production and consumption, alongside a reorientation of economic institutions toward collective wellbeing within planetary boundaries. While post-growth and degrowth scholarship has increasingly shifted from critique to policy proposals, limited attention has been paid to the political agency and coalition-building capacity required to implement such policies. This paper asks whether a post-growth policy package can function as an emancipatory tool for building a counter-hegemonic alliance capable of contesting growth-dependent capitalism. We examine perceptions of a “Post-Growth Deal” composed of five non-reformist reforms – Universal Care Income, Universal Public Services, Working Time Reduction, a Public Job Guarantee, and Deliberative Forums – among three strategically positioned actor groups: environmental activists, labor union members, and progressive political party members. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines focus group discussions with a survey, we analyze the desirability, communicability, achievability, and perceived popularity of these measures. Our findings show that work-centered policies, particularly Working Time Reduction and a Green Job Guarantee, display the strongest potential for cross-group alignment, while more redistributive and participatory measures face greater ideological and communicative barriers. The study contributes to ecological economics by empirically assessing the coalition-building potential of post-growth policies, foregrounding compromise and political strategy, and situating degrowth debates within a southern European context, by focussing on the case-study of Italy.

title: ESG performance, tone of earnings calls, and market reaction during an economic crisis
abstract: Abstract This study explores the relationship between firms’ environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, the tone of earnings calls, and market reaction during the COVID-19 outbreak. Using a comprehensive sample of European listed firms and a robust methodology, our findings show a less optimistic tone of the earnings calls during COVID-19 and a negative relationship between ESG and tone, wherein firms with lower ESG project a more positive outlook in their earnings calls to reassure stakeholders. We find a positive market reaction to the tone of earnings calls, which is more pronounced for firms that seek to reassure with an inflated tone, even in presence of lower ESG. This study offers new evidence on the value relevance of non-financial information as a driver of managerial tone and the effectiveness of companies’ communication strategies in reassuring stakeholders and market participants during an economic crisis; it provides insights into how companies could respond to manage stakeholders’ expectations when dealing with significant large-scale disruptions.

title: Insurer Capital and Organizational Forms in Market Equilibrium
abstract: Abstract We explain the coexistence of stock and mutual organizational forms and their relative dominance in different insurance markets in a market equilibrium model. Organizational forms endogenously reflect the benefits and costs of equity and the impact of insurer operating efficiencies. Stock insurers are larger and more efficient than mutual insurers. Mutualization (i) increases with taxes and agency costs, (ii) decreases with the mean and idiosyncratic variability of insuree losses, (iii) increases with aggregate insurer asset and liability risks, and (iv) increases (decreases) with the market return when insuree loss variance is low (high). Evidence from U.S. insurance data supports all our predictions. (JEL G12, G22, G32)

Climate Change and Agricultural Export Margins: The Role of Financial Development

Toward a Behavioral–Institutional Framework of Socially Responsible Investment Adoption: A Bibliometric Review and Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing prominence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations has increased scholarly and market attention to socially responsible investment (SRI) as an approach that combines financial and sustainability considerations. This study examines the development, intellectual structure, and determinants of SRI adoption through an integrated bibliometric analysis, systematic literature review, and thematic analysis. This study analyses Scopus‐indexed publications from 2015 to 2026; it combines bibliometric mapping of 358 documents with a systematic synthesis of 72 eligible studies. The findings indicate substantial growth in SRI research, particularly in recent years, alongside increasing thematic attention to investor behavior, sustainability, ESG, and responsible investment. The systematic review identifies 13 recurring determinants associated with SRI adoption, organized through thematic analysis into five themes: psychological and Behavioral; social, moral and sustainability; knowledge and literacy; financial and risk; and institutional. Building on these themes, the study proposes a Behavioral–institutional framework in which the four individual‐level themes serve as antecedents of SRI intention and adoption, while government policy support acts as a contextual moderator of the intention–adoption relationship. The framework is presented as a conceptual synthesis, with its relationships offered as propositions for future empirical testing. The study offers directions for future research and suggests possible implications for policymakers, financial institutions, and investment practitioners.

title: Measuring digital technology adoption: a multidimensional scale development and validation
abstract: Existing research widely acknowledges the significant effects of digitalisation, yet empirical work often treats it as a unified construct, which obscures its underlying technological diversity. This paper addresses that limitation by developing a psychometrically validated scale of digital technology adoption that captures the multidimensional and functionally distinct nature of digital technologies. Drawing on theoretical insights from innovation studies and digital technology research, we identify four core dimensions that structure firms’ adoption profiles: digital communication technology, digital in situ technology, digital data analytics technology, and digital networking technology. We develop and validate a 19-item scale that operationalises these dimensions and reflects the different coordination, optimisation, data access, and location access functions that digital technologies perform. The resulting measurement instrument offers scholars a more precise means to examine how digital technologies shape organisational processes. It also provides managers with a diagnostic tool for assessing adoption patterns and guiding technology investment decisions.

title: The price of a nation: The effects of financial incentives on support for union in Scotland
A Blessing in Disguise: The Long‐Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old‐Age Male Longevity
abstract: The infamous agricultural pest, the boll weevil, spread across southern US counties between 1892 and 1920. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. We show that the estimated effects are robust across a wide array of specifications, are not driven by sociodemographic and socioeconomic compositional change in the final sample, and are not associated with pre-existing trends in the outcome. Further, we find larger impacts among Blacks, children of lower educated mothers, whose fathers work in the farming industry, and those born in high cotton intensity counties. Moreover, the effects appear to be substantially larger among children in states with less restrictive child labor policies, implying the role of these policies in reducing the adverse effects of child labor in the absence of the boll weevil in cotton production counties. Affected children are more likely to migrate, and their destination counties are more likely to be urban and have higher socioeconomic scores. The 1940 census suggests that the exposed children attain higher levels of education and have higher socioeconomic scores. We discuss the policy implications of these results in relation to child labor and school attendance policies in developing countries.

title: Not in Isolation: The Influence of Patient‐Sharing Networks on Psychotropic Prescribing for People With Dementia
abstract: The use of low-value care practices is extensive. Clinical guidelines and alignment in prescribing practice can facilitate a reduction in related medical practices by physicians as part of de-implementation strategies. Peer influence within physicians' networks can significantly impact clinical behaviors, including the adoption or abandonment of certain prescribing practices. We examine the physicians prescribing alignment related to de-implementing low-value psychotropics prescribing to people with dementia. Using Finnish prescription register data (2014-2020), we identified patient-sharing networks and applied instrumental variable estimation to account for reflection and endogeneity. We instrument patient-sharing network prescribing using peers' peers' prescribing behavior-physicians who share patients with a focal physician's peers but not with the focal physician themselves-to isolate peer effects on psychotropic prescribing to dementia patients. We found that a one percentage point higher share of psychotropic prescribing within physicians' patient-sharing network was associated with a 1.5 percentage point increase in the physician's psychotropic prescribing when controls and time-invariant physician characteristics were fixed. Our findings underscore the need for consensus among physicians to facilitate the de-implementation of low-value care in the context of dementia care.

title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
abstract: Abstract The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.

title: Pay incentives to run for local governments
abstract: Local governments in advanced democracies have increasingly struggled to attract political candidates, weakening electoral competition and accountability at the municipal level. While several factors may contribute to this trend, politicians’ salaries represent one of the few policy levers that can be directly adjusted by policymakers. We study a large-scale reform that substantially increased local politicians’ pay, exploiting quasi-experimental variation in election timing across municipalities. On average, we find no evidence that higher salaries increase political entry. Instead, the effects are concentrated in specific local contexts: municipalities with lower entry barriers and less affluent areas experience an increase in candidacies, particularly among first-time candidates. In the poorest areas, the reform further alters the composition of local political elites, shifting recruitment toward candidates with different educational and occupational backgrounds.
