title: EXPRESS: How Gig Sellers Do the Hustle
abstract: We conceptualize and develop theoretical insights related to a neglected category of market actors: gig sellers. Gig sellers are independent agents who sell products on behalf of a specific brand with marketing support. They face semi-entrepreneurial opportunities, meaning that while they are entirely responsible for managing the customer sales funnel, they do not develop new products or services like conventional entrepreneurs. They are compensated solely by sales commissions and do not receive salaries or benefits like organizational salesreps. Drawing on a large set of qualitative data from effective agents, we inductively and abductively draw inspiration both from literature and our analyses to unpack how these agents seize the opportunity to accomplish what is important to them. We find prominent reliance on effectual versus predictive practices is crucial to satisfactory achievement of outcomes. We expand our understanding of the range of outcomes that gig selling may result in, whether it be to remain in gig sales (enacting long-term loyalty, switching teams, or enriching) or enter alternative opportunity corridors (pursuing entrepreneurship, seeking employment). Our theoretical insights contrast with findings regarding salespeople in institutional settings and other categories of independent agents. Practical implications for agents and organizations are developed.

title: Government‐funded experimentation: How startups use R&D contracts to resolve uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded. This paper examines how government‐funded experimentation relates to subsequent performance among high‐tech startups that receive federal awards. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups between 2001 and 2018, I distinguish between technology experimentation, measured by the value of R&D contracts, and market experimentation, measured by the number of agencies awarding the R&D contracts. Market experimentation is positively associated with subsequent employment, sales, and acquisition, while technology experimentation shows weaker associations with these outcomes. The findings are consistent with startups using information from multiple government buyers to learn about market opportunities and improve subsequent performance. Managerial Summary High‐tech startups need to test both whether their technology works and where demand exists, but venture capital often leaves this experimentation unfunded. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups from 2001 to 2018, this paper shows that startups funded by more government agencies subsequently have higher employment and sales and are more likely to be acquired. Larger R&D contract amounts have less consistent relationships with these outcomes. For managers, the findings suggest considering what different government customers can help the firm learn. For policymakers, they suggest that the diversity of a startup's public customer base is a vital margin to consider alongside the overall size of its R&D awards.

title: EXPRESS: Slim Shading in Ad Auctions: Adjustment of Bidding Strategies to First-Price Rules
abstract: We study how bidders adjusted to a switch from second-price to first-price auction rules on a large online advertising exchange. Under first-price rules, bidders should strategically reduce (“shade”) their bids. To assess whether observed bid reductions were sufficient given the competition each bidder faced, we develop a nonparametric estimator of a lower bound on the valuation underlying each bid. The estimator relies on localized measures of competition and does not require assumptions of bidder symmetry, valuation independence, or equilibrium bidding. Applying the method to more than 40 million auctions involving eight major demand-side platforms, we find pervasive insufficient bid shading after the switch. The implied lower bounds on valuations remain substantially above pre-switch levels for at least three months after the transition, indicating that none of the bidders we study shaded sufficiently. This finding is robust to alternative definitions of local competition, richer conditioning information, and variations in the assumptions underlying the estimator. The results suggest that adjustment to major auction-design changes can be surprisingly slow even among sophisticated algorithmic bidders, with implications for marketplace design and the interpretation of short-run “A/B test” experiments.

title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use our theory model prediction as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using our model predictor, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05427 .

title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore [Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022]. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not reflect the views of the Social Science Research Council (Singapore) and the Ministry of Education (Singapore). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08443 .

title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

title: When meaningful work becomes inaccessible: Disability, ableism and passive agency
abstract: Why does meaningful work become inaccessible to certain groups? Existing literature increasingly recognizes that access to meaningful work is shaped by both subjective experiences and objective conditions, yet it remains less clear about how and why such access becomes systematically constrained. In particular, prior studies tend to foreground workers’ active agency in engaging with, negotiating or resisting these conditions of meaningful work, but they offer limited insight into how this capacity itself may be restricted. Drawing on Archer’s distinction between active and passive agency, we conceptualize passive agency as a mechanism through which structural constraints limit workers’ capability for purposive action. Based on 33 interviews with disabled workers in China, we show how ableism acts as a structural constraint, positioning disabled workers as passive agents, restricting their capacity to experience work as meaningful by limiting opportunities for autonomy, dignity and recognition. In doing so, we extend current understanding of meaningful work by specifying how structural constraints give rise to passive agency, thereby systematically foreclosing access to meaningful work. We also clarify contingent conditions under which more active forms of agency may be enacted, and thus meaningful work can be sustained.

title: Unethical Leadership and Employee Creative Unethicality—Do Dark Personalities Matter?
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that employee creativity may also be unethical; however, our understanding of such behaviour is limited. Existing literature suggests that certain leadership behaviours foster creativity; hence, employee creative unethicality may be similarly underpinned by unethical leadership—that is, leadership that rejects accepted norms. Building on the focus‐strand logic of self‐regulation theory, we argue that the degree of unethical leadership has an inverted U‐shaped relationship with employee creative unethicality, and that this relationship is conditional on employee Dark Triad personality traits. A time‐lagged survey of 468 employees from 26 firms in Bangladesh, India and Malaysia confirms the hypothesized inverted U‐shaped effect and finds that this relationship is positively moderated by employee Machiavellianism and psychopathy. The findings contribute to understanding when creative unethicality escalates within organizations by showing that unethical leadership does not invariably translate into employee creative unethicality. Under high unethical leadership, employees guided by self‐regulation may instead pursue more ethical solutions. However, when employees possess Machiavellian or psychopathic traits, their self‐regulatory tendencies are compromised, thereby increasing the likelihood of creative unethicality under unethical leadership.

title: From Biospheric Values to Employees' Green Supply Chain Engagement: The Dual Mediating Roles of Generative Concern and Environmental Attitude
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks how employees' biospheric values translate into engagement with their organization's green supply chain practices, and why some employees act on those values more readily than others. Although environmental attitude is a well‐established predictor of pro‐environmental engagement, the motivational role of generative concern, the disposition to contribute beyond oneself to future generations, has received limited attention. Framed by the natural‐resource‐based view and drawing on Value‐Belief‐Norm theory, the study develops and tests a moderated‐mediation model in which biospheric values relate to employees' perceived green supply chain engagement through the parallel mediating roles of generative concern and environmental attitude, with generative leadership as an enabling condition. Data were collected through purposive, department‐stratified sampling from employees across nine public‐sector departments in Pakistan and analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling, complemented by an artificial neural network analysis as a predictive robustness check. Biospheric values were positively associated with perceived green supply chain engagement, both directly and through generative concern and environmental attitude, operating as distinct parallel mediators. Generative concern remained a significant predictor alongside the established value‐to‐attitude pathway, and generative leadership strengthened the value‐driven pathways while showing no direct association, consistent with a contextual‐enabler role. Discriminant validity and full collinearity checks supported construct distinctness and reduced common‐method‐bias concerns. By positioning generative concern as an underexamined motivational driver of sustainability engagement, the paper offers a focused extension of value‐based environmental research, points to a possible micro‐foundation of green organizational capability, and offers practical guidance for strengthening employee sustainability engagement in public‐sector organizations.

title: Extending the Strategy Tripod View to Explain Circular Economy Implementation in SMEs: A Systematic Review
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how interorganisational arrangements shape circular economy ( CE ) implementation in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). Existing research identifies resource‐, institution‐ and industry‐related influences but insufficiently specifies how external arrangements condition their contribution to implementation. We systematically review 139 studies through the strategy tripod view's constituent perspectives and assess the strength of evidence supporting a system‐level extension. We develop circular value system architecture (CVSA), comprising connectivity, coordination locus and participation terms, and distinguish these attributes from resource access, deployment, capability augmentation and focal‐SME coordination burden. Seven proposition groups specify how arrangements may shape implementation across the three strategic paths. Along the resource path, deployment capability conditions the usefulness of external access, while coordination allocation shapes the SME's burden. Along the institutional path, environmental information exchange may condition the pressure–implementation relationship, depending on circular innovation orientation. Along the industry path, weaker bargaining positions may constrain implementation through less favourable participation terms. The framework identifies a participation tension: Resource shortages may increase SMEs' need for external complements while restricting their capacity to obtain and sustain them on viable terms. Material constraints further qualify which arrangements are useful. The review contributes by explaining how arrangements condition established strategic determinants, when external resources become operationally useful and why external provision may inadequately compensate for internal scarcity. The framework offers managers and policymakers a basis for diagnosing CE implementation constraints.

title: Structuring Firms' Alignment With the Sustainable Development Goals: ESG and Broader Corporate Performance Indicators
abstract: ABSTRACT The literature on ESG indicators highlights the relevance of corporate contributions to sustainable development. However, fragmentation and a lack of standardized indicators limit alignment between corporate performance and global sustainability goals. This study examines how the literature has addressed the relationship between Corporate Performance, the SDGs, and ESG indicators in recent years, identifying prevailing approaches, measurement strategies, and reported findings. We conduct a systematic literature review complemented by bibliometric and content analyses. Results suggest a marked increase in publications after 2019 and a predominance of governance indicators in studies linking ESG to corporate performance and the SDGs. Across the sample, more than 300 distinct ESG indicators are identified, evidencing heterogeneity in measurement practices. Based on these findings, we develop a conceptual framework that clarifies structural patterns in the ESG–SDG–Corporate nexus and contributes to greater conceptual integration in corporate sustainability research.

title: Are Supply Chain Relationships Characterised by Similar Carbon Policies? An Exploratory Study Using Social Network Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT The carbon footprint from manufacturing companies' supply chains presents significant opportunities for climate change mitigation. Supply chain emissions management is gaining increasing importance in the EU, where regulations target both firms' direct and supply chain impacts. Yet the consistency of carbon regulatory requirements across supply chains and their effects on business relationships remain unclear. This study uses empirical data to explore the association of similar national carbon regulations with the likelihood of observing a tie between two companies in undirected buyer–supplier networks. Using an exponential random graph model (ERGM) on 6027 firms and 11,483 edges, we assess whether companies under similar regulatory conditions are more likely to form undirected buyer–supplier ties. Results indicate that national carbon regulation simultaneously is associated with clustering among regulated firms and cross‐regulatory ties that can enable spillovers. Unregulated firms show weaker clustering, suggesting that even when national regulation is absent, firms remain indirectly exposed to decarbonisation requirements through their connections to regulated partners. Our findings advance sustainable supply chain management by demonstrating how regulatory homophily creates the network conditions through which coercive pressures originating from national carbon regulation may extend indirectly across international supply networks.

title: Double Materiality Assessment Profiles Under Institutional Pressure: Early Evidence From the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
abstract: ABSTRACT Companies reporting under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) identify required disclosures through a double materiality assessment (DMA)—a complex process for which no established practice existed in the first reporting years. Organizations facing such uncertainty are known to orient themselves toward practices prevalent in their institutional environment. While this phenomenon, institutional isomorphism, has been used to explain reporting practices and the design of materiality assessment processes, assessment results have not been studied. This study asks whether DMA profiles converge within the sectoral and national reference groups implied by mimetic and normative isomorphic pressure. DMA results are hand‐coded from CSRD‐compliant sustainability reports for the financial years (FY) 2024 and 2025 of 244 large listed EU firms, yielding 4697 decisions at the reporting‐standard level and 18,040 at the impact, risk, and opportunity (IRO) dimension level. These profiles are analyzed using logistic regressions, linear probability models, and permutation tests on pairwise profile distances. Firms' DMA profiles are more similar to those of their sector and country peers than to the remaining sample. Between years, which reporting standards a firm assesses as material converges only within sectors. At the IRO‐dimension level, convergence is observed for both reference groups, but only for the impact materiality half of the profiles. Institutional pressure is thus associated with the topics firms report and with how they frame impacts related to such topics, but not with how they frame risks and opportunities.

title: Financial Innovation for Sustainable Development: The Mediating Role of Green Credit in Advancing Human Well‐Being
abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates the links between traditional and digital financial inclusion, green credit and selected dimensions of human well‐being across 32 high‐ and upper‐middle‐income nations from 2011 until 2020. Two‐step system GMM models are used to investigate infant mortality, life expectancy and undernourishment, supplemented by a principal‐component‐based well‐being index. Commercial bank branches and ATMs are linked to lower infant mortality and higher composite well‐being. Bank branches are also linked to higher life expectancy, whereas the ATM–life expectancy relationship and both indicators' relationships with undernourishment are statistically insignificant. Digital financial inclusion shows heterogeneous relationships. Debit cards are linked to lower infant mortality, higher life expectancy and a weakly significant increase in composite well‐being. Credit cards are linked to lower infant mortality but lower life expectancy and composite well‐being, and higher undernourishment. E‐banking is linked to lower infant mortality and weakly higher life expectancy, but higher undernourishment and lower composite well‐being. Green credit is linked to lower infant mortality and undernourishment and higher life expectancy and composite well‐being. The reported mediation estimates suggest favourable indirect channels via green credit for traditional banking infrastructure and debit cards, but adverse indirect channels for credit cards and e‐banking. The findings show the significance of differentiating financial instruments and the environmental orientation of debt allocation. They represent country‐level relationships rather than definitive causal effects.

title: Digital Technologies to Address Transparency and Traceability for Sustainable Supply Chain Management: A Stakeholder Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT The concept of supply chain transparency and traceability as a crucial aspect of sustainability is gaining traction among academics, practitioners, and policymakers. In this perspective, digital technologies are recognized as essential enablers to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in organizations. Despite the increasing global shift in digitalization in various industries, the adoption of digital technologies in the agricultural sector in developing economies remains limited. Hence, this exploratory study aims to investigate the use of digital tools enabling stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in the Sri Lankan tea sector. A qualitative research methodology was used and 24 semistructured interviews were conducted with 13 participants holding different positions in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Drawing on the resource‐based view and stakeholder theory, the study findings highlighted various digital tools as valuable resources facilitating upstream, midstream, and downstream stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for achieving economic, environmental, and social sustainability in tea supply chain operations. The study contributes to the existing literature through detailed investigation and empirical mapping of digital technologies used by supply chain actors across upstream, midstream, and downstream activities in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Using the perspectives and in‐depth insights of 13 stakeholders across the Sri Lankan tea supply chain, the findings present a grounded picture of how digital technologies are operationalized in a specific agricultural supply chain in a developing economy context.

title: From Green Innovation to Legitimacy: The Roles of ESG Engagement and Institutional Context in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental innovation does not automatically confer legitimacy: firms must also persuade institutional audiences that their actions merit recognition. This distinction matters in state‐capitalist economies, where the state evaluates firms alongside investors and communities. Using panel data on Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, we examine the association between green innovation and state‐oriented legitimacy (SOL), the mediating role of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) engagement, and the moderating role of regional institutional quality. We distinguish green innovation as a substantive activity, ESG engagement as a potential signal, and SOL as a state‐oriented legitimacy measure. Green innovation is positively associated with SOL, partly through ESG engagement. Institutional quality appears to strengthen this indirect relationship mainly through the link between innovation and ESG engagement. The findings extend research on how institutional context shapes the relationship between environmental activity, corporate signalling, and legitimacy.

title: Climate Change and Energy System Dynamics in Sub‐Saharan Africa: New Evidence From the Role of Institutional Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate pressures have become an increasingly decisive force shaping the evolution of energy systems across sub‐Saharan Africa (SSA). This study examines how climate change and shocks affect energy intensity, renewable electricity output, and electricity access across 19 SSA countries from 1995 to 2023 using a high‐dimensional fixed effects estimator. The analysis introduces the Notre Dame Climate Vulnerability Index (ND‐CVI) into energy transition analysis and formalizes an institutional resilience mechanism that specifies how government effectiveness and regulatory quality moderate the climate–energy relationship through distinct governance channels. The results show that climate vulnerability persistently constrains renewable electricity generation but has weaker effects on energy intensity and electricity access in the baseline specifications. Institutional moderation is heterogeneous across energy outcomes. Government effectiveness weakens the vulnerability–renewable relationship, while regulatory quality shapes the vulnerability–access relationship. Heterogeneity analysis identifies hydro‐dependence as the key transmission channel, with the adverse renewable effect concentrated among the most hydropower‐reliant economies. Temporal comparisons reveal that climate vulnerability effects on renewable output emerged more clearly in the post‐2010 transition era, as regional renewable capacity expanded but remained climate‐sensitive. Findings are robust to alternative shock specifications, outlier adjustment, panel‐corrected standard errors, and instrumental variables estimation using lagged climate vulnerability. The results highlight the importance of renewable diversification, sequenced governance reforms, and integrating adaptation finance into long‐term energy transition strategies in SSA. Trial Registration: Not applicable

title: Unraveling the Factors of Sustainable Market Competitiveness: Strategies of Digitalization, Circular Economy, Green Finance, and Gender Equality
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the central role of digitalization, circular economy, green finance, and gender equality in the European Union (EU) sustainability and competitiveness agendas, the mechanisms through which these factors jointly shape sustainable market competitiveness remain insufficiently understood. Existing research has widely examined these factors in isolation, whereas rare attention has been given to their combined direct, mediating, and moderating relationships grounded in the dynamic capabilities view, ecological modernization, and feminist institutionalism theories across the EU member states. Hence, this study primarily aims to examine the direct association among the outlined factors. Secondly, it examines the mediating role of circular economy between digitalization and sustainable market competitiveness, the mediating role of circular economy between green finance and sustainable market competitiveness, and the mediating role of green finance between digitalization and circular economy. Third, it seeks the moderating role of gender equality between digitalization and circular economy, the moderating role of gender equality between digitalization and green finance, and the moderating role of gender equality between green finance and circular economy across the EU nations. To this end, the study extracted country‐year level data from Eurostat and the OECD for 2014–2023, with a sample size of 270, and analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS‐SEM) to clarify hypothesized associations among constructs. The outcomes indicate that all the direct and mediating paths are positive and statistically significant in the defined settings. In addition, gender equality significantly moderates the relationship between digitalization and circular economy but does not significantly moderate the relationships between digitalization and green finance or between green finance and circular economy. These outcomes extend the existing literature by directing EU policymakers on how to leverage these factors in digital‐to‐green transition, clarify the conditional mechanism of gender equality, and offer evidence‐based guidance to achieve sustainable market competitiveness. The study also contributes by integrating the dynamic capabilities, ecological modernization, and feminist institutionalism theories to draw comprehensive theoretical map for the sustainable market competitiveness. Hence, this study is unique in aligning the outlined factors in a multitheoretical framework for digital‐to‐green transition to achieve sustainable market competitiveness across the EU nations.

title: How firms and NGOs align resources and knowledge to address biodiversity loss: a network perspective
When the Ground Shifts: Why Artificial Intelligence Requires Both Policy and Debate
abstract: Overview This editorial introduces the new Business & Society artificial intelligence (AI) policy developed through an 8-month collaborative process. The policy builds on a central premise: humans remain in the driver’s seat while AI serves as an assistant, and is guided by four core principles: Accountability , Integrity , Responsibility , and Transparency (AIRT). Accordingly, we establish boundaries between acceptable and prohibited practices of authors, reviewers, and editors, and call for disclosure of all AI use by authors. Beyond presenting the policy, we reflect on difficult questions that emerged during its development, particularly regarding transparency, disclosure, and the process of policymaking itself. Rather than claiming to resolve these issues, we explain the reasoning behind the choices made. We also acknowledge unresolved challenges related to governance and the rapid evolution of AI technologies, and invite ongoing dialog on the environmental, social, and institutional implications of AI for scholarship.

title: Deriving value from mobile shopping apps: mediating and moderating mechanisms across countries
abstract: Purpose This study focuses on how consumers derive value from mobile shopping apps, investigating how service quality dimensions are associated with utilitarian, hedonic and social value perceptions and how these value perceptions, in turn, relate to app loyalty. Grounded in Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) theory, it empirically tests a model of direct, mediating and moderating effects across consumers in the USA, UK and UAE. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 543 shopping app users in the USA, UK and UAE. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modelling, with separate structural models estimated for each country to allow detailed within-country examination and cross-national comparison. Mediation and moderation analyses were also conducted. Findings The results provide empirical evidence of associations that are consistent with the notion that service quality dimensions shape value perceptions, with significant variations across countries. Efficiency and contact are consistently associated with multiple value facets across all three countries, while fulfilment and responsiveness are context-specific, primarily in the UAE. All value dimensions are positively associated with app loyalty and mediate the association between service quality and app loyalty. The positive association between hedonic value and app loyalty is consistently stronger at higher levels of intrinsic enjoyment. The pattern of significant pathways differs across the three national contexts. Originality/value This study provides a cross-national investigation of how established quality–value–loyalty pathways operate across three culturally distinct markets: the USA, UK and UAE. By comparing these regions, it reveals where the associations between service quality and value remain consistent and how the associations between utilitarian, hedonic and social value and app loyalty differ.

title: ‘Flying under the radar’: job crafting when menopause disrupts neurodivergent coping
abstract: Human Resource Management increasingly recognises the importance of job crafting, which relies on personal structures of coping. This study foregrounds workplace job crafting using a critical case approach, focusing on neurodivergent individuals whose coping mechanisms may be destabilised during menopause. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 45 neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms (UK and US) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings provide insight into how intersecting vulnerabilities shape person-led workplace adaptation. Specifically, neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms were found to engage in different forms of avoidance job crafting (behavioural avoidance demand crafting, behavioural avoidance resource crafting, cognitive avoidance demand crafting). Moreover, a newly identified preservation orientation drives a combination of avoidance and approach job crafting, evidenced by crafting strategies that primarily focus preservation, or maintaining the status quo, to align personal resources within maintaining job performance. This article contributes to the job crafting literature by demonstrating distinctive job crafting practices of individuals whose life-long coping strategies (of neurodivergence) are temporarily and transitionally destabilised (by menopause symptoms). Organisations have a critical role to support potentially stigmatised employees, thereby nurturing inclusive human resources support policies that provide support to individuals experiencing multiple stigmas.

title: How does open government data promote firm digital innovation? An ability-motivation-opportunity perspective
When leader workplace impostor thoughts spill over into abusive supervision: The roles of identity threat and moral identity internalization
abstract: Abstract Research on the psychological origins of abusive supervision has highlighted leaders' elevated self‐views and entitlement‐related expectations. We examine a contrasting evaluative experience—leader workplace impostor thoughts, characterized by the belief that others overestimate one's competence—as a potential source of abusive supervision. Drawing on an identity threat perspective, we propose that leader impostor thoughts heighten role‐legitimacy identity threat, which shapes abusive supervision in ways contingent on moral identity internalization. We examined this process in two studies: a scenario‐based experiment with 138 participants and a multi‐wave, multi‐source field study with 185 matched leader–subordinate dyads. Study 1 showed that experimentally induced leader impostor thoughts increased identity threat, which in turn was positively associated with abusive supervision intentions. Study 2 supported a positive indirect association between leader impostor thoughts and abusive supervision through identity threat. Moral identity internalization moderated the identity threat–abusive supervision relationship: the association was positive when moral identity internalization was low but negative when it was high. This research advances abusive supervision scholarship by identifying an evaluative mismatch–identity threat pathway rooted in perceived overestimation and extends leader impostorism research by articulating an identity‐based interpersonal spillover mechanism.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: What non-financial disclosure research can (and cannot) learn from financial disclosure research about impression management – a structured literature review
abstract: Purpose This paper reviews the literature on impression management (IM) in corporate disclosures and systematically compares research on financial disclosures (FD) and non-financial disclosures (NFD), particularly sustainability reporting. Given the maturity of IM research in FD and the recent acceleration of IM research in NFD driven by societal and regulatory pressures, the study aims to identify commonalities, differences, and research gaps between both streams, and to assess how insights from FD research can inform future IM research in NFD. Design/methodology/approach We conduct a structured review of 83 archival studies published since 2000 in leading accounting and sustainability journals. The review compares FD and NFD studies along key dimensions, including motivators of IM, disclosure instruments, sample characteristics, and econometric approaches, thereby enabling a systematic assessment of methodological and conceptual differences between the two research streams. Findings The review yields four main findings. First, theoretical frameworks in NFD research remain largely disconnected from capital-market considerations that anchor FD research. Second, NFD research focuses predominantly on sustainability performance as a motivator of IM, leaving other motivators – such as CSR contracting, investor sustainability preferences, and political influence – largely unexplored. Third, prior studies emphasize textual IM instruments, while visual and structural elements central to sustainability reporting remain underexamined. Fourth, NFD studies typically rely on smaller samples and less rigorous econometric designs than FD research, limiting robustness and replicability. Originality/value This study systematically compares archival IM research across FD and NFD. By synthesizing insights from the mature FD literature, it develops a research agenda that broadens the scope of IM motivators, advances the measurement of visual and structural disclosure practices, and strengthens methodological rigor in future NFD research.

title: Overconfident chief executive officers in capital structure decision-making – a systematic literature review
abstract: Purpose This systematic literature review (SLR) synthesises and integrates the growing body of research on CEO overconfidence and corporate capital structure decisions, with particular attention to how alternative measures of overconfidence may contribute to divergent findings. Design/methodology/approach This review systematically searched EconLit, Scopus, Web of Science, Business Source Ultimate and Google Scholar using terms covering CEO overconfidence and capital structure. After screening and eligibility assessment, we reviewed 53 studies and coded them by overconfidence proxy, research method, treatment of endogeneity, identification strategy and findings. Findings The review finds substantial heterogeneity in the operationalisation of CEO overconfidence. These measures are not conceptually equivalent and differ in construct validity and susceptibility to endogeneity and measurement error. The apparent inconsistency in findings should be interpreted cautiously: differences may reflect measurement and identification choices as well as institutional and firm-level context. Originality/value This review clarifies how measurement heterogeneity and differences in empirical identification shape conclusions about CEO overconfidence and capital structure. It also identifies priorities for future research, including construct triangulation, stronger causal designs and transparent reporting of alternative measures.

title: Do mandarins dream of electric fleets? Path dependency and British EV transition
abstract: The UK government’s plans for a zero-emission vehicle transition by 2035 is contingent upon the replacement of new petrol and diesel automotives with Electric Vehicle (EV) technology. The need for technology change, primarily motivated by climate change mitigation strategies driven by niche, regime and landscape pressures, has led to EVs becoming the dominant transport technology solution. This paper critically examines whether path dependencies of existing transport technologies influence EV adoption and presents the results of a survey of UK drivers gauging their attitudes to Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) and their purchasing intent. Our survey data captures four important attitudes towards BEVs: views on current adoption practices, views on impending technological transition, views on replacement technology, and the likelihood of uptake. The findings show that expectations of future performance are influenced by current experiences of Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles, with consumers seeking comparable cost, comparable infrastructural support, and comparable performance from BEVs. On the whole, willingness to change remains a low priority, with notable differences in attitude between young and old drivers as well as low- and high-income households. The study also uncovers discernible regional variations. Important policy implications flow from our findings, also to address the root causes of path dependency and resistance to change as well as the risk of new self-reinforcing mechanisms emerging.

title: A matter of course or controversy: Balancing AI expertise and domain experience in “AI for science”
Definitely Original: The Effect of the Definite Article in Brand Names on Perceived Originality and Consumer Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate the effect of the definite article “ the ” in brand names on consumer responses. We theorize and demonstrate that the positive effect of the definite article is driven by perceptions of brand originality, defined as the perception that the brand is the source of its kind—the origin from which later versions emerge. Drawing on research from linguistics, we argue that the definite article presupposes its referent as the prototypical, identifiable entity in a context. Consumers encountering a brand name starting with the definite article accommodate this presupposition through perceptions of brand originality, which in turn leads to more positive brand outcomes. However, this effect attenuates for imitator brands and brands in highly competitive categories. We test our framework across six studies, including five controlled experiments using fictitious brands and one analysis of real‐world data. We show that brand names beginning with the definite article (e.g., The Body Shop ) generate more favorable brand attitudes and behavioral intentions than those without it (e.g., Body Shop ). Practical implications of our findings are also discussed.

title: Perceived Authenticity in GenAI‐Mediated Luxury Services: The Role of Delivery Configuration and Need for Uniqueness (NFU)
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing integration of GenAI into luxury services raises important questions in a domain where exclusivity, authenticity, uniqueness, and human touch are central. Integrating sociotechnical theory with AI‐in‐service and luxury research, this study uses two experiments to examine how human‐only, GenAI‐only, and hybrid luxury service delivery configurations influence customer evaluations. Findings show that hybrid delivery produces the most favorable luxury service outcomes, with perceived authenticity explaining these effects and need for uniqueness (NFU) shaping customer responses across configurations. This research advances understanding of GenAI in luxury services by showing that its value depends on how human and technological capabilities are combined rather than on either mode in isolation. It also contributes to extant knowledge by showing that authenticity is not merely a stable attribute of luxury offerings, but a psychological mechanism affected by how the luxury service is delivered. Finally, it establishes NFU as a motivational boundary condition that explains variation in customer responses to different luxury service delivery configurations and its interplay with perceived authenticity. Practically, this research offers guidance on integrating GenAI in ways that preserve rather than undermine customer evaluations of luxury services.

title: Through the eyes of an observer: the role of perceived effort in addressing online incivility in social media service recovery
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to examine how firms use different responses to consumer-to-consumer incivility on social media during service recovery. The authors use attribution theory and service climate to examine outcomes of observer perceptions of two response styles, justifying versus denouncing incivility. A key mediator (observers’ perceived effort) and moderator (observers’ consumer-to-consumer justice) are tested. Design/methodology/approach Study 1’s online content analysis illustrates the phenomenon. Study 2 (incivility from a troll) and Study 3 (incivility from a loyal customer) use service failure and complaint scenarios to assess complementary mediation of observers’ perceived effort and service climate. Findings Study 1 finds that firms justify incivility more than denounce it in practice. Studies 2 and 3 reveal that denouncing incivility leads to greater observer purchase and engagement intentions through increased effort perceptions but only if observers perceive incivility as an injustice. Effort’s mediation is robust to controlling another mediator, perceived service climate. Research limitations/implications The authors extend attribution theory with a distinct action and stakeholder conceptually different from a firm’s effort to handle a complainant’s failure. Effort perceptions attributed to a firm are based on an action of handling a nonconsumption failure of consumer-to-consumer incivility (rather than an action of correcting a product or service consumption failure), and this is perceived by observer stakeholders who did not suffer a failure (rather than a complainant stakeholder). Practical implications Firms are eight times more likely to justify incivility than denounce it. However, denouncing unjust incivility from trolls or loyal customers can increase engagement and purchase intentions. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first inquiry into observers’ attribution of perceived effort of a firm when it handles consumer-to-consumer uncivil interactions on a digital service channel.

title: Algorithmic confinement: How AI-powered travel recommendations narrow destination and temporal diversity in tourism?
When AI Says No: AI-Driven Service Rejection and Its Impact on Customer Satisfaction
abstract: Service rejection is common in the service sector and a routine part of commercial interactions. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into service delivery, it is important to understand how AI-driven rejections affect customer satisfaction compared with rejections made by human agents. This research shows that consumers are generally less satisfied when an AI agent, rather than a human agent, rejects their applications. This is because consumers are more likely to assign greater blame to AI agents, perceiving them as having lower decision-making ability. We also examine how explanations shape consumer responses to AI-driven rejections. Our findings indicate that providing a teleological explanation, clarifying why a rejection occurred, effectively mitigates negative reactions compared with providing a mechanistic explanation, which clarifies how the rejection was made, or providing no explanation at all. This research contributes to the ongoing discussions about consumer responses to AI-based decisions, particularly when those decisions deliver unfavorable outcomes.

title: Organizational Frontlines the Next Frontiers: The Intersection of Context, Intent, Asymmetric Information, and Technology at B2C, B2B, and Back-Office Boundaries
Ambiguous Consumer Vulnerability: How Transgender Consumers Navigate the Co-Constitution of Agency and Harm
abstract: Consumer vulnerability research treats harm and agency as oppositional: vulnerability arises when restricted access to marketplace resources erodes agency, and restoring agency is assumed to reduce harm. Current research also presumes that vulnerable consumers occupy a stable, if constrained, legal position. Through an ethnography of UK-based transgender consumers, we problematize both assumptions and develop the concept of ambiguous consumer vulnerability: a condition in which harm arises not only when market access is withdrawn and agency is constrained, but also when consumers assert their agency by participating in the marketplace. Because the marketplace is inescapable and central to identity and well-being, exiting is not an option; consumers instead engage in the volitional absorption of harm to maintain market access. We show how this co-constitution of agency and harm is intensified by legal precarity, which renders the ambiguity persistent and unevenly distributed across services. We identify three strategies—circumventing, educating, and conforming—through which consumers navigate, rather than resolve, ambiguous consumer vulnerability, and then explore how legal precarity complicates the efficacy of these navigation strategies. We contribute to service research by reexamining the relationship between vulnerability, agency, and harm, and offer managerial guidance—seamless service inclusion and inconsequential fluidity—for more inclusive services.

title: From Symbolic Action to Substantive Outcomes: The Positive Relationship Between Ideologically Aligned CEO Activism and Employee Productivity
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue CEO activism has become increasingly prevalent among top executives, yet we know little about whether it is associated with substantive effects on firm effectiveness and the conditions under which such effects arise. Research Findings/Insights Using a panel of 1026 S&P 1500 CEOs observed between 2015 and 2019, we find that CEO activism alignment with employee ideology is positively associated with employee productivity. We further find that this positive relationship is amplified in highly polarized industries and firms. Supplemental mediation analyses provide evidence consistent with our proposed mechanism. Theoretical/Academic Implications The study integrates the stakeholder‐alignment view of CEO activism with the meaning‐making view of executive symbolism to theorize CEO activism as a symbolic action with substantive organizational consequences. Our findings suggest that CEO activism may extend beyond stakeholders' evaluations and attitudes to also relate to the contributions they make to the firm. We also identify ideological polarization as an important contextual condition under which these relationships are stronger, as it makes CEO activism more salient, distinctive, and meaningful to employees. In doing so, we connect CEO activism to a more relational view of stakeholder governance, suggesting that symbolic executive actions may eventually contribute to such governance insofar as they relate to stakeholders' willingness to cooperate with and contribute to the firm. Practitioner/Policy Implications CEOs' public stances on sociopolitical issues can be associated with firm effectiveness when those stances align with employees' prevailing ideological values. Ideologically aligned activism can be associated with more favorable employee attitudes and, in turn, is associated with greater employee productivity, particularly when firms operate in ideologically polarized industries or employ internally polarized workforces. CEOs should therefore consider not only the prevailing ideology of their employees but also the broader ideological context in which their activism will be interpreted.

title: Corporate Acquisitions: Operating and Financial Performance of Czech Companies—Industries Analysis
abstract: This study explores the impact of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) on financial performance across industries in Czechia. Framed by the shareholder value theory and agency theory, it analyzes all mergers in 2016 using Altman’s Z-score, IN05, Taffler’s Z-score, and Kralicek’s Quick Test. The dataset comprises financial statements of 1,077 companies, providing a robust basis for long-term performance analysis. The results reveal that merging production, retail, and wholesale companies, which had been stagnating prior to the merger, experienced accelerated positive development in financial performance in the years following the merger. In contrast, the post-merger development of companies in the service and real estate sectors does not significantly differ from the pre-merger trajectory, suggesting a limited financial impact in these industries. This study highlights the industry-specific effects of M&A within a transitioning EU economy and emphasizes the importance of contextual, sectoral and managerial factors in determining financial success in emerging economies.

title: Policy Design and Polarization: How Policy Characteristics Moderate the Relationship Between Issue and Social Polarization
Home Rule, Local Autonomy, and Voters: Explaining Government Growth
abstract: This paper examines local government growth by analyzing how municipalities respond to increases in taxing autonomy and whether their responses are conditioned on voter preferences. Specifically, we investigate the fiscal impact of home rule when the shift to home rule status (HRS) is independent of voter preferences versus when voters adopt home rule. We find that home rule has no effect on tax collections when changes in HRS are unrelated to voter preferences. However, the tax structure shifts to one that more closely aligns with the preferences of the median voter. In contrast, when voters select into HRS there is a significant and sustained increase in tax revenues that is driven by increases in property and sales taxes. These findings indicate that local fiscal policy is responsive to the preferences of the median voter.

Who Consumes What? Characterization of Violent Pornography Consumers in the Young Adult Population Living in Spain
abstract: Abstract Studies about violent pornography consumers until now could be biased by social desirability. This study aimed to explore violent pornography consumption in young adults in Spain with an instrument that minimized social desirability. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 3607 women and men aged 18–35 years. By using multinomial logistic regression models, we identified the sociodemographic characteristics associated with the consumption of different types of pornography, considering consumption frequency and social desirability. In the last year, 84.6% of men and 45.2% of women have viewed pornography, and 82.2% of men and 74.4% of women have viewed violent pornography. Sexual orientation was associated with the likelihood of viewing pornography with degrading/humiliating practices without physical violence (OR_gay_bisexual: 1.92; OR_lesbian_bisexual: 2.36) and with the likelihood of viewing pornography with physical violence (OR_gay_bisexual: 2.38; OR_lesbian_bisexual: 3.15). In women, the place of origin was associated with consuming pornography with physical violence (OR_stranger: 1.92). In women, both associations were explained by consumption frequency. In men, the association of sexual orientation did not depend on consumption frequency (Degrad/humi: OR_gay_bisexual: 1.75; Physical: OR_gay_bisexual: 1.96). The higher the social desirability, the lower the consumption of pornography with physical violence (OR_men: 0.87; OR_women: 0.91) and degrading/humiliating practices without physical violence (OR_men 0.93). The type of pornography consumed is defined by sexual orientation in men and by the frequency of consumption in both sexes.

title: Beyond Beliefs: Exploring the Lasting Effects of Purity Culture Exposure on Sexual Shame and Satisfaction Among Adult Religious Disaffiliates
abstract: Abstract Purity culture, a socioreligious framework promoting strict sexual abstinence, has been qualitatively linked to sexual shame and distress. However, no studies have explored whether developmental timing of purity culture exposure differentially impacts later sexual outcomes. This study examined relationships between purity culture beliefs, sexual shame, and sexual satisfaction among religious disaffiliates through a cross-sectional survey design. A total of 345 religious disaffiliates (predominantly White, cisgender women from Christian backgrounds, particularly Evangelical and Latter Day Saints traditions; ages 19–77) completed measures of purity culture, sexual shame, and sexual satisfaction, and recalled their ages and duration of religious affiliation. Multiple regression with robust standard errors identified significant developmental periods, while bootstrapped mediation analyses assessed mediating relationships. Purity culture exposure during early adolescence was significantly associated with higher purity beliefs and sexual shame. Purity beliefs partially mediated the relationship between early adolescence exposure and sexual shame, while sexual shame completely mediated the relationship between purity beliefs and sexual satisfaction. Early adolescence emerged as a sensitive period for internalizing purity messaging, showing strongest associations with beliefs and shame. Complete mediation suggests interventions targeting sexual shame may effectively improve sexual well-being among religious disaffiliates.

title: Child Sexual Abuse, Sexual Function, and Sexual Distress in Couples Coping with Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder: A Dyadic Longitudinal Study
Restructuring Accountability Through Participatory Grantmaking: Towards a Dialogic Approach
abstract: Traditional grantmaking practices have been criticised for reinforcing hierarchical power dynamics and perpetuating the very inequalities they aim to alleviate. Participatory grantmaking (PGM) is an alternative approach that seeks to redistribute decision-making power to communities. Despite the growing advocacy for PGM, little is known about how it transforms accountability. Drawing on nine global community meetings and webinars involving 28 pioneering practitioners, we outline a cohesive, interrelated framework of values-led, co-produced and institutionally buffered accountability relationships. Our findings contribute to the critical dialogic accountability literature by mapping the micro-processes of downward power-sharing and illustrating how intermediaries actively buffer institutional friction to protect community-led relational spaces. Consequently, it repositions PGM as a site of values-led relational praxis, extending critical non-profit scholarship and demonstrating how accountability is co-produced as an ongoing, political dialogue rather than bureaucratic compliance.

title: Why policy actors choose not to coordinate in policy conflicts
abstract: Research on advocacy coalitions in public policy highlights the importance of coordination among policy actors seeking to influence policy making. Less attention has been devoted to why actors sometimes choose not to coordinate, even when they share similar beliefs or interests. In this study, we explore the rationales behind actors’ decisions to refrain from publicly visible coordination in wind power development projects in two Swedish municipalities over a 16-year period. Our findings show that, while most actors engage in coordination at some point, they also refrain from coordinating with others for several reasons. First, they perceive alternative means of exerting influence as more cost-effective; second, they have concerns about the trustworthiness of like-minded actors; third, they view the long-term consequences of coordination as uncertain; and fourth, they are less willing to coordinate when conflict is high, unless they represent political parties. These findings show that shared beliefs or interests do not necessarily translate into coordination and identify conditions that can constrain collective action among policy actors. The study contributes to research on advocacy coalitions by bringing decisions not to coordinate more explicitly into explanations of collective action in contested policy subsystems.

title: Explaining policy stasis on same-sex unions in Peru
abstract: This article advances understanding of how policy monopolies sustain policy stasis in morality policy, where scholarship has explained policy change more fully than its absence. It develops the concept of a moral policy monopoly to examine how interlocking mechanisms can sustain policy stasis in contexts of high religiosity. Using abductive, mechanistic and analyticist process tracing, and drawing on documents and interviews, the study examines three decades of legislative inertia on same-sex unions in Peru, where 17 Bills were submitted to Congress between 1993 and 2024 and none advanced to plenary approval. The analysis identifies five interlocking mechanisms through which ultraconservative religious actors sustain stasis under conditions of high religiosity, substantial church capacity and a religiously embedded party system. Forging alliances, building moralised policy images and capturing politics operate continuously, while joint opposition campaigns and competing Bills operate episodically in response to triggering events. Each mechanism presupposes or reinforces the others, so stasis emerges from interlocking and deliberate activity rather than dispersed opposition. By showing how these mechanisms work together to prevent policy change, the article demonstrates how policy monopolies can actively sustain stasis in morality policy. These mechanisms also reveal religiosity not as a background condition but as a resource that actors convert into political capacity.

title: The politics of policy transfer: political dynamics in OECD accession
abstract: While recent scholarship has called for greater attention to the political dynamics of policy transfer, this dimension remains under-theorised in policy studies. Existing work has convincingly shown that transfer is politically motivated yet often lacks analytical tools capable of systematically unpacking these dynamics. This article examines the politics of policy transfer empirically. Drawing on political sociology, it conceptualises policy transfer as a process of mobilisation by interested actors occupying positions within organisational fields. These actors use policy transfer as an opportunity to mobilise resources and advance their positions, while seeking to legitimate their choices among national and transnational audiences. Building on three analytical dimensions – fields, opportunities, and legitimacy – the article examines policy transfer associated with the accession of Chile and Colombia to the OECD during the 2010s and 2020s. The analysis shows that transfer was driven, at the transnational level, by the OECD’s efforts to reinforce its relevance within the multilateral field, particularly in the Latin American region, while domestically it was shaped by governing elites seeking economic capital in the form of foreign investment and symbolic capital through international recognition. The article concludes by showing how attention to fields, opportunities, and legitimacy can advance understanding of the political dynamics that shape policy transfer.

title: Does policy evaluation depend on the quality of democracy?
abstract: Policy evaluation contributes to the quality of democracy, but does the quality of democracy, in turn, contribute to the production and use of policy evaluation? Existing research provides evidence for the former claim but not for the latter. Addressing this research gap, this article examines the pertinence of democratic characteristics alongside or in combination with economic, bureaucratic and educational capacities and analyses the extent to which they are necessary or sufficient for the production and use of policy evaluation. Drawing on Bertelsmann’s Sustainable Governance Indicators (SGI), the analysis applies fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to all 41 OECD and EU countries. The results suggest that a strong balance of powers and access to information are necessary, but not sufficient conditions for the production and use of policy evaluation. Instead, democratic settings provide an enabling context that must be matched by strong bureaucratic and educational capacities for policy evaluation to be produced and used. Conversely, pathways involving weak democratic accountability, insufficient educational and economic capacities, or insufficient bureaucratic capacity, result in the absence of the production and use of policy evaluation. By shedding light on the tenuous relationship between policy evaluation and democracy, this article carries important implications for policy evaluation and evidence use in countries facing democratic decline and the political erosion of state capacities.

title: Who Benefits From Robots? Gender and Technology on the Shop Floor
abstract: ABSTRACT The introduction of robots has produced uneven benefits for workers with different skills, occupations, and genders. We examine a qualitative case study of a Norwegian auto‐supply plant to ask why gender inequalities often persist on the shop floor, even in a gender‐progressive institutional context. The introduction of CNC machines in the plant made machining more like the female‐dominated assembly line in skill and strength demands, yet machining remained male‐dominated, with higher pay and greater investment in automation compared to the assembly line. The authors argue that persistent assumptions about economic value and gendered institutions and practices explain these unequal outcomes.

Decarbonising industrial hydrogen supply systems under EU taxonomy regulation: A multi-objective decision-support framework for existing facilities
abstract: Hydrogen is a crucial vector for decarbonising hard-to-abate industrial sectors, but its deployment increasingly depends on regulatory sustainability criteria alongside economic performance. In Europe, frameworks such as the EU Taxonomy and RED II impose life cycle emission thresholds that directly influence hydrogen system design. This work proposes a flexible multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming framework for the design of lowcarbon hydrogen supply systems for industrial applications. The model integrates renewable and biogenic resources, electricity generation, hydrogen production technologies, inter-monthly hydrogen storage, and resource-specific transport. Economic performance and life cycle CO2eq emissions are optimised simultaneously by using an augmented epsilon-constraint method, while regulatory sustainability thresholds are assessed a posteriori. Water consumption is explicitly included, enabling analysis in regions were water scarcity constraints production. The framework is applied to western Andalusia (Spain) and the Republic of Ireland, which differ in resource availability and hydrogen demand. Regional resource-to-demand ratios strongly shape Pareto front structures and technology portfolios. Biomass gasification emerges as the most cost-effective pathway in resource-abundant settings, while electrolytic routes dominate in resource-constrained regions. All Pareto-optimal solutions comply with the EU Taxonomy emission threshold, although the economic cost of compliance differs between regions. Overall, the framework provides a transparent and adaptable decision-support tool for assessing cost-emission trade-offs and regulatory compliance in regional hydrogen planning. It supports the development of context-specific, policy-consistent hydrogen roadmaps that balance economic competitiveness, environmental performance, and sustainability requirements.

Magnetic Properties of Heated Fe-Rich Soils as Proxies for Burn Temperature and Nanoparticulate Formation
abstract: Abstract Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity worldwide, exposing large populations to iron-oxide aerosols and metal-bearing particulates generated during soil burning. Yet the formation and thermochemical alteration of iron oxides during fire, and their implications for exposure and risk assessment, remain poorly constrained. Here, we investigate how iron-oxide populations evolve with temperature using heating-based experiments on Fe-rich serpentinite and greenstone soils. A comprehensive suite of magnetic measurements reveals systematic shifts toward more oxidized phases and finer particle sizes with increasing temperature. Different magnetic measurements resolve complementary aspects of temperature-driven iron-oxide transformations: hysteresis properties most clearly track changes in the single-phase-dominated serpentinite soils, whereas remanent coercivity distributions effectively resolve the evolution of multiple coexisting magnetic phases in the greenstone soils. Across both lithologies, the relative contribution of magnetite and its associated low-temperature Verwey transition diminishes with increasing oxidation, while ultrafine (<∼30 nm) magnetic particles and hematite become increasingly abundant, particularly under the highest heating conditions (600–800 °C). More broadly, our findings highlight the potential for rock magnetic methods to aid in reconstructing past burn intensities and quantifying fire-induced nanoparticulate formation, with the latter providing information relevant to assessing potential public health risks in fire-prone regions.

title: Origins, Current Practice, and Future Directions of Life Cycle Assessment
abstract: Abstract Life cycle assessment (LCA) has evolved from a niche method for evaluating product systems into a widely used approach for assessing the environmental sustainability of products, services, supply chains, technologies, sectors, economies, and scenarios. This article reflects on its historical roots, current state, and future developments. The early development was marked by pioneering methodological frameworks, inventory databases, and impact-assessment methods. Since then, LCA has matured into a robust and versatile method. Today, scientific, industry-related, and regional inventory databases support routine assessments, while impact assessment has increased in scope, accuracy, regional representation, and policy relevance. Advances in inventory modeling, impact assessment, regionalization, uncertainty analysis, and prospective assessment have substantially broadened the questions that LCA can address and the decision contexts it can support. While LCA traditionally focused on comparative assessments, recent advances introduced absolute approaches that benchmark impacts against planetary-boundary-based thresholds. Looking forward, artificial intelligence promises to transform LCA by facilitating data collection, enabling large-scale scenario analysis, and accelerating assessments. Moreover, increasing spatial and temporal resolution will be a game-changer for assessing impacts such as biodiversity loss and climate change.

title: Endocrine-Disrupting Effects and Reproductive Toxicity of Metal-Based Nanoparticles through DRP1-Mediated Mitophagy within an Adverse Outcome Pathway Framework
abstract: The widespread use of metal-based nanoparticles (NPs), including Ag, ZnO, and TiO2 NPs, in industrial and consumer products has raised concerns about their potential endocrine-disrupting effects and reproductive toxicity. Conventional safety assessment approaches may not adequately capture the complex mechanisms underlying NP-induced toxicity. To our knowledge, this study is the first to integrate OECD-recommended assays, high-throughput screening, an adverse outcome pathway (AOP) framework, and the Toxicological Prioritization Index (ToxPi) to investigate the endocrine-disrupting effects and reproductive toxicity of metal-based NPs. The results showed that ZnO and Ag NPs increased estrogen receptor (ER) transcriptional activity, whereas TiO2 NPs inhibited it. All NPs increased 17β-estradiol production, while ZnO and TiO2 NPs reduced testosterone production. ZnO NPs induced the generation of reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial dysfunction, and DRP1 activation, which were associated with subsequent apoptosis, mitophagy, and autophagy. In contrast, Ag NPs did not induce apoptosis or autophagy, suggesting distinct cytotoxic mechanisms. TiO2 NPs caused no significant cell death in MLTC-1 cells, even at high concentrations. ToxPi ranked COOH-ZnO NPs as the most toxic, followed by NH2-ZnO NPs, Ag NPs, and TiO2 NPs. This integrated framework could provide a practical approach for toxicity screening, mechanistic investigation, and hazard prioritization of NPs.

title: Temperature Does Not Universally Accelerate VOC–OH Reaction Kinetics: Implications for Ozone Formation
Spatiotemporal Orchestration of Dual Functional Sites Enables Efficacious NH3-SCR and CO Oxidation: Synergy of Zeolite-Associated Cu Sites and Cu-O-Co Interfacial Ensembles
abstract: Abstract Integrated abatement of NOx and CO is highly desirable for industrial flue-gas purification, yet competitive adsorption and mismatched kinetic requirements between NH3–SCR and CO oxidation hinder the realization of a unified low-temperature reaction window. Herein, a spatiotemporally organized Cu–O–Co/Cu-ZSM-5 architecture was constructed to provide differentiated catalytic environments and reduce mutual interference between the two reactions. The optimized Co0.2@Cu/Cu-Z5 catalyst delivers a broad co-operational window of 150–350 °C at 45,000 mL·h–1·g–1 and sustains simultaneous NO and CO conversions above 80% from 175 to 350 °C even at 175,000 mL·h–1·g–1, with high N2 selectivity and robust tolerance to 5 vol % H2O. In situ DRIFTS and transient cross-interference experiments indicate that zeolite-associated Cu species preferentially sustain NH3–SCR functionality, whereas Cu–O–Co interfacial ensembles preferentially enhance CO/NO oxidation, thereby alleviating mutual inhibition under coupled conditions. Theoretical calculations further reveal interfacial electron redistribution, Cu 3d-Co 3d hybridization, and more favorable oxygen-vacancy formation at the CuO/Co3O4 interface, and the CuO/Co3O4 interface lowers the activation barrier of the carbonate-forming elementary step from 2.12 to 0.36 eV via a carbonate-assisted MVK-like pathway, whereas its low activation barrier for the first NH3 dehydrogenation step (0.41 eV) suggests the necessity of confining NH3 activation to Cu-zeolite sites to avoid parasitic oxidation. This dual-center pathway differentiation alleviates adsorption and kinetic conflicts between competing reactions, offering a strategy for improving compatibility in multifunctional environmental catalysis.
