Projected climate warming reduces occurrence probability of the imperiled Athabasca rainbow trout
abstract: Freshwater salmonids often occupy narrow ecological niches defined by tight physiological constraints, limited dispersal pathways, and strong dependence on local habitat conditions. As climate warming, land use, and habitat fragmentation reshape riverine environments, many species may shift distributions or experience population declines, creating species-specific conservation challenges. We integrated two decades of Athabasca rainbow trout ( Oncorhynchus mykiss ) inventory data from Alberta, Canada, with geomorphic and anthropogenic predictors in a gradient boosting species distribution model and projected occurrence probabilities under moderate and high future air-temperature scenarios while holding non-climatic predictors constant. Mean August air temperature had the greatest relative influence in the final model, and fitted occurrence probability was highest across an intermediate range of about 12–15 °C. Mean predicted occurrence probability across the stream network declined from 0.205 under current conditions to 0.107–0.068 under future air-temperature scenarios, equivalent to reductions of 47.7–66.9%. Although 54.8–97.4% of future stream-network sampling points fell outside at least one predictor range represented in the training data, increasing uncertainty in the magnitude and spatial distribution of projected change, the direction of change was consistent across all scenarios. These declines are projected across a landscape also characterized by roads and watercourse crossings, highlighting potential conservation conflicts where recovery objectives intersect with ongoing land use. These conditional projections provide a spatially explicit basis for prioritizing monitoring and conservation planning where climate-associated declines and existing landscape pressures coincide.

Diminishing Hysteresis in Cyclic Underground Hydrogen Storage: A Field-Scale Numerical Investigation
abstract: Underground hydrogen storage (UHS) in saline aquifers involves repeated drainage and imbibition, during which hysteresis can strongly affect hydrogen recovery. Most field-scale models commonly treat hysteresis as a persistent process that continues to evolve with local saturation history throughout cyclic operation. However, recent laboratory evidence suggests that cyclic displacement during UHS may stabilize hysteresis and trapping behavior after repeated drainage-imbibition events. Here, we propose a cell-wise diminishing hysteresis framework to investigate the impact of local hysteresis stabilization on cyclic UHS. Each gridblock independently tracks its gas saturation history and drainage-to-imbibition reversal count; once the prescribed number of local reversals is reached, the local hysteresis state is fixed and no longer updated. The framework is implemented in a heterogeneous saline aquifer model and compared with non-hysteretic and full-hysteretic cases over four annual injection-withdrawal cycles. The results show that full hysteresis substantially increases residual trapping and decreases hydrogen recovery relative to the non-hysteretic case. In contrast, diminishing hysteresis limits further growth of residual trapping once the local hysteresis state is locked, thereby increasing the mobile hydrogen fraction and recovery factor. The effect is strongest when residual trapping potential is high (i.e., at lower Land trapping coefficients) and locking occurs early, with residual trapping reduced by up to 18.67 percentage points and recovery factor increased by up to 8.51 percentage points relative to the full-hysteresis case. These results suggest that persistent hysteresis assumptions may overestimate trapping losses in long-term cyclic UHS and highlight the importance of local hysteresis evolution in field-scale performance assessment.

From project outputs to environmental assessment: A framework for structuring project-generated knowledge
abstract: Research and innovation projects generate practice-grounded environmental knowledge, but their heterogeneous outputs are rarely organised for discovery and appraisal beyond the project context. This paper addresses this gap by developing a systematic approach for structuring project outputs for environmental assessment and knowledge synthesis, using the EU Horizon 2020 MERLIN freshwater-restoration project as a case study. Its portfolio comprises 122 outputs spanning 18 European case studies. We characterised this portfolio using seven knowledge pillars, contributor metadata, and four analytical themes informed by interpretive mapping against the IPBES Second Global Assessment (GA2) scoping report. Theme-specific keyword analysis, normalised term-frequency metrics, relevance filtering, principal component analysis, and k-means clustering identified three thematic domains: Ecosystem Restoration, Mainstreaming & Transformative Change, and Finance & Scaling Pathways. Equity, Inclusion & Knowledge Systems emerged as a cross-cutting theme. Qualitative interpretation related the domains to three assessment questions: what restoration achieves and under which conditions; how it is institutionally embedded and implemented; and how it can be financed and scaled. These results were integrated into a filterable, document-level interface linking thematic information, knowledge functions, contributor characteristics, representative documents, and original sources. The interface supports the discovery and prioritisation of potentially relevant project knowledge while retaining traceability to original documents for expert appraisal and synthesis. Although motivated by IPBES GA2, the approach is not assessment-specific. It provides a reproducible, ex post means of making heterogeneous project portfolios more transparent, navigable, and accessible to environmental assessments and other science–policy synthesis processes.

title: Effects of Avalanches and the Vaia Storm on Land Use Changes and Erosion Susceptibility in the Eastern Italian Alps
abstract: ABSTRACT In Alpine catchments, extreme weather events and avalanches contribute to alterations in soil characteristics and land use conditions, thereby affecting hillslope stability and increasing erosion‐prone areas. The effects of major natural hazards on land use land cover (LULC) changes and erosion susceptibility remain poorly understood in steep mountainous areas. Therefore, this study aims to (i) assess the dominant LULC change dynamics using high‐resolution orthophotos before and after the 2014 and 2018 hazards (avalanches and the Vaia storm, respectively) in an Alpine catchment in northeastern Italy, (ii) develop multi‐temporal erosion susceptibility maps (ESMs) under varying LULC conditions and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) using Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis, (iii) validate the predicted ESMs using hydrogeological hazard inventory data. Orthophoto analysis conducted for 2015 (following the 2014 avalanche events) showed localized conversion of grassland to bareland on hillslopes, particularly at high elevations. Following the Vaia storm in 2018, the catchment experienced a substantial net loss of grassland (23% reduction) and a 2% decrease in forest cover, which was largely converted into bareland. These land cover changes, together with other conditioning factors, contributed to a ~4% increase in erosion‐prone areas by 2021, with moderately susceptible hillslopes accounting for ~22% of the catchment. Slope (27.2%), LULC (13.1%), lithology (9.6%), and soil texture (7.5%) were the most influential conditioning factors in determining erosion susceptibility. Integrating temporal LULC and NDVI as dynamic factors proved effective in predicting the changes in erosion susceptibility after the considered natural hazard events.

title: Lithology Is Strongly Associated With Soil Free‐Living N 2 Fixation in Subtropical Forests
abstract: ABSTRACT Free‐living N 2 fixation (FLNF) mediated by soil diazotrophs constitutes a fundamental nitrogen (N) input, critically shaping N availability within terrestrial ecosystems. Despite its ecological importance, the determinants of FLNF across distinct lithological types in karst forest ecosystems remain insufficiently elucidated. In this study, we delved into the patterns, predictors, and underlying mechanisms of soil FLNF within two typical karst forests situated on limestone (LS) and dolostone (DS), alongside a proximate non‐karst forest on clasolite (CS) in southwest China. By quantifying FLNF (indicated by acetylene reduction activity, ARA) rates, nifH gene (N fixation) abundance, and an array of soil, rock, and microbial properties, we uncovered significant associations of lithology with soil ARA and N‐fixing microbial abundance ( p < 0.001). Our results indicated that soil ARA in karst forests (DS and LS) was 2.3–4.7 times that in non‐karst forests (CS). Correlation and random forest analyses pinpointed soil reactive minerals (M d and M o ) and N‐fixing microorganisms ( nifH gene) abundance as primary predictors of ARA variability. Partial least squares path modeling (PLS‐PM) further demonstrated that lithology indirectly associated with ARA dynamics through pathways involving soil minerals (M e , M d , M o , M p , and Clay+Silt), N‐fixing microorganisms ( nifH gene) abundance, and microbial stoichiometric C/N balance (BG/(LAP+NAG)). These findings shed light on a comprehensive understanding of the intricate FLNF dynamics, highlighting the pivotal role of lithology in regulating soil N cycling in karst forest ecosystems.

title: Scaling Practices for Digital Servitization and Industrial Sustainability: How Manufacturing Firms Scale Digital Solutions
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing interest in digital servitization, limited understanding exists of how industrial original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) scale digital solutions beyond localized deployments. Particularly underexplored are the concrete practices through which scaling occurs across organizational and ecosystem boundaries and generates environmental, economic, and social sustainability value. This study examines how industrial OEMs enact and coordinate practices to scale digital solutions across markets and generate industrial sustainability value. Drawing on a qualitative multiple‐case study involving 37 in‐depth interviews with three globally operating OEMs and their ecosystem partners, we identify three interconnected levels of scaling practices: intraorganizational, ecosystem, and customer. These practices operate through three scaling modes: expansion, replication, and synchronization, generating three forms of industrial sustainability value: operational optimization, resource efficiency, and lifecycle extension. Each form encompasses environmental outcomes, including reduced emissions and resource consumption; economic outcomes, such as improved productivity and asset utilization; and social outcomes, particularly improved workforce safety, working conditions, and operator competence. This study contributes to digital servitization and scaling research by uncovering the practices underpinning market scaling, explaining how they are coordinated across organizational and ecosystem boundaries, and demonstrating how distinct scaling modes generate interconnected environmental, economic, and social sustainability value.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Travel‐Leisure Firms: Modelling Risks and Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT The travel and leisure (T&L) industry faces increasing uncertainty from climate policies, geopolitical developments, and oil markets, with implications for equity performance and financial risk management. This study examines how climate policy uncertainty, geopolitical risk, and oil price uncertainty predict T&L equity returns across global, North American, European, and Asia‐Pacific markets. Using daily data from May 14, 2007, to March 28, 2024, the study applies cross‐quantilogram, wavelet quantile correlation, and causality‐in‐quantiles approaches to assess dependence across market conditions and investment horizons. The findings reveal nonlinear, asymmetric, and geographically differentiated relationships. Climate policy uncertainty shows mixed short‐term associations, stronger positive dependence at intermediate horizons, and regional differences over longer horizons. Geopolitical risk becomes more pronounced over medium and longer horizons, particularly in global and Asia‐Pacific markets. Oil price uncertainty exhibits adverse short‐term relationships, whereas intermediate‐horizon dependence varies across market conditions. Overall, the findings show that uncertainty‐related financial exposure depends on the source of uncertainty, market conditions, and investment horizon. The study provides market‐based evidence to inform climate‐transition risk assessment, investment decisions, portfolio diversification, and strategic financial planning in the T&L industry.

Advanced chemical looping-based reverse water–gas shift for methanol production: A techno-economic analysis
abstract: The transition to a low-carbon economy has driven significant interest in green methanol as a sustainable energy vector and potential platform chemical intermediate; however, the incumbent production pathway via the reverse water-gas shift reaction is hindered by thermodynamic equilibrium limitations and energy-intensive separation steps. This study presents a comparative techno-economic assessment of a novel chemical looping reverse water-gas shift process against the conventional reverse water-gas shift route. Integration of experimental reactor data into rigorous process models demonstrates that the chemical looping pathway overcomes equilibrium constraints, achieving high single-pass carbon dioxide conversion (94% at 650°C) and inherent product separation. This process intensification eliminates the need for syngas recycling, resulting in a reduction of approximately 21% in feedstock requirements and a decrease of 49% in electricity consumption compared to the conventional benchmark. Economically, these technical advantages translate into a net production cost of 2.17 USD per kilogram of methanol, representing a 30% reduction from the 3.12 USD per kilogram estimated for the conventional route. Finally, sensitivity analysis identifies the market price of low-carbon hydrogen as the critical economic driver, revealing that, despite the superior efficiency of the chemical looping design, the commercial viability of both pathways remains fundamentally tied to future reductions in feedstock costs.

Why Indonesia captures limited value from cottonii - linking quality incentives, processing and environmental management
abstract: Indonesia is a major supplier of cottonii, used here for cultivated Kappaphycus alvarezii, yet much is exported as raw dried seaweed. This narrative review integrates evidence on market structure, quality incentives, regulatory requirements, processing economics and environmental burdens to identify conditions for greater domestic value capture. Trade data indicate concentrated market exposure, with China receiving 85.9% of Indonesia's seaweed and other algae export volume during 2022-2024. Procurement studies show that better handling does not consistently attract higher prices, while payment terms, credit and transport services shape suppliers' net returns. Processing viability depends on reliable feedstock, buyer-accepted output and achievable utilisation, with extraction gains sometimes accompanied by lower functional quality. Water, chemical and energy requirements make environmental management integral to investment appraisal, but incomplete plant balances and inconsistent boundaries limit comparisons among upgrading routes. Laboratory studies demonstrate ethanol production from selected carrageenan residues without establishing commercial viability or environmental benefits for industrial filter cake. We propose a staged roadmap linking quality measurement and transparent payment rules with product qualification, working capital, testing and wastewater management. Residue conversion warrants investment only where characterised streams, measured recovery and credible demand support an advantage over current handling and alternative uses. Evaluation should distinguish supplier returns, processing profitability and environmental outcomes, while tracking how costs and benefits are distributed. Linking transaction records with plant-level material and energy balances would make these conditions testable and strengthen investment and policy decisions.

title: Coastal protection and restoration with stabilised large driftwood: What we do (and do not) understand
abstract: Stabilised large driftwood (woody debris fixed in place with anchors, ballast or burial) is increasingly promoted as a nature-based alternative to hard coastal defences, offering erosion protection alongside co-benefits including sediment trapping, dune rebuilding and habitat provision. Yet this promotion has outpaced the evidence, raising the question of what design and implementation principles can guide effective use of stabilised driftwood as a nature-based solution (NbS) for coastal protection and restoration. We systematically review the global evidence base, synthesising experimental, field and observational studies to evaluate its design, implementation and performance. We identify 45 documented installations worldwide, predominantly North America, with single examples in South America and Australia, underpinned by two flume experiments and two field investigations. Cross-shore placement relative to the still water level is a key control on performance; wave attenuation, though widely assumed, has not been directly measured; and scour from buoyancy-driven log movement is a recurring, mechanistically explainable failure mode. Outcomes are sensitive to beach-sediment characteristics and wave-energy regime, so no single design generalises across sites. While the evidence base remains too sparse and narrow for validated design criteria, findings suggest genuine potential for stabilised driftwood as a coastal protection tool, pending research targeting these process-level uncertainties. Notably, because driftwood naturally stabilises in the backshore rather than the foreshore where deployed, burial may outperform anchoring by bypassing the mobilisation problem and inserting the log further along the wave-sediment-wood feedback loop. These findings provide a foundation for guidance to improve stabilised driftwood's reliability and uptake as a coastal NbS.

title: Crystallinity-dependent dual role of iron oxides in regulating SOC mineralization and sequestration in paddy soil
Impacts of traditional and industrial approaches to oil palm cultivation on bird biodiversity and conservation in a West African rainforest landscape
abstract: Agricultural expansion threatens tropical ecosystems worldwide. Oil palm is cultivated primarily in Southeast Asia, but production in West Africa (its native range) is increasing rapidly. Here, oil palm is cultivated under traditional and industrial management, and the impacts on native West African ecosystems are poorly understood. Working within the framework of the Sustainable Oil Palm in West Africa (SOPWA) Project in Sinoe County, Liberia, we derived bird occurrence data using point count surveys across 54 plots in January-February 2023, spanning rainforest ('forest'), traditionally managed oil palm ('country palm'), and industrial oil palm systems, to investigate differences in bird species richness, community composition and community-level trait associations. Forest and country palm had comparable species richness, which was significantly higher than industrial oil palm. Taxonomic community composition differed across systems, with assemblages in country palm representing a mix of those in forest and industrial oil palm. Further, communities in forest and country palm were more associated with foraging in high strata, ant-associated behaviour, and an invertebrate diet. We detected four species of conservation concern in all systems, showing no consistent collective response to any specific system. Our findings show that country palm offers a promising option to preserve relatively high biodiversity as well as traditional cultivation practices in Liberia's managed landscape, although country palm is likely less productive than industrial oil palm. Oil palm systems are no replacement for rainforest ecosystems, and protection and designation of reserves and remnant forest patches are critical for wider bird conservation across West Africa.

abstract: -S/L/d, depending on temperature, solid substrate, and supplemented electron donor supply. Lactate and nutrient additions enhanced sulfate reduction, although elevated total organic carbon (TOC) concentrations were detected in the effluent. Elevated TOC concentrations in the potato peel columns indicated ongoing hydrolysis and fermentation, particularly at higher temperatures. The highest sulfate removal efficiencies were observed in biochar reactors at 15 °C (up to ∼100 %) and in potato peel reactors at 5 °C (up to 53 %). Characterization of the microbial community by 16S rRNA gene-based sequencing revealed changes in community composition across experimental stages. Sulfate removal aligned with the enrichment of sulfate-reducing bacteria, with Desulfovibrionia being the dominant class. The results show that temperature-dependent performance can be mitigated through substrate selection and supplementation. At low temperatures, readily degradable substrates such as potato peels are advantageous, whereas biochar-amended systems perform best under heated conditions. Shifts in community composition further indicate that process performance is not limited by slow microbial turnover but can respond dynamically to operational changes. Exploring Canadian beef farmers’ perceptions of participation in climate change mitigation: Insights from Prince Edward Island
abstract: Beef farmers can play a significant role in reducing and sequestering greenhouse gas emissions through specific farm management practices. Understanding how farmers perceive this role is essential for effective knowledge exchange and communication strategies that promote climate change mitigation. This study investigates how beef farmers in Prince Edward Island (PEI), Canada, perceive their involvement in farm-level mitigation efforts. Using identity theory as a framework, the study conducted a framing analysis to examine how participating farmers communicated their actions through four identity lenses: productivist, conservationist, hero, and scientist. Through purposive sampling, nine in-depth interviews were conducted with PEI beef farmers actively engaged in mitigative practices. Findings reveal that farmers often drew on multiple identities, with the productivist frame emerging most prominently. To foster broader engagement in climate mitigation, communication strategies should reflect the range of identities farmers associate with. Future research should explore perceptions among those not currently participating in mitigative practices.

Is the river clean? Comparison between public perceptions and water quality monitoring reveals divergences in the understanding of pollution sources in Arequipa, Peru
abstract: Public perceptions of water quality are crucial in shaping water-related behaviors and management decisions that influence water conditions. Yet these perceptions, formed through social, cultural, and environmental experiences, do not always align with scientific assessments of water quality. This study combines a face-to-face survey of 692 adult residents of Arequipa, Peru, conducted in 2022, with an analysis of river water quality data from the prior decade to examine the congruence between perceived and measured water quality in the city's largest water body, the Chili River. Results indicate that residents correctly perceived the river as polluted but misidentified the main source of pollution, with the majority focusing on mining and litter. Analysis of longitudinal and temporal water quality profiles indicates degradation during urban and peri-urban transit, with signatures consistent with untreated sewage discharges and urban/agricultural runoff, but limited mining influence. Supporting this interpretation, the 2016 commissioning of the La Enlozada wastewater treatment plant, which intercepts municipal wastewater before it reaches the river, was associated with improved water quality downstream of the interceptors, while upstream conditions deteriorated. Despite these improvements, thermotolerant coliform levels generally remained above regulatory standards throughout the urban area and downstream. The pollution sources emphasized by the public, whether visible or assumed, explain only part of the contamination measured in this watershed. This discrepancy could hinder environmental progress and highlights the need to address gaps between public perceptions and measured conditions by improving environmental communication, ensuring data quality and transparency, and encouraging community involvement in watershed management.

title: Integrating the marine domain into the Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem nexus: A data-driven framework for Mediterranean environmental management

Furthermore, we provide evidence of bidirectional coupling, where phytoplankton blooms can actively modulate the physical environment by influencing surface temperature and mixing depths. These results demonstrate that the marine domain is not merely a geographic backdrop but a primary engine of the nexus. By quantifying these spatiotemporal responses, this study provides a predictive window for resource managers and supports the integration of nexus-based indicators into regional policy frameworks such as the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and Maritime Spatial Planning.

Beyond single-stage classification: A hybrid AI–expert validation framework for environmental monitoring of European food waste prevention
abstract: European food loss and waste prevention records are reported through heterogeneous sources and formats, limiting their comparability and reuse for environmental monitoring. We developed a hybrid Zero-Shot Learning and Human-in-the-Loop framework to transform these records into a traceable, multidimensional corpus while retaining expert oversight. The workflow integrated 1164 Action Tracker records with 161 expert-curated records. 1324 records were retained after one semantically insufficient entry was excluded. A confidence-based routing step sent 331 Action Tracker records to full expert review, while a separate blind audit examined 125 of 832 higher-confidence records. Expert review showed that classification confidence and eligibility as a discrete prevention action are distinct quality dimensions. On 75 qualifying audit records, model-expert agreement remained limited, supporting automated inference as a first-pass routing tool rather than a substitute for expert assessment. The resulting taxonomy also showed that 512 of 1163 classified Action Tracker records (44.0%) were assigned to two or more food supply chain stages. These are model-assigned labels rather than verified proportions of qualifying interventions, but they retain cross-stage information that a strictly single-stage representation would omit. The framework does not estimate environmental impacts directly. Instead, it structures heterogeneous prevention evidence so that intervention characteristics, data gaps, and cross-stage coverage are explicit before subsequent linkage to activity data, life-cycle inventories, and policy assessment.

Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
abstract: In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. We identify organizations in which meritocracy is likely to give way to favoritism and entrenchment, and investigate policy interventions (such as affirmative action, quality-based or diversity-based funding, discretionary overruling of majority decisions, blind hiring processes) and their unintended consequences.

title: Earnings Instability
abstract: Abstract This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

title: Automation and Gender: Implications for Occupational Segregation and the Gender Skill Gap
abstract: We examine the differential effects of automation on the labor market and educational outcomes of women relative to men over the past four decades. Although women were disproportionately employed in occupations with a high risk of automation in 1980, they were more likely to shift to high-skill, high-wage occupations than men in over time. We provide a causal link by exploiting variation in local labor market exposure to automation attributable to historical differences in local industry structure. For a given change in the exposure to automation across commuting zones, women were more likely than men to shift out of routine task-intensive occupations to high-skill, high wage occupations over the subsequent decade. The net effect is that initially routine-intensive local labor markets experienced greater occupational gender integration. College attainment among younger workers, particularly women, also rose signicantly more in areas more exposed to automation. We propose a model of occupational choice with endogenous skill investments, where social skills and routine tasks are q-complements, and women have a comparative advantage in social skills, to explain the observed patterns. Supporting the model mechanisms, areas with greater exposure to automation experienced a greater movement of women into occupations with high social skill (and high cognitive) requirements than men.

title: The consequences of cellphone restrictions in classrooms
abstract: We examine teacher-level cellphone permissiveness in a setting where phones are often used for instructional support and teachers retain discretion over classroom cellphone use. Using linked Chilean administrative and survey data, we exploit variation in cellphone policy within teachers across cohorts and within students across subjects. Greater restrictiveness modestly reduces eighth graders’ cellphone use in class, but not tenth graders’. It also lowers eighth graders’ self-perceived academic capability, with no detectable effects on test scores. These findings inform settings, more common in low- and middle-income countries, involving uneven classroom enforcement within schools and where phones serve as low-cost instructional tools.

title: Comments on: “Unpacking non-tariff measures: Beyond the tip of the iceberg”
A mandate to multiply: the effects of pro-birth policies on fertility in colonial Congo
abstract: Abstract Like other colonial powers, Belgium enacted pro-birth policies in its colony starting in the 1920s. We investigate their impacts on women who grew up in colonial Congo, using individual fertility outcomes for a sample of 30,000 women. Given that Catholic nuns implemented these policies, we exploit temporal and geographic heterogeneity in exposure to different types of missions, Catholic, Catholic with nuns and Protestants. We find that Catholic nuns succeeded in stimulating fertility, unlike other missionaries. We investigate mechanisms and show that Catholic female education – and its promotion of domesticity – played a decisive role. Finally, we find modest traces on fertility today.

title: Enclaves and Assimilation in the Age of Mass Migration: Evidence from Ethnic Catholic Churches
abstract: Abstract Local ethnic amenities can foster the growth of immigrant enclaves, affecting economic and cultural integration. We study the centralized placement of “ethnic” Catholic churches in the United States during the Age of Mass Migration (1900-1930), focusing on Polish and Italian immigrants. Polish immigrants relied more heavily on the local parish to organise communal life. Following the opening of a Polish (but not Italian) church, co-ethnic residents experienced declines in occupation-based earnings but strengthened communal ties, measured by in-group marriage and naming, relative to matched neighbourhoods. These effects persist into the second generation and are not observed among other local residents, including Jews and non-Polish Catholics.

title: The old lady of economic history: 100 years of the Economic History Review
abstract: Abstract This article traces the evolution of the Economic History Review over its first century and places it within the broader transformation of economic history as a discipline. Drawing on a new database covering 2761 articles published in the journal between 1927 and 2025 by 2011 authors from 571 institutions in 50 countries, it analyses changes in editorial leadership, research topics, historical periods, geographical coverage, methods, authorship, and citation patterns. The findings suggest that the journal evolved from a predominantly UK outlet into one of the leading international journals in economic history. Over time, it converged towards the model of the major international field journals, with citation networks revealing a shift from stronger links with history to closer connections with economics. At the same time, however, the journal retained a distinctive profile, preserving a more historical orientation than the leading American journals. The article also documents a marked process of internationalization, reflected in both the geographical scope of published research and the growing presence of scholars from continental Europe. Finally, citation analysis shows that articles addressing long‐run and geographically comparative questions achieve the highest scholarly impact.

title: Indigenous communities and the shaping of a lithium labour regime in Jujuy’s salt-flat ecologies
abstract: This article examines how Indigenous communities shape the lithium-mining labour regime in the Atacama Puna of Jujuy, Argentina. Drawing on ethnographic research, it shows how global mining arrangements are territorially reconfigured through communal landownership, community negotiation, subcontracting, salt-flat ecologies and historically constituted forms of social reproduction. These articulations produce distinctive recruitment practices, labour segmentation, uneven occupational risks and gendered reproductive burdens. The article advances labour-regime analysis by demonstrating that communities actively constitute the labour regimes of the energy transition through their political organisation, property relations and livelihood histories within the specific ecological conditions of the salt flats.

title: Can shadow prices from energy system optimization models serve as reliable electricity price indicators?
abstract: Shadow prices from large-scale energy system optimization models (ESOMs) are widely used as long-term electricity price proxies in research and policy analysis. While their structural limitations are broadly acknowledged, no systematic empirical evidence exists on their reliability as market price proxies. We address this gap with a novel three-stage statistical framework (Kruskal–Wallis tests, t -tests, Pearson correlations) applied to ENTSO-E day-ahead prices and shadow prices from GENeSYS-MOD — one illustrative example among many cost-minimising ESOMs — across 22 European countries and four temporal resolutions. We find that shadow prices are compressed relative to observed market prices across all temporal resolutions. Volatility compression is most pronounced at the day-of-week level ( 10 × on average) and at the hour-of-day level ( 7 × on average). Month-of-year and season resolutions show smaller but still substantial compression (3– 4 × on average). Despite this, day-of-week, month-of-year, and season price patterns are structurally aligned with ENTSO-E observations. Hour-of-day alignment improves with model year but the observed market pattern is structurally shifting, making it the resolution hardest to use reliably. Independent literature projections from other LP-based models fall in the same compressed range, indicating that compression is a model-class property rather than a single-model artefact; direct empirical validation across other ESOM families remains an open task. Addressing these structural limitations is a promising avenue for future model development. In the interim, we propose resolution-conditional guidelines to support more principled shadow price applications.

title: When Grant Writing Becomes Cheap: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Efficiency of Agricultural Research Funding
abstract: ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (AI) reduces the time and effort required to prepare competitive research proposals, potentially reshaping the allocation of agricultural research funding. We study these implications in the context of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)'s Agriculture and Food Research Initiative (AFRI), the primary federal mechanism supporting U.S. agricultural research and innovation. Using a formal economic model of the AFRI grant market developed from a no‐AI benchmark, we analyse two AI scenarios: independent adoption , in which AI use is uncorrelated with researcher quality, and correlated adoption . AI‐driven reductions in preparation costs can increase submissions from marginal projects, weaken peer‐review signal informativeness and amplify institutional funding advantages even when underlying research quality is comparable. Allowing AI adoption to correlate with researcher quality shows that compensatory adoption—a negative adoption–quality correlation deepens signal degradation, whereas the correlation must exceed approximately 0.10 before fixed‐pool informativeness improves relative to the no‐AI benchmark. In the calibration, uniform high adoption increases equilibrium submissions by 18.0%. Under a heterogeneous scenario in which 70% of potential investigators receive high‐intensity AI assistance and 30% receive none, submissions increase by 6.2%, while mean funded quality falls by 3.5%. These allocative effects coexist with proposal preparation resource savings. We evaluate second‐best responses implementable within USDA's existing authority, including mandatory pre‐proposals, meritorious‐pool lotteries, AI‐use disclosure and targeted AI‐access programmes for historically Black land‐grant and other minority‐serving institutions. Generative AI can therefore raise applicant productivity while weakening the information and selection mechanisms underlying efficient and equitable research funding.

The baby boom and the US divorce boom
abstract: The United States experienced two major demographic ’booms’ during the second half of the twentieth century, in births after 1945 and in divorces 25 years later. This paper argues that the two booms are linked. As the baby-boomers were entering marriageable age, men in previous cohorts were faced with exceptionally good remarriage prospects. I find that across states people in the pre-boom generations were more likely to have ever divorced the bigger the relative supply of young women (instrumenting the size of the baby-boom with WWII mobilization rates). I construct a simple dynamic marriage and remarriage model (matched to the pre-1970s matching patterns) that illustrates how age-gap preferences can translate a cohort-size variation into a rise in divorce.

The nuanced role of government credit in monetary policy transmission
Managerial Ability and Employee Workplace Health and Safety
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between managerial ability to efficiently convert capital into revenue (which we refer to as “managerial ability”) and employee workplace health and safety violations. We document a positive association between managerial ability and employee workplace health and safety violations. This relation is more pronounced in firm environments with weaker labor unionization, and becomes weaker in more innovative firm environments, when executive compensation includes stronger employee workplace health and safety incentives and when CEOs have longer horizons. Collectively, these findings suggest that while higher managerial ability is associated with greater employee workplace health and safety violations, firm environments that emphasize stakeholder protections and longer‐term managerial horizons attenuate this relation. Finally, while employee workplace health and safety violations do not significantly affect short‐ to medium‐term financial performance, they appear to harm long‐term financial performance in firms led by high‐ability managers.

title: Credit Tightening and Earnings Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate the effect of credit tightening on firms’ earnings quality (EQ). During periods of credit tightening, agency conflicts between lenders and borrowers intensify, prompting firms to adjust their EQ to compete for scarce credit resources. Leveraging a unique setting in China, where credit tightening is induced by the crowding‐out effect of local government debt and varies across cities, we find that firms improve EQ in response to credit tightening. The effect is less pronounced for state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) and more pronounced for firms with greater financial constraints and higher growth opportunities. Moreover, we find evidence that firms with improved EQ secure more debt financing and enjoy a lower cost of debt. Our evidence highlights credit tightening as a crucial macroeconomic determinant of firms’ EQ.

title: 1918 Influenza pandemic across America - New evidence using county-level data
Antitrust Enforcement and Market Power: Evidence from DOJ Field-Office Closures
Regional green growth coalitions and the eco-social-growth trilemma: the case of the automotive industry in West Sweden
abstract: This study analyses how and why a regional green growth coalition is constructed in West Sweden, and how this coalition shapes the organisation and prioritisation of economic, ecological and social objectives in the green transition. Drawing on the transition of the region’s automotive industry, the analysis shows that while Sweden’s national growth model has shifted away from green export-oriented growth, regional actors continue to align around this trajectory. The coalition is sustained by perceived state withdrawal, intermunicipal collaboration and a framing of the transition as essential for regional competitiveness and welfare provision. Within this regional growth model, economic competitiveness takes precedence, while social objectives are largely treated as outcomes of successful green growth. The article contributes to growth model research by showing how regional coalitions can sustain growth trajectories that diverge from national strategies, and how this shapes the incorporation and prioritisation of social objectives in green growth.

title: Private global finance and climate governance: de-risking, assetized vulnerability, and domination in the Global South
abstract: Private finance has become central to climate governance, especially to strategies for mobilizing investment in climate-vulnerable states. This article argues that de-risking can do more than reallocate project risk: it can make historically produced vulnerability revenue-bearing. Assetized vulnerability names the process through which hazard exposure, fiscal and monetary fragility, and infrastructural weakness are rendered calculable and connected to premiums, yields, guaranteed payments, or protected cash flows. The concept adds to research on de-risking by identifying both a valuation mechanism and a selection effect. Vulnerabilities that can be stabilized by public authority may become investable; needs that cannot support protected revenue streams remain excluded. A structured comparison of wind power in Kenya, catastrophe-risk finance in the Caribbean, and geothermal exploration in Indonesia shows that the result is not uniform. De-risking becomes domination-based exploitation where investors or intermediaries gain from a dependent state’s constrained alternatives while public institutions bear residual risk and surrender policy space. It can instead support transformation where it builds public capability, preserves public control, and shares risks and gains reciprocally. The article therefore offers a relational test for distinguishing investor-centered de-risking from public, capacity-building climate finance.

title: Local corporate taxation and the mobility elasticity of the tax base: Evidence from Japan
Nonpredictive approaches in marketing
abstract: Abstract Much academic research is focused on the application of predictive data, forecasts, and models to inform practical marketing decision-making. Such work offers powerful insights to marketers directing their firms and interacting with the environments in which they operate. The present study is devoted to the smaller, alternative, and equally potent body of work that seeks to enable decision-making without reliance on prediction. We term this category of approaches ‘nonpredictive’ because their operative basis for action does not depend on prior estimation of future states or outcomes. Instead, decision paths are generated and revised through mechanisms of action, interaction, commitment, recombination, experimentation, and imagined direction. This foundation enables nonpredictive approaches to function across a wide variety of marketing decisions, including truly uncertain situations where prediction cannot reliably guide action. Interest in nonpredictive approaches is emerging but has yet to be consolidated. We inventory and synthesize nonpredictive approaches in the marketing literature, contributing to academic discussion at the foundation of marketing decision-making. In the process, we clarify conceptual specifics of nonpredictive approaches, construct a taxonomy that distinguishes among them, and develop a series of propositions to inform future research. The payoff from our work lies in bringing attention to a class of approaches for making decisions in an increasingly uncertain world.
