title: Doing bad by doing good? The impact of philanthropy on perceptions of organizational leader morality and organizational trust and support
The Impacts of Host Culture Heterogeneity on Learning from Success Versus Failure in Foreign Direct Investments
abstract: Abstract This study examines the differentiated influences of host culture heterogeneity on the learning outcomes of multinational enterprises' (MNEs) success and failure experiences in foreign direct investments (FDI). We posit that host culture heterogeneity among prior successful FDIs reduces the beneficial effect of an MNE's success experience on a subsequent FDI, particularly when the cultural differences between the subsequent FDI and the MNE's prior successes are significant. In contrast, host culture heterogeneity among prior failed FDIs enhances the learning benefits of failure experience, and this effect is more pronounced when the subsequent FDI is culturally distant from the prior failures. Using FDI data of South Korean MNEs between 1990 and 2016, we find support for our hypotheses, demonstrating that host culture heterogeneity has divergent impacts on the learning outcomes of MNEs' success versus failure FDI experiences. This study enhances our understanding of the conditions under which host culture heterogeneity may weaken or strengthen the learning benefits of an MNE's FDI experience.

title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .

title: Connectors and Influencers
abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .

title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00747 .

title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .

title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06801 .

title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

title: Role conflict, growth mindset, and financial misreporting
Emission Differentiation as a Self‐Financing Transition Mechanism: The Case of Sustainability in Automotive Repair and Maintenance
abstract: ABSTRACT Global commitments to reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions have focused policy and managerial attention on upstream production and use‐phase emissions, leaving downstream repair and maintenance services (RMS) largely overlooked. This paper examines whether lower‐emission service provision can become a self‐financing differentiation strategy for capital‐constrained, small‐ and medium‐sized service firms. We develop a price‐competition model where firms choose between traditional and cleaner service offerings, and customers exhibit heterogeneous emission sensitivity. From this framework, we derive a self‐financing condition that links emission‐sensitive demand, market size, operating‐cost variations, and upfront abatement investments. To ground the model empirically, we collect detailed operational data from 13 German and 6 Australian RMS shops, combining these inputs with life cycle assessment (LCA) estimates to map Scope 1–3 emission channels and characterize abatement pathways. The results show that energy‐related measures in heating and electricity provide low‐risk entry points that reduce or stabilize operating costs. Conversely, spare parts and material strategies dominate total lifecycle emissions; while they offer higher absolute abatement potential, they demand greater capital investment and value‐chain coordination. This study contributes to the business case for sustainability literature by demonstrating that environmental differentiation operates not only as a demand‐side premium driver but also as an operating‐cost and investment‐feasibility mechanism. Finally, we offer actionable guidance for RMS managers, insurers, Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), and policymakers on sequencing decarbonization pathways within service industries dominated by small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs).

title: Does Nationality Matter? Foreign CEOs and Green Innovation: The Role of Institutional Pressure
abstract: ABSTRACT Drawing on upper echelons' theory and legitimacy theory, this study examines whether and under what conditions foreign CEOs enhance green innovation in Chinese firms. Using data from firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, our multivariate regression results provide robust evidence that firms led by foreign CEOs exhibit significantly superior green innovation performance than those led by local CEOs. Importantly, this advantage is more pronounced in firms located in economically developed regions, firms subject to greater media scrutiny, and firms operating in highly competitive industries. Furthermore, our results show that environmental initiatives led by foreign CEOs are positively associated with enhanced shareholder value. Furthermore, we address endogeneity using firm, year, and province fixed effects, supplemented by lagged specifications and a difference‐in‐differences approach exploiting CEO transitions from local to foreign CEOs. By highlighting the contingent value of foreign CEOs in emerging economies, our findings extend upper echelons and legitimacy theories and contribute to the corporate social responsibility and green innovation literature, while offering meaningful implications for boards, policymakers, and regulators.

title: Digitalization, Sustainability‐Oriented Practices, and Resilience in SMEs: An Integrated Capability‐Based Model
abstract: ABSTRACT In volatile and sustainability‐constrained environments, small and medium‐sized enterprises increasingly face the challenge of advancing digital transformation and sustainability simultaneously while preserving their capacity to adapt, recover, and remain competitive. Although the simultaneous pursuit of digitalization and sustainability has attracted growing scholarly attention, empirical research that has examined the internal capability pathways linking digital technologies and sustainability‐oriented practices to organizational resilience has been limited. Drawing on the Resource‐Based View, the Natural‐Resource‐Based View, and the Dynamic Capabilities View, this study develops and tests an integrated model linking digital technologies, green corporate culture, organizational learning, innovation capability, environmental training, social and environmental management, and organizational resilience. Using survey data from 206 SMEs located in Andalusia, Spain, and applying structural equation modeling, the results indicate that digital technologies are positively associated with green corporate culture, organizational learning, and innovation capability. Organizational learning emerges as a central mechanism associated with both innovation capability and environmental training. Environmental training, in turn, is positively associated with social and environmental management practices, while organizational learning and innovation capability show robust positive associations with organizational resilience. Social and environmental management is positively associated with organizational resilience in the hypothesized model, although this direct relationship is more sensitive to fuller structural specification. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying how the simultaneous pursuit of digitalization and sustainability is associated with organizational resilience through a sequence of learning‐, innovation‐, and sustainability‐oriented resources, capabilities, and practices. The study also provides relevant implications for SME managers, suggesting that digital investments may generate greater strategic value when embedded in learning systems, environmental training practices, and proactive sustainability management.

title: Political Influence as Strategic Substitution: Carbon Performance and Corporate Lobbying in US Climate Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms facing environmental regulation can respond through both operational adjustment and political engagement, yet existing research provides limited insight into how these strategies interact. This study addresses the theoretical question of how firms allocate resources between market and nonmarket strategies and whether corporate lobbying functions as a complement to, or a substitute for, environmental abatement. Drawing on public choice theory, we argue that firms allocate resources across alternative strategies based on relative costs and expected benefits, such that firms with poor carbon performance, facing higher compliance costs, are more likely to substitute towards lobbying. We further propose that this relationship is contingent on the credibility of the regulatory environment. We test these arguments using panel data on US firms' carbon emissions and lobbying expenditures from 2010 to 2020, exploiting the US withdrawal from the COP21 Paris Agreement as an empirical setting capturing a broader class of deregulatory shocks. The results show that firms with higher emissions systematically engage in more lobbying and that this relationship weakens following the decline in climate accountability. This study contributes to the literature by conceptualising corporate lobbying as part of a strategic allocation between market and nonmarket responses, by identifying carbon performance as a key driver of firms' strategic behaviour and by demonstrating how changes in regulatory credibility shape the interaction between environmental performance and corporate political activity.

title: Labels Versus Substance: Regulation, ESG Signals and Fund Pricing in Sustainable Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether sustainable finance regulation affects the pricing of investment funds labelled as having environmental, social and governance attributes. Focusing on the European regulatory framework, we analyse how the EU Taxonomy and the introduction of the European Securities and Markets Authority naming guidelines influence fund fees across Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation classifications. Using a panel of mutual funds from 2020 to 2025, we assess whether regulatory tightening leads to systematic changes in pricing. Our findings provide no evidence of a persistent fee premium for sustainable funds. However, we document heterogeneous pricing responses across SFDR categories following regulatory intervention. In particular, Article 8 funds exhibit a significant increase in fees relative to Article 6 funds following the application of the EU Taxonomy, whereas no significant differential response is observed for Article 9 funds. A similar heterogeneous pattern emerges when the ESMA naming guidelines are considered as a distinct regulatory intervention. Moreover, the Morningstar sustainability rating does not exhibit a statistically significant incremental association with fund fees after controlling for SFDR classifications. Overall, these results indicate that the pricing response to sustainable finance regulation varies across SFDR categories and highlight the importance of considering such heterogeneity when assessing the effects of regulatory intervention.

title: ESG Performance, Corporate Profitability, and Capital Market Trust: Evidence From Chinese A‐Share Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the associations between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, corporate financial performance, and capital market trust among 1353 Chinese A‐share listed firms over 2010–2023. Drawing on stakeholder, information asymmetry, and signaling theories, capital market trust is operationalized through a composite measure combining analyst coverage, institutional ownership, and absolute analyst forecast error. Baseline estimates show that ESG performance is positively associated with corporate profitability and the composite capital market trust measure. Under firm fixed effects, ESG remains positively associated with accounting‐based profitability, as measured by ROA and ROE, but is not statistically significantly associated with Tobin's Q. Exploratory split‐sample analyses indicate a stronger ESG–profitability association among nonstate‐owned enterprises and a slightly stronger association in heavy‐pollution industries. Overall, the evidence is stronger for accounting‐based profitability than for market valuation and is interpreted as documenting context‐specific, conditional associations rather than causal effects.

title: The Paradox Between Comprehensive ESG Performance and Cost of Capital in the Aerospace and Defense Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the relationship between comprehensive ESG performance and the cost of capital in the Aerospace and Defense industry, a sector characterized by intrinsic controversies and strong financial dynamism. Using a panel of 118 publicly listed firms worldwide from 2018 to 2025, we find that the ESG combined score, which incorporates controversy‐related information, is associated with a lower cost of debt, particularly in firm fixed‐effects specifications. In contrast, we find no significant evidence for the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), and the evidence for the cost of equity is weak, marginally significant, and not robust to the comprehensive ESG performance measure. The findings suggest that creditors, rather than equity investors, tend to price overall ESG performance in Aerospace and Defense firms, consistent with the notion that sustainability signals may operate mainly through the debt channel.

title: Innovation Activity and Green Business Practices in European Firms: The Role of Environmental Management
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how innovation activity relates to green business practices among European firms and considers, rather than directly tests, the implications of these practices for sustainability communication. Using establishment‐level data from 4666 firms across Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Estonia, Germany and Ireland drawn from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys, the study employs survey‐weighted logistic and fractional‐response models to account for complex survey design, firm characteristics, country effects and industry heterogeneity. Green business practices are measured through CO 2 emissions monitoring, energy management, on‐site solar adoption and solar electricity intensity. The findings reveal that broader innovation activity is positively associated with CO 2 monitoring and, more strongly, energy‐management adoption. However, innovation does not significantly predict on‐site solar adoption, indicating a boundary between general innovativeness and capital‐intensive renewable‐energy investment. Disaggregated results further show that R&D activity primarily drives CO 2 monitoring, whereas process innovation is particularly important for energy management. Importantly, energy management is associated with an approximately 13–14 percentage‐point higher probability of solar adoption, suggesting that organisational environmental readiness is more closely associated with renewable‐energy investment than innovation breadth alone. The study concludes by recommending that firms strengthen their environmental management systems to translate innovation into measurable green practices and renewable energy investments.

title: Navigating Stormy Waters: Strategic Responses to Regulatory Uncertainty in Sustainability Reporting
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory uncertainty poses complex strategic challenges, but firms' responses to it are often reduced to a binary choice between compliance and noncompliance. This study examines how companies manage regulatory uncertainty when facing changing sustainability reporting requirements, focusing on the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and its partial reversal under the Omnibus I package. Through a multiple‐case study of 35 German companies, we combine regulatory uncertainty with a dynamic capabilities lens to develop a typology of four strategic responses. We advance three arguments. First, firms' responses extend beyond compliance and noncompliance. Second, regulatory uncertainty is partly self‐induced, as the firms shaping the rules generate the uncertainty others must navigate. Third, regulatory relief falls unevenly, unsettling firms without prior reporting experience while others facing release continue building capabilities they may no longer need.

title: Talk Without Substance? Institutional Pressures, the Rule of Law, and the Symbolic Decoupling of Corporate Green Innovation After the Paris Agreement
abstract: ABSTRACT International climate agreements are widely presumed to push firms toward substantive environmental change, a presumption that hardens where domestic institutions are expected to hold firms to their word. Drawing on institutional theory, namely, legitimacy‐seeking, isomorphic pressure, and decoupling, this study interrogates that presumption, asking whether the Paris Agreement produced substantive corporate green innovation or chiefly symbolic environmental disclosure and how the rule of law conditions the response. Using 174,056 firm‐year observations across 51 countries and economies from 2007 to 2025 and a difference‐in‐differences design that interacts a common post‐treaty indicator with time‐invariant institutional characteristics while absorbing firm and year fixed effects, the analysis finds no robust average effect of the Paris Agreement on substantive green innovation once firm characteristics and ESG controls are absorbed. Rather than amplifying disclosure, the institutional setting separates the two channels: the post‐Paris interaction with a strong rule of law registers on environmental disclosure yet is indistinguishable from zero for real innovation. The sharpest evidence comes from legal origin, where common‐law firms raise environmental disclosure after Paris without any matching gain in substantive innovation, a pattern read here as institutional decoupling operating at the level of the international treaty. The study offers a large‐scale, cross‐country quasi‐experimental test distinguishing environmental talk from environmental action and cautions investors, boards, and policymakers against reading disclosure intensity as evidence of genuine innovation.

title: Linking environmental-based corporate digital responsibility to green innovation: The roles of digital leadership, dynamic capabilities, and environmental dynamism
From observation to silence: Bystanders’ reaction to coworkers’ cyberloafing in the hotel industry
Projecting for Sustainability Transitions: Where Are We Now?
Projecting for Sustainability Transitions: The Research Contributions
Different shades of green: diverging effects of employee and organizational green signals on hotel customers
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how hotel customers’ perceptions of sustainability influence their behavioral intentions-toward hotels (BI-TH), specifically comparing perceived-employee green behavior (P-EGB) and perceived-environmental corporate social responsibility (P-ECSR). Utilizing signaling theory, social exchange theory and the stimulus–organism–response model, it examines how these pathways lead to revisit intention (RI), word-of-mouth (WOM) and willingness to pay price premium (WPPP) as BI-TH outcomes. In addition, it tests whether perceived-green value (P-GV) and Green trust (GT) serve as sequential mediators. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative methodology was applied using a cross-sectional structured survey design. Data were collected from 309 hotel customers in North Cyprus with a hotel stay in the previous year and several employee interactions. PLS-SEM assessed the measurement model, structural paths and serial mediation effects. Findings P-ECSR positively relates to all BI-TH outcomes. P-GV and GT provide partial serial mediation between P-ECSR and RI, WOM and WPPP, whereas full serial mediation was found between P-EGB and all three BI-TH outcomes. Practical implications Hoteliers must recognize that macro-level corporate environmental initiatives directly drive customer loyalty. Furthermore, frontline employee green behaviors influence customer outcomes via value and trust. Therefore, managers must use Green HRM to train and empower staff to communicate green value effectively during customer interactions. Originality/value This study measures employee green behaviors from the customer perspective and shows the diverging effects of organizational-level and employee-level green signals on BI-TH.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Fan or Foe: How Human Versus Virtual Influencers and Review Type Drive Consumer Brand Hate
abstract: This research explores consumer brand hate reactions to influencer-generated reviews, focusing on differences between human influencers (HIs) and virtual influencers (VIs) and review types (unfair negative, fair negative, positive/control). Using a 2 × 3 between-subjects design, two experiments were conducted: Study 1 in a low-involvement context (café), and Study 2 in a high-involvement context (airline). Across both studies, HIs elicited stronger soft (non-purchase intention, brand switching) and hard (brand boycott, negative word-of-mouth) brand hate intentions than VIs, particularly following unfair negative reviews. Psychological contract breach emerges as the key mechanism linking influencer reviews to brand hate perceptions and intentions. This research introduces a theoretical framework to elucidate psychological factors contributing to brand hate reactions. The findings can help brands and advertisers adjust influencer strategies, including those involving generative artificial intelligence-enabled VIs, to meet consumer expectations, strengthen connections, and prevent brand rejection. The findings help brands manage influencer, including artificial intelligence-enabled VI, communications to mitigate brand hate.

title: Market-shaping visions: A conceptual analysis and typology
Generative AI adoption and brand competitiveness in B2B manufacturers: The roles of digital service innovation and digital leadership
Viewpoint: human agency as the transcending concept of human service systems
abstract: Purpose This viewpoint positions human agency as the transcending concept of human service systems, provides a practical, evidence-based framework for this new logic, develops the concept of collaborative agency and applies collaborative agency to reconceptualize the role of money in financial service systems. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on transformative service research, this research employs an interdisciplinary synthesis to establish human agency as a strategic design requirement. The methodology involves reframing service system interactions into a hierarchy of dominance and service and developing a practical toolkit based on Elinor Ostrom's core design principles. This synthesis is then applied to demonstrate the redesign of exploitative financial service systems into collaborative commons. Findings The concept of “collaborative agency” is introduced because systems designed for collaboration foster full human agency. When financial service systems are designed as collaborative common-pool resources, they transform from tools of control that undermine agency into enablers that liberate agency. Practical implications Eight core design principles are developed as a practical toolkit for practitioners to design and evaluate service systems that serve humanity. This toolkit provides a detailed framework for redesigning financial service systems, shifting them from exploitative mechanisms to collaborative commons. Originality/value This research contributes a comprehensive framework, adapted from Elinor Ostrom's principles, for designing human agency-centered service systems. Applying this framework to redesign financial service systems as common-pool resources demonstrates its novelty, creating a new research pathway for inclusive human service systems.

title: Open-System Orchestration as a Strategic Response to Paradoxical Demands in Social Enterprises
abstract: This study examines how social enterprises (SEs) engage in open-system orchestration to navigate paradoxical social and business demands. Drawing on a multi-case study of four SEs in the UK assistive technology sector, we develop a process model distinguishing two sets of practices: (1) recurring tactical practices— accommodating prescribed social benefit provision and fence-sitting on social and business demands —through which SEs respond to immediate resource opportunities and support open-system orchestration, and (2) continuous strategic practices— uncovering social beneficiaries’ untapped potential , facilitating shifts in modes of beneficiary participation , and fostering social benefit provision and income flows —through which open-system orchestration unfolds. Our findings offer a processual refinement of orchestration research by showing how SEs cultivate conditions for contribution among beneficiaries not initially recognized as contributors. A paradox lens further shows that the underlying contradiction between social impact and financial viability persists, while SEs reconfigure participation pathways and forms of beneficiary contribution through which they pursue these demands. The study offers practical insights for SEs and informs broader debates on social value creation.

title: The Atikamekwization of the Commons: Reclaiming Indigenous Territorial Governance on Unceded Land
abstract: How do negative commons and Indigenous commons operate simultaneously when an Indigenous nation repurposes a Western legal instrument on unceded public land? This article presents the first phase of a collaborative, decolonial inquiry into how the Atikamekw Nation in Quebec (Canada) reinterprets Commons theory through what community members call Atikamekwization. Through the development of the Fiducie Ickapitcikan, a social utility trust designed for private property and repurposed to enact collective stewardship over public forest territory, the study examines how the Commons are translated, contested, and reconfigured within Nitaskinan. This evolving institutional experiment reveals how inherited extractive legacies (negative commons) and relational territorial governance (Indigenous commons) converge in a single legal form. Reading the case critically, we trace how a community moves from consulted stakeholder to institutional architect, enacting self-determination through epistemic resistance to, and within, a legal grammar inherited from dispossession.

title: Corporate Culture and Cost Stickiness
Task reflexivity as a pathway linking task interdependence and knowledge sharing
abstract: Abstract Based on a dynamic perspective on knowledge sharing, we examine how and why daily task interdependence relates to knowledge sharing. Drawing on cybernetic control theory, we propose that task interdependence is associated with greater coordination and information demands among employees, which may be linked to task reflexivity. We expect task reflexivity to serve as a within‐person cognitive pathway linking task interdependence and knowledge sharing. We further examine feeling envied as a social‐evaluative condition that strengthens the relationship between task reflexivity and knowledge sharing. We tested our hypotheses using a daily diary study of 156 construction workers in South Korea, yielding 1404 observations. Results from within‐person analyses indicated that daily task interdependence was positively related to task reflexivity, which in turn was positively associated with daily knowledge sharing. The hypothesized mediating role of task reflexivity and moderating role of feeling envied was also supported. Based on these findings, we discuss theoretical and practical implications.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: Embracing nature virtually: how virtual reality helps to promote pro-environmental consumption
Listening to consumers via live streaming: Live streaming comments and their impact on consumer continuance engagement behaviors
AI as Psychological Surrogate in Consumer Search: A Conceptual Framework and Future Research Directions
abstract: ABSTRACT Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.

title: Different Strokes for Different Folks: Exploring Algorithmic Fairness and Trust in Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely used to personalize recommendations, yet questions remain about the representativeness of algorithmic recommendations to recognize diverse consumer needs. This research integrates the stimulus‐organism‐response model and social identity theory to inform how personalization influences recommendation acceptance through algorithmic fairness and trust and how communication style affects these processes, which may differ between ethnic groups. Using a sequential explanatory design, Study 1 ( n = 136) shows that high personalization increases recommendation acceptance, perceived algorithmic fairness and trust compared with low personalization based on an experiment. Study 2 ( n = 300) identifies a positive sequential indirect effect through algorithmic fairness and trust, with competence‐oriented communication producing a stronger effect than warmth‐oriented communication based on an experiment. Study 3 ( n = 340) further reveals differences in these relationships across ethnic groups using a quasi‐experiment. Study 4 ( n = 14) employs semi‐structured interviews to contextualize these findings and explore the underlying reasoning. Theoretically, the findings extend GenAI personalization literature by identifying fairness and trust as key pathways to recommendation acceptance and highlighting ethnic differences in these processes. Practically, the findings guide strategies for GenAI developers to create more equitable and context‐sensitive design across diverse consumers.

title: EXPRESS: A boundary perspective on open strategy
abstract: Open strategy (OS) is often intended to relax formal organizational boundaries in the performance of strategy through transparency and inclusion. However, empirical evidence suggests that openness triggers defensive behaviours, which affect the implications of OS. This essay addresses the conceptual puzzle of why both formal and informal boundaries may persist, intensify, shift, or newly emerge rather than be dissolved when strategy is opened up. We adopt a boundary work perspective to illuminate how boundaries are enacted, contested, and reconfigured. We identify specific practices (defending, challenging, and orchestrating) in which both ‘strategists’ and ‘non-strategists’ engage, and we illustrate the dialectic and moderating relationships between those practices. In addressing how the episodic nature of OS and the temporal coexistence of openness and closure reconfigure the boundaries around strategy work, we posit that OS depends not on the removal of boundaries but on the dynamic social work performed at their intersections.

title: Editorial note for the article: ‘’The power of prediction with Google searches and social media posts: Retail investor interest and IPO pricing’’ Information & Management, Volume 61, Issue 5, July 2024, 103972
From Incubation to Recovery: Constructing the Emotional Life Cycle Model of Families Travelling With Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Family travel can enhance the well-being of families with children with autism spectrum disorder, yet it also creates substantial emotional demands for parents. Drawing on life-cycle theory and the circumplex model of affect, this study examines how parental emotions change across travel stages. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 23 parents from a special education school in Nanjing, China. Findings reveal a four-stage emotional cycle of incubation, adjustment, trial and recovery, showing an overall upward but fluctuating trajectory shaped by perceived parent-child benefits, perceived social support, parenting self-efficacy, courtesy stigma, parenting stress and sense of agency. Exploratory findings suggest that higher child support needs may be associated with stronger parental stress and stigma concerns. Practically, schools and tourism organisers should reduce uncertainty before departure, provide sensory-sensitive pacing and quiet spaces, offer timely assistance during demanding activities, and create post-trip reflection opportunities to build parental confidence for future travel and reduce stress. Also available in Chinese. See Supplemental Material for details.

title: Partner selection in project-based software development: the roles of performance, collaboration experience and network governance
abstract: Purpose This study examines supplier selection in project-based software development, where buyers rely on external developers for specialized capabilities while facing substantial safeguarding risks. Adopting a network-governance perspective, we investigate how network overlap – the extent to which a publisher and developer share common partners – moderates the relationships between developer performance, prior collaboration experience and selection outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Using a longitudinal dataset from the electronic video game industry (7,583 products, 4,322 unique developers and 3,016 unique publishers, over 16 years), we model developer selection using a conditional logit framework. Findings Developers with stronger historical product performance, confidentiality performance and greater prior collaboration experience are more likely to be selected. Network overlap substitutes for prior collaboration experience while strengthening the association between confidentiality performance and selection likelihood, highlighting the contingent role of network governance in partner selection decisions in project-based software development. Originality/value This study advances supplier-selection research by examining observed partner selection in project-based software development. It integrates firm-level indicators, dyadic experience and network overlap, showing that network governance can substitute for prior collaboration while complementing confidentiality performance.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Customers' Stakeholder Orientation and Suppliers' Engagement in Supply Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue Amid the growing shift from shareholder primacy to stakeholder primacy in corporate governance, it remains unclear how this governance stance affects economically linked firms. This study investigates whether customers' stakeholder orientation affects suppliers' relationship engagement and economic outcomes. Research Findings/Insights Using data on US supplier–customer relationships from 1991 to 2019, we find that suppliers increase product relatedness, provide more trade credit, and maintain longer relationships with stakeholder‐oriented customers. Instrumenting customer stakeholder orientation with the passage of constituency statutes, we find further evidence supporting a causal interpretation of our main effect. The effect is more pronounced when suppliers exhibit stronger corporate social responsibility performance, when customers face greater industry competition, and during the financial crisis. Suppliers with more stakeholder‐oriented customer bases also achieve higher sales, improved profitability, and greater operational efficiency. Theoretical/Academic Implications Our study contributes to the corporate governance literature by extending research on the economic consequences of stakeholder orientation beyond focal firms to their supply chain partners. Specifically, our findings suggest that customer stakeholder orientation may encourage greater resource commitments from suppliers and is associated with better supplier performance, providing an interorganizational perspective on the benefits of stakeholder‐oriented governance. Practitioner/Policy Implications Our findings offer practical insights into the role of stakeholder orientation in managing supply chain relationships. For customer firms, adopting stakeholder‐oriented policies may encourage greater supplier commitment and help sustain long‐term trading relationships. For suppliers, customer stakeholder orientation can serve as a credible signal of counterparty reliability, informing partner selection and subsequent relationship‐specific investment decisions.

title: Transition risks, banks’ lending premium, and macro-financial impacts: A stock-flow consistent perspective
Unveiling the J-curve: How intangibles drive productivity mismeasurement
abstract: This paper identifies a firm-level Productivity J-curve induced by intangible investment. Using novel microdata on business-to-business transactions for Belgian firms, we construct a comprehensive measure of intangibles covering software, R&D, design, training, and organizational capital. Because these investments are expensed instead of capitalized, conventional TFP measures misclassify them as intermediate inputs, overstating inputs relative to output. Exploiting their lumpy timing in a difference-in-differences event study, we show that TFP is underestimated by about 1.7%–3.0% over seven years. Intangible investment spikes are followed by higher profits and lower marginal costs, indicating that the J-curve reflects mismeasured, rather than absent, returns to intangible investment. Linking intangible capital to systematic mismeasurement provides new evidence on the productivity slowdown and highlights intangibles as a source of downward measurement bias.

title: Learning from success but not from failure in digital experimentation
A perceived tax on privacy? AI misuse concerns as legitimacy deficits in mandatory governance
abstract: As public administrations embed artificial intelligence (AI) in mandatory services such as income taxation, discretion shifts from case-level judgment to system-level design choices. Privacy then concerns not only which data are held but how citizens are judged, as algorithms infer sensitive attributes and categorize individuals. Because citizens can neither opt out of these services nor audit the underlying logic, privacy frameworks built on voluntary use and personal control are inadequate to explain how citizens’ concerns arise or how regulation addresses them. This study draws on a dyadic model in which legitimacy requires shared expectations, perceived conformity to them, and assent. Two AI misuse concerns, reduced judgment and algorithm bias, are conceptualized as perceived violations of the procedural justice expectations: correctability and bias suppression. The resulting model treats perceived nonconformity as an antecedent of assent and regulation as a factor shaping these concerns. It is estimated using partial least squares structural equation modeling on a scenario-based online survey of 312 employed German residents who evaluated AI-based risk classification of tax returns. Perceived effectiveness of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation is positively associated with trust in the tax administration but not directly with either concern. Instead, trust fully mediates its associations with the two concerns. Both concerns, in turn, are associated with a less favorable attitude toward the AI procedure. Where citizens cannot exit, regulatory assurance thus appears to work through institutional trust, so administrations should look beyond compliance and embed visible procedural safeguards that build this trust.

title: Safety risks and governance in the low-altitude economy (2000–2025): a bibliometric study
Training Ab initio eVTOL pilots for regional air mobility missions: A comparison of curricula
Evaluating the effectiveness of automated speed enforcement in San Francisco, California: A Quasi-experimental approach using telematics data
A narrative policy framework approach to measure blame and credit strategies during the Swiss–EU negotiations
abstract: Abstract This article examines how policy actors use narrative strategies to claim credit, attribute blame, and deflect responsibility. Building on the blame avoidance literature, it integrates the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) to conceptualize presentational strategies as combinations of narrative causal mechanisms and devil–angel–solidarity shifts. Empirically, the study analyzes press releases by the Swiss government and the two major political parties during the Swiss–EU negotiations (2013–2025). The findings show that narrative strategies systematically align with credit and blame strategies: credit claiming and attribution are predominantly associated with intentional causal narratives and angel shifts, whereas blame attribution is linked to intentional causal mechanisms and devil shifts. Governmental actors primarily engage in credit claiming, while political parties focus on blame attribution. Credit claiming remains the predominant strategy of the government, even under declining policy support. The study contributes to the public policy literature by linking blame avoidance and NPF research, offering a novel measurement approach, and refining expectations about governmental communication under political contestation.

title: Extreme temperatures and child neglect: A nationwide case-crossover study of Brazilian children
abstract: Background Neglect is the most frequently reported but least studied form of child maltreatment. Because it arises in part from the conditions under which care is provided, neglect may be sensitive to environmental stressors associated with a warming climate. As an act of omission, it may also respond to heat through pathways distinct from those implicated in abusive behavior. However, population-level evidence on this association remains limited. Objective To estimate the association between heat and child neglect in a middle-income setting and examine heterogeneity across child and case characteristics. Participants and setting 150,163 notifications of neglect or abandonment involving children aged 0 to 9, recorded in Brazil's national violence notification system across 3428 municipalities, 2012 to 2019. Methods Time-stratified case-crossover analysis with conditional logistic regression. Each child served as their own control, matched on municipality, calendar month, year, and day of week. Exposure was municipal daily maximum temperature, categorized with 27 to 30 °C as reference. Results Odds of child neglect increase with temperature. On days of 33 °C or above, odds were 6.0% higher than at 27 to 30 °C (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03–1.09). Below 24 °C, they were 6.0% lower (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.92–0.96). Findings were robust to alternative event dates, reference categories, and municipality exclusions. No variation appeared by sex or race. Exploratory age comparison suggested a larger association among children aged 5 to 9 than among those aged 0 to 4 (ratio of odds ratios 1.10, 95% CI 1.02–1.18, p = 0.017), although the difference did not meet the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold. Conclusions Heat is measurably associated with child neglect. Exploratory analyses suggest that these associations are larger in older children, though this effect does not persist after correction for multiple comparisons. Child welfare research and practice should consider environmental conditions as a potentially relevant and modifiable context.

title: “Living just above the poverty line where I will stay for the rest of my life”: Child sexual abuse and long-term financial health
Disruptions in mentalizing trauma across the prenatal and postnatal periods: Stability and associations with environmental stressors and infant development
abstract: BACKGROUND: Disruptions in trauma-specific reflective functioning (T-RF) among parents are linked to poorer mental health and parental functioning, whereas effective T-RF is a key protective factor. However, the natural trajectory of T-RF and its association with infant development remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: This longitudinal study examined trait- and state-like features of disruptions in T-RF from pregnancy to postpartum, and its associations with infant development. PARTICIPANTS AND SETTING: A sample of 185 pregnant women were recruited during the second trimester (T1) and followed up in the third trimester (T2), as well as between five and 14 months postpartum (T3). METHODS: Self-report questionnaires were used to assess T-RF at all three time points and stressful life events and infant development at T3. RESULTS: = 6.40, p = 0.57), supporting its trait-like features. Greater exposure to prenatal stressful life events was associated with greater prenatal disruptions in T-RF (β = 0.17, p = 0.03), a finding that is consistent with, but does not establish, the possibility that T-RF may exhibit state-like characteristic. Higher disruptions in prenatal T-RF prospectively predicted infant developmental difficulties (β = -0.23, p = 0.01). CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that T-RF primarily reflects stable individual differences and is associated with infant development. Future research should examine whether enhancing prenatal T-RF through psychological interventions can promote infant development.

title: Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of a Novel Online Prevention Program Addressing Changes to First-Time Parent Couples’ Sexual Well-Being
abstract: The perinatal period brings persistent changes to couples’ sexual and romantic relationships. Access to perinatal sexuality information benefits sexual well-being, yet sexual health remains neglected in perinatal care. We examined feasibility and preliminary efficacy of the first couple-based online prevention program (Supporting the Transition to Parenthood through Online Sexual and Relationship Knowledge; STORK) targeting perinatal sexual challenges via psychoeducation and cognitive-behavioral skill-building. We examined feasibility (practicality, acceptability, demand) via adherence and self-reports, and preliminary efficacy by comparing primary (sexual satisfaction, desire, distress) and secondary (relationship satisfaction, relationship conflict, depressive symptoms) outcomes among expectant couples with STORK program access (N = 45 woman-man dyads) and a matched control sample from mid-pregnancy/pre-program to three months postpartum/post-program. Feasibility was strong. Most couples adhered to the STORK program and rated it highly. Preliminary efficacy findings were small-to-moderate and positive for birthing parents but mixed for partners. Compared to controls, birthing parents reported smaller declines in sexual satisfaction and desire and smaller increases in conflict and depressive symptoms. Relationship satisfaction declined less for both parents. Unexpectedly, partners reported greater declines in desire and increases in sexual distress. STORK addresses a critical gap in perinatal care by offering an accessible program to support couples’ adjustment, especially for birthing parents.

title: Drivers of household food insecurity in Brazilian Amazonian riverine communities
abstract: Abstract The Amazon Basin faces mounting socio-environmental pressures that threaten both ecological integrity and food security. In this study, we examine socio-environmental, economic and cultural factors that may drive household food insecurity among ribeirinho (riverine) communities in the middle Juruá region of the Brazilian Amazon. We conducted 563 surveys with 348 women across 33 communities near the end of low-water (2023) and high-water (2024) seasons, assessing food insecurity using the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale, and analysing socio-demographic and income-related predictors. Our findings reveal that food insecurity is widespread and seasonally variable: 80% of households reported moderate or severe food insecurity during the low-water season, decreasing slightly to 74% in the high-water season. Significant predictors of food insecurity were low-water season, and absence of a cantina (small community store). This study highlights the mismatch between abundance and food access in Amazonian territories and underscores the importance of culturally appropriate, locally embedded strategies to promote food security. Our results demonstrate the importance of community-based initiatives and targeted public policies to promote dietary resilience and support food sovereignty in the face of environmental and community vulnerability.

title: Age and sex differences in questionnaire-based indicators of motivational anhedonia, consummatory anhedonia, and negative affect among colorectal cancer survivors
Correction to “Institutional Backsliding Under Liberal Democratic Backsliding: Central Bank Independence Reversal in Türkiye”

Water-energy-carbon nexus footprint of seawater desalination and transfer for industrial development: a hybrid life cycle -node-flow framework
abstract: Seawater desalination is becoming increasingly important in arid, industrializing regions, but planning assessments often consider the embodied energy of supply chains and the operational energy of water transfer separately. This study presents a hybrid life cycle and node-flow framework that combines embodied energy and carbon emissions with a spatially explicit model of pumping energy based on elevation gain and hydraulic head losses. The framework is applied to Iran's Persian Gulf Seawater Desalination and Transfer (SDT) project, which supplies 138.76 million m 3 of water annually. Two strategies are compared: Water Transfer (WT), which pumps water inland while transporting products to the coast, and Industrial Transfer (IT), which relocates industries to the coast and transports raw materials from inland areas. Rail and truck freight represent the best- and worst-case transport scenarios, respectively. Pumping-energy intensity ranges from 333.2 to 21,462.4 MWh per million m 3 , depending mainly on transfer distance and elevation. Although industrial relocation reduces long-distance pumping-energy by 99.4%, transporting raw materials offsets much of this saving. Under the grid-average electricity scenario, rail transport results in nearly unchanged total energy use (+0.9%) but reduces carbon emissions by 22.7%. With truck transport, energy use and carbon emissions increase by 121.9% and 53.8%, respectively. Under low-carbon electricity, relocation increases carbon emissions with both transport modes. Benefits also vary by industry: relocation reduces energy use at the steel site under both modes and at the pelletizing site by rail, but not at the copper sites, where raw-material requirements are substantially greater than product output. The water footprint changes only slightly (−4.4%). This framework supports integrated assessments of energy and carbon trade-offs in desalination-dependent industrial systems.

title: Spatial patterns of hybrid PV–CSP–TES configurations for green hydrogen production across Algeria
abstract: Existing studies have optimized hybrid PV–CSP plants or mapped suitable locations for solar hydrogen production, but the spatial dependence of the optimal hybrid architecture remains insufficiently resolved. This study develops a national-scale framework that couples GIS–FAHP screening with hourly PV–CSP–TES–electrolyzer simulation and site-specific NSGA-II optimization to determine how the cost-optimal system design changes across Algeria. At each meteorological location, PV capacity, CSP power-block capacity, TES duration, and solar multiple are jointly optimized for a fixed 50 MW electrolyzer, with the final configuration selected as the lowest levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) solution satisfying annual demand satisfaction (ADS) ≥ 90%. The resulting architecture varies substantially across the country: optimal PV capacity ranges from 70.03 to 168.86 MW, CSP power-block capacity from 50.00 to 92.98 MW, and solar multiple from 2.35 to 3.40, while annual hydrogen production remains comparatively stable at 7.58–7.65 kt H₂ yr −1 . Unconstrained LCOH ranges from 6.00 to 10.78 € kg −1 H₂ and narrows considerably after GIS-based deployment constraints are imposed. At Hassi R'Mel, the selected architecture combines approximately 100 MW PV, 50 MW CSP, SM = 2.80, and 16 h TES, achieving an LCOH of 6.53 € kg −1 H₂, 90.3% ADS and approximately 7.6 kt H₂ yr −1 . Sensitivity analysis identifies the discount rate and CSP capital cost as the strongest economic influences within the examined parameter ranges. A matched-output comparison shows that PV-only production can achieve lower LCOH when intermittency is acceptable, whereas PV–CSP–TES substantially increases electrolyzer utilization and production continuity. The results demonstrate that site-specific optimization is necessary to capture how economically preferred generation capacities and solar-field sizing adapt to local solar-resource conditions.

title: Data-driven distributionally robust planning of coastal distribution networks and PV-storage-EV stations for low-carbon energy transition
Land-use change and flood-risk governance in a peri-urban catchment of Ljubljana, Slovenia
abstract: Urban expansion into natural floodplains has reduced retention capacity across Europe, increasing downstream flood exposure and creating dependence on engineered substitutes such as dry retention basins. These basins are frequently sited on private agricultural land, producing a structural tension: they deliver public flood protection while concentrating hydrological, agronomic, and economic costs on a small group of landholders. How this tension unfolds – and whether governance frameworks adequately address it – remains poorly understood, particularly in peri-urban catchments where development pressure, climate extremes, and agricultural livelihoods intersect. This paper analyses the mechanisms through which progressive floodplain occupation generates and redistributes flood risk, using a two-century land-use reconstruction (~1820–2024), official hydraulic modelling results (Q10, Q100, Q500 scenarios), and qualitative interviews with land users in the Glinščica catchment (Ljubljana, Slovenia), centred on the Brdnikova dry retention basin. Results reveal a pronounced transition from agricultural floodplain to heavily urbanised catchment, with built-up land increasing more than fifteenfold, primarily at the expense of arable land and meadows in low-elevation zones. Inundation under moderate return periods recurrently affects valley-bottom agricultural soils, where farmers report sediment deposition, soil compaction, invasive species pressure, yield losses, and increased labour demands. Recently introduced compensation mechanisms address direct crop damage, but cumulative and indirect impacts remain uncovered. The findings indicate that dry retention basins in peri-urban agricultural settings are best understood as engineered flood-retention infrastructure embedded in multifunctional agricultural land use, rather than as full ecological-restoration measures. They require integrated governance frameworks that anticipate distributional effects, ensure equitable compensation, and coordinate spatial planning with agricultural and environmental policy. Given the single-case design, the study advances context-sensitive governance considerations relevant to comparable peri-urban retention settings.

title: Dealing with credit constraints for households' climate resilience: the role of land ownership and institutional quality in Togo
Land abandonment as a window for transformative change: Response pathways in Europe
abstract: Land abandonment is a persistent and uneven process reshaping rural Europe, with risks for biodiversity, land degradation, and rural socio-cultural and economic resilience. Although it is often framed as a negative condition to be reversed, we argue in this Viewpoint that land abandonment can be approached as a window for change, which in some contexts can take a more transformative form. We put forward four alternative pathways to help understand and strategically shape responses to land abandonment in Europe: sustainable land management; heritage and identity; community and social innovation; and rewilding and nature. To support comparison across pathways, we adapt the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) transformative change framework to make explicit how interventions frame abandonment, their intent for change, and the alignment they mobilise across visions, institutions and practices, including implications for equity, power and decision-making. Drawing on illustrative responses, we suggest that many initiatives prioritise coping or adaptation, while transformative elements tend to sit in specific governance and instrument choices rather than system-wide shifts. Transformative change, where pursued, should therefore be treated as one end of a spectrum rather than a default expectation and requires explicit intent, durable institutional anchoring and legitimacy. The paper offers a heuristic perspective — not a definitive typology of existing approaches — to help planning and policy debates become clearer about aims and limits, better able to match instruments to intent, and more attentive to the governance and distributional conditions under which responses endure, evolve or become contested.

Emergency medicine and sustainability: optimizing a knee trauma care pathway with life cycle assessment
abstract: The carbon footprint of emergency care remains largely under-examined. This study quantified greenhouse gas emissions associated with the full clinical pathway of knee trauma patients treated at an outpatient emergency unit in University Hospitals of Geneva, Switzerland, to better understand the environmental impact of this care trajectory. Life Cycle Assessment methodology was applied to the functional unit of the management of one patient presenting with knee trauma, including diagnosis and initial treatment. Different clinical scenarios were modelled to reflect variations in care complexity and diagnostic imaging use. Results revealed that patient transportation, pharmaceuticals, medical consumables, and diagnostic imaging, particularly magnetic resonance imaging, are major contributors to the carbon footprint. These findings underscore the importance of optimizing care protocols and exploring sustainable alternatives in emergency healthcare to reduce associated greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Developing Partial Characterization Factors for Ship Noise Impacts on Marine Biodiversity in European Seas
abstract: Abstract Shipping is the primary source of underwater noise pollution, yet its impacts on marine biodiversity remain unquantified in Life Cycle Impact Assessment (LCIA). This study presents the first framework for quantifying the regionalized impact of ship noise on marine mammal biodiversity within LCIA, demonstrated for European Seas. Ship noise data from the NAVISON project for 2019 were combined with species-specific sensitivity thresholds for marine mammals to derive spatially explicit Potentially Affected Fractions (PAF). Partial characterization factors (pCFs) for 21 country groups were calculated by integrating PAF values with spatially explicit transport work and maritime trade data, ranging from zero to 1.00 × 10–14 PAF × yr × ton-km–1 (Northern Europe), with a mean of 1.86 × 10–15 PAF × yr × ton-km–1. The total impact of ship noise per country was calculated for 200 countries by multiplying the pCF with each country’s maritime trade. The United Kingdom has the highest total impact (1.34× 10–2 PAF × yr), followed by the United States of America and Spain. This framework represents a first step toward integrating ship noise as a novel impact category in LCIA, supporting comprehensive environmental assessments of global supply chains alongside other maritime stressors such as greenhouse gas emissions and marine invasive species.

title: Distinct Methane-Cycling Pathways Drive Variable Surface Flux in Freshwater Wetlands
abstract: Abstract Freshwater wetlands are the largest natural source of methane (CH4), representing a third of global emissions. Both CH4 production and oxidation are microbially mediated, yet the metabolic controls governing CH4 cycling across wetland types remain poorly resolved. Here, we investigated six hydrologically and geochemically distinct wetlands in the Prairie Pothole Region of North America. By integrating genome-resolved metatranscriptomic data with porewater geochemistry, dissolved CH4 profiles, and chamber-based flux measurements across these wetlands, we assessed how microbial gene expression associated with electron acceptor utilization corresponds to CH4 cycling and identified the dominant methanogenic pathways driving CH4 production. CH4 porewater concentration varied across seasons and sites, with higher concentrations later in the season under more reducing conditions. Wetlands with higher expression of denitrification and sulfate reduction genes exhibited lower methanogenesis and porewater CH4 concentrations. Sites with higher porewater CH4 showed elevated expression of all three methanogenic pathways. Methanogenic activity, however, was not predictive of surface flux. Instead, emissions were modulated by site-specific physical and geochemical controls on methanotrophic CH4 consumption. These findings demonstrate that equivalent CH4 production can emerge through distinct microbial pathways, and that production alone is a poor predictor of atmospheric emissions. This distinction carries important implications for modeling wetland contributions to global CH4 budgets.

title: Robust Dual-Cycle Direct Air Capture Process Enabled by a Novel Biphasic Solvent
abstract: Abstract Traditional liquid-based DAC (L-DAC) technology suffers from high energy consumption and transportation difficulties due to complex intermediate conversion and oxidative degradation, despite its fast kinetics. To address these challenges, this study proposed a dual-cycle DAC strategy using a novel biphasic absorbent ([PZ][1,2,4]-NMP). Atmospheric CO2 was first captured by KOH and converted to K2CO3. Subsequently, under air-isolated conditions, [PZ][1,2,4] selectively displaced CO2 from K2CO3, concentrating it into a flowable carbamate slurry. By confining regeneration to this small-volume slurry, a low-energy penalty of 1.37–1.45 GJ·t–1CO2 was achieved. The closed-loop design effectively prevented oxidative degradation of the active components and significantly enhanced phase separation. This dual-cycle architecture provides a promising pathway for energy-efficient and operationally robust DAC technologies.

title: 60 Years of ES&T in Pursuit of Sustainable Systems

Issue Editorial Masthead
The Acute Exposure Window: A Missing Dimension in Industrial Fire Assessment
Adsorptive Membranes for PFAS Removal: Current Status, Design Principles, and Research Needs
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are contaminants of concern due to their persistence, occurrence in natural waters, and association with adverse health outcomes. Producing potable water from PFAS-impacted sources requires selectively removing PFAS from complex waters. Adsorptive membranes are an emerging strategy for PFAS removal due to their tunable architectures and chemistries, modularity, and high water permeances. However, it is difficult to compare adsorptive membrane performance across studies and identify membrane properties governing PFAS removal due to the diversity of materials, architectures, testing conditions, and reported performance metrics. This review critically evaluates the state of PFAS adsorptive membranes by examining nanofiber membranes, asymmetric membranes, adsorptive nanofiltration (NF) membranes, and ion exchange membranes used for adsorptive PFAS removal. We highlight structure-property-performance relationships, assess current testing strategies, and recommend standard performance metrics to enable cross-study comparisons. We further compare adsorptive membrane performance to conventional reverse osmosis (RO) and NF membranes. Finally, we apply the convection-diffusion-adsorption (CDA) model to published PFAS breakthrough data to gain mechanistic insights into the role of membrane properties and operating parameters on PFAS removal. Overall, this review provides a framework for evaluating adsorptive membranes, identifies key research gaps, and establishes design criteria to advance adsorptive PFAS separations.

title: Developing Complementary Aquatic Sentinel Panels for Cross-Chemical Monitoring and Regional Localization
abstract: Abstract Sparse and uneven multispecies toxicity data make it difficult to select a small panel of aquatic sentinels that includes sensitive species across priority chemicals. We developed COMPASS (Complementarity-Oriented Monitoring Panels of Aquatic Sentinel Species) to select complementary sentinel species using species sensitivity distributions (SSDs). Of 2,026 SSDs fitted within chemical and test-condition groups from 426,588 waterborne toxicity records, 1,613 with at least six species supported focal-species leave-one-out estimation; 413 five-species groups supported supplementary comparisons. The national top-5 comprised Gastrophryne carolinensis, Neocloeon triangulifer, Hyalella azteca, Daphnia ambigua, and Daphnia magna. Chemical-priority-weighted expected capture was 33.8%, 62.4%, and 88.8% at measured lower-5%, lower-10%, and lower-20% targets, respectively. Among 115 chemical–medium combinations meeting U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requirements, the lowest measured protective-apical threshold among panel members correlated with the full-data lower-5% benchmark (Spearman ρ = 0.847; 95% chemical-bootstrap interval, 0.756–0.904). None had measurements for all five members; 54 and 44 had measurements for one and two, respectively. Follow-up rankings for 639 chemicals depended on effect-family aggregation. Localized panels averaged 6.75 percentage points higher model-expected capture than the national panel across 32 states under matched weights; three data-limited states used the national panel. Deployment requires prospective assays, cultivation work, and matrix-specific validation.

title: Light/dark-cycle-mediated microbial selection and metabolic differentiation reshape pollutant removal pathways in microalgal–bacterial granular sludge
