AI dramatically lowers the cost of building software thereby lowering product development costs but may raise the barriers to scaling and sustaining competitive advantage. Value capture depends not simply on innovation, but on a compelling value proposition and access to and control over critical complementary assets, architectural control points, and shifting ecosystem bottlenecks. The paper emphasizes that entrepreneurial success requires dynamic capabilities and human judgment to configure and reconfigure ecosystems as technologies and competitive conditions evolve. Managerial Summary AI makes it easier to start a business as it lowers the cost of software development; but building a durable competitive advantage still requires more than a good product or technology. It requires a compelling value proposition to the customer and participation in ecosystems first as tenant and later as anchor. Accordingly, entrepreneurs need to become sophisticated ecosystem players and aspire to be architects, coordinating partners, platforms, data, technology, capital, and other capabilities they may not own. They should identify early which complementary assets are critical to creating and capturing value, understand where control and bottlenecks lie in their ecosystem, and continually reassess these as technology and competition change. AI can help small teams move faster and operate at greater scale, but it does not replace human judgment. Successful entrepreneurs must combine AI with strong ecosystem relationships, domain expertise, governance, and the ability to adapt as their businesses scale.

title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

title: Phantom Networks: Window on Agency in Social Mechanisms
abstract: Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience — what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure-in-action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work

title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
abstract: ABSTRACT Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

title: Online review effectiveness: The moderating role of macroeconomic conditions
Temporal Intuition and Organization Studies: Surfacing Intangible Time from a Sea Kayak
abstract: Scholarship on organisational temporality has yet to fully take into account intangible time, defined in this essay as the creative connecting of fragmented temporal experiences through ‘temporal intuition’. This essay argues for a stronger attention to temporal intuition to enrich current understandings of temporal forms in organization studies. Inspired by Bergson’s work on lived temporal experience, it reports from the author’s direct experience of time during a 15-day solo sea-kayaking journey from Copenhagen to Oslo in August 2025. It shows how the experience of paddling in challenging weather and sea conditions required continued reliance on intuition to connect the multiple and dispersed temporal experiences encountered during the trip. Retrospective reflection on this experience has yielded three forms of temporal experience that can inspire further temporal theorizing: immanent events, inchoate rhythm, and contemporaneous flows. The essay concludes with suggestions on how to give temporal intuition a voice in organization studies by developing empirical, methodological and analytical aspects, thereby bringing intangible time from obscurity.

title: Constituting Technological Stigma: The Oscillating Stigmatization of Internal Combustion Engine Scooters
abstract: Technologies can themselves become objects of stigmatization, rather than merely serving as vehicles through which stigma is directed at associated individuals or organizations. As technologies evolve, shifts in their benefits and harms may alter the grounds for stigma. Yet it remains unclear how these shifts shape stigma trajectories. We examine this issue through a longitudinal qualitative study of the stigmatization of internal combustion engine (ICE) scooters in Taiwan (2009–2021), a case in which a proposal to phase them out in favor of electric scooters was later withdrawn. We show how stigmatizing and stigmatized audiences, evolving technologies, and infrastructures co-constitute evaluative conditions that shape which attributes and consequences acquire discrediting significance. Stigma first attached to legacy ICE models and then spread to all ICE scooters. Its scope later narrowed as upgraded variants regained acceptance, although legacy models remained discredited. This oscillating trajectory unfolds through three mechanisms: constituting a graded technological order, polarizing this order, and reconstituting technological normality. Our model thus extends audience-centered accounts by explaining how human and nonhuman elements jointly shape the trajectory and scope of technology stigma.

title: Perspectives: A Tale of Three Plots: Advancing narrative theorising in organisation and management research
abstract: Narrative theorising (rather than theorising based on constructs and models) is much called for in qualitative research in management and organisation studies. Despite this, how to emplot, i.e. the process of configuring fragmented events into coherent and meaningful accounts with the objective of sensemaking and understanding remains underexplored. This Perspectives piece showcases recent exemplars illustrating how we can practice narrative theorising using three distinct styles: historical, metaphorical, and discursive narratives. Since narrative theorising is commonly observed in single-case studies, we begin our exploration by drawing on six such articles published in Organization Studies to demonstrate how these styles foreground the temporal evolution of phenomena, bridge between multiple divergent accounts, or highlight conflicts between competing discourses to construct theoretical accounts and understanding. We illustrate each style in terms of its distinctive form, set of paradigmatic assumptions, analytical moves, and intended aims, with the overall aim of advancing the potential of narrative theorising in organisation and management research.

title: From Managerial to Relational Epistemologies: Decolonizing Sustainability Education
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I critically interrogate the epistemic foundations of sustainability education in business schools in the context of escalating climate crises. I argue that business education is complicit in the production and perpetuation of planetary destruction by privileging market‐based, growth‐driven rationalities while simultaneously co‐opting sustainability discourses to reinforce capitalist accumulation. These dominant managerialist regimes are epistemically resistant to the transformations required for sustainability and climate justice. Drawing on insights from decolonial scholarship and critical pedagogy, I explore the (im)possibilities of epistemic transformations that are needed for a more meaningful engagement with sustainability. I argue that such a transformation requires a shift from managerial to relational epistemologies—ways of knowing that emerge through relationships rather than detached observation of isolated, independent entities. Sustainability, from a relational epistemological perspective, cannot be divorced from social and environmental justice and must also confront power dynamics that drive inequality, neocolonialism and the exploitation of marginalized communities. I propose a radical reimagining of sustainability education—one that historicizes, denaturalizes and problematizes sustainability while prioritizing climate justice, relational ethics and pluriversal futures.

title: From Triple Bottom Line (TBL) to Supply Chain Triple Value Bottom Line (SCTVBL): A Sustainable Supply Chain Value Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT In today's competitive business environment where consumers increasingly expect transparency, quality, and value for money, buying a product means interacting with the entire supply chain. As the modern supply chains become more autonomous and interconnected, the effective measurement of their business value necessitates transitioning from the conventional efficiency‐based business models to more holistic, stakeholder‐focused business models. In this regard, although the triple bottom line (TBL) framework offers sustainability of the supply chains via economic, social, and environmental performance dimensions, it does not segregate and comprehensively capture value for the key supply chain stakeholders, thereby disregarding the important stakeholders like employees, customers, suppliers, and partners. Therefore, by evaluating the gaps in the extant supply chain management literature coupled with analyzing, critiquing, and synthesizing the current supply chain performance frameworks, and drawing upon the guiding theories, this research introduces a novel concept, “supply chain triple value bottom line” (SCTVBL), and subsequently presents a SCTVBL framework. While addressing the evolving performance needs of the contemporary supply chains, the proposed framework further extends the conventional TBL framework by offering value‐oriented supply chains perspective. As a whole, by suggesting organizational value creation (via economic value, operational value, and employee value), socio‐environmental value creation (via social value and environmental value), and relational value creation (via customer value and supplier & partner value) as renewed supply chain value dimensions, the SCTVBL framework offers a more stakeholder‐focused perspective for holistically addressing the value creation needs of the supply chain stakeholders. Although the proposed SCTVBL framework is conceptual in nature, it opens new avenues for future theoretical research and empirical practice, thereby paving the way for policy renewals, revitalized industry practices and improved SDG contributions.

title: Green Finance, Environmental Governance, and the Performance of Green Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT Green finance can support green innovation not only by financing research and development (R&D), but also by facilitating the application of green technologies. Drawing on institutional theory and the dynamic capability perspective, this study examines how green finance relates to two stages of the green innovation value chain: green technology R&D and the conversion of technological innovation into economic and environmental outcomes. Using panel data for 284 Chinese cities from 2008 to 2022, we find that green finance is positively associated with performance at both stages of the innovation value chain. The evidence is consistent with improved urban financing conditions and greener consumption, while stronger environmental governance reinforces these relationships. The association becomes stronger after identifiable thresholds in green‐finance development and extends across city boundaries through positive spatial spillovers. These effects are also more pronounced after 2016 and in eastern cities. These findings show that green finance operates not simply by expanding the supply of capital, but also by interacting with firms' resource‐acquisition, market‐sensing, and resource‐reconfiguration capabilities across a sequential innovation process.

title: Independence at a Temporal Cost: How Central Bank Independence Influences Green Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT The standard theory of Central Bank Independence (CBI) establishes that a discretionary policymaker might maximize social welfare but exploit the short‐run trade‐off between inflation and output. Building upon this, we investigate the impact of CBI on green loans using an unbalanced panel of 13,150 observations from financial firms across a global sample over 15 years (2010–2024). We find that financial firms issue fewer green loans in the short‐term with the increase of CBI. We further show that this constraining effect intensifies when interest rates are high, consistent with a borrowing‐cost channel linking CBI to green lending. We also document that the Paris Agreement offsets the negative effect of CBI on green lending in countries that underwent central bank reforms during this period, consistent with the Agreement functioning as a policy signal that tempers central bank neutrality in some contexts. Our findings suggest that the temporal negative impact of CBI on green loans is more pronounced for financial firms with larger size, lower loan growth, greater noninterest income, nonadoption of GRI, lower ESG performance and those who are nonsignatories of the Equator Principles. For financial firms operating in countries with lower capital requirements, regulatory quality and control of corruption, we observe that increases in CBI are associated with temporal reductions of green loans. The results are consistent with robust proxies for CBI and green loans and after accounting for endogeneity issues.

title: Digital Sustainability as an Enabler of Supply Chain Sustainability: A Systematic Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital sustainability is gaining increasing popularity among corporate leaders in global challenges and the competitive landscape. Digital sustainability refers to corporate activities that leverage technology to advance sustainable development goals. The digital dimension of sustainability has not only become standard practice in contemporary business operations but is also instrumental in advancing supply chain sustainability. As companies navigate the complexities of the digital competitive landscape while meeting environmental and social sustainability needs across supply chains, it is increasingly important to understand how technological advancement is connected to sustainable development. In particular, over the past two decades, the field of sustainable supply chain management has evolved into mainstream supply chain management, with a focus on sustainable development. However, there is a significant gap in sustainable supply chain management regarding digital transformation and technological applications. That is, existing studies tend to focus on individual technologies, specific industries, or isolated practices, offering only limited insights into the broader thematic structure, interconnections and evolution of digital sustainability within corporate sustainability. To address the gap, the primary aim of this paper is to map the current state of research on digital sustainability and sustainable supply chain management, identify research gaps and emerging areas, provide a theoretical classification of these results and propose research directions. Using a systematic literature review, this study identified four themes: (1) core digitalisation and blockchain foundations in sustainable supply chain management, (2) digital transformation and performance/innovation outcomes, (3) adoption, governance and implementation challenges of digitalisation in sustainable supply chain management and (4) emerging and integrative digital sustainability pathways. This study provides new insights into the connected fields of digital sustainability and sustainable supply chain management and offers theoretical justifications for the areas in which research should be further developed.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty, ESG‐Based Sustainability Uncertainty, and Sectoral Transition‐Risk Monitoring in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate action requires credible policy implementation, effective sustainability disclosure, and sector‐sensitive transition‐risk monitoring. This study examines how Chinese climate policy uncertainty (CCPU) and ESG‐based sustainability uncertainty (ESGUI) are embedded within China's sectoral stock‐market connectedness network during the low‐carbon transition. Using monthly data for 11 sectoral indices, CCPU, and ESGUI from November 2002 to September 2024, we apply an asymmetric TVP‐VAR framework to estimate total connectedness and connectedness within positive‐ and negative‐return‐component systems. The full‐system estimates identify CCPU and ESGUI as net receivers of shocks associated with domestic sectoral returns. Bootstrap and lower‐dimensional validation analyses show that the receiver position is stronger and more stable for CCPU, while the position of ESGUI is sensitive to system composition. Energy‐intensive, capital‐heavy, infrastructure‐related, and consumer‐linked sectors occupy prominent positions in the connectedness network. Bootstrap inference provides qualified support for stronger connectedness within the negative‐return‐component system. The policy‐period estimates indicate that asymmetric connectedness is highest during the Post‐Paris/pre‐dual‐carbon period, while the intervals for the period differences support a descriptive interpretation of these temporal patterns. The findings show that connectedness involving sustainability‐related uncertainty is sign‐specific and time varying across China's low‐carbon transition and provide insights for firms' investment planning, financing decisions, disclosure practices, risk management, and transition strategies.

title: Strengthening or Straining Resilience? Climate Risk Disclosure and Technology Adoption in Banks
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines bank digital transformation and climate risk disclosure as two concurrent strategic investments and tests their joint effect on market‐implied default risk, a question central to financial‐system resilience under SDG 13. Prior research has largely studied the two strategies in isolation. Drawing on synergy theory, we document negative association between them and show how it evolves across default‐risk horizons. Using a global sample of 543 listed banks from 2000 to 2023, we examine how technology‐firm acquisitions and climate risk disclosure relate to market‐implied default probability. Each strategy is associated with lower perceived fragility when considered separately. However, their interaction is positive and significant, which indicates that pursuing both at once attenuates these stabilizing effects. This pattern is consistent with negative synergy.Scaling both transformations at the same time creates coordination costs, managerial attention constraints, and implementation strain. This negative synergy is strogest at shorter horizons, whereas climate disclosure becomes more relevant at longer maturities. The findings suggest that banks should sequence digital and climate governance investments rather than scale both aggressively at once. For policymakers and supervisors, the results indicate that climate disclosure frameworks and digital transformation policies should be supported by governance capacity, reliable data infrastructures, and implementation guidance consistent with SDG 13.

title: Understanding the Mediating Role of Talent Retention in SMEs' Sustainability Practices
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation and institutional regulation do not consistently translate into more sustainable practices in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). This study, which is grounded in the resource‐based view (RBV) and draws on institutional theory (IT) and talent management theory (TMT), emphasizes talent retention as a theoretically central mediating mechanism that links external institutional and digital drivers with embedded sustainability practices. Applying PLS‐SEM to survey data from 253 SMEs in La Rioja (Spain), our findings reveal no significant direct effects of digital management intensity or the social and regulatory framework on sustainability. However, both of these variables have an indirect effect on sustainability via talent retention. Our results suggest that regulatory and digital drivers are more likely to be effective when supported by a stable “Green Pillar” of human capital that can internalize these external stimuli. By positioning talent retention as the core conduit through which external digital and institutional pressures are converted into sustainable practices in SMEs, the study advances TMT, adds to the Digital Green Twin Transition debate, and offers practical implications for aligning talent management strategies in SMEs with digital and institutional policies.

title: Entrepreneurial Trust and Corporate Green Innovation: Evidence From Chinese Entrepreneurs
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do entrepreneurs respond so differently to environmental innovation imperatives? Prior research emphasizes structural pressures, overlooking the cognitive and social frames shaping environmental decisions. Using survey data from 3163 Chinese micro and small firms, we find composite entrepreneurial trust is positively associated with green innovation. Disaggregating trust reveals a distinct institutional division of labor: Locally embedded in‐group trust accompanies green innovation—particularly local pollution abatement in lower‐pollution sectors—whereas institutional trust is linked to climate‐related innovation specifically among politically connected entrepreneurs. Generalized out‐group trust shows no association. Furthermore, trust aligns with green innovation alongside active behavioral commitments—risk‐taking, employee training, and proactive policy search—rather than passive expectations like future optimism or perceived policy effectiveness. This research advances the microfoundations of environmental strategy by illuminating how distinct trust objects shape responses to uncertainty. Practically, policymakers must lower policy‐information search costs, and entrepreneurs should pair relational trust with concrete capability investments.

title: Is ESG Score Associated With Corporate Outcomes? Empirical Evidence From Europe and Latin America
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable business practices are increasingly central to corporate strategies, partly driven by the pursuit of performance‐related incentives. This study examines the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and corporate outcomes, focusing on operational efficiency, market valuation, and profitability. Using panel data regression models, we analyze two samples: 192 European and 110 Latin American publicly listed companies. Our findings reveal different patterns of association across the two regional subsamples. In the European sample, significant associations emerge particularly for market valuation and selected financial outcomes, whereas in the Latin American sample significant associations are more frequently observed for operational and financial performance. Particular attention is devoted to the environmental pillar, and its associations with corporate outcomes are assessed within the broader ESG framework, using the social and governance dimensions for comparison. These associations persist across all lagged specifications, providing evidence of a persistent ESG performance relationship over time. Overall, the findings reveal context‐specific patterns in the association between ESG performance and corporate outcomes, with relevant implications for corporate decision‐makers, investors, and policymakers.

title: Driving Social‐Ecological Supply Chains Toward Circularity: A Delphi Study on Microfoundations of Transformative Capabilities
abstract: ABSTRACT To remain competitive in turbulent business environments, modern supply chains must undergo radical and systemic transformations, such as moving toward circular supply chain configurations. However, how to initiate and effectively govern such transformative changes is a complex task, not yet fully understood. This paper addresses this research gap by identifying the microfoundations relevant for triggering, envisioning, navigating, and stabilizing transformative capabilities, recently proven to initiate and govern social‐ecological supply chain transformations toward circularity. A three‐round Delphi study is carried out to identify, select, and classify the microfoundations of each transformative capability at the levels of individuals, processes, and structures. Our results suggest the specific set of microfoundations that facilitate the development of triggering, envisioning, navigating, and stabilizing capabilities for supply chain transformations toward circularity. This paper advances the new paradigm of transformative supply chain management by offering valuable theoretical and managerial insights.

title: From green climate to green creativity: the role of environmental practices, resource availability and integration
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how green work climate (GWC) reaches employee green creativity through environmental management practices (EMPs) and how environmental resource availability and employee environmental integration condition that process. Design/methodology/approach The study collected data in three waves from 371 supervisor–subordinate dyads across 27 hotels in Saudi Arabia. The study tested hypotheses via the PROCESS macro (Models 4 and 21). Findings EMPs mediate the relationship between GWC and employee green creativity. GWC influences EMPs more strongly where environmental resources are abundant. EMPs influence green creativity more strongly where employees are highly integrated. Practical implications Hospitality managers should move beyond symbolic green climates and implement concrete EMPs. This requires sufficient environmental resources and a strategy that treats staff as codesigners of environmental solutions. Originality/value This study identifies two distinct points at which a green climate fails to reach creative output. One depends on organizational resources; the other on employee integration. It also distinguishes three practice dimensions that prior work has bundled and provides validated measures for three previously unoperationalized constructs.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Beyond behaviouralism: rethinking sustainability governance
abstract: Purpose This paper critically aims to examine behaviouralism as an influential problem-defining orientation in tourism and hospitality sustainability research, focusing on how it shapes problem framing, responsibility allocation and engagement with sustainability transitions. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a critical conceptual problematisation of recurring research logics. Drawing on purposively selected streams of behaviour-centred sustainability research, critical scholarship and alternative theoretical perspectives, it examines how assumptions about agency, causality, actionability and responsibility shape sustainability knowledge. Findings Behaviouralism can narrow sustainability challenges into behaviourally actionable problems, foregrounding individual or firm responsibility while backgrounding governance, political-economic conditions and justice. The analysis shows how ontological and methodological assumptions influence what becomes visible and actionable as a sustainability problem. The Behavioural Governance Matrix distinguishes individual and collective agency across behaviour-centred and governance-centred forms of actionability. Practical implications The matrix provides a basis for examining when sustainability responsibility is concentrated on individual actors and when wider organisational or governance conditions also require attention. For managers, policymakers and destination authorities, it directs attention beyond behavioural compliance towards the institutional, labour, infrastructural and accountability arrangements that enable or constrain sustainable practice. Originality/value The paper conceptualises behaviouralism as a problem-defining logic rather than a methodological preference and develops the Behavioural Governance Matrix as a diagnostic framework for examining how agency, responsibility and actionability are configured in sustainability research.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Geopolitical Shockwaves: SME Growth and Resilience in times of Political Instability
abstract: We investigate the relationship between geopolitical risk (GPR) and the growth and survival of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across diverse economic and institutional contexts. Using econometric analyses of firm-level data across multiple countries, we find that heightened GPR is associated with lower SME growth and a higher hazard of firm exit. These patterns are consistent with real options theory, which suggests that uncertainty may encourage the postponement of irreversible investments. The negative association between GPR and growth is more pronounced among financially constrained firms, highly innovative SMEs, and domestically owned businesses. Greater gender diversity in firm leadership and workforce composition is associated with a weaker negative GPR–growth relationship, while regional analyses indicate stronger negative associations in the Middle East and North Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean. Survival analyses also identify differences in survival probabilities across firms with different financial, strategic, and operational characteristics. In particular, higher management quality, exporting, certification, internal financing, bank financing, and digital finance use are associated with higher survival probabilities. These findings identify potential sources of SME resilience, although they do not establish causal effects of these characteristics or practices.

title: Institutional changes and the persistence of regional entrepreneurship in China: 1952–2024
Transforming procurement into credit: fiscal–financial coordination and SME innovation in China
Chatroom Democracy: How Digital Tools Shape Governance in Cooperatives
abstract: Digital tools are increasingly used to enhance governance, yet little is known about how they support and hinder democratic governance in multistakeholder cooperatives. This study examines this question through an 18-month digital ethnography of WhatsApp groups within a multistakeholder cooperative in Indonesia, complemented by 28 interviews and 24 Zoom and in-person observations. Drawing on McQuarrie’s lens of participatory technologies, the findings show that the role of digital tools varied across organizational conditions. With a large and geographically dispersed membership base, digital tools facilitated information sharing and coordination. During periods of financial crisis, they enabled member mobilization and amplified collective voice. Yet, as members remained financially dependent on the cooperative and information asymmetries persisted, the same tools were used to reassert managerial control. By extending participatory technology into the digital realm, the study shows that the way participation is organized through the same digital tool can shift over time.

title: Sustaining Membership With the B Corp Certification: Values Work With a Community of Practice
abstract: We investigate how company leaders engage with a prosocial certification over time to sustain their company’s membership, through the lens of values work with a community of practice. Adopting a qualitative approach, we interviewed executives of U.S. B Corp–certified companies at two points in time to investigate how they enacted values work, or the articulation and accomplishment of values through actions, to sustain membership. We found company leaders enacted three types of values work through membership with the B Corp certification, framed as a community of practice: leveraging , participating , and infusing . We develop a conceptual model describing how enacting only “leveraging” values work does not support sustained membership, whereas enacting “leveraging” with “participating” and/or “infusing” values work with the certification as a community of practice does. This study advances theory on framing prosocial certifications as communities of practice, developing values-based processes that support sustained membership over time.

title: Determinants of the commercialization of academic knowledge: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Abstract Over the last two decades, research on the determinants of academic knowledge commercialization has attracted increasing scholarly attention. However, despite this interest, the evidence remains fragmented across levels of analysis, commercialization channels, and outcome measures. This study provides a systematic review and channel-specific quantitative synthesis of 134 quantitative studies. We identify 110 determinants and organize them into five framework components: environmental, organizational, TTO-related, research content and field, and individual. A weighted sign test assesses directional consistency across five channels and mixed outcomes, while a meta-analysis of 68 studies with comparable correlations estimates summary associations for patenting, licensing, spin-off creation, and collaboration. The findings reveal channel-specific patterns. Patenting is associated with organizational resources and prior experience. Licensing is associated with venture capital availability, income from public sources, prior publications, and TTO size and age. Spin-off creation is associated with research quality, income from public and third-party sources, innovation climate, prior collaboration, technology transfer activities, and TTO expertise. Collaboration is associated with technology transfer activities, prior patenting, applied research, and industry experience. The weighted sign-test synthesis extends the evidence to consulting and relationships for which comparable effect sizes are unavailable. Many associations show substantial heterogeneity and should be interpreted as average rather than uniform relationships across settings. Overall, the findings do not support a uniform set of determinants. Instead, they indicate channel-specific configurations across framework components. The resulting framework connects these components with commercialization channels and types and stages of outcomes, providing a basis for future research and channel-specific support measures.

title: Style and content of entrepreneurial stories as dual reference points for the evaluation of crowdfunding campaigns
A future-proof perspective for academic authorship in systematic literature reviews
Diagnosing green innovation collaboration network resilience under shocks: Implications for network orchestration
abstract: Green innovation collaboration networks (GICNs) can drive green technological breakthroughs and innovation upgrading in Chinese manufacturing, but they are increasingly exposed to multiple shocks, such as natural disasters, public crises, technological blockades, and geopolitical conflicts. Dynamic diagnosis and governance of GICNs resilience remain insufficiently understood. We exclusively investigate GICNs centered on Chinese manufacturing firms. Integrating network resilience and network orchestration theories, we develop a “Network Orchestrator-Orchestration Action-Orchestration Outcome” framework. Using green patent co-application data from 2413 Chinese manufacturing enterprises, we construct temporal GICNs and assess their structural resilience (i.e., connectivity and stability) and functional resilience (i.e., transmissibility and redundancy). We further leverage multi-scenario network shock-recovery simulations and a network cascading failure model to diagnose resilience deficiencies and formulate governance strategies. Results show that: (1) Both network structural and functional resilience require strengthening and exhibit clear stage-specific vulnerability. Resilience losses are concentrated in early-shock stage, while network connectivity and transmissibility are most sensitive to failure of critical orchestrators and collaboration patterns. Multiple and superimposed shocks cause greater damage than single shocks, while the impact of shock transmission on resilience jointly depends on orchestrators' bearing capability and shock intensity. (2) Heterogeneous orchestrators can shape GICNs resilience through network orchestration actions. Enterprises, universities, and research institutions sequentially exert diminishing effects on resilience degradation under shocks, acting respectively as chain‑leading, knowledge-bridging, and channel-service orchestrators, while governments provide institutional orchestration support. Network resource acquisition, control and transmission capabilities captured by network positions, together with bridging and tight collaboration patterns, exert differentiated effects on resilience evolution. (3) Building on these diagnostics, we identify three governance measures using simulation analysis: strengthening critical network capabilities, stabilizing valuable collaboration patterns, and forming or reconfiguring collaboration patterns under cost constraints. To promote resilience governance, we further conceptually develop a four-stage dynamic orchestration strategy framework encompassing preventive buffering, protective stabilizing, adaptive reconfiguration, and evolutionary upgrading orchestration strategies.

title: The association between different types of anthropomorphism of artificial intelligence service agents and user trust: A three-level meta-analysis
abstract: As artificial intelligence service agents (AISAs) become increasingly widespread, anthropomorphism is often proposed as a way to foster user trust, yet empirical findings remain mixed. Drawing on competing trust-building and trust-undermining mechanisms, we conducted a three-level meta-analysis of 211 effect sizes from 136 independent samples ( N = 46,071) to estimate the anthropomorphism–trust association and examine its boundary conditions. The average association was positive and robust to alternative dependence models ( r = 0.462, 95% CI [0.420, 0.502]), but varied substantially across settings (95% prediction interval [−0.131, 0.811]). It was considerably weaker for objectively specified design cues ( r = 0.222) than for perception-based measures ( r = 0.543), most of which captured adjacent trait attributions such as competence and warmth. Restricting outcomes to global trust, reliance, or willingness to depend yielded a similar estimate ( r = 0.475), although construct overlap on the outcome side cannot be ruled out. Cognitive and emotional anthropomorphism were more strongly associated with trust than physical anthropomorphism in aggregate, but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for operationalization; among design cues, physical and emotional anthropomorphism did not differ significantly, and no design-based cognitive effect sizes were available. The association was stronger in Eastern than in Western samples and in survey than in experimental studies, whereas no statistically significant moderation was detected for gender composition or the prespecified service-context categories. These findings caution against reading the pooled association as a uniform effect of anthropomorphic design and suggest that anthropomorphic cues should complement, rather than substitute for, demonstrable competence and reliability in AISA design and deployment.

title: From Dysfunction to Socially Embedded Adaptation: A Constructive Pathway for Jealousy Toward Creativity in the Workplace
abstract: ABSTRACT Building on growing interest in social emotions in the workplace, this study examines the social cognitive pathway through which workplace jealousy can contribute to employee creativity. Drawing on social functional theory of emotion, we propose that workplace jealousy increases the focal person's recognition of others' ideas, which subsequently promotes creative performance. Furthermore, we hypothesize that political skills, such as social astuteness and networking ability, strengthen the indirect effect of workplace jealousy on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. To test our hypotheses, we conducted three studies (Study 1: field data from 269 employees and their supervisors; Study 2: an online study based on the critical incident technique involving 276 working adults; and Study 3: a scenario‐based online experiment with 278 participants). Across the three studies, our analysis provides consistent patterns that workplace jealousy has a significant positive indirect effect on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. Our analysis also shows that political skills strengthen this indirect relationship, although the results varied across the two dimensions. These results provide valuable theoretical insights into the constructive social functions of workplace jealousy toward creative processes, particularly for employees who are politically skilled.

title: CEOs’ job-hopping experience and supply chain relationships: insights from the attention-based view
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the attention-based view, this study examines how CEOs’ job-hopping experience shapes supply chain relationships through managerial attention to supplier search and market expansion, and how CEOs’ R&D and production-line experience moderate these effects. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, this study hand-codes CEOs’ job-hopping experience from resumes and measures supplier and customer concentration based on disclosed top-five trading partner shares. We use fixed-effects models, mechanism and moderation tests and a series of robustness and endogeneity analyses. Findings Firms led by CEOs with more job-hopping experience exhibit higher supplier and customer concentration. Upstream, CEOs devote less attention to alternative supplier search, reflected in fewer tender projects and lower procurement-related recruitment, concentrating purchases among established suppliers. Downstream, CEOs give lower priority to market expansion, reflected in lower advertising expenditure and sales- and marketing-related recruitment, concentrating sales among established customers. CEOs’ R&D experience strengthens the supplier-side association, whereas their production-line experience strengthens the customer-side association. Both associations are stronger in non-state-owned firms and those facing greater performance pressure or higher capital intensity, while board production-line experience weakens the customer-side association. Originality/value This study extends supply chain relationship research beyond transactional and firm-level determinants by highlighting CEO career history as an explanation for firms’ different purchasing and sales patterns across trading partners. We extend the attention-based view by showing how experiences accumulated across organizational boundaries shape managerial attention, adding a historical dimension to managerial priorities. By linking managerial attention to observable supplier search and customer development activities, we clarify how CEO career history translates into supply chain relationship management and how prior functional experience shapes this process.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: A Journaling Intervention in Advertising and Public Relations Undergraduate Education: Reflecting on Ethics Increases Moral Reasoning
abstract: Abstract This study examines how reflective journaling encourages college students to explore their moral beliefs and moral reasoning during a time of moral development and exploration. Principled moral reasoning, indicative of autonomous thought, continues during college and emerging adulthood and moral stimuli embedded in coursework can positively impact moral reasoning by serving as educational interventions. Once principled reasoning is stored in long-term memory, it can be accessed later such as during one’s career rife with ethical challenges. While studies have found that college education and specific instructional methods that empower students from a learning-centered paradigm have positive impacts on moral reasoning, these studies often focus on conceptual ethics classes. This moral intervention examines moral reasoning when reflective journaling is used to supplement education on the business practices of advertising and public relations. Utilizing the Defining Issues Test (DIT), quasi-experimental results and moral development gains suggest the potential of reflective journaling as a facilitator of successful educational interventions.

title: Building contract management capacity in government organizations: contrasting priorities of public and vendor managers
abstract: Governments build contract management capacity to improve their contracting practice and performance. Because this may have implications for vendors, assessing governments’ contract management capacity not only from a government but also a vendor perspective can promote understanding of this important organizational capacity and help identify capacity gaps. However, such accounts are rare. Drawing on theories of formal and relational contracting, this article examines which contract management skills public managers need to improve, according to public managers and vendor managers. Survey data from Denmark (n = 364, including public contract managers and vendor managers) reveal significant disagreement: public managers prioritize formal contract governance skills, whereas vendors prioritize relational contract governance skills, with the exception that both parties prioritize contract design. The article shows how governments and vendors value government investments in formal and relational contract management capacity differently and illustrate the utility of analysing this capacity from both perspectives.

title: Why do ‘public service satisfaction surveys’ dissatisfy many people? A process model of the implementation paradox emerging when policy implementation meets co-production fatigue
abstract: Governments worldwide, in pursuing good governance, have increasingly routinized public service satisfaction surveys to advance accountability, responsiveness, and integrated performance. However, when these instruments are institutionalized as performance devices and embedded in hierarchical systems, they may paradoxically generate dissatisfaction among street-level bureaucrats and citizens alike in practice. Employing the Gioia methodology for systematic inductive analysis across five cases in China, this study identifies five aggregate dimensions explaining this contradiction: Ambiguity and Clarity in Policy Potential, Misalignment of Policy Capacity, Policy Compliance Decoupling, Co-production Fatigue, and Feedback Spillover Effect. The primary theoretical contribution is the ‘Dialectic of Policy Implementation Framework’, which integrates four interactive domains and synthesizes temporal and spatial dimensions to elucidate policy implementation processes. Conceptualizing the multidimensional, recursive dynamics of the paradoxical consequences in evaluation systems, the framework advances public administration theory while also proposing a governance pathway optimized through a feedback loop of learning, adaptation, and evaluation.

title: Aim High: The Impacts of Marijuana Legalization on Air Force Recruitment, Drug Use, and Disciplinary Actions
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the labor market impacts of marijuana legalization in a unique setting: a large employer, the Department of the Air Force (DAF), with strict drug use policy for its employees (military service members). US military recruiting has grown more difficult, partly due to declining eligibility among young adults, with drug use cited as a factor. The spread of recreational marijuana laws (RMLs) may affect recruitment, drug use, and discipline among service members. Using a difference‐in‐differences approach, we find that RMLs do not impede recruit quality, although there is some evidence of fewer Black people recruited in RML states. Among serving military members, positive marijuana tests increase for some groups (particularly White enlisted members), but overall illicit drug use shows little evidence of rising, as part of the increase reflects substitution across substances. We find no strong evidence of changes in overall discipline but do find increases in grade reductions (a form of discipline), possibly reflecting differential disciplinary treatment of marijuana relative to other substances or differential behavioral responses to its use.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Into the Echoverse: the role of social media use in eschewing science and scientists
abstract: Recent events highlight conflicts between populist attitudes and the broader scientific community. In the United States, the alt-right is a small but vocal group with populist leanings who use social media to express their beliefs. Previous work has not established whether non-mainstream social media usage increases science skepticism or if instead institutional skepticism drives usage of online platforms. To explore this question, we apply the recently advanced Identity Driven Information Ecosystem approach as a theoretical framework and employ a three-wave longitudinal design to examine the connection between mainstream and non-mainstream social media usage at time 1, science skepticism at time 2, and support for punitive actions against scientists at time 3. Results show that among alt-right identifying individuals, using non-mainstream social media, but not mainstream social media, predicted more science skepticism, which in turn predicted support for punitive actions toward scientists. We discuss these results in the context of ‘alternative’ attitudes toward science becoming more mainstream.

title: Using probabilistic bias analysis to adjust for selection bias in retrospective case-control studies
abstract: Retrospective case-control studies are susceptible to selection bias from differential participation. Knowledge of non-participation proportions by outcome and exposure status is difficult to estimate. This knowledge gap can be treated as a missing data problem through the implementation of imputation strategies to reduce potential bias. We used information about participants' exposure prevalence to inform non-participants' exposure prevalence and applied these estimates in probabilistic bias analysis to address the missing data problem. We conducted a simulation study using four probability distributions (uniform, triangular, trapezoidal, and beta) assigned to the exposure prevalence in non-participants for use in bias-adjustment, identifying the trapezoidal distribution as the most principled approach. We applied the trapezoidal distribution to a meta-analysis on passive smoking and breast cancer, with a recomputed summary OR=1.23 (95% CI, 1.00, 1.51) in retrospective case-control studies and a recomputed summary RR=1.07 (95% CI, 0.92, 1.24) in prospective cohort studies. Applying our bias adjustment to the retrospective ORs, we obtained a summary OR=1.16 (95% CI, 0.99, 1.35) from a meta-analysis of the retrospective studies; closer to the prospective studies' summary estimate. In the simulation and applied example, making defensible assumptions about the exposure prevalence of non-participants yielded more valid estimates compared with ignoring selection forces.

title: Response to: The French Paradox 2, a remake for Norway?
Safety-relevant effects on human-machine interface warning at intersections of limited sight distance: a controlled field driving study
Lane departure accident prevention in foggy conditions: A Prior-Guided Dynamic Feature Fusion Transformer framework for real-time lane detection
Development of the Sexual Experiences Survey-Victimization-Short Forms (SES-V-SF) and a Psychometric Evaluation of SES-V Standard and Short Forms
abstract: The Sexual Experiences Survey–Victimization (SES-V) was substantially revised in 2024 to broaden the range of sexual exploitation victimization assessed. Although the revised SES-V offers important advantages, its length may limit its usefulness in some research and applied contexts. The purpose of this study was to develop a short form of the SES-V and to evaluate the psychometric performance of both the short-form and the standard-form SES-V. Using a predefined process, we selected two to four items from each SES-V module. These items captured 89% to 96% of the victimization reported within each module in a national dataset. We then recruited 1,103 adults through CloudResearch, oversampling groups previously underrepresented in SES-V research. Participants were randomized to complete the standard-form SES-V or one of two short-form versions along with measures to assess convergent validity. A subsample of participants (n = 640) completed the same SES-V form again two weeks later to assess test–retest reliability. The short forms performed well and were comparable to the standard form in convergent validity and test–retest reliability. Endorsement rates on the short forms were similar to the standard form across three of four modules, and the short forms required less than half the administration time (i.e. a median of under five minutes). Findings were generally consistent across demographic subgroups. This study provides psychometric support for the short forms and additional psychometric evidence for the standard form. Future research should further examine whether the short forms capture the full range of victimization across diverse populations.

title: Off the Record? Effects of Interview Audio Recordings on Interviewer Behavior
abstract: Survey interviewers are usually instructed to follow standardized interviewing procedures when conducting interviews. The introduction of computer-assisted interviewing facilitated the collection of interview audio recordings to assess if interviewers indeed follow these standardized procedures. However, in most cases, audio recordings require respondent consent, and thus interviewers know whether an interview is recorded or not. In this paper, we analyze the extent to which interviewers change their behavior when interviews are recorded. Using automatically collected timestamp data and both cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis approaches to account for selection effects, we find that interviewers substantially change their behavior when recorded. Our results show that audio recordings lead to substantially fewer very short and very long questionnaire module durations and increase the average time spent on questionnaire modules, which is in line with a deterrence effect. Concerning substantive outcomes, we find larger interviewer effects for estimates derived from non-recorded than for recorded interviews.

title: Divorce and suicide mortality after prostate cancer diagnosis: a population-based competing-risks analysis
Physical activity and sedentary behavior in middle-aged and older cancer survivors: the ELSI-Brazil study
abstract: Abstract Background Movement-related behaviors, including physical activity and sedentary behavior, play a central role in the health of cancer survivors. However, evidence from middle-income countries with marked social inequalities, such as Brazil, remains limited. Aim To describe the levels of physical activity and sedentary behavior in middle-aged and older cancer survivors and to investigate sociodemographic, environmental, and social factors associated with physical activity and sedentary behavior using nationally representative data. Methods This cross-sectional study used baseline data from the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Aging (ELSI-Brazil), conducted between 2015 and 2016 with individuals aged ≥50 years. The sample included 9396 participants, of whom 504 reported a previous cancer diagnosis. Physical activity and sedentary behavior were assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ). Generalized linear models with Poisson distribution and log link function were used to estimate prevalence ratios (PR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI), accounting for the complex sampling design. Results Cancer survivors showed significantly lower levels of physical activity compared to participants without a history of cancer, with reductions in daily walking time (−21.2%), moderate physical activity (−3.8%), and vigorous physical activity (−27.4%), as well as fewer days of vigorous activity per week (−32.4%) ( p < 0.001). In contrast, sedentary behavior was higher among cancer survivors, with increased sitting time on weekdays (+15.1%) and weekends (+17.3%) ( p < 0.001). In analyses restricted to cancer survivors, male sex and increasing age were consistently associated with lower physical activity across domains. Environmental and social factors, including perceived neighborhood insecurity and fear of falling, were associated with reduced walking time but increased moderate and vigorous physical activity. Awareness of public physical activity programs was associated with higher walking time, whereas participation was associated with lower walking and moderate activity but higher vigorous activity. Conclusions Middle-aged and older cancer survivors in Brazil exhibit lower physical activity levels and higher sedentary behavior compared to individuals without cancer. Among cancer survivors, physical activity was associated with sociodemographic, environmental and social characteristics. Implications for Cancer Survivors These findings may inform strategies to promote physical activity and reduce sedentary time among middle-aged and older cancer survivors, considering sociodemographic, environmental, and social factors associated with physical activity.
authors: Elisa Cristina Alves de Moura Furtado
Samantha Karlla Lopes de Almeida Rizzi

title: Dyadic Effects of Personality on Sexual Behavior and Experiences in Older Adulthood
abstract: Abstract Sex is a central component of intimate relationships. However, much of our knowledge of the psychological factors shaping satisfying sexual lives is limited to younger adults. We examined individual (i.e., actor) and partner effects of the Big Five personality traits on sexual outcomes (i.e., sexual frequency, sexual and relational quality, and sexual dysfunction) among 953 older opposite-sex couples followed over five years as part of the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project ( M age = 70.60 years, SD = 7.92). Individual and partner conscientiousness were linked to more frequent sex and greater physical and emotional relationship quality, whereas neuroticism was linked to more sexual problems and lower satisfaction. Individual and partner agreeableness were associated with more satisfying sex and relationships. Individual extraversion was positively associated with higher sexual and relational satisfaction and fewer problems, but partner extraversion effects were largely non-significant. Both actor and partner openness were related to poorer evaluations of sex and relationships, but had limited associations with sexual problems. Some gender differences emerged, with more nuanced partner effects for women. Longitudinal analyses indicated that most associations wavered in strength over time. These findings highlight the role of both partners’ personality traits in encouraging sexual and relational well-being in older adulthood.

title: Patterns of Sexual Behavior Initiation Among United States Adolescents
abstract: Abstract Most research on adolescent sexual behavior initiation emphasizes penile–vaginal sex, overlooking other behaviors. We descriptively evaluated initiation patterns of five different sexual behaviors (penetration of the vagina or anus with a finger [fingering], oral sex, sex with a toy, penile–vaginal sex, and penile–anal sex) in a diverse cohort of United States adolescents. Data are from the QuaranTeen Health study, an online cohort study of adolescents aged 13–17 years. Participants reported the age they first engaged in each of the five behaviors or indicated no engagement on 5 follow-up surveys over 24 months. Our analytic sample included participants who reported no engagement in all five sexual behaviors at baseline ( N = 924). Among initiators ( N = 267, 29%), the most frequently reported first behavior(s) were fingering, oral, and penile–vaginal sex occurring during a single observation interval (22.8%), fingering and oral sex occurring during a single observation interval (18.7%), fingering alone (17.5%), and oral sex alone (10.4%). By 24 months, 33% of participants still under observation had engaged in fingering or oral sex and 25% had engaged in penile–vaginal sex. Sex with toys and penile–anal sex were less frequently reported and often paired with other behaviors. Most participants who initiated behavior(s) reported a first activity or combination at one observation and did not add additional behaviors under observation. Overall, while penile–vaginal sex was a frequently reported first sexual activity in our sample, fingering and oral sex were also common. Efforts to understand and support adolescent sexual development should consider a full range of sexual behaviors.

title: Comparative analysis of PV allocation rules in heterogeneous energy communities for collective self-consumption
A probabilistic region-based model for evaluating the integrated hosting capacity of photovoltaics and electric vehicles in power distribution networks
A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-enhanced framework for knowledge-guided campus-scale building retrofit design
abstract: Urban-scale building envelope optimization is constrained by the computational burden of iterative simulation. This study proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-enhanced framework that replaces the search phase of conventional optimization: literature-screened envelope solutions are retrieved from a curated corpus and then cross-checked through physics-based EnergyPlus simulation, rather than located through exhaustive parametric search. The corpus comprises 20,247 initially identified publications screened to a core of 338 studies, together with an experimentally characterized database of 502 envelope materials, of which 65 were used in the assemblies evaluated here. A three-stage progressive retrofit strategy — conventional high-performance insulation; vacuum insulation panels, aerogel and phase change materials (PCMs); and optimized PCM hybrid assemblies — was applied to seven reference buildings on Yonsei University's 86-building campus in Seoul, Korea. A systematic literature review established that whole-building field-measured savings are systematically 0.25–0.75× of simulation-only upper bounds, a correction embedded directly in the retrieval thresholds and screening criteria. The seven reference buildings produce a simulated mean building-level EUI reduction of 21.5%, ranging from 9.5% in high window-to-wall-ratio modern buildings to 39.6% in thermally deficient heritage structures, while campus-wide analysis of all 86 buildings yields 15.7% (124.4 to 104.9 kWh/m 2 ·year). EnergyPlus models were not calibrated against sub-metered operational data, so all reported reductions are simulation-based screening estimates. The framework offers a scalable, computationally efficient route to envelope retrofit planning for large institutional portfolios and urban decarbonization programs.

title: Real-time control of sustainable data centers: A two-layer model predictive control framework with workload flexibility and heat recovery
abstract: This paper proposes a two-layer model predictive control (MPC) framework for the real-time operation of data centers integrated with on-site photovoltaic generation, battery energy storage, waste heat recovery, and district heating. The upper layer employs scenario-based stochastic optimization to jointly optimize intraday market participation, workload scheduling, and energy management under uncertainty. The lower layer adopts an adaptive tube-based MPC strategy that compensates for short-term disturbances while tracking the dispatch references given by the upper layer. The framework further integrates multi-horizon forecasting to support real-time decision-making. Microservice-based simulation studies under representative clear-sky, overcast, and oversupply operating conditions demonstrate that the proposed framework accurately tracks dispatch plans despite fast photovoltaic and workload fluctuations. Compared with single-layer control strategies, the adaptive lower-layer controller substantially reduces real-time dispatch deviations and the associated imbalance costs. In addition, the proposed framework naturally adapts to seasonal operating conditions and responds to carbon-aware operating signals, offering a practical approach for economically efficient, sustainable, and grid-supportive operation of future data centers.

title: Land transfer experience and disparity between WTA and WTP: Evidence from China
Aligning mitigation incentives across technologies under the Paris Agreement's Article 6.4 mechanism
abstract: This article examines the incentive structure of the Paris Agreement’s Article 6.4 mechanism and document systematic misalignment of incentives across mitigation technologies and regions. Using project-level data, we estimate levelized emissions reduction costs across a wide range of mitigation activities and analyze their distributions. A machine-learning clustering algorithm classifies projects into seven global cost clusters, from which we derive relative weights per unit of emissions reduction.Our analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity in mitigation costs across technologies and locations. Yet observed deployment and credit issuance patterns are poorly aligned with these differences. High-cost projects account for a disproportionate share of credits relative to lower-cost activities. Across renewable categories, higher-cost projects issue fewer credits, revealing persistent incentive asymmetries. Estimated relative weights differ sharply across clusters, indicating that emissions reductions from high-cost technologies warrant proportionally greater support. Results are robust across alternative specifications.The findings underscore the importance of accounting for both cost and geographic heterogeneity in the design of climate finance under Article 6.4. By providing a transparent, data-driven, and flexible weighting tool, the framework offers policymakers a practical instrument to improve incentive alignment, maintain technological and regional diversity, and strengthen the integrity and effectiveness of global carbon markets.

title: Strategic autonomy and the energy transition: Rethinking Europe's geopolitical alignment
abstract: Europe's geopolitical alignment, its enduring deference to a US-led unipolar order, has come at the expense of its energy security and its ability to carry out the energy transition. This paper argues that greater strategic autonomy, the capacity and willingness to make economic and foreign policy decisions according to its own interests, would allow Europe to pursue both goals more effectively. It develops this argument in four parts. First, it characterises Europe's geopolitical alignment as a pattern of deference to US strategic priorities, sustained despite mounting costs to Europe's material interests, its standing and the multilateral order it claims to uphold. Second, it traces how this alignment shaped Europe's response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, contributing to a partly self-inflicted energy crisis followed by an abrupt and costly pivot to American liquefied natural gas that failed to resolve Europe's energy dependency. Third, it argues that on the energy transition Europe's interests are more closely aligned with Beijing's than with Washington's, although closer engagement deepens its dependence on Chinese clean technologies and critical raw materials. Europe should manage this trade-off by maintaining its de-risking approach and extending it to all its strategic dependencies, including those on the US. Finally, it argues that Europe will be unable to recalibrate its alignment and exercise strategic autonomy without building up its industrial and technological capacities and increasing its investment. Europe's choices will help determine the pace of the global energy transition, and with it, the world's chances of meeting its climate goals.

title: Thermal short-circuiting in enhanced geothermal systems: Mechanisms, field evidence and emerging mitigation technologies
Towards sustainable and circular power semiconductor switches: Methodologies, challenges, and potential solutions
Out of sight, out of mind: Informal used vehicle trade as a blind spot in EV transition governance
abstract: International trade in second-hand vehicles (SHVs) plays an important but poorly documented role in shaping vehicle fleets and the geography of waste streams. In North America, one of the largest SHV trade flows globally occurs from the United States to Mexico, much of which is not captured in official trade statistics due to its informal nature. This study quantifies these unobserved flows, demonstrating how informal SHV trade obscures regional fleet dynamics and material flows and, as electrification accelerates, redistributes economic value and environmental risk embedded in used EV batteries across borders. We develop a novel modeling framework that integrates original on-the-ground vehicle survey data with literature benchmarks and administrative records to estimate Mexico's informal SHV stock. These estimates are embedded in a US–Mexico stock turnover model to reconstruct historical flows and project future dynamics. Results indicate that formal and informal SHV exports represent approximately 12–15% of annual US vehicle retirements but account for nearly 49% of vehicles entering the Mexican fleet, representing up to 70% of new vehicle additions in some states, concentrated in lower-income communities. Downstream, nearly 30% of cumulative US EOL EV battery mass may leave the country embedded in exported vehicles by 2050, while informal SHV imports are estimated to add an otherwise unaccounted 24–45% to vehicle retirements in Mexico. Policy interventions targeting upstream markets, particularly salvage vehicle auctions, could improve transparency and support more effective governance of the global EV transition, with implications for other regions, including the EU and China, where similar dynamics are emerging.

title: Water–nutrient nexus planning for agriculture: A GIS-AHP assessment of reclaimed wastewater suitability and water and nutrient resource potential
Is Regional Conflict an Environmental Risk Multiplier for the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman? Toxicological and Engineering Considerations
Physiological and Transcriptomic Responses of Thalassiosira pseudonana to Coated ZnO Nanoparticles and Their Mixtures under Long-Term, Low-Dose Exposure: The Dominant Role of Dissolved Zinc
abstract: Abstract The escalating production of engineered nanomaterials has raised concerns about their environmental impact. However, conventional short-term, high-dose ecotoxicity studies inadequately reflect realistic exposure scenarios. This study evaluated the long-term, low-dose toxicity of bare zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) and four representative silane-modified ZnO-NPs in the marine diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana. Algal cells were exposed for 14 days to individual ZnO-NPs, their binary mixtures (0.001–1 mg/L) or equimolar Zn2+ (0.0008–0.8 mg/L). Physiological and transcriptomic responses showed dose- and time-dependent toxicity, with largely comparable effects across nanoparticle and Zn2+ treatments. Growth inhibition by all zinc forms peaked at 38.0% within 0.01–0.1 mg/L and exceeded 90.0% at 1 mg/L, accompanied by reduced photosynthetic performance, altered chlorophyll a content, and elevated lipid peroxidation. Transcriptomic profiles of all ZnO-NPs resembled those of Zn2+, particularly for photosynthesis- and oxidative stress-related pathways. These similar responses were likely attributable to the substantial dissolution of all nanoparticles and their mixtures (44.3–89.2%), resulting in comparable cellular zinc bioaccumulation and Zn2+-like toxicity. Together, these findings reflect that the tested ZnO-NPs, whether silane-modified or present in mixtures, may behave similarly to dissolved zinc under chronic, environmentally relevant concentrations, highlighting the importance of incorporating such scenarios into ecological risk assessments of soluble metal-based nanomaterials.

title: Quantifying the Contribution of Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Amines to Nitrogenous Disinfection Byproduct Formation in Wastewater by Chemical Derivatization
abstract: Abstract Disinfection of wastewater effluent during water reuse produces nitrogenous disinfection byproducts (N-DBPs), many of which are more toxic than regulated DBPs. Despite progress in understanding N-DBP formation pathways from model compounds, the precursors of N-DBPs in authentic wastewater effluent remain largely unknown. Using derivatization reactions adapted from the synthetic organic chemistry literature, this study quantified the contribution of 1°, 2°, and 3° amines to the formation of three commonly studied N-DBP classes in wastewater effluent: N-nitrosamines, nitroalkanes, and haloacetonitriles. Derivatization reactions were first adapted to mild reaction conditions, and then derivatization effectiveness at suppressing N-DBP formation was assessed with known N-DBP precursors. Effluent organic matter was similarly derivatized to selectively block 1°, 1° and 2°, or all amines, and N-DBP formation after disinfection was compared to nonderivatized controls. NDMA formation was primarily attributable to secondary amines; nitromethane formation was attributable to primary amines, with secondary amines sometimes contributing significantly; and haloacetonitrile precursors varied by source, chiefly primary amines in two wastewaters, but secondary amines in another. Irrespective of amine order (1°/2°/3°), amines collectively comprised the majority of the N-DBP precursor pool, suggesting that insights from N-DBP formation mechanism studies using amines as model precursors are likely applicable to real wastewater.

title: Toxicity-Weighted Assessment Reveals the Rising Dominance of Non-Exhaust PM2.5 from On-Road Transportation in China
abstract: Abstract Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) emitted from nonexhaust sources, here defined as brake and tire wear, is attracting attention as vehicle exhaust emissions decline due to advanced aftertreatment devices and rapid fleet electrification. However, the relative toxicity of nonexhaust PM2.5 compared with tailpipe emissions remains insufficiently quantified under a unified methodology. In this study, oxidative stress and cytotoxicity potencies of nonexhaust PM2.5 are 5- to 11-fold higher than those of exhaust PM2.5 via dynamometer tests, chemical analyses, and in vitro cellular assays. By integrating these toxic potencies with compiled emission inventories and modeling, toxicity-adjusted emissions of nonexhaust PM2.5 in 2023 expanded to nearly eight times those of exhaust PM2.5 in China. Exposure hotspots were disproportionately concentrated in economically developed regions with dense traffic. Projections forecast the nonexhaust proportion in toxicity-adjusted on-road emissions to surge from 54% in 2014 to an overwhelming 96% by 2050. While fleet electrification eliminates tailpipe exhaust and regenerative braking reduces brake wear, the nonexhaust PM2.5 proportion will keep rising in the absence of dedicated control measures. Our findings underscore an urgent imperative to incorporate nonexhaust sources into future air quality management, prioritizing eco-friendly material innovations and establishing standardized regulatory metrics to safeguard public health.

title: Mind the Leak: Challenges of Riverbank Filtration for Highly Mobile Chemical Pollutants
abstract: Abstract Riverbank filtration (RBF) serves as a natural protective barrier for groundwater and drinking water sources.
