title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
abstract: We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Trended Momentum
abstract: Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Distributional and efficiency impacts of supranational carbon budget allocations
A tripartite stochastic evolutionary game of government, large-scale clean energy bases, and flexibility resources under a novel cost compensation mechanism
Explosive diversification: Cartel adaptation to crackdowns in Mexico
Measuring beliefs causes beliefs to change
Gender identities and relative income in polish households: Implications for marriage, labor supply and marital stability
How do mutual fund management fee changes impact mutual fund flows?
abstract: Management fees are the central price in delegated asset management, but their effect on mutual fund flows is hard to identify because fee levels may reflect unobserved quality and changing demand. We study fee changes instead of fee levels. Our laboratory is the Israeli mutual fund industry, a retail-dominated, bank-distributed market in which every management fee change must be publicly announced. Combining hand-collected announcements of all fee changes with daily fund-level flows for 2012–2020, we find that responses concentrate in the days around the announcement: fee increases are followed by cumulative net outflows of about 10 percent of assets over one hundred trading days, and fee cuts by inflows of about 35 percent. Two quasi-natural experiments (a 2016 regulatory restriction that confined fee increases to the first days of the year and forced the repricing of zero-fee funds into the open, and the 2013 distribution fee reform, a counterpart of the UK Retail Distribution Review and the MiFID II inducement rules), an instrumental variable based on fee changes of other funds in the same family, and a battery of falsification tests suggest a causal relation between fee changes and flows. The evidence points to investor attention to salient repricing, rather than smooth price elasticity, as the operative mechanism. Finally, using unique inflow and outflow data and proprietary data on individual holdings of mutual funds, we find that fee increases affect net flows first and foremost through their negative impact on additional investments by existing investors.
journal_name: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money

title: Strategic regulatory engagement in multipolar value chains: contesting the EU Deforestation regulation in the Global South
abstract: Unilateral sustainability regulation from the Global North has become a central feature of contemporary trade governance. The European Union’s Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which conditions market access on proof of deforestation-free production, exemplifies this shift. Yet, systematic accounts of how producer countries in the Global South interpret, contest, and reshape such external regulatory demands remain limited. This article develops a relational framework of strategic regulatory engagement to analyze how producer states respond to unilateral sustainability rules through the interaction of three arenas: interstate relations, state–society relations, and regulatory network relations. Drawing on documentary analysis and semi-structured interviews, we examine Brazil and Indonesia, two pivotal suppliers of forest-risk commodities targeted by the EUDR. We show that responses are neither simple compliance nor outright resistance. In both cases, strong interstate bargaining leverage, cohesive domestic coalitions, and dense governance infrastructures generate layered engagement combining diplomatic contestation, bilateral embeddedness, and selective institutional adaptation, configurations that differ in substance and outcome depending on governance density and bilateral leverage. The article contributes a relational framework for analyzing producer country agency in sustainability governance and demonstrates that regulatory authority in multipolar value chains is negotiated and contested rather than unilaterally imposed.

title: Does Early‐Life Participation in SNAP Improve Adult Mental Health? Evidence From a Regression Discontinuity Design
Effects of State Paid Sick Leave Mandates on Children's Mental Healthcare Utilization
abstract: Many major mental health conditions first emerge in childhood, when early intervention can produce both immediate and long-term benefits. The United States has no federal paid sick leave (PSL) policy, but 18 states have implemented PSL mandates that give employees job-protected, paid time off to address their own health needs or those of a dependent. We study the effects of these mandates on children's mental healthcare use, combining data from the 2016 to 2024 National Survey of Children's Health with difference-in-differences and event-study methods. We find suggestive evidence that children's mental healthcare use increases following PSL mandate implementation, though the difference-in-differences estimate is imprecise. Event-study analyses suggest a short-run increase in use that dissipates over time. The increases are particularly pronounced among children ages 5 to 11. These findings suggest that PSL mandates may help parents obtain mental healthcare for their children and make other investments in their children.

title: How Long Is Clinical Research Valuable for?
abstract: Value of information methods provide an approach to quantify the expected value of resolving uncertainty in a decision. It provides a quantitative basis to assess the expected value of clinical research projects and to understand the health impact of granting accelerated access to innovative medicines with uncertain benefits. Information generated from a clinical trial can be used to inform decisions for patients in the present and in the future. This means that when estimating the expected value of research we must make a judgment about how long the research will be valuable for, which we define as T. Despite its large impact on results, there is scant research, theoretical or empirical, to inform this judgment. We provide a general approach to estimating T reflecting treatment entry and price changes. In our case study we find T ranges between 13 years and infinity. The specific value depends on the type of parameter (whether it is treatment specific or not), the rate of innovation in the indication of interest and the magnitude of price reduction associated with generic entry. For the first time, this provides a method and starting point for analysts to justify the choice of T in applied contexts.

title: Market and non-market exchange and market-supporting institutions
abstract: How does introducing market exchange into reciprocity-based communities affect welfare, and what role do market-supporting institutions play? We study a repeated-matching model in which non-market transfers are sustained by ostracism, and market trade requires a fixed participation cost and is governed by formal institutions. This article argues that access to the market and non-market exchange are welfare-enhancing relative to the situation in which only one type of exchange is available, despite crowding out. Community welfare rises with the quality of market-supporting institutions whenever the income and discount factors are sufficiently large. The results shed light on the development process.
journal_name: The Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization

title: Which climate risk matters most for macroeconomic outcomes: Physical, transitional, or climate policy uncertainty?
How does innovation success affect corporate payout policies?
Harvesting the Concrete: Urban Expansion and Agricultural Land Productivity
Bimodal spread majorization: bridging inequality, bipolarization, and polarization in income tax policy
Examining Negative Asymmetry in Employee Social Networks: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: Two decades have passed since Labianca and Brass introduced social ledger theory with its focal assumption of negative asymmetry—that the social liabilities created by negative workplace ties are more strongly related to employee outcomes than the social assets created by positive workplace ties. Yet widespread conclusions that negative workplace ties are more consequential have exceeded a surprisingly limited base of empirical tests. This article uses meta-analysis to examine this largely untested assumption by offering 22 original meta-analytic estimates drawn from 248 effect sizes across 71 samples representing 13,369 employees. At the bivariate level, both positive and negative ties have significant relationships with employee outcomes. However, evidence consistent with negative asymmetry emerged only for out-degree ties predicting task performance. In contrast, evidence more consistent with positive asymmetry emerged for in-degree ties predicting task performance and for both in-degree and out-degree ties predicting organizational attachment, although the relationships between in-degree ties and attachment are relatively small. Considerable variation exists around the effect sizes constituting these patterns, suggesting that future research is needed to consider moderating factors that may shift the relative importance of negative versus positive ties. We discuss the implications for refining social ledger theory and for helping practitioners managing social assets and liabilities in organizations.

title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05050 .

title: Bound to grow? How firms can thrive without growth in capitalist market environments
abstract: In capitalist market environments, firms face strong growth pressures resulting from improved access to external financing, economies of scale and scope, network effects and market power as well as enhanced career opportunities for employees. However, ecological and social challenges increasingly constrain unbounded firm growth, creating a tension between economic pressure and sustainability limits to growth. Yet, to date, both the extant literature on firm growth and the literature on post-growth and degrowth provide limited insights into how firms can thrive without growth in capitalist market environments that pressure them to grow. In this paper, we therefore investigate this question by drawing on an inductive, multiple-case study of firms pursuing different business models in the German information technology industry. We show that, to thrive without growth, firms can adopt four major strategies: patient capital, service, niche and mission orientation. Importantly, our analysis also reveals four underlying mechanisms—namely strengthening firms’ financial autonomy, using labour-intensive activities, differentiating products in the market and thriving on employee self-motivation—through which these non-growth strategies help firms compensate for the benefits typically associated with growth. By developing a theoretical framework that explicates the detailed mechanisms of how firms can thrive without growth within the dominant capitalist system, we make important contributions to the literatures on post- and degrowth and alternative forms of organising, as well as to the management literature on firm growth and non-growing firms.

title: Ethical bricolage as ethics-as-practice in criminal organizations. The case of a drug dealing gang
abstract: In this paper, we explore how ethics emerge in contexts of criminal organizations. To do so, we carried out a non-participant observation of a suburban drug dealing gang. Resorting to Lévi-Strauss’ concept of “bricolage”, we posit that actors assemble and recombine available moral resources in practice. We found that the criminals we studied resorted to various practices of ethical bricolage, which we define as a genuine mode of social organizing resulting from individuals collectively mobilizing and recombining available moral resources to promote situated ethical practices aimed at designing and maintaining a delineated moral territory. We contribute to the ethics-as-practice literature in discussing how, in organizations lacking social acceptability, ethical bricolage constitutes a mode of organizing, structuring the boundaries of a “man-made” acceptable life.

title: Bringing culture back in: An institutional analysis of budgeting and power in an emerging economy context
abstract: This paper examines how notions of culture and power intertwine in the shaping of budget-related practices within a large public sector organisation in Bangladesh. Drawing on institutional theory, we advance a view of power as a dynamic and relational, yet institutionally embedded, phenomenon. We examine how the power originating in cultural norms, which are firmly institutionalised in Bangladeshi society, is reinforced and weakened by micro-level dynamics in the organisation under investigation. We also show how the interplay between cultural norms and micro-level dynamics is conditioned by the influence of international donor agencies and other actors, who are relatively peripheral to the organisation, and how this gives rise to variations in the operation of power and budget-related practices. Examining how this interplay manifests itself under conditions of institutional stability, we provide a nuanced perspective on how power is implicated in budgeting and a systematic, contingent conception of how variations in budget-related practices emerge. We discuss the implications for institutional research on budgeting and institutional theory in general.

title: Green Marketing Research: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Bibliometric Analyses With an Integrated Future Research Agenda
abstract: This umbrella review synthesizes 168 systematic reviews and bibliometric analyses of green marketing published between 2005 and 2025. It maps the intellectual foundations of the field, identifies dominant themes, evaluates the quality of existing evidence, and proposes a structured future research agenda. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive Scopus search (January 2026) yielded 168 review publications. Bibliometric synthesis quantified publication trends, citation patterns, and collaboration networks using VOSviewer 1.6.19; systematic content analysis identified thematic clusters, theoretical frameworks, and research gaps. Two independent coders achieved acceptable interrater reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.84). Quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews ( n = 62) and adapted criteria for bibliometric studies ( n = 106). Green marketing reviews have grown exponentially since 2015, with 49.4% published in 2025 alone. Five dominant themes emerged: consumer behavior, green product attributes, firm strategy and performance, sustainability and policy, and education and awareness. The Theory of Planned Behavior and Theory of Reasoned Action dominate theoretical frameworks, with structural equation modeling as the predominant analytical technique. Only 29% of systematic reviews and 23% of bibliometric analyses met high‐quality standards, and only 13% of systematic reviews reported conducting formal publication‐bias assessment. Critical gaps include theoretical homogeneity, methodological concentration, limited circular economy integration, insufficient digitalization and AI research, weak cross‐cultural comparisons, and the absence of reviews with corresponding authors affiliated with institutions in low‐income countries. Practitioners should prioritize authentic sustainability communication, leverage digital platforms strategically, and integrate circular economy principles. Policymakers should support credible eco‐labeling, address greenwashing through deterrence and facilitation, and cultivate policy–marketing synergies. This is the first umbrella review to synthesize the green marketing review literature, offering a structured research agenda organized around four strategic priorities: circular economy integration, digitalization and AI, cross‐cultural comparisons, and policy‐driven strategies. It provides the first systematic analysis of publication‐bias assessment practices within the review corpus and identifies the low‐income‐country authorship gap as a critical limitation.

title: Beyond Acknowledgement: A Strategic Assessment of Decarbonization Measures in Global Steel Firms
abstract: Decarbonization of the iron and steel industry is critical to achieving global carbon reduction goals. Existing studies have proposed multiple decarbonization strategies, yet there is limited knowledge on firm adoption of these strategies. In this study, we develop a Decarbonization of Iron and Steel Strategy Classification (DISC) framework for assessing firm‐level strategies for emission reduction based on the transition literature. Using a sample of global steel producers, we evaluate firms' decarbonization strategies under three categories: awareness, planning, and action. We use content analysis of companies' disclosures to score strategies and Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to estimate relative efficiency within the observed sample. The decarbonization strategy index scores are then compared with the companies' relative efficiency. The results of our study suggest that large steel firms have implemented incremental strategies, but few firms have moved beyond acknowledgement to adopt transformative strategies. The study provides implications for policymakers and steel firms to transition to low‐carbon steel while ensuring long‐term competitiveness.

title: Beyond the Boardroom: Nonlinear and Conditional Institutional Quality Effects in the Women on Boards—Sustainability Performance Nexus
abstract: This study examines nonlinear and conditional relationship among women on boards (WOB), institutional quality, and sustainability performance in global banking. Using a cross‐country panel of 641 banks from 2011 to 2023, we apply fixed‐effects. Quadratic, conditional marginal effects, and instrumental‐variable models. WOB improves sustainability performance, but its marginal benefit diminishes beyond a model‐implied turning point, extending critical mass theory from a minimum threshold toward an optimal‐range perspective. Institutional quality exhibits a U‐shaped association, consistent with a transition from legitimacy‐oriented responses toward more substantive sustainability integration as regulatory credibility and legal enforcement strengthen. The conventional WOB and institutional quality interaction is insignificant; however, marginal effects and regime‐based estimates show stronger WOB effects in higher‐quality institutional environments. These findings suggest that effective sustainability governance contingents not simply on increasing female board representation, but on maintaining meaningful gender diversity within supportive institutional surroundings. For policymakers, strengthening regulatory credibility and legal enforcement may enhance the sustainability benefits associated with gender‐diverse boards.

title: The power of a number: why and when precise carbon labels make restaurants look more committed
Beyond speak-up: A multidirectional framework for employee voice issue processing
abstract: Employee voice research explains why employees speak up or remain silent and how managers respond when they do. This article develops an organizational-level framework of employee voice issue processing to explain how HRM systems handle voiced concerns and why those concerns lead to different consequences. The framework shifts attention from voice occurrence to the movement, handling, and fate of employee voice issues within HRM voice architecture. It identifies five component pathways—voice up as upward expression, voice down as authoritative response, voice around as lateral voice testing, voice in as inward translation, and voice out as outward escalation—and argues that their consequences depend on how pathways are configured and integrated. The article introduces voice integration capacity as the organization's ability to link, interpret, coordinate, and respond to employee voice issues across these pathways. By connecting voice research with HRM system design, the article explains why opportunities to speak can lead to learning and correction in some settings but pseudo-voice, fragmentation, or external scrutiny in others. It treats employee voice not only as an individual act of expression but also as an HRM issue-processing challenge.

title: From farm to fine dining: trust is the backbone of luxury food supply chains
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how trust is built, maintained and challenged along the understudied luxury food supply chain, which is characterised by more personal transactions and higher quality stakes than conventional agri-food sectors. Design/methodology/approach Using the French Riviera caviar market as the focal empirical setting, the authors conducted 21 semi-structured narrative interviews with chefs (n = 11), distributors (n = 5), and producers (n = 5) selected through purposive and snowball sampling. The authors analysed the interviews using structuring qualitative content analysis, combining main categories derived from a theory-informed interview guide with inductively developed subcategories. Findings Trust in luxury food supply chains emerges as a relational and symbolic construct, shaped by cultural capital, artisanal values and sustained interpersonal engagement. Participants relied primarily on repeated interaction, personal credibility and proactive transparency, rather than on the transactional, system-based trust models typical of conventional food sectors. Trust expectations vary systematically across supply chain roles, while luxury value is symbolically co-created through shared narratives of rarity, craftsmanship, authenticity and heritage. Trust is also particularly fragile: operational failures can simultaneously undermine relational confidence, personal credibility and the symbolic legitimacy of the product category. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study offers the first systematic investigation of trust dynamics across the producer–distributor–chef triad in the luxury supply chain. It contributes to the supply chain management literature by empirically specifying how three interdependent trust layers, namely, operational, relational and symbolic, are activated differently in luxury than in conventional contexts, and offers managerial guidance for preserving quality, authenticity and reliability in premium food networks.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: Socioemotional wealth and the social behavior of family firms
Architecting future entrepreneurial orientation–performance research: how accumulated evidence informs modeling
abstract: Entrepreneurial orientation (EO) is positively associated with firm performance, and a large literature examines additional constructs around this relationship. What the accumulated findings reveal about how EO relates to performance is less clear. Synthesizing 211 samples from 208 publications that use unidimensional EO measures, we combine meta-analysis with coding of how environmental, organizational, and upper echelon constructs are measured and positioned in primary models. The evidence base is broad, but much of it is thin. About two thirds of the pairs of frequently studied constructs have never been measured in the same sample, leaving their interrelationships untested. In terms of construct use, although EO theory stresses managerial decisions, executives are commonly included in models using demographics such as age and tenure, and mainly as controls. In terms of model positioning, market orientation and organizational learning correlate similarly with EO and performance, yet studies most often position the former alongside EO and the latter between EO and performance, which raises theoretical questions regarding model placement. Surprisingly, the task-environment conditions long associated with EO are also seldom modeled as reasons firms differ in EO. Taken together, our synthesis suggests that before building on a recurring correlation, EO–performance researchers should check how the underlying constructs were measured and positioned in the studies that produced it. Applying this approach to EO as a theory of new value creation, we specify the measures and relationships needed to test how learning and resource flexibility enable firms to create customer value through successive product-market entries.

title: When Corporate Biodiversity Measurement Rises While the State of Biodiversity Declines
abstract: The measurement of corporate biodiversity performance is expanding, with firms disclosing risks, adopting biodiversity targets, and developing reporting tools. However, biodiversity continues to decline. We argue that this tension reflects ecological scope decoupling: corporate measurement is structured around organizational units, sites, and reporting cycles, whereas the state of biodiversity changes across ecological places, under cumulative pressures, and over longer recovery horizons. This mismatch is not simply a problem of measurement quality but a unit-of-analysis issue for management research. Firm-year evidence can support claims regarding firm performance, but it cannot by itself demonstrate biodiversity improvement. We develop three forms of scope fit—spatial, temporal, and collective—to clarify when corporate metrics can support ecological claims. We argue that claims of biodiversity progress require ecological baselines, defined boundaries, and evidence that reductions in pressure on ecosystems translate into improvements in their ecosystem condition over ecological time.

title: Artificial intelligence in international marketing: a systematic review and integrative framework
abstract: Purpose This article examines the current state of research on the integration of artificial intelligence-driven techniques in international marketing. It seeks to clarify how the field has evolved, which themes dominate existing scholarship and which conceptual and empirical gaps limit cumulative knowledge development. Design/methodology/approach The article applies a systematic literature review and integrates descriptive mapping, thematic synthesis, a structured risk of bias assessment and an unsupervised topic modeling procedure implemented in Python. This combined approach enables a multi-layered evaluation of how artificial intelligence is being conceptualized, applied and assessed within international marketing research. Findings Our review shows that artificial intelligence adoption in international marketing is advancing, although its development remains uneven across technical, organizational and contextual dimensions. Existing research concentrates heavily on algorithmic capability, while persistent data heterogeneity limits cross-country applicability. Decision integration varies from experimental uses to fully embedded applications. Contextual alignment, organizational readiness and governance mechanisms appear underdeveloped, despite their relevance for generative and agentic artificial intelligence. Topic modeling reveals five dispersed thematic clusters, consistent with the fragmented structure of the field. Originality/value Our article delivers a consolidated assessment of how artificial intelligence-driven techniques are shaping international marketing and introduces a seven-construct framework that links technical, contextual, organizational and strategic dimensions. This integrated perspective clarifies the field's current trajectory, exposes areas requiring theoretical consolidation and offers guidance for scholars and practitioners seeking to navigate artificial intelligence adoption in multinational environments.

title: Gamification for international marketing across cross-cultural consumer journeys: the role of regulatory fit and self-construal
abstract: Purpose Gamification offers international marketers significant opportunities to design engaging and experience-driven consumer journeys akin to those offered by games. However, its success as an international marketing strategy largely depends upon four critical but underexplored factors – industrial/cross-cultural contexts of implementation, longitudinal testing of gamification effects, systematic phase-based deployment of game mechanics and consumers' goal perspectives. This study aims to address these research gaps. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a mixed-methods approach comprising two studies: Study 1 involves a systematic literature review of 238 articles to examine trends in industrial/cross-cultural contexts and methodological approaches in gamification-based marketing research. Building on these insights, Study 2 adopts theory elaboration by abductive reasoning, drawing on regulatory fit theory and self-construal concept to underpin a longitudinal multi-case study research involving leading international retailers in the USA, United Kingdom, India and Malaysia. Findings Study 1 reveals a lack of longitudinal analyses on gamification in hedonic retailing contexts within international markets. In Study 2, through multi-case analyses of leading global retailers, we demonstrate that the goal-motivation fit between consumers' regulatory promotion-prevention goals and their self-construal-oriented gamified user types is dynamic and changes across different stages of consumer buying journey, necessitating phase-based implementation of game mechanics. Practical implications This study offers actionable insights for international marketers utilizing gamification to market hedonic product offerings. It can assist marketers and game designers to tailor their international marketing strategies according to goal-motivation fit by matching consumers' promotion (prevention) goals with their self-construal oriented gamified user types, which can vary in pre, during purchase and post-purchase stages of cross-cultural gamified consumer journeys. Originality/value This study offers two key contributions. First, it interprets the industrial/cross-cultural contexts and methodological approaches in existing gamification-based marketing research, clarifying the field's trajectory. Second, it extends these insights through a longitudinal multi-case study, developing a framework and propositions that synthesize conceptual associations between goal-motivation fit in cross-cultural gamified consumer journeys. This study can be considered the first to examine such phenomena in gamification and international marketing research.

title: The Endurance of Government Connections after the Anti-corruption Campaign in China
Greening from the Top: Post-IPO Government-Guided Fund Entry and Corporate ESG in China
A Direct Method to Imply Activity-Level Required Returns: Evidence From Firms With Bifurcated Business Models
abstract: Implied cost of capital (ICC) models have been limited to the firm level because activity-level market values are unobservable. We develop a novel method for firms with two main activities that resolves this challenge by using share price pairs to solve simultaneous accounting-based valuation equations for each activity. We empirically validate the method using a specific dataset of international banks with bifurcated business models, demonstrating that the resulting ICCs have an appropriate dependency structure, are correctly rank-ordered, and are economically rational. While our empirical analysis focuses on this distinct set of firms, use cases illustrate the method’s broad applicability to other multi-activity contexts, such as asset management, divestitures and commercial lending. Our method has the potential to improve accuracy in capital budgeting, managerial performance evaluation, and business valuations.

title: Fiscal policy and innovation discourse: exploration language in SBIR and STTR award abstracts around the TCJA R&D amortization rule
CEO family circumstances and firm growth: contrasting effects of marriage and parenthood
abstract: Chief executive officers (CEOs) play a pivotal role in shaping organizational outcomes through their strategic decisions.While upper-echelons research has shown that executives' demographic characteristics and early-life experiences influence these decisions, comparatively little is known about how ongoing family experiences affect firm strategy.Drawing primarily on the upper-echelons framework, we propose that marriage and parenthood shape CEOs' attention, cognitive and emotional resources, and strategic priorities, thereby influencing firm growth.Using panel data on CEOs of S&P 100 firms, we find that firms led by married CEOs exhibit significantly higher growth, whereas firms led by CEOs with children exhibit significantly lower growth.We further show that the positive relationship between CEO marriage and firm growth is weaker when firms face greater financial risk.Our findings extend upper-echelons research by demonstrating that CEOs' ongoing family experiences constitute an important source of executive heterogeneity with implications for firm growth.

title: Digital Affordances for Customer Engagement: The role of Co-Creation Climate, Social Media Manager’s Characteristics, and Creative Brand Content
Taxing Pollution, Conserving Energy: Evidence from China’s Environmental Protection Tax Reform
abstract: Can environmental taxation deliver durable energy savings rather than merely temporary emission reductions? We study this question using China’s environmental protection tax (EPT) reform as a quasi-natural experiment. Our analysis links the National Tax Survey Dataset (NTSD) to firm registration records from the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (SAIC) and satellite-based pollution measures from NASA. Difference-in-differences estimates show that the reform lowers firms’ fossil energy use and air pollution and raises fossil energy efficiency. The evidence points to higher expected penalties generated by higher tax rates and more credible tax enforcement as the principal mechanisms. Firms respond by upgrading their production equipment while also expanding their end-of-pipe treatment. The effects are concentrated among small and privately owned firms and among firms in resource-based cities, places with weak prereform environmental regulation, and regions with greater tax collection effort. Although the reform shifts firms’ energy mix toward cleaner inputs, we detect no statistically significant change in overall carbon emissions. Our research highlights the importance of cost-effective regulation and provides evidence on the effectiveness of environmental taxation.

title: Challenges, opportunities, and policies for dual use innovation
“Unseen and unheard”: Recognition and Its Role in Shaping Administrative Burden
abstract: Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with 33 individuals (16 young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and 17 social and outreach workers). We argue that recognition, and its denial, are part of the mechanism through which psychological costs are produced, and that whether an encounter carries a message about a person's standing sorts the category into three analytically distinct types. Affective costs are emotional responses to procedural load and involve no recognition; primary symbolic costs are emotional responses to status positioning; and secondary symbolic costs arise when procedural load itself carries a message about standing. The latter two, in which recognition is at stake, are traced through Honneth's three spheres of rights, solidarity, and care, each producing its own configuration of costs. The types differ in their causes and remedies, with affective costs calling for efficiency reforms and symbolic costs for recognition-oriented ones. Social workers emerge as allies who counter misrecognition, and drawing on these findings we propose bureaucratic recognition, the building of voice, certainty, and validation into procedural design, as a remedy for status-related costs. Finally, misrecognition both constitutes symbolic costs and compounds others, positioning status, alongside distribution, as a critical axis of administrative burden.

title: Captured governance and diagnostic infrastructures: evidence from municipalities dissolved for mafia infiltration
abstract: Public financial management systems increase visibility, yet captured governance can maintain compliance while redirecting budgeting, accounting, and procurement routines. We conceptualize these systems as diagnostic infrastructures that can conditionally expose such distortions. Anchored in Italian municipal dissolutions for mafia-type infiltration, theory-informed analysis of 50 dissolution reports identifies four core configurations and three cross-cutting dimensions. Across 7,802 municipalities (2016–2024), combined accounting and procurement indicators outperform single-source benchmarks and retain discrimination among Southern and fiscally distressed municipalities. We specify when such systems retain diagnostic capacity under staged compliance, informing data infrastructure design and existing scrutiny procedures, not municipal screening.

title: Who Should Do Clinical Ethics Work? Defining Appropriate Roles for the “Ethics-Interested”
abstract: The publication of the third edition of the Core Competencies for Healthcare Ethics Consultation reflects the growing professionalization of clinical ethics consultation and marks an important advancement of the field. However, clinical ethics work extends beyond consultation to include education, policy development, liaison work, moral distress support, and institutional leadership. In many settings, these activities are undertaken not only by trained ethicists but also by “ethics-interested” individuals without formal training. This raises questions about appropriate roles and how institutions can ensure adequate expertise across ethics-related activities. This paper argues that ethics programs should align clinical ethics activities with required competencies, using ethical risk as a guiding concept. Clinical ethics consultation carries the highest ethical risk and requires specialized training and oversight, while lower-risk activities may involve ethics-interested contributors with support. We propose a framework that uses example activities to differentiate proficiency levels and clarify when specialized ethics expertise is warranted.

title: The Patient-Regarding Reasons Principle: A New Intervention Principle for Surrogate Decisions
abstract: The bioethics literature focuses on ideal surrogate decision-making for adults, with less attention paid to the threshold at which that decision-making becomes unacceptable. That is, when the medical team should intervene in surrogate decision-making. The limited work on these adult intervention principles has focused on either the surrogate’s knowledge or reasoning, largely suggesting that there will be many cases where a surrogate should be overruled by the medical team. Others have written in favor of wide latitude for surrogate decision-makers on both legal and ethical grounds. In this paper, we first argue that competent surrogates of adult patients should rarely be overruled. We then propose a clear set of intervention principles for surrogate decision-making: the necessary but insufficient traditional harm principle and an adjoined principle that we term the patient-regarding reasons principle. Lastly, we call for more research into these aspects of surrogate decision-making.

title: Privacy and Cybersecurity Guardrails for AI in Healthcare: Consensus-Based Guidance
Assessing the Robustness of Growth Mixture Models with Distal Outcomes Across Different Time Coding Approaches
abstract: Growth mixture models (GMMs) with distal outcomes identify groups following different trajectories and examine group differences in subsequent outcomes. Although time coding is often treated as a matter of parameter interpretation, it may also affect model estimation, class recovery, and distal-outcome inference. We examined this sensitivity through two empirical illustrations and simulation studies varying time coding, data conditions, and population trajectory patterns. Alternative codings sometimes selected different numbers of classes. Even with the number of classes fixed, fitted models differed in convergence and attained log-likelihood solutions, accompanied by differences in class recovery and distal-outcome estimates. These discrepancies were most pronounced when the population contained more classes. Moreover, the relative performance of each coding varied across trajectory patterns, with no coding performing consistently best. Researchers should therefore select a primary coding based on substantive interpretation and examine sensitivity across alternative codings, particularly when many classes are considered, or estimation is unstable.

title: Sampling Schemes and the Recovery of Within-Person Dynamics in Intensive Longitudinal Data: A Two-Timescale Continuous-Time Approach
abstract: Intensive longitudinal designs space observations unequally. Fixed schedules leave overnight gaps, signal-contingent protocols randomize prompt times, and measurement-burst designs separate dense bursts by weeks, yet standard discrete-time vector autoregressive analyses treat all intervals as equal. This article derives what such analyses estimate under design-generated interval mixtures. The probability limit implies design-specific attenuation of cross-lagged effects, and occasion-level measurement error combined with contemporaneous correlation produces spurious cross-lagged effects even under stationarity. Unmodeled slow change inflates false-positive rates further, to .31 in single series and .94 under two-stage pooling with burst sampling. A two-timescale continuous-time state-space model, separating fast latent dynamics, a correlated slow trend, and occasion noise, maintained nominal Type I error and drift coverage across equidistant, diurnal, random, and burst schemes in 32,000 simulated series. Reanalysis of a 239-day experience sampling study shows model choice reversing substantive conclusions. All code and results are openly available.

title: The influence of pre-diagnostic allostatic load on mortality after incident colorectal cancer
abstract: Allostatic load is an emerging stress biomarker capturing immune, cardiovascular, and metabolic dysregulations. We evaluated associations between allostatic load and mortality after colorectal cancer (CRC) diagnosis, comparing allostatic load to metabolic syndrome to determine if including additional domains beyond metabolism strengthens associations with mortality. Southern Community Cohort Study participants who developed incident CRC after enrollment (2002-2009) were included; most self-identified as Black (69%) and report <$15,000 annual household income (55%). Enrollment samples were analyzed for immune, metabolic, and cardiovascular biomarkers. A standard metabolic syndrome definition was used (3/5 traits); most (N=1007) had available information to calculate metabolic syndrome. To calculate allostatic load, biomarkers above clinical risk cutoffs were summed; counts above median indicated high allostatic load (4/10 traits). A subsample of 303 had additional information to calculate allostatic load. Mortality was ascertained through 2020 via National Death Index linkage. Multivariate-adjusted Cox models estimated hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals (HR[95%CI]). High allostatic load was associated with higher risk of all-cause (1.81[1.25-2.62]) and CRC-specific mortality (HR:1.81[1.07-3.07]). The latter attenuated after controlling for health behaviors (HR:1.57[0.91-2.70]). Metabolic syndrome was not associated with mortality (all-cause: 1.06[0.88-1.28]; CRC-specific: 1.08[0.83-1.40]). Allostatic load may be a clinically actionable biomarker to readily identify cancer patients with comorbidity.

Men’s Engagement in and Enjoyment of Sex Toy Use with Female Partners: Exploring Differences in Masculinity, Sexism, Male Genital Image, and Sexual Esteem
abstract: = 15.29) who had ever had at least one female sexual partner completed an online survey. Multivariate and discriminant function analyses revealed that sex toy users demonstrated less conformity to masculine norms, fewer precarious manhood beliefs, lower sexism, and greater genital self-image and sexual esteem than non-users. Among users, enjoyers exhibited lower masculine conformity, precarious manhood beliefs, and sexism, alongside greater sexual esteem, compared to non-enjoyers; genital self-image did not differ significantly between groups. Hierarchical logistic regressions further indicated that sexual esteem - but not genital self-image - predicted use of phallic-style toys. Findings suggest that masculine ideology and traditional sexual scripts may pose meaningful barriers to partnered sex toy engagement among men who have sex with women, with possible implications for sexual health education.

title: From bedroom to bond: examining patterns of cross-activation between sexual and pair-bonding motivational systems
Socioeconomic disparities in access to care among patients with a rare cancer: a systematic review
Strong will to survive: patients’ experiences of self-management of multiple cancer-related symptoms in cancer survivors—a systematic review of qualitative studies
abstract: This review aimed to synthesise qualitative evidence on cancer survivors’ experiences of living with multiple cancer-related symptoms, the self-management strategies they use in daily life, and the individual, interpersonal, and contextual factors influencing these efforts. This qualitative systematic review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute meta-aggregation methodology and was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Cochrane) were searched for English-language qualitative studies published from January 2005 to September 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and appraised quality using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Findings were synthesised using meta-aggregation. Fifteen studies published between 2013 and 2025 across nine countries were included. Three themes were identified: (1) what remains after therapy—the burden and impact of multiple symptoms; (2) strong will to survive—self-management strategies for adapting to the new normal; and (3) travelling a challenging path—barriers to self-management. Survivors’ experiences highlighted the importance of symptom literacy, symptom prioritisation, and accessible systems that support timely symptom reporting and ongoing guidance in community contexts. Survivors may benefit from clear guidance on treatment-related symptoms, support in prioritising competing symptom demands, and a named contact who can facilitate timely access to appropriate clinical and community services. Self-management of multiple, fluctuating cancer-related symptoms is shaped by individual resources and broader social and healthcare contexts. The findings suggest a need for treatment-specific education, patient navigation, and coordinated interprofessional follow-up during and after treatment. Digital resources may complement this support when linked to professional assessment and care responsive to symptom severity and complexity. Implications for Cancer Survivors may benefit from clear guidance on treatment-related symptoms, support in prioritising competing symptom demands, and a named contact who can facilitate timely access to appropriate clinical and community services. title: Marital Adjustment and Sexual Quality of Life in Consanguineous Marriages: A Sociocultural Perspective from Married Women in Southeastern Turkey
abstract: This study examined differences in marital adjustment and sexual quality of life between women in consanguineous marriages (between first cousins) and women in non-consanguineous marriages. Comparing these unions is important because consanguineous marriages are embedded in distinctive kinship, family, and partner-selection structures that may influence women’s relational and intimate well-being. However, empirical evidence regarding these outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. The sample consisted of 277 married women recruited from Family Health Centers in southeastern Turkey, including 133 in consanguineous and 144 in non-consanguineous marriages. Data were collected using a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Marital Adjustment Test, and the Sexual Quality of Life-Female scale. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and moderation analyses were conducted, while controlling for age and number of children. No significant differences were found between consanguineous and non-consanguineous marriages in marital adjustment ( p = .26, d = 0.13) or sexual quality of life ( p = .98, d = 0.00), suggesting limited practical differences between groups. Higher income and self-selected marriage were positively associated with both outcomes ( p ≤ .01), whereas longer marriage duration and a greater number of children showed negative associations ( p < .001). Marriage type moderated the association between consanguinity and marital adjustment, but not sexual quality of life. The findings should be interpreted within a sociocultural context in which shared family structures and extended kin involvement may shape relational experiences beyond kinship status. Socioeconomic and relational factors were more consistently associated with marital and sexual well-being. Future longitudinal and cross-cultural studies are needed to clarify these relationships.

title: The Politics of Retirement Age Reform Under Xi Jinping
abstract: Raising the legal age for receiving pension benefits is a highly sensitive decision for any government, even for an authoritarian regime. This article addresses how the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) under Xi Jinping 习近平 proceeded cautiously for over a decade to raise China’s retirement ages, which had been established in the 1950s and, by the 2020s, ranked as the youngest retirement ages in the world. The CCP undertook strategies to make reforms possible and more palatable to the public, before a legal measure was finally enacted in 2024. Given the CCP’s ability to deter large-scale public protests, it did not expect anything like the fierce public opposition to recent retirement age increases seen in France (2023) and in Russia (2018). Why was retirement age reform in China deferred for so long? This article reviews policy documents and public messaging to understand Xi Jinping’s guarded approach to enacting retirement age increases, and the constraints that the CCP faced as it considered the timing and substance of the measure.

title: Representative bureaucracy and the career trajectories of female STEM students: a retrospective interview study
abstract: Demographic representation in public organizations shapes how the interests of diverse citizens are seen and heard. Previous studies show how a more representative bureaucracy encourages underrepresented groups to feel a greater affinity with the public organizations that serve them, for example, by increasing their trust in and engagement with those organizations. STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) education is an important context to examine, as most teachers are male, leaving female students with fewer role models of their own gender for this increasingly important field of knowledge. This lack of female role models, moreover, is especially critical at young ages, when students often decide whether to pursue STEM professions. Through in-depth interviews with STEM students from five Israeli universities, we explore how the active representation of female high school teachers encouraged their female students to develop a sense of self-efficacy and to succeed in STEM. Furthermore, we also demonstrate how these teachers’ past representation actions shaped their female students’ professional futures. Our research highlights the importance of early gender representation in shaping educational and professional opportunities.

title: From one cycle to full life: Ultra-early battery degradation assessment for operational assessment and rapid screening
Technology trajectories and critical raw materials in sodium-ion battery innovation: An LLM-assisted patent analysis
A risk-averse bidding and scheduling strategy for process industry VPPs in demand response markets based on thermodynamically-enhanced RTN
Operating-point-dependent power-flow linearisation for joint siting, sizing, and dispatch of long-duration energy storage in distribution grids
Stochastic assessment of eight emergency electricity supply configurations for urban shelters: Performance limits and the role of vehicle-to-shelter
abstract: Emergency electricity planning for urban shelters requires comparing heterogeneous supply resources under uncertain, time-varying demand. This study assesses eight specified emergency electricity-supply configurations, including two Vehicle-to-Shelter (V2S) arrangements, for a 1000-person shelter during a 72-h grid outage. A common framework combines paired Monte Carlo simulation, hourly supply–demand matching, continuous resource-state evolution, and access-conditioned variance decomposition, while retaining configuration-specific constraints on power, usable energy, infrastructure continuity, resource access, and deployment timing. Across nine demand and disaster-severity scenarios, adequacy declined as shelter services expanded and cold-season demand increased, while access-dependent resources were additionally constrained by infrastructure continuity, allocation, and arrival. High coverage of the specified diesel-generator configuration depended strongly on its usable energy in the most demanding scenario, where a 20% stock reduction lowered mean energy coverage ratio (ECR) from 0.819 to 0.659. Similar aggregate coverage also concealed different temporal risks. Under hot conditions with moderate disaster severity, a mobile power-supply truck and a local-plus-external V2S arrangement had nearly identical mean ECRs (0.368 and 0.367) under baseline access assumptions but different temporal shortfall patterns. The truck provided no support before allocation and arrival, whereas locally parked EVs supplied limited early power. Access-state differences accounted for most observed ECR variance for the access-dependent configurations in the two examined scenarios, distinguishing conditional resource capability from unconditional shelter adequacy. These findings support mechanism-based screening by power, endurance, immediate availability, and credible access arrangements, while suggesting a potential role for V2S as a conditional supplement rather than a universal substitute for dedicated backup supply.

title: A continental dilemma: Is centralized or decentralized renewable hydrogen cheaper?
Lost in convergence, found in risk? A dynamic evaluation of Mediterranean land degradation in light of Von Thunen’s theory
What do sustainable agriculture practices really mean? A global review of definitions, thematic discourses, and practices
Energy transition and energy poverty: Uneven policy outcomes across indicators and climate contexts
abstract: As countries accelerate energy transitions, ensuring that decarbonization advances social as well as environmental goals has become a defining global challenge of Energy Justice. Using Chile, a country spanning six climate zones and marked by high socioeconomic inequality, as an empirical laboratory, we assess how twelve national energy transition policies (ETPs) reshape the geography of energy poverty (EP). Across 346 municipalities and eight complementary indices, our modeling shows that full policy implementation would reduce EP by 24.8%, yet benefits remain spatially and socially uneven. Cold, humid southern regions achieve the strongest declines (Cfc −44.4%; Cfb −34.5%), while arid areas improve by only ≈21%. Higher-income households gain disproportionately (−29.1%) compared to low-income ones (−23.5%). Under the full-implementation scenario, the National Energy Policy is associated with the largest modeled reduction (−38.2%), whereas the Atmospheric Decontamination Plan produces a 2.4% increase in measured national EP that reflects a statistical reclassification effect, driven by shifts in the sample-dependent reference values used to classify non-intervened municipalities. Taken together, these results reveal that climate and inequality are jointly associated with the distributional outcomes of energy transitions, highlighting the urgent need for spatial-sensitive and redistributive policy design to achieve truly just global decarbonization.

title: Cybersecurity in DC microgrids: Threat taxonomy, detection techniques, resilient control, and open challenges

Proton-Coupled Oxidation Mechanisms in the Ferrate System: Unraveling the pH Dependence of Fe(VI), Fe(V), and Fe(IV) for Contaminant Abatement
abstract: Like conventional water treatment oxidants, ferrate exhibits highly pH-dependent reaction kinetics, classically attributed to its acid–base speciation. However, while this dissociation equilibrium accurately describes the kinetics of ferrate decay, it cannot account for the anomalous pH-dependent kinetics observed during contaminant oxidation. By combining acid–base model with the pyrophosphate sequestering method, we reveal that highly reactive Fe(V) and Fe(IV) intermediates drive this deviation. To trace these species, aniline, theophylline, and sulfamethoxazole were employed as model contaminants for oxidation processes dominated by Fe(VI), Fe(V), and Fe(IV), respectively. By quantifying their specific contributions, we found that decreasing pH enhances the reactivity of the intermediates and amplifies their oxidation contributions by 13–63%. Consequently, the systems dominated by Fe(V) or Fe(IV) exhibit apparent rate constants surging far beyond the predictive capacity of the Fe(VI) speciation. Solvent kinetic isotope effects and proton inventory analyses elucidated distinct proton-assisted pathways: Fe(VI) undergoes a rapid protonation pre-equilibrium before rate-limiting electron transfer, Fe(V) reacts via a concerted proton–electron transfer pathway, and Fe(IV) proceeds through an inner-sphere electron transfer pathway associated with coordinated water release. Exploiting these insights, we demonstrate a proton-activation strategy where rapid proton exchange significantly enhances both reaction kinetics and oxidant utilization efficiency in ferrate-based water treatment.

title: Mechanochemistry-Induced Hydrated Salt Activation for Green Recovery of Palladium and Platinum via O 2 -Mediated Oxidation
abstract: Palladium (Pd) and platinum (Pt) are essential precious metals in modern catalytic applications, while their sustainable recovery remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report a room-temperature, AlCl3·6H2O-assisted mechanochemical strategy for efficient recovery of Pd and Pt from industrial spent catalysts and automotive three-way catalysts without the addition of external oxidants. Mechanistic investigations reveal that mechanochemical treatment promotes catalyst fragmentation and the activation of hydrated salt, creating an ion-rich, liquid-like interfacial environment that facilitates O2-mediated oxidation of metallic Pd and Pt and stabilizes the oxidized metal species through chloride coordination. High-purity Pd and Pt products were successfully recovered through water extraction and N2H4·H2O reduction, while the recyclable AlCl3·6H2O medium enabled a closed-loop process with reduced reagent consumption. A preliminary lab-scale cost assessment indicated treatment costs comparable to those of conventional aqua regia treatment, highlighting the potential of hydrated salt-assisted mechanochemistry as a mild, recyclable, and economically promising approach for sustainable Pd and Pt recovery.

title: Characterizing the Composition and Reactivity of Dissolved Organic Matter: New Insights from Complementary Methods
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays important roles in numerous processes in both natural and engineered systems, ranging from carbon cycling to metal complexation to disinfection byproduct formation. Characterizing the composition of this complex mixture, which is comprised of thousands of molecules that vary in time and space, is critical for understanding its role and reactivity. This review highlights major developments and notable limitations in the most commonly used DOM analytical techniques and, importantly, summarizes state-of-the-art knowledge on DOM composition and reactivity gained from each approach. The selected techniques include simple but fundamental approaches for DOM analysis (i.e., chromatography and optical spectroscopy), more complex molecular techniques (i.e., nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and ultrahigh- and high-resolution mass spectrometry), and methods designed to investigate reactivity (i.e., electrochemical analyses). The review also assesses prospects and needs for future developments within each technique, which range from further advancing analytical capabilities to making instrumentation more accessible to improved data analysis. Finally, because each technique is only able to partially describe DOM composition and reactivity, the review provides a forward-looking outlook on combined analytical approaches and opportunities for data synthesis, leveraging the potential of complementary analytical techniques to establish a more integrated understanding of DOM composition and reactivity.

title: Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) in Textiles: Attributing the Fluorine Inventory via Polymer-Specific Analysis
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are widely used in functional textiles for water- and stain resistance, yet their polymer compositions, quantities, and potential environmental release remain poorly resolved by conventional analyses. Here, we analyzed 22 commercial textiles using an integrated approach combining total fluorine (TF) by combustion ion chromatography, targeted PFAS analysis, the total oxidizable precursor (TOP) assay, and pyrolysis–gas chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (Py-GC-HRMS); the latter enabled polymer-specific identification and semiquantitative estimation of fluoropolymer and side-chain fluorinated polymer (SCFP) contributions. Fifteen textiles contained low-to-moderate TF concentrations (0.03–2.57 mg F g–1) and were predominantly associated with SCFPs containing 6:2 and/or 8:2 fluorotelomer moieties, whereas three high-fluorine textiles (143–158 mg F g–1) contained polytetrafluoroethylene together with SCFP-based treatments. Targeted PFAS accounted for ≤0.021% of TF, while TOP-derived PFAS also represented only a small additional fraction, indicating that conventional extractable and oxidizable PFAS measurements captured little of the total fluorine inventory. Simulated laundering, UV exposure, and wet abrasion caused limited TF loss in most textiles but substantial losses in some SCFP-treated materials, indicating treatment-dependent potential for PFAS-associated fluorine release during use and aging. This approach improves polymer-specific characterization of PFAS in textiles and helps assess their potential environmental emissions.

title: Mobilization of Geogenic Contaminants Induced by Seawater Intrusion in Coastal Aquifers Globally
abstract: Seawater intrusion deteriorates freshwater quality in coastal aquifers, threatening billions of people worldwide. While its impacts on freshwater scarcity and salinization are well documented, the associated mobilization of geogenic contaminants remains unclear. This study critically reviews the current knowledge on the global distribution, underlying biogeochemical mechanisms, specific triggering scenarios, management implications, and predictive modeling advances of seawater-intrusion-induced contaminant mobilization. A synthesis of 343 studies across 55 countries confirms the widespread occurrence of geogenic contamination in coastal aquifers. Among these, studies from 19 countries (n = 50) document seawater-intrusion-related contaminant mobilization. At the microscale, contaminant release is driven by altered water–rock interactions, disrupted microbial metabolism, and colloidal transport. These biogeochemical shifts are further modulated by specific seawater intrusion scenarios such as groundwater overexploitation, sea-level rise, and tidal oscillation. Of particular concern, conventional strategies for mitigating seawater intrusion may inadvertently alter aquifer hydrochemistry and intensify contaminant release, underscoring the urgent need for optimized synergistic solutions. While some reactive transport models attempt to capture these dynamics, their field-scale accuracy remains constrained by hydrogeological heterogeneities and computational bottlenecks. Addressing these challenges requires multidisciplinary collaboration and high-resolution monitoring of databases. These advances are critical to informing science-driven governance frameworks that ensure the long-term sustainability of coastal groundwater resources.

title: Physiological Adaptation of Comammox Nitrospira to Acidic pH Suppresses N2O Production
abstract: Nitrous oxide (N2O), a potent greenhouse gas, is a major byproduct of microbial nitrification, yet how environmental pH governs N2O production by complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox) remains poorly understood. We conducted controlled culture experiments with comammox Nitrospira inopinata at pH 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5. Under mild acidification (pH 6.5), nitrification activity was largely maintained, but cellular growth declined sharply, and both N2O yield and extracellular hydroxylamine (NH2OH) accumulation fell substantially relative to neutral conditions. Strikingly, this reduced growth was accompanied by pronounced transcriptional upregulation of core nitrification, stress response, and pH homeostasis genes, whereas carbon fixation genes remained largely unchanged. This decoupling of growth from gene expression indicates that acid-stressed cells reallocate energy away from biosynthesis toward cellular maintenance and proton extrusion, tightening intracellular handling of NH2OH and limiting its extracellular release. Isotopomer analysis (site preference ∼28–36‰) confirmed that NH2OH-driven chemistry remained the dominant N2O source across all pH conditions, and complementary abiotic assays indicated that chemical N2O formation was likely influenced by the diminished NH2OH pool. These results establish that comammox suppresses, rather than enhances, N2O production under mild acidification, opposite to the response reported for canonical ammonia-oxidizing microbes. This distinctive trait carries important implications for predicting nitrification-derived N2O fluxes and refining greenhouse-gas budgets in acidifying ecosystems.

title: Decoding and Harnessing Microbial Resilience for Anaerobic Digestion: Mechanisms, Strategies, and Sustainability under Environmental Stress
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) is central to the circular bioeconomy, yet its application is limited by the vulnerability of microbial consortia to diverse stressors from endogenous metabolic inhibitors to exogenous contaminants. This Review synthesizes current evidence on microbial resilience mechanisms in AD, distinguishing resistance from perturbation to functional recovery through a sensing-activation-adaptation cascade. The thermodynamic basis of stability is examined through discoveries in direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) and metabolic bifurcation, revealing how syntrophic networks overcome thermodynamic barriers under stress. Multiscale resilience mechanisms are considered from molecular sensors and signal transduction pathways to community-level reorganization associated with functional redundancy and niche differentiation. Bridging microbial ecology with process engineering, resilience-enhancing strategies are evaluated, including quorum sensing manipulation, conductive material amendment, and bioaugmentation with immobilized consortia, strengthening syntrophic networks under internal and external perturbations. A shift from reactive monitoring to proactive management is discussed, using interpretable deep learning models and genome-informed digital twins to predict failures. Critical knowledge gaps include single-cell phenotypic heterogeneity and the synthetic consortium design. Resilient AD systems require a framework integrating techno-economic viability with life cycle assessment, ensuring that they are biologically robust, environmentally sustainable, and economically competitive under variable operating conditions.

title: Underappreciated Role of Free Troposphere–Boundary Layer Exchange in Ozone Pollution over the North China Plain
abstract: Ozone pollution control is mainly based on the ozone chemistry sensitivity to precursor emissions. However, despite stringent reductions in precursor emissions, severe summer ozone pollution persistently engulfs the North China Plain (NCP), urgently calling for effective ozone controls. Here, we show that there is strong interfacial ozone exchange between free troposphere (FT) and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), which renders FT ozone a potential source of surface ozone, but has not been well accounted for in previous ozone controls. We quantify FT-ABL interfacial ozone exchange using an online diagnostic scheme implemented in a coupled meteorology-chemistry model and reveal a significant yet spatially heterogeneous correlation between observed surface ozone and interfacial exchange over the NCP. In high-correlation area, strong downward transport from FT to ABL exceeds chemical production, contributing 52% of afternoon ozone sources under polluted conditions. In low-correlation area, ozone pollution is dominated by chemical production. Derived from these spatially differentiated pollution causes, we propose an expanded ozone pollution formation regime to divide the NCP into exchange-dominated, chemistry-dominated, and mixed conditions. This new regime can better explain observed and modeled spatial differences of ozone trends in response to precursor reductions in 2019–2025. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating FT-ABL interfacial exchange into ozone pollution control frameworks beyond conventional chemistry-based regime.

Navigating spatial dynamics in multifunctional landscapes: understanding tradeoffs in conservation, agricultural production, and climate resilience in the Canadian Prairies
abstract: Meeting global commitments to biodiversity conservation, climate and sustainable development requires integrating policy frameworks with local priorities in order to reconcile competing objectives in multifunctional landscapes. A key challenge lies in navigating spatial dynamics of ecosystem services (ES), where anthropogenic activities, particularly in agricultural landscapes, create trade-offs. We evaluated ES provisioning in the prairies of Canada to analyze trade-offs and synergies among three management objectives – conservation, agricultural production, and climate resilience – using a spatial multi-criteria and multi-objective framework with multivariate clustering. Using landscape data from the Soil Landscapes of Canada, we identified five distinct landscape clusters, each reflecting a unique combination of the three objectives. These clusters highlight regions dominated by trade-offs, such as high agricultural production with conservation and climate resilience challenges, particularly in landscapes that have been heavily modified for agricultural production. The clusters also identify areas where synergies between objectives create opportunities for land management strategies that enhance landscape resilience, often in regions with protected areas and conservation initiatives. Our analysis revealed that over a quarter (27%) of the prairie region is characterized by at least one significant trade-off, where high agricultural production occurs at the expense of conservation and climate resilience objectives. In contrast, approximately 9% of the region falls within a cluster characterized by high agricultural production and climate resilience scores and intermediate conservation scores, indicating comparatively stronger alignment among the three objectives. Our analysis highlights priority areas where conservation and agricultural production objectives can be strategically aligned, providing a basis for spatial prioritization that can inform targeted interventions aimed at maximizing multiple benefits subject to local conditions and implementation feasibility.

Lung-deposited surface area as a personal exposure metric for short-term heart rate variability responses to sub-micrometric particles in healthy adults
abstract: Sub-micrometric particles, including the ultrafine fraction, have been associated with short-term changes in cardiovascular autonomic markers, but the exposure metric most informative about short-term changes in heart rate variability (HRV) remains uncertain. This study compared particle number concentration (N) and instrument-estimated lung-deposited surface area concentration (LDSA) as personal exposure metrics for minute-level HRV responses in healthy adults monitored under real-life conditions. Thirty-five healthy volunteers were equipped with portable particle monitors, a wearable cardiac monitoring device, and activity monitors. Minute-resolved particle exposure, posture, heart rate (HR), and time-domain HRV indices were aligned and analyzed. Subject-adjusted distributed lag models were fitted over exact-time lags of 0–10 min for the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN), and the percentage of successive normal-to-normal intervals differing by more than 50 ms (pNN50). Models included subject fixed effects and posture adjustment, and cumulative effects were expressed as percent changes after doubling the exposure. Additional exposure-level analyses were conducted using quartiles of the 0–10 min lagged average exposure, and spline models were used to characterize the shape of the LDSA-HRV association. Over the full 0–10 min window, an LDSA doubling was associated with lower RMSSD and SDNN, with decreases of 5.7% (95% CI: −10.0, −1.2) and 5.4% (95% CI: −8.6, −2.0), respectively. A negative association was also observed for pNN50. Corresponding estimates for N were weaker and not statistically significant. Quartile-based and spline analyses supported lower HRV at higher LDSA exposure levels, particularly for RMSSD and SDNN, whereas pNN50 showed directionally consistent but less robust associations. HR showed weaker and less consistent associations than HRV indices. These findings suggest that instrument-estimated LDSA may provide a more consistent personal exposure metric than particle number concentration for detecting short-term HRV responses to sub-micrometric particles.
