Design and operation of district heating and cooling grids integrating a borehole heat exchanger field and multiple regeneration sources
abstract: District heating and cooling grids with central borehole heat exchanger fields present an efficient option for space heating and cooling. Especially in an urban context, space limitations as well as the availability of additional low-temperature heat sources, make multi-source regeneration of the borehole heat exchanger field attractive. This study aims to provide new insights for the design and operation of such grids with multiple regeneration sources. With this aim, the optimisation potential of a small district heating and cooling grid with waste heat from two combined heat and power plants and passive space cooling as regeneration sources is analysed. Modelling approaches for the sub-systems are developed and validated with measured data where appropriate. Passive cooling is modelled using an heat exchanger effectiveness approach, while the waste heat production is modelled as a linear correlation to the thermal power of the combined heat and power plants. Additionally, the short- and long-term behaviour of the borehole heat exchanger field is taken into account. Various designs and operational strategies are simulated numerically and compared to each other. The evaluations reveal, that simultaneous operation of the heat pumps and regeneration sources as well as hydraulic decoupling of the heat pumps and the different heat sources, achieve the most promising results regarding system efficiency (+3% and +5% over 20 years in the considered case) and net thermal energy extraction from the borehole heat exchanger field (−7% and −27%). While this study evaluates a concrete setup in central Germany, the findings are transferable to other sites and future projects.

Ecosystem Service–Driven Assessment of Ecological Network Stability Under Urban Expansion: A Case Study in Chengdu
abstract: The spatial fragmentation and increasing isolation risk of Ecological Networks (ENs) pose a serious threat to the stable provision of regional ecosystem services. Taking the rapidly urbanizing Chengdu metropolitan area as a case study, this study proposes a dynamic assessment framework coupling Ecosystem Service Flow (ESF) with Ecological Networks. First, an Ecological Service Index (ESI) was constructed by integrating the InVEST model with multi‐source remote sensing data, and the spatial flow paths of ESF were quantified by identifying Service Providing Areas (SPAs) and Service Benefiting Areas (SBAs). Ecological Networks for 2000, 2010, and 2020 were then delineated by combining Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis (MSPA), the Minimum Cumulative Resistance (MCR) model, and circuit theory. On this basis, the Urban Ecological Isolation Index (UESI) and Ecological Source Isolation Index (ESII) were constructed to evaluate the dual isolation effects of urban expansion on both EN structure and service flow delivery, followed by complex network attack simulations to assess topological stability. A multi‐scenario simulation of EN configuration evolution under three development pathways was further conducted for the year 2035. The results showed that: (1) the built‐up area in the study region increased by 86.2% over two decades, primarily through encroachment on cropland; the ESI remained generally stable, with vegetation recovery in mountainous areas driving significant increases in habitat quality and net primary productivity, whereas regulatory services exhibited a slight decline; (2) the total area of ecological sources increased to 3589.3 km 2 , yet intensified fragmentation led to a greater number of corridors with shorter average lengths, exposing the EN to the risk of structural disintegration; the UESI rose by approximately 269% over the 20‐year period, with the most pronounced isolation risk concentrated in the central plain and the outer edges of the Longquan Mountains; (3) the EN's aggregate structural metrics exhibited a positive trajectory, yet isolation risk continued to escalate and network stability remained heavily dependent on a limited number of key nodes—under intentional attack, the removal of merely the top 5% of high‐centrality nodes precipitated a sharp decline in robustness. The multi‐scenario simulation results further demonstrated that corridor connectivity under the Environmental Protection (EP) scenario was substantially superior to that under the Free Development (FD) scenario, with the central plain zone facing the highest degradation risk. By integrating the spatially explicit identification of ESF with EN topological stability assessment within a unified framework, this study bridges the feedback mechanisms among ecosystem service supply, service flow delivery, and network structural stability. It reveals the contradictory interplay between ecological restoration processes and the oppressive effects of urban expansion in complex terrain, thereby providing both a theoretical basis and methodological support for accurately identifying ecologically vulnerable nodes and formulating differentiated conservation strategies in rapidly urbanizing regions.

title: Toward an Integrative Model of Layoff Effects: A Strategic Human Capital Resources Framework
abstract: Despite decades of research yielding rich theoretical insights and empirical evidence, the layoff literature remains fragmented. It lacks an overarching framework integrating findings across levels of analysis (e.g., organizational, group, and individual), stakeholder groups (e.g., layoff decision‐makers, executioners, survivors, and displaced employees), and outcomes from proximal processes to distal performance consequences. This fragmentation impedes understanding of how layoff effects unfold and why they vary across individuals and organizations. We review and synthesize layoff research and integrate insights from recent advancements in the strategic human capital resources literature. Our framework explains how layoffs first trigger an outflow of human capital and then reshape the quality, complementarity, and deployment of remaining human capital resources, while shaping the social‐psychological reactions of stakeholder groups. We further identify layoff characteristics as contingencies that determine whether layoffs produce negative or positive shifts in strategic human capital resources states, shape stakeholder reactions, and condition whether individual outcomes aggregate to the organizational level. In doing so, we delineate the organizational‐, individual‐, and cross‐level pathways through which layoffs influence individual performance and, ultimately, organizational outcomes. We offer implications for firms seeking to plan layoffs strategically, manage social and psychological processes, and leverage human capital resources before, during, and after layoffs.

title: Implementation of Circular Economy Strategies Across the Plasterboard Value Chain: Prioritisation and Improvements
abstract: As environmental pressures and stakeholder expectations increase, construction organisations are exploring circular economy (CE) strategies to build resilient and sustainable business models. In the plasterboard sector, inadequate segregation, contamination and logistical challenges often divert gypsum waste into downcycling, limiting its CE potential. Few studies have examined the extent to which CE strategies are implemented across the plasterboard value chain to improve closed‐loop plasterboard waste recovery. This study investigates the implementation, prioritisation and improvement of CE strategies throughout the value chain using a participatory workshop design, including a pre‐workshop questionnaire and an in‐person workshop with 23 senior managers grouped into five value‐chain clusters. Findings show that ‘segregating demolition plasterboards’ is nearly fully implemented, whereas strategies such as ‘digital product passports’ and ‘data sharing on maintenance’ remain rarely adopted. Thirteen CE strategies were prioritised, and stakeholders suggested improving awareness, partnerships, recycled gypsum quality, installer guidance and measures to reduce gypsum waste losses.

title: Forecasting defense-industrial diversification: relatedness, weak signals, and the political limits of predictability in the global arms trade
Opulent and Environmentally Responsible?: Brand‐ and Consumer‐Related Factors Shaping Consumer Responses to Sustainable Product Innovation Signals by Luxury Brands
abstract: Academic Summary Luxury and environmental sustainability often appear fundamentally at odds: luxury derives its value from exclusivity, symbolic aspiration, and resource‐intensive craftsmanship, while sustainability demands restraint, reduced environmental impact, and responsible production. Yet luxury brands such as LVMH and Gucci are increasingly introducing sustainable product innovations, seeking to align with evolving consumer expectations and regulatory demands. For consumers, this creates a genuine tension: does a sustainably produced luxury personal good elevate its desirability, or quietly erode what makes it special in the first place? Despite the urgency of this question for both consumers and brands navigating the luxury‐sustainability interface, research on consumer responses to sustainable product innovation in luxury personal goods remains limited. Drawing on signaling and cue‐diagnosticity theory, this study examines how, why, and when consumers respond to luxury brands'' environmentally sustainable product innovation. Across a pilot and three main experimental studies, it explores consumer responses to sustainability signals, particularly considering skepticism surrounding the sustainability–luxury interface. Results show that consumers have more positive attitudes, higher purchase intentions, and greater willingness to recommend luxury brands engaged in sustainable versus conventional product innovation. This effect is partially mediated by consumers' feelings of specialness, a proximal, state‐like psychological mechanism. Moreover, transparency as a brand‐level signal and socially responsible consumer behavior as a consumer‐level characteristic strengthen the effectiveness of sustainable product innovation signals. These findings advance understanding of how environmentally sustainable product innovation creates value in luxury markets by shaping consumers' interpretations, experiences, and responses. Managerial Summary Luxury brands face growing pressure to integrate sustainability into their products while preserving the exclusivity, prestige, and craftsmanship that define their appeal. This research offers practical guidance on how they can navigate this challenge through sustainable product innovation. Across four studies involving more than 2450 consumers, introducing eco‐innovative products improves consumer attitudes, increases purchase intentions, and strengthens willingness to recommend. A key insight is that consumers respond positively because sustainable product innovations make them feel special, unique, and privileged, reinforcing rather than undermining luxury's core appeal. Managers can cultivate these perceptions by embedding environmental sustainability into limited editions, exclusive collaborations, and bespoke offerings. Experiential storytelling highlighting material origins, craftsmanship processes, and environmental significance transforms these initiatives into emotionally engaging experiences rather than purely ethical propositions. Transparency is equally critical. When brands are transparent about their sustainability practices, the positive impact on consumer attitudes and purchase intentions is significantly stronger. These results offer clear guidance for luxury brand managers and innovation teams: integrate sustainable product innovation into new product development not as a trade‐off but as a source of differentiation, prioritize transparency to meet consumer demand for accountability, and tailor communications to eco‐conscious consumer segments, positioning the brand as a forward‐thinking leader in luxury innovation.

Distinct Phyllosphere Microbiome-Linked Stress Pathways of Conventional and Biodegradable Plastics in Vallisneria natans
abstract: Microplastics negatively affect submerged macrophytes, but the phyllosphere pathways associated with these responses remain poorly understood, particularly for biodegradable microplastics. Using a mesocosm experiment that distinguished fresh and withered leaf microhabitats, the stress pathways induced by conventional polystyrene (PS) and biodegradable polylactide acid (PLA) in Vallisneria natans were directly compared. Withered leaves emerged as the key microhabitat where the two polymers differed most clearly. PS was mainly associated with host-centered physiological adjustment and a modular microbial network, whereas PLA was associated with broader phyllosphere reorganization, particularly in fresh-leaf bacteria and withered-leaf algal assemblages. Direct measurements in the highest-exposure treatments detected PLA hydrolysis products (lactic acid and oligomers) and PS oxidation products, providing chemical evidence consistent with these contrasting pathways. Mantel tests and structural equation modeling further supported a divergence between a predominantly host-centered PS pathway and a broader PLA pathway involving nutrient balance and phyllosphere organization. These results indicate that conventional and biodegradable microplastics may differ not only in their direct interactions with submerged macrophytes but also in the extent to which microbiome-linked indirect pathways are involved.

Microbial Resurgence in Degraded Soils: Early‐Stage Recovery of Biological Quality by Legume Cover Crops in Alluvial Gold‐Mining Areas
abstract: Artisanal and small‐scale gold mining in the southeastern Amazonian department of Madre de Dios, Peru, has caused severe soil degradation characterized by extreme sand dominance, nutrient depletion, and disrupted microbial communities. Conventional restoration approaches have often resulted insufficient, highlighting the need for evidence‐based strategies. This study evaluated five legume cover crops— Stylosanthes guianensis , Pueraria phaseoloides , Canavalia ensiformis , Centrosema macrocarpum , and Crotalaria juncea —and a control as nature‐based solutions for soil health recovery. Plots were arranged in a completely randomized block design with three replicates, comparing treatments and post‐establishment years (11 and 22 months). Soil Quality Index (SQI) integrating 15 biological, physical, and chemical indicators through principal component analysis was developed to quantify soil recovery. All cover crops improved soil quality relative to bare controls (SQI = 0.070), reaching values between 0.092 and 0.197, although still below the reference forest benchmark (0.461). Stylosanthes showed the highest SQI (0.197), associated with greater aggregate stability and increased actinobacterial abundance, while Pueraria promoted strong fungal proliferation and enhanced potassium availability; Canavalia also improved potassium levels. Microbial respiration increased across all treatments compared with the control, and biomass production was highest under Stylosanthes , suggesting greater potential for organic matter inputs. Overall, the SQI framework captured multidimensional recovery patterns and revealed complementary ecological functions among species. Although limitations in organic matter content and cation exchange capacity persisted, these findings demonstrate the short‐term potential of legume cover crops to initiate soil recovery processes and support long‐term ecological restoration in Amazonian ecosystems affected by gold mining.

The life-cycle dynamics of wealth mobility
abstract: We use 25 years of tax records for the Norwegian population to study the mobility of wealth over people’s lifetimes. We find considerable wealth mobility over the life cycle. To understand the underlying mobility patterns, we group individuals with similar wealth rank histories using agglomerative hierarchical clustering, a tool from statistical learning. The mobility patterns we elicit provide evidence of segmented mobility. Over 60 percent of the population remains at the top or bottom of the wealth distribution throughout their lives. Mobility is driven by the remaining 40 percent, who move only within the middle of the distribution. Movements are tied to differential income trajectories and business activities across groups. We show parental wealth is the key predictor of who is persistently rich or poor, while human capital is the main predictor of those who rise and fall through the middle of the distribution.

Heterogeneous Farmer Education, Technology Gaps, and Technical Efficiency in Ghana
abstract: Education is widely viewed as a driver of agricultural productivity, yet its association with technology gaps and farming efficiency remains ambiguous. Ghana provides a revealing case, where major educational reforms have coincided with persistent yield gaps. Using nationally representative data from 19,862 households in the sixth and seventh rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, we apply a stochastic metafrontier framework combined with Euclidean distance matching to assess how farmer education is associated with estimated technology gaps (TGRs) and technical efficiency. Our results show that farmer education is associated with higher managerial capacity and larger estimated TGRs. Educated farmers record higher technical efficiency (0.799 vs. 0.606 for uneducated peers), but they also face a 10% points estimated technology gap. When disaggregated, receiving some formal education and training, being literate and numerate and current school enrolment are all associated with significant efficiency gains. Other education measures are either not statistically significant or are negatively associated with efficiency, underscoring the heterogeneous relationship between education and farm performance. These findings point to the possible value of combining education with measures that ease potential technological constraints. Sector‐specific training and targeted incentives may be relevant to technological endowment and sustained productivity growth.

title: Regulatory Information and Consumer Acceptance of Novel Foods: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
abstract: Ensuring food safety, food security and food sustainability has become increasingly essential in the current global context, characterised by growing food demand, environmental pressures and resource constraints. Technological innovations and the adoption of non‐traditional food sources may contribute to achieving sustainability goals. However, their effectiveness ultimately depends on consumer acceptance. Indeed, even a balanced integration of safety, security and sustainability objectives may prove insufficient if individuals are reluctant to consume novel foods. Using a survey experiment on a representative sample in terms of age, gender, and macro‐geographical area of residence of the Italian adult population ( N = 2012), we investigate whether regulatory information influences consumer acceptance of novel foods. We analyse the effect of providing information about the European Union's marketing authorisation process concerning novel foods on willingness to consume cell‐based meat and products based on insect flour. Results show that informed respondents express significantly higher acceptance of both types of products, compared to a control group. We also administered an obfuscated follow‐up survey to the same sample of subjects, with varying time gaps between the first and second waves to assess whether the informational effect persisted over time while controlling for demand and priming effects. Evidence from the obfuscated survey indicates that the informational effect progressively declines over time, eventually fading out completely. Findings highlight the role of regulatory knowledge in shaping consumer trust and suggest the need for targeted communication strategies to support the diffusion of sustainable food innovations.

Development interventions in Africa’s historical borderlands: Evidence from colonial missions
abstract: Africa’s historical borderlands are persistently associated with low levels of economic development. This paper examines how these regions respond to development interventions, analysing whether the long-run development advantage associated with colonial Christian missions persists near historical homeland borders. Combining georeferenced data on 3365 pioneering mission stations with high-resolution satellite night-time luminosity data, we show that the positive association between proximity to missionary activity and contemporary economic development weakens sharply in these borderland areas. This result is robust across a wide range of specifications and is corroborated by evidence on household wealth and human capital from the Demographic and Health Surveys Program. Our findings suggest that the success of development initiatives in the historical borderlands reflects not only the interventions themselves, but also the institutional environments in which they were implemented.

title: A typology of green and climate jobs: Towards eco-social political economy
Did the UK ‘build back better’? It's hard to say…: A socioecological analysis of the United Kingdom's green recovery
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, global governments pledged to ‘build back better’ through green recovery initiatives. Rather than attempting a linear causal evaluation of these claims, this study conducts an immediate post-lockdown structural diagnostic of the United Kingdom using Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism (MuSIASEM). By generating a multi-scale metabolic profile, we evaluate the extent to which underlying biophysical structures shifted toward a more sustainable orientation by 2022. At a high scale, our diagnostic reveals a highly resilient metabolic system that is largely resistant to state steering, exhibiting an elastic ‘bounce back’ to its pre-crisis state. While consumer-facing sectors showed superficial signs of greening, the Energy/Fuel Production sector emerged as a major structural anomaly, exhibiting a 159% surge in territorial emissions. Rather than a setback in decarbonisation, we interpret this spike as the repatriation of previously offshored emissions as the UK prioritised domestic supply security during the 2022 energy crisis. Additionally, we identify a structural equity trade-off where localised environmental improvements in the household sector are exchanged for the market stabilisation of paid work. Ultimately, these mixed results demonstrate that post-crisis evaluations depend entirely on the chosen criteria of structural change. These findings detail how a systemic shock can be absorbed to preserve an entrenched socio-technical regime, offering critical insights into the material and institutional limits of state-led green transitions.

Media coverage and stock price synchronicity: the roles of opinion dispersion and common media coverage

Do Institutional Investors’ Environmental Concerns Improve Corporate Environmental Sustainability Practices? Evidence from Textual Analysis in China

Left in charge: Political rule and the rise of local welfare
How Generative AI Reshapes Analysts’ Information Intermediation: Evidence From China
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption propensity in analyst reports and stock price informativeness. Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2023 to 2024, we document that greater GenAI adoption propensity in analyst reports is associated with lower stock price informativeness, reflected in a weaker relation between current stock valuations and future firm profitability. This relationship remains robust across alternative specifications and empirical approaches addressing potential endogeneity concerns. The negative association is more pronounced among non‐state‐owned firms, firms without cross‐listings, during analysts’ busy periods, and for firms receiving greater analyst attention. At the report level, higher GenAI adoption propensity is associated with more cautious language, reflected in abnormal negative tone and greater linguistic hedging, and with greater textual convergence across reports covering the same firm. We also find weaker investment–price sensitivity among firms with higher GenAI adoption propensity, consistent with a reduced informational role of stock prices in corporate investment decisions. Overall, our findings suggest that greater GenAI adoption propensity does not necessarily coincide with more informative stock prices, highlighting potential trade‐offs in analysts' information intermediation.

title: Collusion Detection with Graph Neural Networks
Best-Price Provision under Loss Aversion
Good news, better credit? The role of internet media tone in trade credit financing
The supply chain of credit: Collateral-based easing and firms' trade credit provision
Improvements in labor market prospects and the fertility and location decisions of immigrants
Organizational Goal Hierarchies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Dynamic Behavioral Perspective
abstract: This paper theorizes how artificial intelligence (AI) disrupts organizational goal hierarchies by altering the rate and rhythm at which strategic purposes and operational means evolve. Rather than assuming that goals shift uniformly, we introduce the concept of goal flow: a dynamic and nonuniform change across a system of goals. AI technologies play a dual role in goal flow, as they disintegrate goal systems by accelerating goal evolution at different intensities across strategic and operational goals, while simultaneously enabling new forms of integration by augmenting social processes of learning, bargaining, and control. By elaborating this dual role in four types of integration work—aligning, directing, filtering, and sustaining—the paper reconceptualizes goal hierarchies as dynamic systems, augmented by AI.

title: Why Time Management Leads to Well-Being (and Performance)
abstract: Time management is usually seen as a way to get more done. Yet research suggests that it is more strongly associated with well-being than with performance. Why time management improves well-being and why the benefits vary remain unclear. This article proposes three pathways linking time management to well-being and productivity. First, structure brings order to daily life by giving people a sense of control and predictability. Second, synchrony aligns activities with social and biological rhythms, reducing conflict and strengthening social ties. And third, concordance aligns activities with personal values and long-term goals, giving daily life meaning and strengthening the connection between present and future selves. These benefits depend on both individual practices and organizational conditions. Fragmented work, excessive demands on people’s time, and a focus on short-term results can obstruct the pathways. An imbalance among the pathways can also turn otherwise useful time management practices into sources of strain. By distinguishing these mechanisms and their limits, the framework helps explain why time management can improve well-being and productivity in some circumstances, have little effect in others, and sometimes make things worse.

title: Stakeholder Governance
abstract: Stakeholder governance has become central to debates about stakeholder capitalism, yet research remains fragmented about the configurations through which non-shareholder stakeholders gain authority and firms become credibly bound to stakeholder claims. We systematically review 171 articles in management and related fields to develop a framework organized around stakeholder authority (i.e., the participatory rights or recognized standing through which stakeholders can engage in governance), and firm commitment (i.e., the obligations organizations assume toward stakeholder claims in ways that are costly to reverse or ignore). We identify five recurring configurations: (a) disclosure and evaluation; (b) monitoring and verification; (c) contracting, formal rules, and adjudication; (d) governance rights; and (e) rule-making rights. These configurations generally move from informational authority and very weak firm commitment to constitutional authority and very strong firm commitment. We also identify two off-diagonal configurations—constrained authority and embedded commitment—that reveal how authority and commitment need not align. Our framework distinguishes stakeholder governance that remains largely symbolic from arrangements that create durable constraints on organizational discretion. We conclude by outlining a research agenda on institutional settings, organizational forms, transitions across governance configurations, and the implications of learning dynamics for stakeholder authority and commitment.

title: It’s a System: Shareholder Activism, Corporate Harm, and the Role of Regulators, NGOs, and Media
abstract: Research on shareholder activism has focused largely on the direct, dyadic relationship between activists and the firms they target, leaving open a broader question: When does activism actually change corporate behavior? We argue that the answer depends on the wider system of stakeholders surrounding the firm. Integrating stakeholder influence research with institutional theory, we theorize that shareholder demands more effectively motivate organizational change when other actors in the institutional environment reinforce the issues those demands raise. We test this in the context of environmental and social (E&S) shareholder proposals, asking whether they reduce firms’ stakeholder violations, which are regulator-sanctioned acts of misconduct that can harm non-shareholding stakeholders. Using data on E&S proposals at 428 U.S. firms from 2007 to 2021 , we find that proposals reduce stakeholder violations, and that this effect operates through managerial receptivity, defined as a firm’s behavioral pattern of engaging rather than resisting activist demands. Critically, this relationship is amplified when firms face greater scrutiny from two institutional pillars: regulative pressure from regulators and cultural-cognitive pressure from NGOs. By showing that non-shareholding stakeholders condition whether shareholder activism translates into reduced corporate harm, we move beyond the activist–firm dyad and offer a systems-level account of when, and through what mechanisms, shareholder activism succeeds in achieving its aims.

title: EXPRESS: The Relationship Between a Salesperson’s Past and Future Performance
abstract: A salesperson’s past performance is widely assumed to predict their future performance, and thus often guides managerial decision-making. Contrary to that assumption, this study uncovers why and under what conditions past performance becomes a less reliable predictor of future performance. A grounded theory study in a solution-selling context reveals that recent wins generate after-sales workload that lowers the odds of converting the next lead, particularly when those wins are complex, as occurs when customer relationships are new or procurement is formalized. Analysis of seven years of CRM data covering 3,669 sales leads at a Fortune 500 firm confirms that the link between past and future wins weakens as recent wins grow in complexity. Behavioral experiments causally confirm this attenuation effect, showing recent wins reduce effort on the next lead when those wins are complex. Finally, a single-dataset meta-analysis offers convergent evidence for workload as the underlying mechanism, revealing the relationship also weakens when workload is decoupled from winning and rooted in organizational change instead. For managers, these findings imply that using past performance to guide forecasting, quota setting, and coaching risks suboptimal decisions. They also underscore the importance of resourcing salespeople to balance after-sales responsibilities with new business development.

title: Dismantling organized crime's “protective umbrella”: How the downfall of corrupt officials fuels urban entrepreneurship in China
Giving More in a Non-Native Language: The Effect of Language on Monetary Donations
abstract: How does the language of a charitable appeal, whether communicated in a potential donor’s native or non-native (but proficient) language, influence monetary donations? Whereas research finds that people behave more morally in their native (vs. non-native) language, eight preregistered experiments (N = 7,447) and one archival analysis (N = 3,142) find that people donate less in response to appeals in their native language. People facing a donation decision need to determine whether and how much to give, with the appropriate action varying across situations. Situational considerations that inform this decision are more accessible in a native language, making donation decisions seem less diagnostic of the self, reducing giving. Consistent with this process, perceived self-diagnosticity mediates the effect of language on donations, and manipulating self-diagnosticity attenuates this effect. Reconciling these findings with prior research, the relationship between language and moral behavior depends on the type of moral decision under consideration: a native language promotes adherence to moral rules when decisions involve moral violations (stealing; lying), but reduces giving for donation decisions, which we refer to as moral aspirations. Beyond advancing theory on language, self-diagnosticity, and moral behavior, this research offers practical guidance to maximize charitable giving when communicating with multilingual audiences.

title: EXPRESS: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
abstract: The authors study the estimation of causal treatment effects on demand when treatment is randomly assigned but prices adjust in response to treatment. They show that regressions of demand on treatment or on treatment and price lead to biased estimates of the direct treatment effect. The sign of the bias in both cases depends on the sign of the correlation of price with treatment, and the two biases point in the same direction. In most cases including an endogenous price control reduces bias but does not remove it. The authors also show how to test whether bias from an endogenous price response arises and how to recover an unbiased direct treatment effect using a price instrument. They apply the approach to the estimation of feature advertising effects across several product categories using supermarket scanner data and show that the bias when not instrumenting price can be substantial.

title: EXPRESS: Making the Shelf Work for You: How Shelf Dimensions and Brand Types Influence the Shelf Placement Effect on Product Performance
abstract: This study examines how vertical and horizontal shelf position and shelf space affect product sales, and how these effects vary across brand types and shelf dimensions. Using sales data and detailed planogram changes from a leading convenience-store retailer, the analysis distinguishes primary NBs (market-leading national brands), secondary NBs (other nationally distributed brands), and PLs (private labels), and compares tall versus short and wide versus narrow shelves. On tall shelves, primary and secondary NBs perform best between the middle and top, whereas vertical position has little effect for PLs. On short shelves, NBs perform better toward the top and bottom, while PLs tend to perform better near the top. On wide shelves, primary NBs perform best slightly left of center, while horizontal position has little effect for secondary NBs and PLs. On narrow shelves, primary NBs perform best near the center, PLs left of center, and secondary NBs show only modest differences across positions. More shelf space increases sales most strongly for PLs. A shelf-optimization analysis suggests substantial model-implied sales improvements from shelf rearrangement. Overall, the findings help retailers assess and justify requests for contested premium positions and shelf space by showing which brand types benefit most across shelf types.

title: The Effect of Cost Elasticity Choice on Loss Reversal
Anger and gender bias in leadership evaluations: A stereotype-context competition model
abstract: Why do female leaders face professional penalties for the same expressions of anger that often benefit male leaders? Despite decades of research, gender bias in leadership evaluations remains a stubborn hurdle for women seeking career advancement. In this theoretical paper, I develop a stereotype-context competition model to explain how gender bias arises in the evaluation of leaders who express anger, and to identify conditions under which such bias is less likely to occur. I argue that evaluations of angry leaders are shaped by two competing forces: a pro-bias force driven by stereotype information and a counter-bias force driven by contextual information. I further propose that the pro-bias force generally prevails, resulting in the persistence of gender bias in initial evaluations of angry leaders. Finally, I identify three categories of factors—related to the leader, the observer, and the situation—that can reduce the likelihood of gender bias. I conclude by discussing the theoretical and practical implications of the model.

title: Organizing critique at critical organizations: Digital transmediality and critical positionality
abstract: Critical organizations, whose missions involve producing social critique, such as academic, journalistic, and activist organizations, face what we term a dilemma of “critical positionality,” meaning that they must respond to contradictory demands for critical proximity and distance. This dilemma arises because legitimate critique must remain “close to the ground” to access “lived experiences” yet also adopt sufficient distance from practice to allow for problematization. Critical positionality is an organizational challenge that is exacerbated during moments of digital transitions, when proximity and distance are reconfigured through transmediality—that is, movement of content across media types—which can disrupt organizational practices oriented toward critical positionality. To understand how organizations navigate digital transmediality to maintain their critical positions, we studied a Brazilian progressive news outlet during a digital transition. Organizational attempts to build proximity to users were followed by a reactive attempt at repositioning, which cascaded into further efforts to stabilize a position consistent with the organization’s critical mission. By analyzing approximation and distancing dynamics, we contribute to understanding critical positionality in practice, discussing how critique is shaped by evolving requirements of digital transmediality, and illustrating organizational tensions developed in this process in a critical news outlet.

title: Creating meaning at work or providing career support? How servant leaders enhance followers’ vocational outcomes
abstract: Do servant leaders shape their followers’ vocational outcomes by the career support they provide or by helping followers find meaning at work? Drawing on self-determination theory, we test these two accounts, examining their competing effects on followers’ thriving at work, career satisfaction, and job search behaviors. Using the critical incident method (Study 1), we found that servant leaders influence vocational outcomes by deepening followers’ meaning at work, but not by providing career support. In a four-wave study (Study 2), both pathways were significant. A field study (Study 3) again supported only the meaning at work pathway, showing that meaning at work was most salient for followers with lower levels of work volition. An internal meta-analysis confirmed that both pathways carry a positive indirect effect in aggregate, but that the pathway through meaning at work is significantly stronger. Taken together, our results indicate that servant leadership is more vocationally consequential through the meaning followers internalize than the career support they receive, particularly among followers whose vocational agency is more constrained.

title: Renewing Defense Roadmaps Through Open Innovation
abstract: This article investigates how a defense firm manages open innovation initiatives to respond to the challenges facing the sector, including the renewal of its roadmaps to rapidly changing environments. Leveraging the framework of dynamic capabilities, we identify how a highly bureaucratic organization can integrate changes through the study of twelve open innovation initiatives and their link and impact on its roadmaps. We reveal sensing, seizing, and transforming activities involved in this process. We specifically identify four transformations of roadmaps: reduction, enrichment, creation, and marginalization. We therefore propose ways through which rigid organizations can accommodate high-uncertainty innovations without fully disrupting formal strategic commitments

title: Circular Supply Chain Strategies for Mitigating Partial and Full Disruptions in Distribution Centres
abstract: Supply chain disruptions are unwanted events that can create problems in maintaining the flow of goods and services, delivering and fulfilling demand, managing costs, and potentially hurting resilience performance. Adopting appropriate strategies and the use of precise decision‐making models can help mitigate the disruptions and improve profitability and resilience performance. Previous studies developed models and generated mitigation plans using resilience strategies. However, there are limited studies that quantitatively investigate the usefulness of circular strategies in mitigating disruptions. This study makes the first attempt to develop quantitative models and generate supply chain mitigation plans for mitigating partial and full disruptions in distribution centres (DCs). To do so, we develop a mathematical modelling and simulation approach to develop models under three situations: an ideal plan when there is no disruption, the impacts of disruptions when no strategies are used, and mitigation plans with circular strategies. We use a distribution plan of a smartphone in Australia to demonstrate the results and findings. The results reveal that full disruptions in multiple DCs have the most damaging impacts on demand fulfilment and total profit. Results also reveal that the use of circular strategies, such as utilisation of spare capacity, repair and reuse of products, can improve demand fulfilment and total profit by reducing penalty costs for not meeting the demand. We also compare the results under different situations, such as when no strategies are implemented vs. when strategies are implemented in case of partial and full disruptions in single and multiple DCs. In all situations, circular strategies show a positive influence on demand fulfilment and total profit, which are indicators of improved resilience performance. In practice, the models and findings can assist managers to solve real‐life situations when DCs are partially or fully disrupted and end up with reduced capacities.

title: Long‐term Orientation and Proactive Environmental Strategies in Emerging Markets: Evidence From India
abstract: This study examines how emerging market firms characterized by a long‐term orientation (LTO) develop the organizational routines that support proactive environmental strategies (PES). These strategies are essential for sustaining operations within evolving institutions and for adopting environmentally friendly practices in institutionally weak settings. Thus, building on the perspective of organizational routines, this study establishes a positive association between firms' LTO and their likelihood of adopting PES in emerging markets. Furthermore, drawing on informal institutions and transaction‐cost reasoning, the findings suggest that informal competition and crime in emerging markets discourage firms from investing in PES, thereby weakening the baseline relationship. Based on a sample of 6547 Indian firms, we find support for all hypotheses. This research advances the literature on PES by providing insights into how firms' LTO, industry‐level informal competition, and societal‐level crime collectively influence their sustainability strategies in emerging markets.

title: Beyond Green Rhetoric: How Human Resource Management Bridges Strategy and Sustainability in Hotels
abstract: Drawing on the natural resource‐based view (NRBV) and social cognitive theory (SCT), this study examines the relationships among strategic green intentions, green human resource management (Green HRM) practices, sustainable business performance and employee outcomes in Ghana's hospitality industry. Two independent quantitative studies were conducted in star‐rated hotels. Study 1 surveyed 282 managers and supervisors to examine Green HRM practices as mediating mechanisms linking strategic green intentions to economic, social and environmental performance. Study 2 surveyed 302 frontline employees to investigate employee green commitment as a mediator of the relationships between Green HRM practices and employee green behaviour and turnover intention. Data were analysed using a disjoint two‐stage PLS‐SEM approach. Study 1 revealed that strategic green intentions were directly associated with social performance but not with economic or environmental performance. Green HRM practices exhibited significant positive indirect effects across all three performance dimensions, with indirect‐only mediation for economic and environmental performance and complementary mediation for social performance. Study 2 demonstrated that employee green commitment significantly mediated the positive relationship between Green HRM practices and employee green behaviour. However, neither Green HRM practices nor employee green commitment was significantly associated with turnover intention, and the corresponding indirect effect was nonsignificant. The findings refine NRBV and SCT‐informed explanations by demonstrating differentiated relationships between environmental strategic intentions and sustainability performance, while highlighting the outcome‐specific relevance of employee green commitment. Practically, the research underscores the importance of embedding environmental priorities in credible Green HRM practices while recognising that broader employment outcomes may require complementary employee‐support strategies.

title: Sustainability Orientation in New Product Development for High‐Involvement Business‐to‐Business Innovations
abstract: Adapting to climate change has led to innovative sustainable products, yet their market adoption remains uncertain. This underscores the need to explore the link between companies' new product development and their customers' orientation to sustainability in a B2B context. To address this, we developed a path model examining winemakers' willingness to adopt a microtechnology‐based crop‐protection product to mitigate the effects of climate change. A survey of 78 German winemakers, analyzed by partial least squares structural equation modeling, revealed a positive link between sustainable product‐feature orientation and willingness to use, mediated by trust in science and product interest. Sustainable product‐feature orientation showed a negative relationship with trust in science and willingness to use, while trust in science positively influenced product interest and adoption willingness. Our study uniquely connects approaches to new product development with novel technology and high‐involvement products for small and medium‐sized enterprises in the agricultural sector.

title: Navigating digital paradoxes in hospitality: How AI-enabled engagement and techno-invasion shape employee creativity
Work vs. play: Linking generative AI use to hospitality employees’ innovative behavior via intrinsic motivation
Pricing latitude in restaurant transactions: Transaction role effects on price knowledge and acceptable price spread
More ethics, better outcomes? Revisiting ethical leadership in hospitality through a curvilinear lens
Sustaining coordination under compounded volatility: How coordination practices develop and combine in multi-partner R&D projects
Virtual reality booking systems: drivers and ESG outcomes
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how technological, organizational and environmental factors influence the integration of 360° virtual reality-enhanced booking systems (VRBS) and examines the subsequent impact on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance in the hospitality industry. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in the technology–organization–environment (TOE) framework and stakeholder theory, quantitative data were collected from 588 four-star, five-star, and Chinese gold and platinum diamond hotels and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings Relative advantage, digital infrastructure and competitive pressure significantly drive VRBS integration, whereas cybersecurity concerns and organizational agility are nonsignificant antecedents. VRBS integration enables hotels to use resources more responsibly, while enhancing stakeholder trust and transparency, thereby improving ESG performance. Hotels prioritize visible advantages, competitive dynamics and peer behavior over internal capabilities when deciding on integration. Practical implications Hotel managers can adopt VRBS without substantial restructuring because organizational agility and cybersecurity concerns pose minimal barriers. Given the influence of competitive pressure, late-adopting hotels should implement VRBS proactively to remain competitive and meet evolving stakeholder expectations. Originality/value This study broadens the TOE framework by linking it to ESG performance and positioning VRBS as strategic sustainability assets. This addresses the theoretical gaps related to the ESG construct by unbundling the ESG construct and specifying how experiential technology leads to different sustainability outcomes. It shows traditional barriers in adoption literature are not significant at frontline for experiential technologies.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Closing the Knowledge Gap: How Moral Obligations, Perceived Benefits, and Dispositional Greed Shape Influencer Advertising Code Compliance
abstract: The rapid growth of influencer marketing has outpaced regulatory enforcement and has increased the risk of noncompliance through misleading promotions and inadequate sponsorship disclosures. This study investigates whether and how enhancing influencers’ advertising code knowledge affects their intentions to comply with advertising regulations. Specifically, it examines whether increased knowledge enhances compliance intentions, whether this relationship is mediated by moral obligations and perceived benefits, and whether dispositional greed moderates these mediating pathways. Across four studies, involving 1,082 U.K.-based social media influencers, we employed diverse research designs. Study 1 uses a single-session pre–post design (N = 154); Study 2 adopts a two-wave pre–post design (N = 213); Study 3 applies a third-person, between-subjects design (N = 228); and Study 4 employs a randomized experimental design (N = 487). The findings reveal that greater advertising code knowledge significantly increases influencers’ intentions to comply. This effect is mediated by stronger moral obligations and heightened recognition of the compliance benefits. Furthermore, dispositional greed moderates the influence of knowledge on both moral obligations and perceived benefits. These findings highlight the importance of targeted education and training that build influencers’ advertising code knowledge as a lever for strengthening ethical conduct and regulatory compliance.

title: Implicit Algorithm Aversion: How Consumer Characteristics Shape Perceptions of Ads Designed by Undisclosed AI Versus Human Advertising Professionals
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the marketing landscape, providing scalable efficiencies in ad creation. However, the consumer side of AI integration remains underexplored. Drawing on algorithm aversion theory, this research extends the literature by examining how consumer characteristics moderate the persuasive impact of AI- and human-designed ads. Across a pretest and six large-scale experimental studies involving 6,579 consumer evaluations in Japan, this research finds that advertisements with undisclosed AI authorship often outperform human-designed advertisements in enhancing ad perceptions of creativity, credibility, clarity, and mental imagery (i.e., stimulating vivid consumer imagination) and, consequently, increasing purchase intentions. However, AI-generated ads are less effective among consumers with more generative AI experience, higher education, greater product category involvement, and lower interest in science. In these consumer segments, human-designed ads often have the advantage. These findings extend algorithm aversion theory by providing indirect evidence consistent with an implicit mechanism through which consumer characteristics trigger implicit algorithm detection (i.e., sensing algorithmic markers) and implicit algorithm aversion (i.e., subconscious devaluation of perceived artificiality) without requiring explicit disclosure of AI authorship. The findings inform marketing practice by emphasizing the importance of consumer segmentation.

title: Equity crowdfunding and employee growth: the role of legitimacy and founder nationality diversity
Decoding AIoT adoption across borders: a meta-analysis of cultural and country-level moderators
abstract: Purpose As Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIoT) technologies reshape global markets, understanding why adoption patterns diverge across countries is a pressing challenge for international marketers. This study addresses a critical gap by synthesizing how cultural and national contexts shape consumer adoption of AIoT innovations. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a meta-analysis of 262 effect sizes from 56 independent studies (N = 19,165), categorizing 25 antecedents of AIoT adoption across five domains – individual, social, functional, emotional, and conditional – grounded in the theory of consumption values. We further examined the macro-level moderating roles of Hofstede’s cultural dimensions (i.e. power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance) and country-level innovativeness. Findings Meta-analytic synthesis reveals that perceived value (ρ = 0.77), satisfaction (ρ = 0.76), and attitude (ρ = 0.75) are the strongest adoption predictors, while usage barriers (ρ = −0.44) and privacy risks (ρ = −0.22) are the key inhibitors. Cultural moderator analyses demonstrate that adoption drivers exhibit directional robustness, consistently pointing toward adoption across cultures, but magnitude cultural contingency, varying significantly in strength across all five cultural dimensions. Notably, trust weakens as uncertainty avoidance rises, and utilitarian value is significantly moderated across all cultural dimensions examined. Constructs including attitude, perceived value, and hedonic value demonstrate cross-cultural robustness, while trust and optimism are conditionally relevant. Practical implications Findings support a directionally standardized but magnitude-adapted global strategy: core AIoT value propositions can be standardized across markets, while communication emphasis should be culturally calibrated. In high uncertainty avoidance markets, trust-building should emphasize institutional endorsement and regulatory compliance; in innovation-leading markets, functional and utilitarian appeals will be most effective. Originality/value This is the first meta-analytic synthesis specifically theorizing AIoT, rather than IoT broadly, as a distinct consumption phenomenon, and the first to replace dichotomous East–West cultural classifications with continuous, multi-dimensional Hofstede moderator analyses. The study introduces the conceptual distinction between directional robustness and magnitude cultural contingency, offering an empirically grounded resolution to the standardization-versus-adaptation debate in international marketing.

title: The relationship between language ideologies and workplace mistreatment towards North Korean defectors
abstract: Previous studies on Social Identity Theory (SIT) have revealed the role of social categorisation in power imbalances between languages, linking it to negative acts in workplaces (e.g. discrimination). We focus on subtle social categorisation along the linguistic dimension, investigating whether North Korean Defectors (NKDs) working at South Korean organisations perceive workplace mistreatment as a result of linguistic discrimination. Repeat interviews were conducted with 20 NKDs, and one-off interviews with 6 NKDs. Our study shows that the use of North Korean accents or lexical items has been regarded as illegitimate in South Korean workplaces, leading NKDs to feel mistreated. We also investigate NKDs’ identity formation in response to workplace mistreatment. Our results show that the majority of NKDs hide their North Korean ethnicity in the workplace for fear of being mistreated due to ingrained stereotypes about NKDs.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: University entrepreneurial ecosystems and graduate start-up creation across stages of entrepreneurship and regional contexts
abstract: Research has shown that entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs) shape universities’ entrepreneurial activities. However, limited attention has been paid to how university entrepreneurial ecosystems (UEEs) support graduate start-up creation across different stages of entrepreneurship and how their effectiveness varies across regions with different quality of the EE. We draw on a quasi-balanced panel data of 130 English higher education institutions (HEIs) over six years. The analysis shows that UEEs support graduate start-ups across both ideation and business development stages. However, the effectiveness of these support mechanisms is conditioned by the quality of the EE in which universities operate and is subject to diminishing returns. We conclude that support mechanisms for university-based entrepreneurship should be designed with greater consideration of the linkages between the UEE and the regional context to avoid overlapping efforts and a potential detrimental impact on graduate start-up creation.

title: A dual‐pathway approach for explaining constant connectivity and its paradoxical effects
abstract: Constant connectivity—being highly available and connected to work through digital tools—is associated with both beneficial and detrimental outcomes, but the mechanisms driving these divergent effects remain under‐explored. Using self‐regulation theory, we undertake a 10‐day diary design ( N = 341), applying a dual‐pathway approach to find that both momentary job demands (within‐person level) and a compulsive, habitual person factor (between‐person level) independently predict higher levels of daily connectivity. Mediation analysis reveals that higher levels of connectivity are associated with decreased levels of psychological detachment (within‐person path) and increased work‐life conflict (both paths). However, the combined indirect effects reveal that—in both pathways—the negative effects on well‐being outcomes are superseded by the positive effect of constant connectivity on work performance. These findings suggest a self‐regulation trade‐off, whereby constant connectivity is a strategy to sustain performance at the expense of well‐being, both when momentary job demands increase and for those with habitual, compulsive tendencies towards digital communications. In applying a dual‐pathway approach, this study enhances understanding of self‐regulation processes in modern, digital work and we reflect on both theoretical and practical implications.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: Structuring corporate social performance: a definitional framework from five decades of research
abstract: Corporate social performance (CSP) has been debated for more than five decades yet remains characterised by conceptual ambiguity and fragmented definitions. This lack of definitional clarity undermines cumulative research, hinders cross-study comparability, and complicates organisational practice. This paper reviews the definitional landscape of CSP and provides a framework that clarifies its boundaries. Building on a structured literature review of 55 papers published in leading journals, we analyse and structure definitional debates into a five-dimensional framework. The framework distinguishes targets of CSP, components, levels of engagement, strategies of response, and perspectives. Rather than proposing a prescriptive definition, it systematizes alternative approaches, enabling researchers to position their work more explicitly and practitioners to articulate their social performance more credibly. An ex-post exercise applying the framework to eight recent CSP studies illustrates its capacity to integrate diverse theoretical and methodological perspectives. The paper contributes by structuring fragmented debates, enhancing methodological clarity and comparability, and offering practical guidance for organisations facing increasing demands for transparency and accountability.

title: Tax Pitfalls in Cross-Border Deals: Evidence from SPACs
journal_name: The Journal of the American Taxation Association

title: From exposure to imprint: CEO formative experiences and the architecture of accounting and financial decisions
abstract: Purpose This review explains how chief executive officers' formative experiences become organizationally consequential and why apparently similar exposures are associated with different accounting, financing, risk and stakeholder decisions. Design/methodology/approach Following the Search-Appraisal-Analysis-Synthesis (SAAS) workflow, the study maps 105 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2011 and 2026 using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer and conducts a structured content synthesis of 102 studies whose focal construct is an executive formative experience. Findings The literature converges around upper-echelons and imprinting perspectives but does not support a uniform “adversity produces conservatism” account. The synthesis distinguishes four adversity-related imprint families – threat vigilance and loss avoidance; uncertainty habituation, resilience or self-efficacy; scarcity orientation; and prosocial reorientation – while treating institutional socialization as conceptually distinct. Persistent imprints become observable only when later situations activate them and when executive discretion permits expression. Accounting and financing architecture provides particularly discriminating tests of these mechanisms. Originality/value The review moves beyond exposure–outcome associations by separating exposure formation, imprint content, activation, expression and observed decision bundles. It recentres accounting and corporate finance in the chief executive officer formative-experience literature and develops an auditable mechanism-based research agenda.

title: EXPRESS: Reexamining the Implications of CEO Outside Directorships on CEO Compensation and Firm Performance: A Quasi-Replication and Extension Study
abstract: This study revisits the implications of CEO outside directorships for CEO compensation and firm performance by quasi-replicating and extending the findings of Geletkanycz et al. (2001) and Geletkanycz and Boyd (2011). We examine their hypotheses, originally tested with data from 1987, using a cross-sectional sample of Fortune 1000 firms in 2019 and panel data from 2010 to 2019. Our findings suggest that most relationships observed in the original studies may not hold in contemporary contexts. For CEO compensation, we find a positive association in the direct replication but not the extension replication. Diversification negatively moderates this association only in the extension, reversing the original result. For firm performance, we find no significant main effect in either analysis. The direct replication reveals a positive association under high industry concentration, opposite to the original finding under low concentration, while the extension does not reproduce the original moderating findings.

title: Strategic organization under geopolitical uncertainty
Performance feedback and the use of corporate prosocial claims as a marketing strategy
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the behavioural theory of the firm, this study aims to investigate when firms strategically deploy prosocial claims – statements about their commitment to social goals beyond profit – as a marketing tool. Design/methodology/approach Using panel OLS regression with firm/year fixed effects, the authors analysed 19,526 firm-year observations from Chinese public firms (2012–2019). Data from CSMAR and annual reports was used to test the hypotheses. Findings The findings indicate that firms experiencing underperformance make more prosocial claims, whereas those recording outperformance tend to reduce their focus on such strategies. Moreover, when a higher proportion of a firm’s TMT members have marketing backgrounds, underperforming firms are more likely to increase their prosocial claims, while outperforming firms become more conservative in making such claims. Furthermore, we find empirical support for the argument that firms with better social evaluation and financial performance below aspirations are less likely to make prosocial claims, suggesting that for firms consistently excelling in CSR, prosocial claims may not be viewed as effective or novel solutions. Research limitations/implications Generalisability may be limited by China’s emerging CSR context. Claims were measured via annual reports only; future research should examine diverse disclosure channels. Substantive vs symbolic claims (greenwashing) were not distinguished. Future work should test findings cross-nationally, integrate alternative CSR metrics and analyse long-term effects. Practical implications This study not only expands the theoretical understanding of prosocial marketing but also provides practical insights into how firms can integrate CSR into their overall marketing strategies to achieve better performance outcomes. Originality/value Firstly, this study enriches the CSR literature by demonstrating the strategic use of prosocial claims as a marketing tool. Secondly, this study contributes to the ongoing debate on the relationship between financial performance and CSR by offering new insights from a BTOF perspective. Thirdly, this study contributes to the emerging literature on green marketing.

title: Employee-based brand competitiveness (EBBC): how internal stakeholders’ evaluations of outperformance drive employee-based brand equity
abstract: Purpose Research on brand competitiveness has focused on company and customer perspectives, leaving the employees’ perspective underexplored. As employees play a critical role in a brand’s success, this study aims to introduce employee-based brand competitiveness (EBBC) and investigate its influence on employee-based brand equity (EBBE). Design/methodology/approach Leveraging social exchange theory and social identity theory, this article develops a conceptual model of the EBBC–EBBE relationship. It uses a mixed-methods approach, comprising 20 in-depth qualitative interviews and a quantitative survey conducted among 496 employees. Findings The qualitative interviews provide initial evidence for the effect of EBBC on employee behaviour, confirm conceptually derived mediators and reveal additional mediators. The quantitative study confirms the impact of EBBC on EBBE, finds evidence for trait competitiveness as a moderator and validates mediating effects through brand pride, prosocial motivation and career opportunities. Research limitations/implications Due to this study’s cross-sectional design and the country-specific context of data collection, future research is encouraged to use longitudinal and experimental designs and to validate the EBBC–EBBE model across different industries and cultures. Practical implications This study offers actionable insights for practice. Managers should actively communicate their company brand’s competitiveness to employees and emphasise how it benefits them. Competitive brands can further leverage the EBBC effect by prioritising the recruitment of employees with high trait competitiveness. Originality/value This research addresses the call for investigating brand competitiveness from the employee perspective and contributes to the literature by introducing the novel concept of EBBC. It advances research on internal and employer branding and enriches the brand competitiveness literature by providing the theory-based, empirically validated EBBC–EBBE model.

title: Co-caring consumer socialisation: adolescents’ perspectives on sustainable eating
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine adolescents’ perspectives on their experiences of agency in shifting family food consumption towards greater sustainability. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on 20 interviews with 26 Danish adolescents on family dietary practices using innovative, engaging tools embedded in in-depth, semi-structured interviews. Findings The adolescents interviewed revealed a paradoxical “climate pragmatism”; although aware of sustainability issues related to food consumption, they preferred to adhere to (unsustainable) family eating habits. Family negotiations were characterised by “family diplomacy”, with consumer decisions based on dialogue, consensus, mutual care and the inclusion of all family members in what we term “co-caring consumer socialisation”. Adolescents were unwilling to push green consumer practices unless other family members supported them. Co-caring consumer socialisation, thus, plays an ambivalent role in the green transition. It gives adolescents a voice in family consumption, however, climate pragmatism and family diplomacy keep them from using that voice to drive change. Transforming family food consumption towards more climate-friendly food practices, therefore, remains a challenge. Research limitations/implications The findings of this study demonstrate that studies of family consumption should approach the family as a co-caring unit, in which care is jointly produced through family members’ consumption practices. This study draws on a sample of adolescents from primarily middle-class, White, Danish families and future research should investigate co-caring consumer socialisation in sustainable eating and beyond in families of different compositions and origin. Practical implications Emphasising taste, health and well-being seems to be a more relevant argument for adolescents than climate protection. Social implications Adolescents do not seem to lack information about climate issues, and therefore, expectations that pro-environmental education in schools will result in a greening of households will not be fulfilled. On the contrary, the results of this study indicate that adolescents, who have practical experience with green eating in contexts where it is seen as the norm, are powerful in changing behaviour towards more sustainable family food consumption. Originality/value This article contributes to the marketing literature by unfolding the concept of “co-caring consumer socialisation” in family decision-making practices which goes beyond “reverse consumer socialisation”.

title: Negotiating AI at work: motivational tensions and the redefinition of marketing expertise
abstract: Purpose Artificial Intelligence Marketing (AIM) tools are increasingly transforming how marketing work is performed. However, its impact on individual practitioners remains underexplored. This study aims to examine how marketing professionals experience and negotiate the contradictory motivational consequences of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled work. Rather than treating AI as either empowering or threatening, the study explores how these effects coexist and how practitioners respond to them. Design/methodology/approach Twenty in-depth interviews were conducted with marketing practitioners using an exploratory, theory-informed qualitative design. Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, Self-Determination Theory and the Job Characteristics Model were used as complementary sensitising lenses to orient interpretation, while coding procedures informed by grounded theory techniques were used to develop themes inductively from the data. Findings The findings reveal that AIM simultaneously empowers and destabilises practitioners. AI enhances efficiency, capability, strategic focus, confidence and creative possibilities, while also generating uncertainty regarding task ownership, professional identity, technological dependence and future relevance. These effects are not experienced as separate outcomes. Instead, practitioners continually negotiate competing tensions by reframing expertise, selectively integrating AI, preserving human control over consequential tasks and reaffirming distinctively human sources of professional value. Motivation therefore emerges as dynamic and continually reconstructed rather than as a stable outcome of AI adoption. Research limitations/implications The design prioritises interpretive depth rather than statistical generalisability. Future research could develop measures of AI-enabled empowerment, destabilisation and negotiation using larger and more diverse samples. The research sample did not analyse differences across career stages, and warrants future investigation. This paper examines broad AIM tools rather than isolated technologies. Future studies should explore how particular AI capabilities change dimensions of professional value and motivation. The findings highlight negotiation as a continuing process, but the cross-sectional design provides only a snapshot of the process. Longitudinal research could establish whether empowerment-destabilisation tensions persist, intensify, diminish or change form over time. The findings suggest potentially important roles for trust, employee participation, work design, organisational support and AI governance. Future research could investigate the organisational conditions that facilitate productive negotiation of AI-related tensions for marketing practitioners. Practical implications Organisations should consider: Evaluating AI in terms of how it changes employees’ experiences of expertise, ownership, autonomy and professional value; Approaching AI capability development as workforce transformation, rather than technical training alone; Preserving meaningful human ownership of work; Addressing the efficiency-intensification paradox. Providing employees with meaningful agency over AI adoption; Treating AI governance as a crucial part of the employee experience. Social implications AI simultaneously empowers and destabilises marketing practitioners, generating tensions around expertise, autonomy, identity and employability. Rather than passively accepting change, individuals actively negotiate these tensions through adaptation, reframing and human–AI collaboration. AI’s long-term impact will depend not only on technological capabilities, but also on how organisations sustain meaningful work, professional development and human agency. Originality/value This study contributes a new tension-based framework that explains how motivation is continuously constructed under AI-driven work environments. In addition, it advances the understanding of AI-enabled work in three ways. Firstly, it conceptualises employee motivation as shaped by simultaneous empowerment and destabilisation rather than by uniformly positive or negative effects. Secondly, it shows how AI redefines marketing expertise from task execution towards judgment, interpretation, contextual understanding and human–AI orchestration. Thirdly, it identifies ongoing negotiation as a central process through which practitioners sustain professional value and motivation under technological change.

title: Multiple Sources, Mixed Signals: How Supervisor and Coworker Undermining (In)congruence Affects Employee Deviance
abstract: Although studies have shown that employee well‐being and work behavior are affected by incongruent mistreatment over time, from a single perpetrator, and across targets, there is comparatively less research examining the effects of mistreatment incongruence across sources (i.e., multiple perpetrators). This raises novel and important questions about how and why supervisors and coworkers, as two salient sources of potential mistreatment, jointly influence employee well‐being and behavior. Drawing on ambivalence theory, we propose that undermining incongruence across sources—that is, the divergence between the levels of undermining that employees experience from supervisor and coworker referent groups—influences employee well‐being and behavior. We test our predictions with two field studies that employ within‐person and between‐person designs. In Study 1, we demonstrate that the effects of supervisor–coworker undermining incongruence on employee CWB are transmitted by reduced feelings of thriving (or languishing). In Study 2, we constructively replicate and extend these findings by demonstrating that the effects of undermining incongruence on employees' thriving and CWB are driven by felt ambivalence. Implications for theory and research are discussed.

title: Do Organizational Researchers Report Their Priors? Reporting Guidelines for Bayesian Methods
abstract: Bayesian methods are increasingly used in management and organizational research, yet the prior distributions on which they depend are often poorly reported. A systematic review of 89 empirical Bayesian studies across 15 leading journals (2001–2025) finds that more than a third do not disclose specific prior distributions and only half of those that mention priors justify their specific choices. In response, we offer seven reporting guidelines for authors, reviewers, and editors that span the specification, justification, and evaluation of priors, organized as a guide from considering Bayesian methods through to reporting priors. Each is grounded in a gap this review documents or in an established methodological practice. As Bayesian adoption broadens in this field, these checkpoints offer a minimum standard for ensuring that prior assumptions remain visible and evaluable.

title: Impact pathways: flexibility on the factory floor – expanding gig labor research into the manufacturing context
abstract: Purpose Manufacturers have begun to experiment with gig labor due to persistent workforce shortages. This article develops impact pathways that specify what manufacturers must resolve for gig labor to function as an effective flexibility lever, and where operations and supply chain management (OSCM) research can advance implementation.
