Design/methodology/approach We conducted 13 semi-structured interviews, 11 with manufacturing executives and two with CEOs of manufacturing-focused gig labor platforms. Transcripts were analyzed with a Gioia-style coding process. Findings We identify four impact pathways shaping whether gig labor can work in manufacturing: (1) designing flexible workflows for gig labor integration; (2) building plant-level legitimacy for hybrid core–gig workforces; (3) enablement of gig labor through platform mediation; and (4) governing the manufacturing gig labor supply chain. The pathways highlight implications for managers, platform designers, and policymakers. Managers should modularize suitable tasks, design quality into processes, and make the benefits of gig labor visible to incumbent workers. Platforms should embed skills-based matching without increasing income instability, and policymakers should assess whether safety, liability, and worker-classification rules fit flexible arrangements. Originality/value Gig labor research, developed mainly in consumer-facing platform settings, rests on a largely unexamined plug-and-play assumption in which tasks arrive pre-bounded, gig workers operate apart from a permanent workforce, workers are interchangeable, and governance is a two-party relationship between platform and worker. This article shows where each premise breaks down in a manufacturing context and offers a future research agenda for OSCM.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Intergenerational Succession and Family Firms’ AI Engagement
Financial fragility and inequality in emerging markets: wealth distribution and sovereign debt crises
Cooperative Needs and Competitive Opportunities: Lobbying for Technology and the Expropriation of Knowledge
abstract: Despite the importance of regulations regarding new technologies, there has been limited research on the competitive dynamics that may unfold among firms engaged in lobbying. In this article, I explore the potential for knowledge expropriation when firms lobby for technology-related regulations. I propose a framework that distinguishes two processes underlying knowledge expropriation—knowledge leakage and uptake—and argue that employing lobbyists creates opportunities for both. Given the different roles of internal and external lobbyists, I predict that increases in internal lobbyists will lead to a greater risk of leakage, while increases in external lobbyists will give rise to more opportunities for uptake. I test these predictions on a unique dataset of U.S. firms that employed lobbyists to influence technology policy and the patents for which those firms applied. I use an embedding approach on the text of patents to directly detect both knowledge leakage and uptake. Overall, the results suggest that lobbying enables opportunities for knowledge expropriation because firms share information that is useful, reliable, timely, and therefore strategically valuable to competitors. In this way, my study identifies a new competitive dynamic at the intersection of firms’ political and innovation strategy.

title: Detecting digital dependence: Inferring government use of hyperscale cloud from internet infrastructure data
abstract: Understanding where government digital services are hosted is critical for assessing technological dependence and countries' progress toward digital sovereignty, yet hosting arrangements are rarely disclosed and difficult to observe from the outside. We ask whether the hosting providers of government digital services can be inferred from publicly observable Internet data. To this end, we develop and publish a unique ground truth dataset of the verified hosting arrangements of 269 public sector digital services, primarily obtained through Freedom of Information (FOI) requests in three countries. The data reveal that 77% of sampled UK digital public services are hosted on US hyperscalers, compared to 64% in Finland and 33% in the Philippines. Using these verified labels, we evaluate whether supervised machine-learning models can infer a service's hosting provider type from its NS, MX, ASN, and TLS records. Even with a limited training set, the best model distinguishes US hyperscaler from non-hyperscaler hosting with 83% accuracy and 0.83 macro-F1, a 13-percentage-point improvement over the single-feature heuristic inference used in prior large-scale studies. By demonstrating the feasibility of empirically estimating hosting dependencies from public data, the study opens a pathway toward systematic cross-national and longitudinal assessment of the extent of government dependence on foreign hosting infrastructures.

title: The Urban Politics of Homelessness Management: Municipal Decision-Making and Spatial Displacement
abstract: Although increasing acknowledgment of homelessness as a housing issue, the spatial government of the un-housed people is highly political. This study uses a spatial political approach to assess how the practice of municipal decision-making generates geographically varied rates of homeless displacement in three large cities in the U.S. (Los Angeles, Portland, and San Francisco) between 2016 and 2023. We combine GIS-based encampment clearance data, council voting data, and political features of the neighborhood and apply the difference-in-differences estimation by taking advantage of three exogenous shocks: the 2018 Martin v. Boise judicial decision, mayoral changes, and COVID-19 emergency orders. The spatial lag and spatial error models reproduce the effects of diffusion across jurisdictions and neighborhoods. The findings indicate that conservative-leaning council districts expanded clearance work by 34% after Martin, whereas progressive districts cut by 18%. Mayoral changes created dramatic changes in displacement patterns, with new administrations showing 41% greater clearance rates during the first year. Spatial analysis reveals that there are substantial spillover impacts whereby aggressive enforcement in one neighborhood leads to a 23% encampment formation in nearby areas. These results indicate that the displacement of homelessness is not a technical management problem but rather a systematically distributed consequence of purposeful political decisions that have extensive consequences regarding the way cities can manage underprivileged groups in society.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Mirror Life, Thrice: Three Levels of Mirror Biology and Three Ethical Conditions
abstract: Mirror biology is drawing urgent calls for governance, from the WHO to the UN Scientific Advisory Board. Yet the term "mirror life" lumps together phenomena with very different risk-benefit profiles. We distinguish three levels. Mirror molecules already deliver therapeutic benefits at manageable risk; mirror organisms threaten catastrophic and irreversible harm and warrant prohibition; mirror subsystems occupy contested middle ground. For this last category, we propose three conditions that any research with a plausible pathway to catastrophic harm should meet: necessity, commensurate benefit, and intolerable cost of delay. Applied to the mirror ribosome, the principal bottleneck on the path to mirror organisms, none of the three is currently satisfied. Much apparent disagreement in the literature dissolves once we recognize that commentators are addressing different levels of complexity.

title: A Measurement Invariance Study of the Sexual Cognitions Checklist Across Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity
abstract: The Sexual Cognitions Checklist (SCC) provides a unique framework for assessing both positive (PSC) and negative sexual cognitions (NSC). Few studies have examined sexual fantasies and cognitions in sexual orientation and gender diversity (SOGD) populations. This study tested the measurement invariance, reliability, and validity of the Spanish SCC scores across sexual orientation and gender identity groups. Using a nationwide strategy, a sample of 2,000 adults was recruited: 443 bisexual, 693 gay, and 829 heterosexual individuals; by gender, there were 963 cisgender men, 856 cisgender women, and 181 transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals. Results supported strict or partial strict invariance for both positive and negative subscales (SCC-PSC and SCC-NSC), supporting meaningful cross-group comparisons. Significant differences emerged across sexual orientation and gender identity in PSC and NSC dimensions. PSC showed the most consistent associations, in a positive direction, with self-reported sexual functioning (i.e., desire, arousal, and penile erection/vaginal lubrication), whereas NSC showed fewer, negative associations. These findings address a critical gap by including underrepresented populations and extending the evidence base beyond cisgender heterosexual samples. To our knowledge, the SCC is currently the only instrument in the Spanish context with psychometric evidence supporting its use across SOGD groups, making it a potentially valuable tool for inclusive research and clinical practice in sexual health.

title: A Qualitative Exploration of Self-Identity within BDSM/Kink Sexuality
abstract: BDSM and kink are umbrella terms broadly describing the consensual and often erotic manipulation of power dynamics and/or pain/sensation experiences. While prior research has largely focused on BDSM/kink behaviors and fantasies, recent research has also included a focus on BDSM/kink as an identity. This research describes diversity and complexity within self-identities among kink-identified individuals in mostly geographically limited samples. The current project adds to this literature as a qualitative inquiry of the self-identities of 262 individuals with BDSM/kink sexual experiences from around the English-speaking world. Participants in the current sample varied in their connection to a BDSM/kink identity. Many described their identities as tied to specific BDSM/kink pursuits, while others rejected the framework of BDSM/kink as an identity altogether. Participants also described fluidity and intersectionality within their BDSM/kink identities, connected their BDSM/kink identity to consent, and qualified their identities according to strength and specificity. Our findings contribute to the literature on the diversity of BDSM/kink identity and experience.

title: Traffic-scenario-recognition-based energy management strategy with variable prediction horizon for connected fuel cell buses
Recultivation of abandoned cropland in China: Spatial patterns and determinants
Mapping the drivers of generative AI adoption in land use policy making: A T-spherical fuzzy WINGS-ISM analysis
Research progress on data-driven fault diagnosis of lithium-ion batteries: A technical review from data representation to diagnostic decision-making
A critical review of bio-geotechnical interventions in porous geomaterials for energy systems: stabilization, selective sealing and thermal upgrading
Hot box testing of building envelopes for sustainable energy design: A critical review
abstract: Amid the urgent challenges of climate change and energy transition, improving the thermal performance of building envelopes has become a key requirement for renewable and sustainable energy development. This issue is especially important for nearly-zero energy buildings, where accurate assessment of envelope thermal behavior is needed to reduce energy demand and improve the integration of passive and renewable energy strategies. Among available experimental methods, hot box testing is widely regarded as the reference approach for evaluating thermal transmittance. However, its application in sustainable and renewable envelope research has not yet been systematically reviewed. This paper addresses this gap through a critical review of hot box applications in building envelope studies, with emphasis on sustainable materials, advanced envelope systems, and energy related technologies relevant to nearly-zero energy buildings. Although the review is mainly centered on U-value assessment, other indicators, such as thermal resistance, thermal conductivity, heat transfer coefficient, and temperature distribution, are also considered where relevant. The study further examines how complementary methods, including numerical simulation, theoretical calculation, heat flux measurement, and infrared thermography, are used to validate and interpret hot box results. Based on the reviewed literature, a future roadmap is further proposed for hot box testing, including realistic climatic exposure, broader thermal response indicators, exergy evaluation, environmental and economic evaluation, and AI-driven data integration. The findings clarify the capabilities and limitations of hot box testing and confirm its continuing importance in the assessment of sustainable and renewable ready building envelopes.

title: Prefecture-level circular economy savings potential for emissions and resources in the Japanese residential building sector
abstract: The circular economy (CE) is a promising strategy to decouple the Japanese residential sector from resource depletion and climate change. We provide a high-resolution analysis of CE potentials in the sector at the prefectural level. In addition, we develop an integrated framework to model the turnover of buildings by including new construction, demolition, and renovation targets, and include a scenario that accounts for inequalities in the provision of floorspace service. Our results suggest that CE strategies alone save ~14% (Base_CEs) while 31% can be expected when CE strategies are coupled with a more compact living space (LEMD_CEs). The cumulative 2020-2050 savings in GHG emissions are expected to reach 22%, with values ranging from 12% (Okinawa) to 31% (Toyama) at the prefectural level. We estimate that vacant stock will rise from 0.3 billion m2 in 2015 to 1.1 billion m2 in 2050, mostly due to low demolition rates.

title: Detecting and interpreting potential illegal construction and demolition waste landfills using remote sensing and machine learning: evidence from Scotland
abstract: Illegal landfilling of construction and demolition waste (CDW) creates a critical loophole in circular economy and net-zero transitions. Although remote sensing and deep learning have improved CDW-site detection, previous studies have mainly focused on mapping suspected waste locations, with limited attention to linking detected candidate sites with spatial conditions associated with their occurrence. This study develops a framework integrating high-resolution satellite imagery, ensemble deep learning, and interpretable machine learning. Using Scotland as a case study, U-Net, U-Net++, and DeepLabV3+ were trained to detect landfill-like surface disturbances, with soft-voting ensembles combining their predictions. Retained candidate sites were combined with remote sensing-derived environmental and socioeconomic indicators to construct a spatial analysis dataset. Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM were compared for occurrence modelling, with Shapley additive explanations used to interpret the selected model. The U-Net++ and DeepLabV3+ ensemble performed best (test intersection over union, IoU = 0.6746). After spatial filtering, 43 potential illegal CDW landfill sites were retained across Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Aberdeen. XGBoost achieved the highest cross-validated area under the precision–recall curve and was selected for interpretation. The model explanations show that building density made the largest contribution to model predictions, followed by vegetation cover, distance to roads, crime rate, and income deprivation, with candidate sites mainly associated with low-density areas. By integrating site detection with interpretable spatial explanation, this study shows how spatial evidence can support a shift in illegal CDW landfill governance from reactive clean-up towards proactive, risk-informed monitoring, while providing a potential basis for circular construction, enforcement, and waste governance that may be adapted to other data and regulatory contexts.

title: Mapping circular economy indicators for the agri-food sector: Insights from research and technical standards
Integrated sustainability assessment framework for emerging nutrient recovery technologies from wastewater
Meta Life Cycle Assessment, Techno-Economic Analysis, and Risk Assessment of Carbon Mineralization Pathways to Inform Policy Frameworks
abstract: Carbon mineralization can reduce both point-source and legacy CO2 emissions while minimizing long-term risk, and it is essential, urgent, and disconnected. There is no holistic governing carbon mineralization policy in the US or EU, even though carbon capture is already factored into all major global climate models, with mineralization (converting CO2 into stable carbonates) representing a major subset. If mineralization is to bolster the suite of climate mitigation strategies, it is vital that academic guidance be provided to inform the currently underinformed policy direction. To address this, this study presents a meta life cycle and techno-economic analysis of carbon mineralization pathways from both academia and industry, normalizing independent techno-economic, life cycle, and risk assessment (Monte Carlo) results within the context of US and EU policy. Results demonstrate that in situ mineralization achieves the greatest life cycle GHG emission reductions at the lowest cost and is the only pathway capable of gigaton-scale emission reductions commensurate with climate goals. Enhanced rock weathering also consistently delivers net-negative GHG removal at relatively low costs, but ex situ pathways achieve lower GHG emission reductions at higher costs, where several proposed pathways are net-CO2 positive as CO2 emitted throughout the process (transportation, electricity use, and natural gas combustion) offsets CO2 sequestered. Risks of leakage, hazards, global capacity, financial impact, and reversal are also quantitatively and qualitatively compared among the mineralization pathways, demonstrating that in situ mineralization has low financial risk when bolstered by state entities, faces uncertainties in non-governmental organization objection, and, ultimately, all pathways are victims of uncharted policy.

title: Enhancing Sewer Sediment Permeability via Micro-nano Bubble–Mediated Structural Remodeling and EPS Reduction
abstract: Sewer sediments contain dense biofilms enriched with extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), which severely impede chemical infiltration and hinder sediment control. This study uses micro-nano bubbles (MNBs) for the first time to remodel the three-dimensional structure of sewer sediments and reduce their EPS content, thereby enhancing their permeability. Three-dimensional structural analysis revealed that sewer sediments consist of cluster (0.78 mm) and bridged (0.12 mm) biofilms, forming a dense gel network with low porosity. When 20% MNBs were introduced, the complete tracer penetration time decreased from 36 to 8 h, representing a 3.5-times faster migration speed than the baseline group. X-ray computed tomography revealed that MNBs disrupted the sediment matrix: tortuosity decreased from 1.754 to 1.352, the pore volume fraction increased from 0.083 to 0.105, and the number of cluster biofilms decreased from 280 to 178. EPS analysis indicated substantial depth-dependent reductions in protein (5.6 to 1.4 mg/g VSS) and polysaccharide (3.8 to 1.9 mg/g VSS) contents. Finally, the oxidation–reduction potential increased from −280 to −88 mV, shifting the dominant microbial community from anaerobic to aerobic. The underlying mechanism involved the synergistic effects of structural remodeling and EPS reduction, providing theoretical support for applying MNB technology to urban sewage pipe maintenance.

title: Source Attribution, Driving Force Interpretation, and Nature-Based Mitigation of Anthropogenic Water Pollution
abstract: Anthropogenic pollution induced by combined sewer overflow (CSO) threatens urban aquatic ecosystems, yet the source contributions and driving mechanisms of its pollutants from surface runoff and domestic wastewater remain unclear. Here, we propose an analytical framework coupling high-resolution water quality modeling with climatic and socioeconomic (SSP-RCP) projections to characterize spatiotemporal dynamics and source contributions of CSO pollution under changing environments. Random Forest (RF) with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was employed to identify critical drivers of each source. Lorenz curves and Gini coefficient were introduced to evaluate nature-based solutions (NbS) against extreme CSOs. Application of the framework in a typical urban area demonstrated the dominant contribution of runoff pollution (78–88%) to annual loads of 2500–4200 tons, with uncertainty bounds (UB) of 2300–5800 tons. RF-SHAP analysis revealed nonlinear pollution exacerbation around transition points of approximately 8 days for dry-weather period, 0.45 for surface imperviousness, and 2000 inhabitants/km2 for population density. NbS practices mitigated 19–77% of runoff pollution and 52–76% of domestic pollution, decreasing Gini coefficients from 0.69 to 0.49 (UB: 0.40–0.82). The findings provide quantitative support for compliance with the EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, offering a replicable reference for pollution attribution, driver identification, and mitigation assessment under changing environments.

title: Shrinking Non-CO2 Emission Inequality in China’s Municipal Wastewater Treatment
abstract: Integrating emission equity into climate mitigation is essential for sustainable development but remains poorly understood in the wastewater-treatment sector. Here, we develop a long-term, high-resolution emission inventory covering 8703 municipal wastewater treatment plants across China from 2001 to 2020 to assess methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emission trends and their spatial inequality. National emissions increased substantially, although growth rates slowed after 2010 for CH4 and 2015 for N2O. Discrepancies with IPCC-derived estimates highlight the limitations of population-based approaches in capturing emission trends. Economic development dominated emission growth, with wastewater treatment intensity (wastewater treated per unit of GDP) contributing positively, even under scenarios that account for potential changes in emission factors associated with technological and management improvements. Significant emission inequality persisted, with economically developed cities (9% of the population) contributing 16% and 15% of CH4 and N2O emissions in 2020, whereas the least developed group (45% of the population) accounted for 28% and 32%, respectively. Nonetheless, this disparity narrowed over time with Gini coefficients falling from 0.54 to 0.26 for CH4 and from 0.51 to 0.22 for N2O. These findings support geographically differentiated mitigation strategies that prioritize high-emitting areas to promote effective and equitable climate mitigation.

title: Depth-Dependent eDNA Abundances across Ecosystems Inform Deep-Sea Sampling Strategies
abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys are increasingly used to assess marine biodiversity and inform deep-sea environmental decision-making, including mineral resource management and fisheries oversight. Yet standard low-volume protocols inherited from coastal work may be inadequate at depth, and recent findings indicate that depth- and productivity-aware sampling, often requiring high-volume in situ filtration, is needed. Currently no quantitative framework links depth and ecosystem context to define defensible filtration volume targets. We compiled 841 eDNA samples from eight expeditions across the North Atlantic, Wider Caribbean Region, and Pacific (surface to 4000 m) to quantify how recoverable eDNA scales with depth and surface productivity, and to derive depth- and productivity-aware sampling targets. Total eDNA concentration declined with depth as a power law, with attenuation exponents (b) modulated by surface productivity: most gradual in eutrophic waters (b = 0.67), intermediate in mesotrophic (b = 0.90), and steepest in oligotrophic systems (b = 1.25). Volume-weighted models explained 66–88% of the variance. At a fixed extract-concentration target, required filtration volumes diverged ∼7-fold between oligotrophic and eutrophic systems at 200 m and ∼38-fold at 4000 m. Conventional Niskin sampling therefore undersamples deep-sea animal eDNA, particularly in mid- to low-productivity systems. Among laboratory parameters, the assay-specific extract-concentration target exerted greater leverage on required volume than extraction efficiency or elution volume. Volume-aware sampling paired with optimized recovery should be routine in deep-sea eDNA surveys.

title: Drivers of Regional Aerosol pH Differences over Eastern China Quantified with a Thermodynamic Framework
abstract: Aerosol pH governs atmospheric multiphase chemistry, yet quantifying its regional drivers consistently across meteorologically and chemically diverse regions within a single thermodynamically accurate framework remains challenging. Here, we couple the regional chemical transport model Weather Research and Forecasting-Goddard Earth Observing System with Chemistry (WRF-GC) with the Extended Aerosol Inorganics Model (E-AIM) to compute wintertime aerosol pH over six key target regions of eastern China, decompose the drivers of regional pH differences and intramonthly variability through an ammonia gas-particle partitioning framework, and extend this framework to a scenario-response analysis. Monthly mean pH ranges from 2.54 to 4.32, more acidic in the south and more alkaline at higher latitudes. Temperature is the leading driver of the regional pH deviation in the YRD, PRD, and NEP (contributing 58%–63%), whereas in the high-emission NCP and FWP the deviation is instead dominated by NH3 (41%–58%). Negative covariance among the drivers substantially damps intramonthly pH fluctuations, consistent with multiphase buffering. The sensitivity of pH to ammonia reduction rises sharply as aerosols approach an ammonia-poor regime, such that large emission reductions of ammonia would decrease wintertime aerosol pH well beyond linear expectations, with pronounced inter-regional differences. By resolving these drivers on benchmark-level thermodynamics, these results provide a quantitative, region-specific basis for anticipating how aerosol pH responds to differentiated emission-reduction strategies.

title: GCI-TPs: Identifying Potentially Hazardous Transformation Products of Global Chemical Inventory Compounds
abstract: Environmental contamination from an ever-increasing number of chemicals is a subject of high concern, with over one hundred thousand discrete chemicals listed in a recently compiled open global chemical inventory (GCI). As these compounds enter the environment, they often form transformation products (TPs) which may have persistent, mobile, and toxic (PMT) properties. Despite this, less than 1% of compounds have openly available TP information. Although TP prediction can fill some data gaps, the models are prone to combinatorial explosion, and predicted TPs must be prioritized. This study implemented multistep environmental biotic and novel abiotic TP prediction of the ZeroPM GCI chemicals using BioTransformer 4.0, combined with toxicity and mobility models to prioritize which TPs are potentially persistent, mobile, and toxic. The resulting GCI-TPs database contains over 13 million predicted TPs, including 5481 compounds labeled as potential dead-end compounds (compounds that are not predicted to transform further), of which 478 were predicted to be either PMT or PvM compounds. From this, 38 substructures that can act as flags for potential PMT-TP formation were identified. The dead-end PMT-TPs are available on the NORMAN Suspect List Exchange and through the GCI-TPs website (https://gcitps.lcsb.uni.lu/).

title: Dual Pathways of Fe2+ Uptake Drive Intracellular Fenton Chemistry and Ferroptosis-like Cell Death of Escherichia coli upon Exposure to Reduced Nontronite
abstract: Reduced iron-containing clay (RIC) minerals display strong antibacterial activity, yet the intracellular processes underlying bacterial cell death remain poorly understood. Herein, Escherichia coli knockout strains were exposed to a model RIC mineral, reduced nontronite (rNAu-2), to dissect iron influx pathways and the resulting oxidative damage. Two complementary mechanisms of Fe2+ influx were identified: (i) active transport through FeoB proteins and (ii) passive permeation across oxidatively compromised membranes. At low rNAu-2 loading, a feoB mutant accumulated less labile Fe and survived better than the E. coli wild-type (WT), whereas at higher loading, passive permeation dominated and the genotypic differences diminished. Intracellular radical analysis revealed hydroxyl radicals (•OH) as the predominant cytotoxic species. Deleting superoxide dismutases (sodA or sodC) improved bacterial survival by limiting H2O2 availability, whereas loss of peroxidase (ahpC) or catalase (katG) activity elevated H2O2 and •OH production, and heightened cellular vulnerability. rNAu-2 exposure promoted lipid peroxidation and malondialdehyde accumulation, while increasing reliance on glutathione biosynthesis (gshA), indicative of ferroptosis-like cell death. Correspondingly, a recombination-deficient mutant (recA) was hypersensitive to rNAu-2, underscoring the role of oxidative DNA damage in bacterial cell death. These results elucidate the molecular mechanisms of RIC-mediated bacterial killing and significantly advance the current model of antibacterial clay activity.

title: An Innovative Ion Chromatography Method for Determination of Hydroxymethanesulfonate (HMS) in Ambient Air
abstract: Hydroxymethanesulfonate (HMS) is a substantial contributor to atmospheric particulate sulfur, yet its accurate quantification remains challenging due to chemical instability, poor chromatographic separation from sulfate, and the lack of a robust routine filter method. Here, we developed a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-based differential ion chromatography method that overcomes these limitations. Under optimized conditions (n(H2O2):n(HMS) ≥ 4:1, 60 °C, 30 min), HMS conversion to sulfate reaches 97.5 ± 0.3%, enabling indirect quantification via the stable sulfate signal. Recovery on spiked filters was 99.6 ± 1.4% across 0.025–10 mg L–1, with a method detection limit of 0.018 mg L–1. Application to ∼180 PM2.5 samples from a rural North China Plain site shows HMS is not confined to winter haze: autumn concentrations (mean 0.59 ± 0.70 μg m–3, maximum 3.75 μg m–3) were comparable to or higher than winter values, associated with high relative humidity and elevated formaldehyde. Archived filters lost ∼25% of HMS within one month, suggesting historical data may be biased low. The relative contribution of HMS to particulate sulfur increases as total sulfur loading decreases, implying SO2 emission reductions alone may not diminish HMS chemistry. This method provides a robust framework for accurate HMS measurement and improved sulfur budget closure.

title: Tire-Derived Chemicals in Human Populations: A Global Review of Exposure Pathways, Biomonitoring Evidence, Health Outcomes, and Risk Assessment Implications
abstract: Tire wear generates diverse tire-derived chemicals (TDCs), including antioxidants, accelerators, and their transformation products, yet human internal exposure remains poorly characterized. This review provides the first systematic synthesis of global biomonitoring evidence for TDCs in human populations, integrating exposure pathways, biological barrier penetration, and preliminary epidemiological findings. Biomonitoring data spanning four continents reveal widespread detection of multiple TDC classes such as p-phenylenediamines (PPDs), p-phenylenediamine quinones (PPD-Qs), benzothiazoles (BTHs), and benzotriazoles (BTRs), in urine and blood, with urinary concentrations consistently exceeding blood levels. Compound-specific patterns, including the predominance of 6PPD-Q over its parent compound 6PPD and substantial contributions from additional congeners (e.g., DPPD-Q, IPPD-Q, 1-OH-BTR), indicate that single-compound biomarkers are insufficient for capturing overall TDC exposure. TDCs have been detected in cord blood, amniotic fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, breast milk, and semen, documenting occurrence across multiple biological compartments and potential exposure during critical developmental windows. Preliminary epidemiological associations link TDC exposure to adverse birth outcomes, neurodevelopmental effects, and carcinogenic risks, though evidence remains constrained by limited sample sizes and narrow geographic representation: China-based studies dominate the literature, while regions with extensive environmental TDC monitoring (e.g., Europe, North America) largely lack corresponding human data, a mismatch that hinders exposure pathway attribution. Collectively, these findings indicate that TDCs represent a ubiquitous but underrecognized human exposure, and we outline priority considerations for risk assessment, including vulnerable population protection, congener-specific mixture effects, analytical standardization, and interim biomonitoring reference values.

title: Quantifying the Vehicle Emission Reduction Required to Offset Warming-Driven Ozone Increase in Beijing
abstract: Vehicle emissions (VE) reductions are a key pathway for mitigating urban ozone pollution, but their effectiveness under the condition of warming-driven biogenic emission responses remains unclear. An ozone formation path tracing (OFPT) method coupling an observation-based model (OBM) with Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) was used to quantify the contribution of different VOCs for different emission sources to the ozone production rate (PO3). In this study, initial VOC concentrations were reconstructed by correcting for photochemical losses, and an additional constraint on isoprene was applied to improve the assessment of ozone production in Beijing. The results show that initial VOC reconstruction substantially increased PO3 and changed source attribution. Biogenic emissions became the largest single contributor to PO3, whereas VE remained the dominant controllable anthropogenic source because it supplied both VOCs and NOx. After considering the temperature response of isoprene emissions, a 10.7 ± 3.5% reduction in VE was required to offset the O3 increase caused by a 1 °C temperature rise under current conditions. Future-scenario simulations showed that the required VE reductions were lower under the Clean Air scenario (7.1 ± 0.7%) than under the Baseline scenario (11.3 ± 0.1%). These results highlight the need to integrate vehicle electrification, biogenic VOC responses, and warming effects into future ozone control strategies.

Thermo-economic optimization of waste heat-integrated hydrogen production and liquefaction systems
abstract: Liquid hydrogen (H 2 ) is a promising energy carrier for large-scale transport and storage, although its deployment is constrained by high energy consumption, cost, and boil-off losses. To address these challenges, this study investigates the optimization and integration of industrial waste heat recovery (WHR) through hybrid refrigeration and power generation pathways into H 2 liquefaction systems. A base H 2 production and liquefaction system consisting of a proton exchange membrane electrolyzer, a mixed-refrigerant liquefaction cycle, and an ortho–para H 2 conversion unit is developed. Building upon the base configuration, three WHR scenarios utilizing medium-temperature industrial heat sources are proposed and evaluated: (i) an auto-cascade refrigeration process coupled with a Kalina/Rankine power cycle, (ii) a steam-Rankine power plant, and (iii) a combined absorption refrigeration unit and Kalina/Rankine power cycle. Multi-stream heat exchanger networks are designed using pinch analysis to maximize thermal integration and reduce utility consumption. Energy, exergy, and economic assessments are performed by coupling Aspen HYSYS process simulations with MATLAB-based computational modeling. Among the configurations, the steam-Rankine power cycle demonstrates superior thermodynamic and economic performance, achieving a net energy efficiency of 56.69% and a net exergy efficiency of 62.2%. Economic indicators include a payback period of 3.98 years, an annual profit of $9.71 million, and a liquid H 2 prime cost of 5.54 $/kgLH 2 . Sensitivity analysis reveals that the liquid H 2 market price and capital investment are the most influential economic parameters, with the payback period remaining below 6 years when the liquid H 2 price exceeds 6.58 $/kgLH 2 and the capital cost remains below $48.10 million.

OXIDATIVE TORREFACTION OF SUGARCANE BAGASSE: EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE AND CARRIER GAS OXYGEN CONCENTRATION ON FUEL PROPERTIES
abstract: Sugarcane bagasse (SB), a byproduct of the sugar industry, is an abundant and renewable biomass widely used in Brazil for energy production. However, its high moisture content, low energy density, and poor grindability limit its efficiency as a fuel. This study investigates oxidative torrefaction as a thermochemical pre-treatment to improve SB’s fuel properties, comparing the effects of different oxygen concentrations in the carrier gas (0%, 10%, and 20%) at torrefaction temperatures ranging from 200 °C to 300 °C for 30 minutes. The results show that oxidative torrefaction enhances the fixed carbon content and high heating value of SB, while reducing volatile matter and mass yield. Notably, the presence of oxygen in the carrier gas promoted internal heat generation, a phenomenon known as overheating, which enabled improved biomass quality at lower temperatures. This study aims to address a gap in literature by exploring the oxidative torrefaction behavior of sugarcane bagasse and reporting the occurrence of the overheating phenomenon, both of which have received limited attention in previous studies. Despite lower energy and mass yields, the enhancement factor increased significantly under oxidative conditions, indicating improved fuel quality. These findings suggest that oxidative torrefaction offers a promising route for upgrading sugarcane bagasse for bioenergy applications.

Urban perforation under population shrinkage: Insights from trajectory-derived shrinkage typologies in Northeast China
abstract: Intensifying demographic polarization has placed a subset of cities on a trajectory of persistent population decline, accompanied by extensive vacant land and, in some cases, urban perforation. Previous studies have linked population decline to vacant land, but how vacancy varies with the intensity and trajectory of shrinkage remains underexplored. Using shrinking cities in Northeast China, we refined shrinkage typologies with explicit spatio-temporal trajectories, mapped vacant land in central urban areas with a VGG16–U-Net segmentation model, and applied generalized linear mixed models to examine associated factors. Between 2010 and 2020, the region lost more than 10% of its population; 35% of cities experienced severe or extreme shrinkage, and nearly 20% of central urban areas contained vacant land (364.7 km 2 ). By refining shrinkage in both space and time, we find a nonlinear relationship between urban perforation and shrinkage severity. A one-standard-deviation increase in standardized shrinkage is associated with 5% higher odds of perforation. Core districts show lower odds of perforation, while inner suburban and peripheral areas are more heterogeneous. In contrast to the inverted U-shaped relationship reported for increasing urbanization, our study finds a non-monotonic pattern across shrinkage-severity groups. It rises under slight shrinkage, flattens under moderate shrinkage, and resurges under severe shrinkage. Economic vitality most strongly suppresses perforation, whereas building density amplifies it; both peak under moderate shrinkage.

title: Mapping on-street parking using street view imagery: An integrated approach of parking sign and vehicle detection
abstract: The distribution and availability of on-street parking in a city have important implications for transportation, economic, and environmental planning. However, few cities maintain comprehensive mapping of street parking beyond metered zones. Recent studies have proposed computational approaches to automate street parking prediction, but data availability remains a challenge. To address this challenge, this study introduces an integrated framework for mapping street parking using widely available Google Street View images. We develop a computer vision model to detect parking signs and a geometric algorithm to identify stationary vehicles from sequential street view images. A decision tree classifier combines sign and vehicle detection results to predict the presence of street parking at the road-segment level. Trained with 765 ground-truth labels combining official metered-zone records and manual annotation of street-view imagery, the classifier correctly identifies approximately 85% (103 out of 121) of the true cases in the validation set. The two detection approaches offer complementary information for predicting street parking beyond regulated zones, especially in residential areas. Our framework can support municipalities with limited databases in developing city-scale street parking maps.

title: Rivers, peaks and the Car–Transit time gap: Evidence from cross-river travel in Wuhan, China
abstract: Rivers funnel urban travel onto a few crossings, but whether this increases the car–public transport (PT) travel-time gap, and how the gap changes in congestion, remains uncertain. We integrate one week of mobile phone origin–destination flows and route-planning travel times for 426 one-kilometre cells in central Wuhan. The modal competitiveness gap (MCG) is the demand-weighted mean log ratio of car to PT travel time. We contrast cross-Yangtze with other trips using fixed effects, measure peak narrowing of the gap (ΔMCG) and link it to place characteristics with spatially cross-validated random forests. PT takes 2.4 times as long as the car off-peak but 1.8 and 1.6 times in the morning and evening peaks, because car times rise by 34% and 43% while PT times change very little. For given origins and destinations, crossing the Yangtze raises the PT/car ratio by 9-12%; simple comparisons obscure this because cross-river trips end where PT is relatively good. At the morning peak PT still takes over twice the car’s time for 33% of cross-river trips, mostly far from direct cross-river metro stations. Static place characteristics explain little of the narrowing. Peak gains arise from car congestion, yet make metro-based PT an effective complement for river crossing.

title: Coordinating interactive and automated operations in generative urban design: The FLEXUrban prototype
abstract: Generative urban design (GUD) offers an important methodological approach for exploring urban morphology configurations under complex constraints. Despite continued advances in generative techniques, coordinating automated operations with editable intermediate states and local intervention across multi-stage workflows remains a challenge. This paper presents FLEXUrban, a web-based GUD prototype that connects interactive editing and batch parameter assignment within a shared workflow. The system comprises three interrelated modules: tensor-field-guided hierarchical site subdivision organized around division-line dependencies; type-based parametric massing that maps planning controls to building geometry and calculated metrics; and grayscale image mapping that distributes area weights, target FAR, and buildable-area settings across regions. Controlled system-level tests examined local subdivision edits, massing responses to parameter changes, and batch generation under multiple grayscale fields. The results show that local edits reconstructed indexed dependency branches while retaining unaffected regions, planning-control inputs produced corresponding geometric and metric responses, and grayscale fields generated distinct spatial distributions with approximate target matching. FLEXUrban demonstrates how established GUD techniques can be organized around explicit parameter mappings, editable intermediate objects, and inspectable outputs for early-stage morphological prototyping.

title: Uncertainty and Real Estate Return Predictability: Evidence from U.S. REITs
abstract: We show that fluctuations in financial uncertainty generate substantial and predictable variation in U.S. real estate returns. Using six real estate return series and a comprehensive set of predictors, we document strong forecasting performance both in-sample and out-of-sample, with out-of-sample $$R^2$$ exceeding 8%. A one standard deviation increase in financial uncertainty is associated with an approximately 1.5% decline in next-month REIT returns. To uncover the mechanisms behind this predictability, we apply the Campbell–Shiller present-value decomposition, which separates unexpected returns into cash-flow news, capturing revisions to expected future earnings, and discount-rate news, capturing revisions to expected returns. These components are derived from a parsimonious VAR that includes asset-specific dividend–price ratios, allowing us to trace the information content of financial uncertainty. The evidence reveals that financial uncertainty is associated primarily with negative cash-flow news, rather than innovations in expected returns. Relative to the aggregate stock market, real estate assets respond more strongly and persistently to uncertainty shocks, potentially reflecting both information frictions and delayed changes in underlying real estate fundamentals. In line with these findings, simple forecast-based strategies deliver economically meaningful gains, with annualized utility improvements exceeding 10%.

title: When Does Business Strategy Increase Climate‐Change Exposure? The Contingent Role of Managerial Ability
abstract: Why does the same business strategy simultaneously mitigate and amplify firms' exposure to climate‐related risks? Prior research offers conflicting predictions regarding the environmental implications of innovation‐oriented Prospector strategies, suggesting that they can both mitigate and amplify risk. We address this puzzle by developing a contingency framework that reconceptualises climate‐change exposure as arising from how firms organise and govern strategic flexibility. Drawing on organisational theory, the natural resource‐based view and a Neo‐Durkheimian perspective on risk governance, we argue that Prospector strategies embed a fundamental flexibility–control tension that simultaneously enhances adaptive capacity and increases coordination complexity. Climate‐change exposure therefore reflects how organisations manage and resolve this tension. We conceptualise managerial ability as a governance‐structuring capability that organises attention, prioritises competing risk signals and aligns dispersed activities under uncertainty. Using 13,547 firm‐year observations of US public firms from 2001 to 2024 and a machine learning‐based measure of climate‐change exposure derived from earnings call transcripts, we find that Prospector strategies are associated with higher exposure, but this relationship is attenuated in firms with higher managerial ability. Our findings advance a governance‐based perspective in which exposure emerges from the interplay between strategy, managerial capability and the organisational construction of uncertainty.

title: Board Human Capital Heterogeneity, Eco‐Initiatives and Carbon Performance: The Mediating Role of Firm Size
abstract: We examine the relationship between board human capital heterogeneity (BHCH), eco‐initiatives (EI) and carbon performance (CP). Further, we examine the mediation of firm size (FS) between BHCH and CP. Drawing on multi‐theoretical framework, we argue that heterogeneous boards enhance monitoring quality and provide access to diverse knowledge and resources, which collectively support superior environmental decision‐making. Our sample consists of 9608 global firms from 71 countries during the period between 2015 and 2022. Our results report that BHCH and EI are positively and significantly related to CP. Moreover, we find that FS partially mediates the relationship between BHCH and CP. Our study documents that firms should have board with BHCH, and better EI strategies aim at capturing carbon issues. Besides, our findings evidence that FS is the crucial factor that assures resource base in the firm, which facilitates the board of directors to take timely and quick decisions regarding corporate contemporary issues like climate change issues. The findings contribute to the corporate governance and sustainability literature by moving beyond traditional demographic measures of board diversity and emphasising the strategic importance of human capital heterogeneity. The study also highlights the conditional nature of governance effectiveness, demonstrating that board attributes must be aligned with firm‐level capabilities and environmental strategies to achieve meaningful carbon performance improvements. Our study findings have greater implications in policy‐making levels and industry practitioners.

Field Aging of Biochar Drives SOC Accumulation by Promoting Photosynthetic Carbon Input and Shifting Soil Microbial Communities
abstract: Biochar application is an effective strategy for enhancing the soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration. However, the extent to which biochar aging affects the SOC sequestration remains unclear. In this study, we investigated SOC dynamics, photosynthetic carbon allocation patterns, and soil microbial characteristics across a 1- to 5-year biochar aging gradient in a wheat farmland. The results revealed that the SOC content increased by 20.7% after 1 year of biochar application, primarily because of an increase in particulate organic carbon (POC), and increased by an additional 14.8% over the next 4 years, which resulted from additional increases in both POC and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC). The total 13C assimilation increased by 19.9% and 33.0% after 1 and 5 years of biochar application, respectively. Moreover, biochar application promoted the accumulation of 13C in POC, while 5 years of biochar application also increased the assimilated 13C in MAOC. Furthermore, biochar aging altered the soil bacterial community and increased the abundance of saprotrophic fungi, which were strongly related to SOC dynamics. In summary, our results indicate that biochar aging promotes SOC sequestration by promoting photosynthetic carbon assimilation and facilitating the transformation of plant-derived carbon into SOC related to shifts in the soil microbial community.

title: Application-dependent transmit power for auto-induced uplink exposure assessment from in-situ mobile phone usage in four European countries
abstract: Radiofrequency electromagnetic field (RF-EMF) exposure from smartphones depends strongly on user behavior and network conditions, particularly in modern 4G and 5G networks due to increased spatio-temporal variability in uplink transmissions. Understanding exposure differences between realistic usage scenarios is essential for accurate personal exposure assessment. Previous studies mainly focused on legacy technologies or were limited to one country. This study quantifies and compares in-situ average transmit (Tx) powers for voice calls, WhatsApp voice calls, WhatsApp video calls, and uplink file transfers across four European countries, and analyzes how differences between applications, signal strength across locations, and exposure duration relate to uplink Tx power variability. Measurements were performed in 148 outdoor microenvironments in Belgium, France, Hungary, and Switzerland. Trained researchers executed four standardized usage scenarios while network monitoring tools (QualiPoc, Nemo) recorded network parameters from the phone. Uplink file transfers showed the highest Tx powers (median 19.50 dBm), followed by WhatsApp video calls (8.67 dBm) and WhatsApp voice calls (4.20 dBm). Voice calls resulted in the lowest Tx powers (0.27 dBm). 4G dominated usage in Belgium and Hungary, while Switzerland and France showed predominantly simultaneous 4G and 5G operation. The average Tx power exhibited increasing trends with duty cycle and throughput, and an inverse relationship with Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP). Uplink file transfer duration also depended strongly on RSRP. Uplink exposure was shown to be highly application- and location-dependent. These findings support improved personal RF-EMF exposure and dose assessment and provide the first multi-country comparison between applications including non-standalone 5G.

The Real Effects of Credit Ratings on Credit Default Swap Market: The Sovereign Ceiling Channel
abstract: We examine whether credit ratings convey incremental information to the credit default swap (CDS) market. We use sovereign‐ceiling‐induced rating downgrades as an exogenous shock in a difference‐in‐differences model to identify the effect of rating changes on CDS spreads. We find that CDS spreads of treated firms increase by 25.96% more than those of control firms following sovereign downgrades. The effect is stronger for firms with lower earnings performance, R&D, intangible assets, and higher leverage, particularly in countries with less private bank lending. CDS portfolio strategies based on these downgrades generate abnormal returns, indicating that rating downgrades convey non‐public information.

title: Environmental Strategic Alliances and Corporate Environmental Investment
abstract: Environmental degradation has intensified the need for firms to expand environmental investment, yet its firm‐level antecedents remain underexplored. We examine environmental strategic alliances (ESAs) as one such antecedent. Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2007 to 2022, we find that ESA participation is associated with higher environmental investment. Mechanism tests show that ESAs promote investment by easing capital constraints and facilitating the transfer of partners' environmental know‐how. The effect is stronger in firms with collaborative cultures, but weaker for contractual alliances and when partners have poor regulatory compliance records. Our findings highlight ESAs as a key collaborative driver of environmental investment.

title: Ethical concern without collective power: consumer agency and labour precarity in Indonesia’s platform economy
abstract: This study examines consumer agency and ethical concerns in Indonesia’s ride-hailing economy regarding labour precarity and regulation. Surveying 928 users (May 2025), the research challenges the ‘self-interested consumer’ model, revealing strong normative support for fairness: over 98% of respondents favour stronger regulation and social protection for workers, while 83.9% support driver reclassification as employees. However, the findings highlight the limits of consumer ethics. Agency is primarily enacted through individualised, platform-based actions – like tipping or ratings – that mitigate symptoms without addressing structural issues. Extra-platform advocacy remains episodic and lacks the institutional backing of unions or civil society. The article argues that the political impact of consumer agency depends on organisational channels to collectivise moral concern. Without such infrastructure, individual ethical acts may inadvertently stabilise the reproduction of labor precarity rather than transform it.

title: Disaggregating workplace domination: supervision, governance, and ownership
abstract: Recent debates on the future of work have foregrounded platform labour, automation, and digital management as central sites of contemporary domination. Much literature however analyses domination in the firm at a high level of abstraction. Less attention is paid to how different configurations of authority across firms and sectors organise discretionary power. Hierarchical firms institutionalise authority through distinct configurations of managerial supervision, organisational governance, and ownership-level strategic control. Drawing on republican political theory as a diagnostic lens, this article conceptualises firms as regimes of rule and distinguishes three types of work in which arbitrary power is structured in different ways: supervisory-intensive employment, professional and technical work, and work undertaken under conditions of financially mobile ownership. The relative salience of these loci of authority shapes both the form domination assumes and the institutional reforms capable of constraining it. Regulatory constraints on supervision, workplace democracy, and reforms to ownership and residual control rights do not bear equally across these contexts. By shifting attention away from technological change alone towards the institutional organisation of authority within contemporary firms, the article shows how different types of institutional reform address distinct sites of domination.

title: Climate extrapolation and relative asset prices: Evidence from Bordeaux Premier Cru wine auctions
Cognitive Ambidexterity: Balancing Algorithmic Efficiency and Contextual Judgement in AI-Enabled Decision Systems
abstract: AI-enabled decision systems make algorithmic recommendations appear objective and ready for action before contextual, ethical, and stakeholder concerns are fully considered. This study examines how leaders preserve judgment under these conditions. We develop cognitive ambidexterity as a leader-level meta-cognitive capability through which managers balance algorithmic exploitation with contextual exploration in AI-mediated decisions. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first examine five U.K. procurement and infrastructure organizations and identify four mechanisms of cognitive ambidexterity. We then examine these mechanisms through vignette experiments with managers. The findings show that leaders preserve contextual judgment by treating AI outputs as interpretive cues, calibrating trust under ambiguity, slowing decisions when reflection is needed, and building supports that make algorithmic recommendations contestable. The study extends ambidexterity theory by showing how exploration–exploitation tensions are cognitively regulated when exploitation is embedded in algorithmic decision processes. It also uses leadership cognition and Upper Echelons Theory to explain why leaders differ in their capacity to enact this regulation. Together, these insights position cognitive ambidexterity as a critical leader-level capability for using AI’s efficiency gains while preserving the contextual judgment.

title: War and Entrepreneurship: A Synthetic Control Study of the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
abstract: Is war good or bad for entrepreneurship? Entrepreneurs are often situated in extreme environments characterized by violent conflict. Yet existing entrepreneurship scholarship has largely examined war and conflict only at the micro or meso level, leaving the aggregate, macro-level entrepreneurial consequences of large-scale war underexplored. We provide a synthetic control study of entrepreneurial dynamics in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict during 2009 to 2019 as a first step toward bridging this gap. Relative to the synthetic counterfactual, registered LLCs in Ukraine declined by approximately 13% at the 2016 peak (74,000 missing firms) before recovering toward the synthetic trajectory by 2019. Self-employment in Ukraine dropped by approximately 4 percentage points (pp) at the 2015 peak, corresponding to roughly 680,000 Ukrainians no longer self-employed relative to the counterfactual, with partial recovery to a residual shortfall of approximately 280,000 by 2019. For Russia, the gap is delayed but accumulating, widening from −0.4 pp in 2015 to −1.6 pp by 2019. This corresponds to approximately 1.56 million missing LLCs relative to the counterfactual, a 32% relative loss. The contraction in Russian LLCs accumulates rather than attenuates over time. In Ukraine, we also observe a gender gap in post-2014 self-employment deviations from the synthetic counterfactual, with female self-employment falling more than male self-employment. To interpret these findings, we propose a conceptual framework that combines critical-junctures theory with the literature on entrepreneurship under authoritarian and democratic institutional regimes, arguing that the divergent post-2014 institutional trajectories of Russia and Ukraine help explain the contrasting entrepreneurial patterns we observe.
