title: Disclosing work-from-home flexibility to compete for talent? Evidence from job postings
Does supervisor’s dissociating morality from performance stimulate subordinates to commit instigated incivility?
Generative Artificial Intelligence in Project Management: A Paradox Perspective on Tensions, Responses and Outcomes
Bridging project management and circular economy research
From knowledge to agility: transforming B2B marketing agility across GAI maturity configurations
Trusting the interface: conversational AI service quality and partnership outcomes in B2B service relationships
Neurodivergence in B2B markets: examining ADHD among salespeople
When expert screening and crowd validation disagree: signal discordance and venture quality in life-science equity crowdfunding
abstract: Specialized equity-crowdfunding platforms generate three non-equivalent signals about each venture: expert screening before launch, visible early traction during the campaign, and venture outcomes observed years later. These signals are often studied separately, even though platforms and investors must interpret them jointly, especially when they disagree. Using ninety-nine rounds closed on Capital Cell, a life-science equity-crowdfunding platform, between 2016 and 2023, we study this problem as one of signal discordance. We build block-level measures that compare expert evaluations, crowd traction, and lead-investor dominance, and we relate their agreement or disagreement to post-campaign venture quality, measured through venture status and valuation multiples. To analyse a small, noisy, and block-structured dataset under epistemic uncertainty, we use a soft quantum kernel whose softness is calibrated from the dispersion of expert scores. The method is used here as a tool for mixed-signal settings rather than as a claim of general quantum superiority, and we benchmark it against classical alternatives and a hardware implementation on the Quantum Blue QPU at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. The results show that expert screening and crowd traction are distinct informational objects, that their disagreement is especially informative about long-run quality, and that specialized platforms add value when expert signals remain informative where early market validation does not.

title: The Business of Exclusion: Securitising Stray Dogs and the Marketisation of the Commons
abstract: The pursuit of safety has become a moral economy through which the commons are reorganised under the banner of protection. This article examines the governance of stray dogs in Turkey to show how care is moralised, securitised and ultimately monetised. Tracing discourse, law and procurement between 2019 and 2025, the analysis reveals securitisation as a mechanism of enclosure that reconfigures an existing service market through administrative classification and public procurement, converting moral vocabularies of compassion into fiscal infrastructures of control. Business actors appear as co-producers of the resulting field, positioning themselves within an expanding procurement market and translating bureaucratic order into commercial return. Seen alongside contemporary enclosures of digital, ecological and genetic life, the Turkish case exposes a new frontier of accumulation: the marketisation of safety itself, in which protection becomes profitable and the very capacity to care is reorganised as a domain of enterprise.

title: Generative AI collaboration and expatriate career adaptability: a career construction perspective on sustainable career development
abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: The variant similarity sweet spot: how word-of-mouth moderates new product launch in e-commerce
abstract: Online retailers encounter an important decision when introducing a new product variant: how similar should the new variant be compared with existing variants? Too much similarity may lead to cannibalization, while too little may reduce its appeal to existing customers. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness theory, this study examines how retailers should introduce new product variants, focusing on variant similarity’s impact on sales performance and the moderating role of word of mouth (WoM). Analyzing data from an online retailer on a leading e-commerce platform, we find that similarity between new and existing variants exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with both new and existing variants’ sales, highlighting the need for optimal distinctiveness to balance category legitimacy and product differentiation. Furthermore, WoM moderates these relationships by intensifying the curvilinear effects. Findings offer insights for online retailers’ variant introduction strategies and contribute to the literature on e-commerce category management, new product launch, and WoM.

title: Digital economy and circular economy: Pathways to green transition
Does How We Choose Affect What We Choose? Analytic Versus Holistic Thinking in Information Search and the Compromise Effect
abstract: This research examines how consumers' cognitive styles, analytic versus holistic, influence how they choose (information processing patterns) and what they choose (final selection). In an eye‐tracking experiment, we show that participants primed with an analytic thinking style exhibit eye‐movement patterns consistent with attribute‐wise comparisons, whereas those primed with a holistic thinking style exhibit eye‐movement patterns consistent with within‐alternative, brand‐wise comparisons, even after controlling for habitual left‐to‐right reading tendencies. In two behavioral experiments involving product choices, participants primed with an analytic thinking style exhibit a stronger compromise effect (a preference for moderate options over extreme options) than those primed with a holistic thinking style. This pattern is consistent with the proposed explanation that analytic processing heightens sensitivity to extreme attribute values, whereas holistic processing integrates attribute information and reduces the influence of such contextual cues. These findings contribute to the consumer decision‐making literature by demonstrating how cognitive style shapes information processing and choice, and offer implications for marketing strategies and the design of decision aids such as product comparison tables.

title: EXPRESS: Fallacies in Research on Inter-Organizational Strategic Sensemaking: Toward an Ecological Perspective
abstract: In this essay, we critique research in the domain of collective strategy that adopts a reductionist perspective on inter-organizational strategic sensemaking by neglecting its embeddedness within multiple intra-organizational sensemaking processes unfolding simultaneously. To overcome this limitation, we conceptualize inter-organizational sensemaking as an ecology of interrelated inter- and intra-organizational sensemaking processes, advocating for a return to the ecological roots of collective strategy research. This ecological perspective reveals three fallacies that have plagued existing research and produced simplified accounts of inter-organizational sensemaking: the fallacy of isolationism, the fallacy of functional conflation, and the fallacy of transfer logic. By foregrounding the interdependence, heterogeneity, and loose coupling of strategic sensemaking processes, our ecological perspective provides a richer conceptual foundation for understanding how organizations collectively make sense of complex strategic challenges while simultaneously advancing their own organizational agendas.

title: Too lean? Exploring the nonlinear environmental implications of Factory Physics
abstract: Purpose Operations and supply chain managers are continuously pulled between efficiency to reduce costs and buffering for resilience. These endeavors are at the heart of Factory Physics, which theoretically defines the levers managers use to control the physics of an organization. However, organizations are also under pressure to incorporate environmental impacts into their decision-making due to consumer and regulatory pressures. With managerial decisions on inventory turnover and capacity utilization having direct environmental impacts, managers are thus challenged to consider environmental performance alongside economic consequences in an increasingly demanding environment. Taking a Factory Physics lens, this research focuses on the environmental impact of inventory turnover and capacity utilization, while considering potential nonlinearities. Design/methodology/approach A high-dimensional fixed-effects approach is employed with a panel dataset of 4,638 operations and supply chain firms from 2002 to 2026. Findings The results suggest that increasing inventory turnover and capacity utilization improve environmental performance. However, there is a nonlinearity: beyond a certain point, additional inventory turnover no longer improves environmental performance. A similar effect is found for capacity utilization when financial leverage is high. Extending this in a post hoc analysis, the findings suggest that capacity utilization is dominant in reducing environmental harm. Further, increasing inventory turnover only improves environmental performance in later stages of the process. Originality/value This research provides a holistic examination of the environmental implications of Factory Physics, considering the multiple levers managers use to manage Factory Physics and the potential for nonlinear outcomes.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Corporate Misconduct and Artificial Intelligence (AI): Ethical Cost of AI Adoption
Sustainability in Charity Retail: Conflicts in (In)Sufficiency
abstract: Sufficiency has been receiving attention as a means to achieve sustainability. Insights on how to operationalise sufficiency in practice are limited and absent in the context of ecologically constrained organisations, such as, charities. Charities are viewed as critical to sustainability due to their reuse business model; however, charity income is dropping due to the saturation of low-quality and value clothing donations generated by ever-increasing production and consumption of (ultra)fast fashion. This is placing resource (e.g. reliance on volunteer labour) and ecological (e.g. finding reuse routes) burdens on an already constrained sector, highlighting the urgency for charities to future proof the retail businesses foundational to their fundraising efforts. To address this challenge, this research adopts an ethic of sufficiency to introduce business model innovation to charity retail. Drawing on interviews and observations with charity staff, collaborating experts and consumers as donor and retail users, we examine transition to a clothing rental model offering social and ecological sufficiency. We find that the two competing ethics of: (1) sufficiency representing enough and driving deceleration and (2) insufficiency representing not enough and driving acceleration, compete for primacy. While sufficiency can counter challenges arising from insufficiency, competition between them creates contradictory pressures for the charity. This is further exasperated by a misalignment between organisation and consumer experiences of sufficiency. The theoretical and practical implications of the findings for sufficiency, charity retail, rental and consumption are discussed.

title: From Integrity to Entangrity: A Diffractive Reading of a Sustainability Manager’s Entangled Subjectivity
abstract: Integrity is one of the key concepts in business ethics and has conventionally been understood as a quality of the autonomous ethical subject. Relational approaches have challenged this view by showing how integrity is shaped through everyday human encounters and organisational practices. Feminist post-humanist thinking takes this challenge further by questioning human-centred understandings of ethical subjectivity itself. Drawing on Karen Barad’s articulations of entanglement and diffraction, this paper explores what happens to integrity when ethical subjectivity is understood as emerging through more-than-human entanglements. Through a collaborative diffractive reading of theoretical discussions on integrity and entanglement, alongside a sustainability manager’s empirical account, we trace three recurring patterns of entangled subjectivity: sensing that something is not right, carrying the weight of responsibility, and aspiring towards more liveable entanglements. These patterns show how integrity comes to matter through embodied, affective, material, and organisational entanglements. Building on these patterns, this research develops ‘entangrity’ as a relational and lively reconceptualisation of integrity, understood as an expression of entangled subjectivity. Entangrity renews questions surrounding ambiguous ethical subjectivities by pointing to the way ethical tensions are dwelt within, rather than ‘navigated’. It also exemplifies how diffractive reading can enable conceptual development whilst keeping different and even ontologically distinct theoretical perspectives in play. Thus, we invite thinking-with the possibilities of what ethical subjectivity and response-ability might become as posthuman business ethics continues to be developed.

title: Pre-treatment biopsychosocial predictors of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy trajectories in people with breast cancer
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) affects many people receiving taxane treatment for breast cancer. Symptom trajectories vary, with some recovering, and others experiencing persistent, or delayed worsening (coasting) symptoms. The prevalence and predictors of these trajectories remain unclear. This study identified the prevalence and biopsychosocial predictors of CIPN persistence, improvement, and coasting within 3 months post-treatment. This secondary analysis included participants treated with taxanes for stage I–III breast cancer who completed the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy/Gynecologic Oncology Group–Neurotoxicity-4 (FACT/GOG-NTX-4) at baseline, post-chemotherapy, and 3 months later. A minimally important difference (MID) from baseline on the FACT/GOG-NTX-4 defined persistence, improvement, coasting, and no MID-CIPN (below the MID threshold at each assessment) trajectories. Baseline assessments included self-reported pain/well-being, sensory, balance, and lower limb physical functioning measures, and sociodemographic and treatment data were collected. Among 102 participants (51.57 ± 11.24 years), persistence occurred in 34.3%, improvement in 25.5%, coasting in 6.9%, and no MID-CIPN in 33.3%. Compared to no MID-CIPN, older age (OR = 1.120; 95% CI 1.026–1.222), higher expected pain (OR = 1.630; 95% CI 1.082–2.456), and cold hyperalgesia at the foot (OR = 1.130; 95% CI 1.018–1.254) predicted persistence. Greater fatigue predicted improvement (OR = 0.904; 95% CI 0.845–0.968). No predictors were identified for coasting. CIPN trajectories are heterogeneous. Age and pre-treatment pain expectations, cold hyperalgesia, and fatigue differentiate patients with persistent CIPN and those likely to improve from those with no CIPN. Early identification of individuals at risk for persistent neurotoxicity may support risk stratification and guide targeted supportive care strategies.

title: State of temperature estimation for cylindrical lithium-ion batteries: challenges and solutions
Model-based prediction of temperature evolution in solid-state batteries with minimal experimental data: A case study on composite cathodes under thermal ramp
abstract: While solid-state batteries (SSBs) are presumed to be safer than conventional LIBs, recent studies suggest that they can undergo a quicker and more severe thermal runaway than LIB cells. We have developed a modelling framework to investigate safety of SSBs by linking material-scale measurements to electrode- or cell-scale thermal behaviour. The proposed framework directly incorporates differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) heat flow measurements obtained at a single heating rate as a time-dependent heat source to simulate the temperature evolution of electrodes and cells under prescribed thermal ramp conditions. With minimum experimental data and computational fitting efforts, our model allows for consistent thermal-safety comparisons across cell formats and rapid screening of SSB materials. We implemented our model for cathode composites of SSBs, consisting of LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 and eight different oxide- and sulphide-based solid electrolytes, exposed to a thermal ramp and simulated their temperature evolution. The simulations were run in three representative formats for SSBs: coin, single-layer pouch, and multilayer-pouch cells. The results show that the temperature increase in sulphide-based cathode composites is significantly higher than that of oxide-based composites. Among the different formats, the temperature increases considerably higher in cathode composites with multilayer-pouch format, compared to others. The model was also applied to two 24 Ah LIB cells under a 150 °C oven test, whose temperature evolution results has been reported in the literature. The simulated temperature evolution showed good agreement with the experimental measurements and the corresponding kinetic-based model under the investigated thermal conditions, demonstrating the capability of the simplified approach to translate calorimetric heat generation data into full-cell thermal behaviour and its potential applicability to battery systems with different chemistries.

title: Risk-aware operation of electric vehicle aggregators in uncertain electricity markets using game theory and Markowitz framework
Industry–region interactions shape decarbonisation policy effectiveness while renewable deliverability bounds transferability
Evacuation route optimization for mixed bus fleets nder energy consumption uncertainty prior to typhoon landfall
Integrating farm and solar business practices for agrivoltaics financial analysis
Who should govern public energy communities? The role of environmental awareness and privacy cost
abstract: Energy communities are becoming an important instrument of the clean energy transition, but their performance depends on how they are governed. We develop a model in which a municipality invests in renewable-energy infrastructure and chooses between public management and delegation to a private aggregator. Consumers differ in their willingness to pay, value self-produced energy, and incur privacy costs when consumption data are used beyond the operational baseline. Under the symmetric benchmark, private governance produces a smaller community because the aggregator applies a monopoly participation margin and does not internalize the benefit that additional members create for the rest of the community. Public governance therefore expands participation, while investment timing depends on how the operating surplus is allocated between the municipality, members, and the private operator. We then show that correcting the private participation distortion is only a partial alignment result: implementing the public-optimal community size does not by itself align member utility or investment timing. A regulated delegation contract can use a per-member inclusion payment to align participation, a membership-independent concession payment to align investment timing, and data-use restrictions to control privacy exposure. Finally, a numerical example relaxes operational symmetry by allowing the private operator to manage self-consumption more efficiently than the public operator. In this case, regulated delegation can combine public participation objectives with private operational efficiency when the relevant contractual margins are observable and enforceable.

title: Thermodynamic modeling of underground storage caverns in compressed air energy storage systems: Classification, development, and applications
Policy is essential to curb plastic pollution: the example of California’s senate Bill 54
abstract: As plastic pollution continues to rise, policies to curb plastic consumption and waste generation are urgently needed. Using material flow analysis, economic input-output models, and trend projection, we construct a business-as-usual baseline of plastic consumption, and plastic waste generation and management in California for 1950–2050. We then simulate the impact of source reduction, recycled content, and recycling rate mandates on plastic production, waste generation, and associated greenhouse gas emissions using California’s Senate Bill 54 as a case study. We find that, if implemented successfully, Senate Bill 54 could reduce plastic waste by nearly 56 Mt and decrease associated greenhouse gas emissions by 164 Mt CO 2 equivalent between 2025 and 2050. Our results highlight the importance of integrated, multi-faceted policy by showing the effect of policy interventions in isolation and in combination. Our modeling approach provides a broadly applicable framework to support the design and evaluation of evidence-based plastic management strategies.

title: Gas Chromatography-High Resolution Mass Spectrometry Spatiotemporal Screening of River Rhine Suspended Particulate Matter (2005–2022): An Early-Warning Tool for Contaminants of Concern
abstract: Environmental monitoring of archived suspended particulate matter (SPM) provides a basis for retrospective assessment of emerging contaminants in river systems. This study used yearly resolved SPM samples from two sites in the River Rhine, Koblenz and Weil am Rhein, to generate and prioritize gas chromatography high-resolution mass spectrometry (GC-HRMS) data within an early warning system (EWS). The aim was to identify potential contaminants of emerging concern (CEC) showing increasing temporal trends. Of ∼3300 blank-filtered and aligned features, ∼400 exhibited significant trends (p < 0.05), of which ∼80 showed increasing trends. Tentative annotation was performed using spectral libraries which tentatively identified 234 compounds. Cross-referencing tentatively identified compounds showing increasing trends with ECOSAR-modeled aquatic toxicity identified 12 compounds with significant increasing trends and high predicted aquatic toxicity (ρ > 0.6, LC50/EC50 < 1 mg/L). Among the compounds prioritized, tentatively annotated α-methylstyrene oligomers and linear siloxanes accounted for four and three compounds, respectively, indicating recurrent compound-group signals warranting further investigation into their identities, potential co-occurring isomers, concentrations, sources, and subsequently associated risks. Although tentative identification remained a limitation of the GC-HRMS workflow, which relied on hard ionization, these results demonstrate the value of sample archives for temporally resolved prioritization in HRMS-based EWS approaches and highlight their potential for identifying potential CEC.

title: Oxygen Vacancies in Metal-Based Catalysts for Advanced Oxidation Processes: From Defect States to Reaction Pathways
abstract: Oxygen vacancies (Vo) engineering can regulate oxidant adsorption and interfacial electron transfer in metal-based catalysts for advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), thereby overcoming inefficient oxidant activation, sluggish charge transfer, and limited pathway selectivity. Despite rapid advances in Vo synthesis, characterization, and catalytic applications, a unified understanding of how Vo govern the catalytic process remains lacking. This Review first summarizes the construction, classification, physicochemical properties, and characterization of Vo, followed by a critical evaluation of their identification as catalytically active sites. We then elucidate how Vo regulate the adsorption, activation, and transformation of oxidants and reactants, thereby governing both reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated oxidation and electron-transfer processes (ETPs). Particular emphasis is placed on the emerging synergistic interactions between Vo and neighboring active sites, including metal centers, other vacancy defects, and heterojunction interfaces. More importantly, a unified framework is proposed to rationalize the divergent reaction pathways induced by Vo from the perspectives of catalyst–oxidant interactions, Vo concentration, and Vo type. These factors collectively determine local electronic structures, interfacial charge-transfer behaviors, and spin-state evolution, ultimately dictating the pathway selection between ROS generation and ETP. Finally, key challenges in Vo engineering, active-site identification, and pathway discrimination are highlighted together with future opportunities for advancing Vo-mediated AOPs. By shifting the focus from Vo generation to Vo-state regulation, this Review provides guidance for designing next-generation AOP catalysts with tunable reactivity, pathway selectivity, and long-term stability.

title: Interfacial Water Hydrogen-Bond Network Reorientation Accelerates Advanced Oxidation for Micropollutant Abatement
abstract: Interfacial water rigid hydrogen-bond (HB) networks impose significant thermodynamic and mass-transfer barriers in heterogeneous advanced oxidation processes. Herein, we propose a decoupled interfacial water oxidation process (decoupled interfacial oxidation process (DIOP)) strategy that dynamically reorganizes interfacial water to achieve pronounced kinetic acceleration and high decontamination selectivity. Localized electronic polarization drives cooperative reorientation of interfacial H2O, transforming rigid ice-like water clusters into a dynamic zigzag-like HB configuration. This structural relaxation significantly reduces interfacial solvent reorganization energy, shortens electron tunneling distances, and generates angstrom-scale dynamic low-density water microregions. These fluidic microregions selectively enrich small-molecule pollutants over bulky natural organic matter through dipole alignment and surface binding affinities. Density functional theory calculations and electrochemical analyses demonstrate that interfacial H2O reorientation serves as a pivotal gating step, promoting inner-sphere electron transfer between peracetic acid and target contaminants. The quantum probability density microkinetic model was developed to elucidate the crucial role of interfacial water orientation and HB restructuring frequency in mitigating mass-transfer limitations. Furthermore, the DIOP continuous-flow device achieves a 100% micropollutant removal over 180 h with minimal metal leaching. This work elucidates the role of interfacial H2O dynamics in heterogeneous oxidation, offering a generalizable design strategy for advanced wastewater purification.

title: Revisiting the Characteristics and Performance of Acid-Treated Polyamide Membranes: Fundamental Insights and Implications
abstract: Acid treatment of polyamide reverse osmosis (RO) and nanofiltration (NF) membranes is a commonly used approach for membrane cleaning and modification. However, there are contradictory observations on the effects of acid treatment in the current literature. Herein, we systematically characterized the changes in the physicochemical properties of both RO and NF membranes under different acid treatment conditions. Both acid-treated RO and NF membranes exhibited similar surface physicochemical characteristics compared with their respective original membranes. Interestingly, the acid-treated RO membrane showed a nearly doubled water permeance while maintaining high salt rejection. During the acid treatment, the fully aromatic RO membrane underwent selective removal of monomers/oligomers from the bottom region of its asymmetric polyamide layer, as evidenced by the appearance of N-rich molecules in the acid rinsing solution and the increased O/N ratio of the polyamide bottom side. At the same time, the O/N ratio of the polyamide top surface was not affected. In comparison, no release of monomers/oligomers was detected during the acid treatment of the semiaromatic NF membrane. Correspondingly, the NF membrane had a comparable water permeance before and after acid treatment. In the current study, the acid-treated RO membrane demonstrated improved water permeance and stable rejection of NaCl and several micropollutants, suggesting that acid treatment could be used as a polishing strategy to improve the performance of RO membranes for high-efficiency water treatment.

title: Product Formation Dynamics and Sustainability in Chain Elongation Systems: A Cross-Study Analysis
abstract: As a promising strategy for sustainable resource recovery under the global energy crisis, chain elongation in anaerobic fermentation systems has attracted increasing attention. However, its optimization is constrained by limited understanding of dynamic behavior and its role in system-level decision-making. Here, we present a data-driven framework that progressively links dynamic process interpretation with predictive modeling and sustainability-oriented evaluation across heterogeneous chain elongation systems. Literature-derived time-series data were first analyzed to characterize product formation kinetics and identify mode-dependent relationships between process evolution and C6 formation. Building on these mechanistic insights, a random forest model using only initial operating conditions was developed to predict key kinetic descriptors, enabling pre-experimental screening of expected process behavior, while a hybrid dynamic model translated kinetic descriptors into complete product formation trajectories. Environmental and economic assessments further revealed substantial trade-offs among cost, product value, and environmental impact, with only 11 of 893 configurations (1.23%) identified as three-objective Pareto-efficient. Overall, this work provides a data-driven basis for identifying process-control priorities, screening operating conditions before extensive experimentation, anticipating product formation dynamics, and selecting configurations against multiple sustainability objectives.

title: Wildfire-Driven Release of Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals from Tree Biomass
abstract: Fire-prone regions and longer fire seasons are projected to increase with climate warming, intensifying forest disturbance. Many persistent endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs), including polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), can bioaccumulate in forest biomass through long-range atmospheric transport and local deposition, effectively turning forests into contaminant reservoirs. In this Perspective, we expand the concept of wildfire as a driver of remobilization of sequestered EDCs and argue that wildfire can shift forests from sinks to episodic sources of EDC emissions and runoff. We synthesize evidence that EDCs accumulate in tree tissues globally and outline how wildfire may remobilize biomass-sequestered EDCs through coupled atmospheric, terrestrial, and aquatic pathways. Using PFAS as a representative class, we introduce a screening-level model of pre-existing PFAS mass mobilized from burned aboveground wooded biomass. For Greece's 2023 fire season (127,602 ha), a weighted tissue concentration of ∼137.2 ng·g–1 yields a theoretical maximum release of ∼1.22 metric tons (9.6 g·ha–1). Finally, we propose physicochemical criteria to identify EDCs susceptible to wildfire-mediated release and highlight priority research directions to quantify cross-media fluxes in the era of persistent chemical production.

title: Comprehensive Plant Biomarker Profile for Tracing Detection of Sulfur Mustard and Lewisite Exposure and Its Application to Japanese Abandoned Chemical Weapon Samples
abstract: Sulfur mustard (HD) and lewisite (L, mainly containing L1 and L2) from Japanese Abandoned Chemical Weapons (JACWs) in China have persisted for nearly a century, posing ongoing risks to ecological environments and public health. Plants can serve as monitoring sentinels for tracing detection of chemical exposure. However, specific plant biomarkers for HD/L remain unidentified, and their transformation in plants remains unveiled. By nontargeted metabolomics and high-resolution mass spectrometry, 30 novel plant adducts of HD/L were identified. Twelve of these adducts, along with 5 degradation products, were evaluated and assembled into a plant biomarker profile for retrospective detection of HD/L exposure. A sensitive UHPLC–TQ MS method was developed with LODs as low as 0.0200 ng/mL. The profile was detectable in 12 plant species for at least 90 days after exposure. Adduction, hydrolysis, oxidation, and trimerization of HD/L agents have been detected in plants, and transformation diagrams were portrayed. Real samples from JACW remediation sites in northeastern China were analyzed, and free biomarkers were detected at obviously higher levels in plants than in soil. Analytical results indicate that plant leaves may serve as sensitive monitoring media for the exposed agents. This work provides a reliable approach for long-term monitoring of JACW exposure and shows that possible plant accumulation and soil-to-plant transport of CWA products are valuable for further study.

title: Nonlinear associations between urban green infrastructure morphology, landscape configuration, and waterlogging severity in Beijing
Global evolution of dietary water, land, carbon footprints and human health impacts over 2010-2020
Assessing footwear durability and reliability as ecodesign indicators: a methodology based on real-world end-of-life data
abstract: Durability and reliability are relevant product aspects under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), but footwear requires methods that distinguish laboratory performance from real-world retirement. This gap is critical for footwear, where multi-material construction, component-specific degradation and real-world end-of-life datasets generate incomplete technical information. Here, we present a methodological framework with a preliminary empirical demonstration, integrating donated footwear retirement records with a traceable A–B–C–D imputation hierarchy calibrated from 10,117 historical INESCOP laboratory tests. Of 159 collected records, 157 had a valid retirement time and entered a right-censored Weibull accelerated failure time model (141 events; 16 censored); 66.5% of laboratory cells required imputation. A 1500-replicate joint bootstrap propagated sampling/model-parameter and imputation uncertainty. The sample-conditional median time to study-defined retirement was 2.99 years (90% interval 2.52–3.41); descriptive class medians were 1.92, 2.99 and 2.91 years for A, B and C/D (Specification 1, all retirements). Under Specification 2, censoring non-failure sizing retirements (131 events; 26 censored), the Class A median rises to 2.90 years (90% interval 1.53–4.95), approaching Classes B (3.04) and C/D (3.15). This is consistent with child growth shortening Class A service time under Specification 1, without establishing causal attribution or equivalent material durability. The technical score was not independently associated with retirement time (β = 0.006, SE = 0.211, LR p = 0.976), and no covariate model improved out-of-sample log predictive density over an intercept-only model. The framework supports transparent data integration and evidence-gap identification; predictive validity and regulatory suitability are not demonstrated.

title: Sulfur-driven module enhances resilience and detoxification of antibiotic-stressed partial nitrification/anammox system
Combining experiments and density functional theory to study the decomposition mechanism of phenolic wastewater in supercritical water
Molecular-level insights into co-pyrolysis behavior of rubbers and coal model compounds via complementary TG-FTIR and Py-GC/MS
Maize eco-efficiency among Chinese farm households: Measurement and scenario simulation
Comparison of profitability and load matching of vertical bifacial and conventional monofacial photovoltaics across Europe
abstract: This study compares the hourly load-matching of East-West vertically mounted bifacial PV (VBPV) and traditional south-facing monofacial PV (MPV) electricity production profiles across Europe, to find ways to reduce self-cannibalization of PV production. In several countries, such as Germany, the MPV production sinks the electricity price around noon, and current literature has overlooked possibilities of VBPV with its production peaks in the morning and evening to ease this situation. The literature provides only the total annual yields when comparing the performance of MPV with VBPV on a European or a global level. To fill this literature gap, the focus and the key novelty of this study is to assess on how well the PV generation aligns with national electricity demand and electricity price in three European countries (Finland, Germany, and Italy, two locations per country), covering the latitudes 38-64°N. This study also presents a novel cosine-similarity application to analyze load matching. Our results show that VBPV systems consistently offer improved load alignment, with an average 9.6% increase in similarity across all locations. Germany offered better profits per panel with VBPV compared to MPV with an increase of 11.8 % in Germany, where as in Finland and Italy both systems were close to even with an increase of 1.42% in Finland and decrease of 0.22 % in Italy. Although the benefits of VBPV are the largest at high-latitudes due to low solar elevation and expected to grow when considering future projected prices, the improved load-matching allows VBPV to be competitive compared to MPV already now even in Southern Italy. Overall, this contribution highlights that there is significant, utilized potential to cost effectively increase the matching of photovoltaics production with typical electricity consumption across all European latitudes to decrease cannibalization of profits as well as to alleviate the need for electricity storage.

title: Techno-economic and environmental investigation of Power-to-X at various greenfield and brownfield levels – A structured multi-level infrastructure access framework for PtX
abstract: Existing infrastructure can have a significant impact on the production costs and emissions of Power-to-X (PtX) processes. This paper presents a new structured multi-level infrastructure access framework for PtX. The framework was applied to a techno-economic and environmental analysis of the production of ammonia, methanol, methane and kerosene in Chile, Germany and South Africa. Various infrastructural conditions were systematically examined, including grid connection, access to CO 2 , N 2 and H 2 supply and existing synthesis plants. Chile achieved the lowest production costs and emissions due to the significant number of wind full-load hours. In contrast, production in South Africa is dominated by low electricity procurement costs from coal, resulting in high emissions. The impact of existing infrastructure can be so significant that PtX production can be more economical and have a lower global warming potential in locations that are less favourable for renewable energy. The largest cost reduction of 8–34% can be achieved through an additional grid connection. Switching from direct air capture to a site with CO 2 from biogas results in a 14–23% cost reduction. Notably, purchasing renewably produced hydrogen in Germany and Chile can offset the environmental drawbacks of grid electricity and lead to lower-emission production than a greenfield scenario based solely on wind and PV electricity. This creates an interesting scenario when comparing structurally weak sites in Chile with highly developed sites in Germany, where the production costs and emissions are very similar.

Beyond connectivity: Ecological corridors as socio-ecological governance arrangements
abstract: Ecological corridors are among the most adopted environmental policies to address habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss, yet the research supporting them is uneven. Spatial and biophysical questions dominate, while the governance, organizational, and distributive processes that determine whether corridors work in practice remain underexplored. Drawing on a social-ecological systems lens, we systematically review 1871 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025, coded across six analytical dimensions. Two asymmetries stand out. Corridor scholarship advances faster in modeling potential connectivity than in validating realized ecological outcomes, so a mapped corridor is a hypothesis rather than evidence. And only 1.6% of the corpus engages with equity, justice, or gentrification, leaving the question of who gains and who bears the costs largely unasked. We propose a three-dimensional framework linking biophysical and territorial conditions, governance and implementation, and socio-environmental outcomes, and disaggregate the third dimension into distribution, procedure, and recognition. Corridors emerge not as ecological design problems but as socio-ecological arrangements whose effectiveness depends on coordination across actors, institutions, and scales, and whose benefits and burdens fall unevenly. For territorial management and urban planning, the framework supports a sequential prioritization that distinguishes protecting intact linkages, restoring degraded bottlenecks, and creating new connections in urbanized landscapes.

Foster Care or In‐Home Support: Differences in Mental Health Treatment, Education and Crime
abstract: This study traces the trajectories of children before and after their first involvement with Child Welfare Services (CWS), comparing outcomes for those placed in foster care with those who received home‐based services. Leveraging administrative data covering more than 2 decades, we follow these children from infancy through childhood and into adulthood, tracking outcomes in health, education, crime, welfare dependence, and labor market participation. We follow children around the time of their initial CWS contact. We show that children placed in foster care are substantially more likely to receive mental health treatment in the years following the first intervention, with the increase substantially larger for girls than for boys. In contrast, we observe only modest later differences between the two groups across other outcomes. Using geographical variation in the likelihood of being assigned to foster care, we corroborate the finding that foster care placement increases mental healthcare use. One interpretation of this pattern is that foster care placement compensates for childhood adversity by improving access to mental health care services.

Social judgments of faces across world regions are predicted better by distinctiveness than masculinity
abstract: Social judgments of faces influence important social outcomes. Although many researchers have argued that facial masculinity plays a key role in perceptions of both valenced social judgments and dominance, whether these effects are consistent among people from different world regions is highly contentious. Consequently, we investigated possible relationships between masculinity and ratings of 120 faces made by 11,484 participants from eleven world regions (Africa, Asia, Australia and New Zealand, Central America and Mexico, Eastern Europe, Middle East, Scandinavia, South America, United Kingdom, United States and Canada, Western Europe). Surprisingly, masculinity did not significantly predict either perceived valence or dominance. By contrast, facial distinctiveness (i.e., atypicality) was significantly and negatively correlated with valenced perceptions across world regions and predicted valenced perceptions better than did masculinity. Collectively, our results suggest that distinctiveness (or correlates thereof), but not masculinity, shows a consistent association with social judgments of faces across different world regions, potentially due to an “anomalous-is-bad” stereotype whereby people ascribe negative traits to individuals with atypical face shapes.

Multi-product evidence qualification for air quality hotspot screening under retrieval gaps and column–surface divergence
abstract: Satellite hotspot maps can support air-quality screening, but recurrent enhancements are difficult to interpret when retrieval support is uneven, gap handling affects inference, or atmospheric columns diverge from surface conditions. Using British Columbia and California as contrasting test beds, we developed a retrieval-aware, multi-product Sentinel-5P Tropospheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) evidence-qualification framework for carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), sulfur dioxide (SO₂), formaldehyde (HCHO), and the absorbing Aerosol Index (AI) during 2019–2025. Rather than treating hotspot detection as an endpoint, the framework sequentially qualifies retrieval support, sensitivity of temporal and spatial conclusions to gap handling, false-discovery-rate-adjusted Local Moran's I hotspot persistence, and product-specific correspondence with regulatory surface measurements. California's four gaseous columns were higher; apparent AI and Californian seasonal-NO₂ increases failed a July-2021 processor-break sensitivity analysis, precluding atmospheric-trend interpretation. Temporal reconstruction performance varied, but gap-handled spatial analyses retained 96.2–100.0% overall classification agreement and 86.8–100.0% High–High-specific Jaccard agreement versus observed-only analyses. All products exhibited significant spatial dependence and recurrent High–High clusters; NO₂ showed small, stable urban-associated hotspots, while AI showed the strongest regional contrast. Satellite–surface consistency was product-specific: NO₂ was strongest (California: r = 0.73; British Columbia: r = 0.63), CO was weaker, SO₂ was negligible, California HCHO showed stronger rank than linear correspondence, and the AI–PM₂.₅ relationship was weak and contextual. The framework therefore distinguishes robust recurrent column enhancements from those that also support near-surface interpretation, providing a transferable basis for prioritizing follow-up monitoring without conflating satellite hotspots with surface exposure or emission sources.

Quantifying the relationship between prescribed burning and wildfire severity in south-eastern Australia
abstract: High-severity wildfires can pose a critical threat to society and forest ecosystems. While prescribed burning is widely applied to mitigate these risks, evaluation of its effectiveness at the landscape level remains challenging. Factors hindering these assessments include a lack of spatial data quantifying the amount of fuel treatment within burns, and challenges in controlling for variation in environmental conditions (e.g., weather, topography) that affect wildfire severity. We evaluated the effect of historical prescribed burns on wildfire severity in south-eastern Australia. We accounted for spatial variation in fuel treatments by objectively classifying the severity of ∼1300 prescribed burns conducted in the decade preceding each wildfire. Using a Random Forest modelling approach, we identified the key drivers of wildfire severity and employed counterfactual scenarios to quantify the landscape-scale influence of these prescribed burns while controlling the influence of environmental covariates. Overall, fire weather and aridity were the strongest drivers of wildfire severity. Recent prescribed burning reduced the extent of higher severity classes, relatively consistently across climatic conditions. Counterfactual scenarios showed that prescribed burning reduced the total area of the two highest wildfire severity classes (high canopy scorch and canopy burnt) by 6.2% (2882 ha) and nearly doubled the area that remained unburnt within treated areas. Our findings support the strategic use of prescribed burning to reduce the extent of high-severity fire. However, managers must remain mindful of the ecological trade-offs from increased frequency of low intensity prescribed fire, to ensure that fuel reduction prescriptions support forest resilience in an ever-warming climate.

title: Life cycle assessment of marine biodiversity restoration: Case study of European flat oyster (Ostrea edulis) in Nora Lagoon
abstract: Marine ecosystem restoration is increasingly recognized as a key strategy to reverse biodiversity loss and support the recovery of ecosystem services. However, the environmental burdens generated by restoration activities are rarely quantified. This study investigates whether Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) can support the design and management of environmentally sustainable marine restoration interventions. Using the restoration of the European flat oyster ( Ostrea edulis ) in the Nora Lagoon (Italy) as a case study, a cradle-to-deployment LCA was performed, including adult collection, hatchery stage at laboratory scale, transportation, and field deployment. Environmental impacts were assessed and complemented by LCA-based biodiversity indicators, sensitivity analyses, and an evaluation of shell-based carbon sequestration potential. Results showed that the deployment phase was the main contributor to global warming potential, marine eutrophication, and biodiversity impacts, whereas hatchery stage dominated cumulative energy demand and water use. The nursery stage of laboratory rearing and the use of imported commercial feed emerged as major hotspots. Alternative scenarios based on renewable electricity and modified transport logistics reduced several impact categories, with local feed production providing potentially the most balanced improvements. Although restored oysters stored biogenic carbon, sequestration remained negligible compared with project emissions over a 10-year period. The study demonstrates that LCA is an effective decision-support tool for identifying environmental hotspots, optimizing restoration strategies, and integrating sustainability considerations into marine biodiversity restoration planning.

title: Does inequality harm the climate? An agent-based model with endogenous climate policy
abstract: This paper examines how income inequality affects environmental outcomes through the interplay of household consumption and political support for climate policy. We develop an agent-based model in which households differ by income, consumption patterns, and climate policy attitudes. Our results show that the relationship between inequality and emissions is dynamic and non-monotonic: relative to a baseline calibrated to the U.S., lower income inequality initially increases emissions due to rising consumption among formerly low-income households. Over time, however, reduced inequality fosters broader political support for tighter climate action, as a more equal income distribution lowers the relative cost of carbon taxation for households at the bottom of the distribution. This stronger support enables more ambitious policies and ultimately reduces emissions. Moreover, we find that lower inequality consistently produces the lowest cumulative emissions across scenarios. The findings highlight the importance of distributional considerations in designing effective and politically sustainable climate policies.

title: Appropriating managerial identity regulation through collective tactics: The case of environmental insider activism
abstract: How can employee groups influence identity regulation within their organisation? While recognising that employees have agency in their response to organisational identity control, the literature has largely positioned identity regulation as a managerial prerogative enforced through disciplinary power. Some research, however, finds that groups of employees are able to shape their members’ identities and oppose or negotiate managerial attempts to influence them. This article extends the identity regulation research by showing how employee groups can go beyond merely reacting to managerial identity regulation; they can also appropriate and redirect it to influence other employees. Using an in-depth case study, we analyse how an environmental insider activist group managed to do so through two interrelated tactics: augmenting the ideal employee identity built and promoted by management and repurposing existing identity regulation practices and discourses. By demonstrating how employee groups without disciplinary power can appropriate and transform managerial identity regulation for a cause they care about, these findings contribute to knowledge on identity regulation dynamics within organisations and on the relationships between identity regulation and broader societal norms.

title: AI-Generated Images in E-commerce: Mitigating Perceived Uncertainty with Two Compensatory Control Strategies
The Impacts of Choice Assortment Structures in Influencers’ Recommendations on Consumers’ Destination Attitude
abstract: While travel influencers frequently recommend portfolios of multiple destinations, extant research has primarily focused on single-destination endorsements. Drawing on choice assortment theory, this study examines how assortment structure (size, complementarity, diversity) affects destination attitudes. Evidence from a large language model-assisted text analysis of social media posts ( N = 9,823) and three experiments ( N = 815) demonstrates that larger, substitute-based, and high-diversity complement-based assortments enhance tourists’ attitudes toward the focal destination. These effects are explained by assortment structure acting as a diagnostic cue for persuasive motive inference, thereby reducing the situational activation of persuasion knowledge. Furthermore, these effects are stronger under exchange (vs. communal) influencer-consumer relationships, where consumers are more sensitive to persuasive intent. These findings identify an additional motive-diagnostic function of assortment structure beyond comparing options and provide implications for destination management organizations on when and how to manage influencer-curated portfolios.

title: Bond Price‐Level Mispricing: A Multifactor Identity
abstract: This paper develops a new estimator of abnormal bond prices, defined as the deviation of market prices from the present value of future coupon payments and accrued interest under a multifactor stochastic discount factor (SDF). Existing price‐level approaches rely on restrictive assumptions and single‐factor SDFs that are poorly suited to fixed‐income markets. We propose an identity‐based estimator grounded in the Fama and French five‐factor bond model (FFBM). It mirrors traditional abnormal return tests while avoiding overlapping return windows and reducing sensitivity to SDF measurement error. We document four findings. First, the FFBM leaves substantial valuation gaps in bond prices. Second, Credit Risk, Downside Risk, Default Risk, Liquidity Risk, Economic Policy Uncertainty and Market Returns strongly predict abnormal price. Third, a novel composite signal, refined value, parsimoniously captures systematic mispricing. Fourth, refined value subsumes the explanatory power of 23 firm‐ and market‐level characteristics. The results highlight the importance of price‐level analysis in fixed‐income markets.

title: A matter of wheels: How fuel prices affect motorcyclists differently, evidence from Spain
When takeovers require cognitive control: Effects of partial automation and cognitive load on driver-initiated responses to traffic hazards on urban roads
abstract: Partially automated driving (PAD) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in consumer vehicles. While drivers are obliged to monitor the roadway and the system during PAD, they do not always comply with this requirement and may engage in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs). Literature has emphasized the detrimental effects of visual–manual NDRTs on drivers’ capability to takeover control from PAD while reporting negligible effects of non-visual NDRTs (e.g., hands-free phone calls) and cognitive load. However, most studies focused on alerted scenarios, with takeover requests lowering drivers’ reliance on anticipation and cognitive load, masking the effects of cognitive load. Related work also examined PAD conditions alone, neglecting the combined effects of automation and cognitive load on drivers’ responses. To address the gaps, we conducted a driving simulator study examining the influence of cognitive load, induced by a 2-back task, on driver-initiated responses to urban traffic hazards (e.g., crossing pedestrians, oncoming vehicles) during both manual driving and PAD. The timing and quality of driver-initiated responses were analyzed separately for each hazard with detail. Results showed that (i) cognitive load effects manifested most when drivers encountered hazards with lower perceptual salience (e.g., a pedestrian gradually approaching the roadway); (ii) driver-initiated responses during PAD were less proactive and relied more on cognitive control; and (iii) this shift led to higher situational criticality and heightened susceptibility of responses to cognitive load during PAD. Together, these findings underscore an elevated safety risk associated with cognitive load during PAD, especially in scenarios requiring cognitively demanding, driver-initiated intervention.

title: Perceived Urgency as the Gateway to Volunteerism: Integrating Sensemaking With the Theory of Planned Behavior
abstract: Research on volunteering follows two broad approaches. Antecedent-based approaches, such as the theory of planned behavior, explain who is predisposed to help through priors such as attitudes, norms, and perceived behavioral control. Antecedent-based research seldom examines the interpretive mechanism through which priors become action, a gap that matters most in disasters, where help must be given immediately. Meanwhile, sensemaking approaches focus on how people interpret ambiguois situations and decide what they call for. This article aligns the two in a mediation design treating volunteering intentions as both dispositionally grounded and interpretively activated, with perceived urgency as a parsimonious token of interpretation. Structural equation models of survey data on a prospective Istanbul earthquake ( N = 331) show that interpretation carries the effects of attitudes and norms and partly those of perceived behavioral control, improving on an antecedent-only baseline. The study adds an interpretive layer to volunteerability, extends recruitability, and recasts organizations as sense-givers.

title: The Art of Alignment: A Sensemaking Perspective on Elite Philanthropy in Higher Education Fundraising
abstract: This paper examines how fundraisers at higher education institutions construct and sustain alignment between elite donors’ expectations and institutional priorities. Drawing on qualitative interviews with fundraising professionals across 16 leading U.S. universities, we conceptualize alignment as a recursive temporal sensemaking process through which fundraisers manage equivocality and develop shared understandings over time. The analysis identifies three interrelated forms of sensemaking. Retrospective sensemaking involves interpreting donors’ biographies, identities, and relationship histories. Circumspective sensemaking focuses on real-time interactions in which fundraisers and donors explore priorities and negotiate philanthropic possibilities. Prospective sensemaking concerns sustaining alignment through stewardship and engagement as institutional priorities and donor aspirations evolve. Together, these processes show how alignment is continually constructed, maintained, revised, and renewed rather than achieved as a discrete agreement. The study reframes major-gift fundraising as an interpretive process through which fundraisers and donors negotiate shared understandings, offering a process-based account of donor influence and fundraising practice.

title: Crowded and Concentrated? A Density Paradox in Nonprofit Markets
abstract: Organizational counts are often used to characterize nonprofit competition, but they do not reveal how revenue is distributed across funding streams. Using 4.7 million organization-years of IRS Form 990 filings from 2012 to 2021, we examine concentration within revenue streams and revenue–share concordance across 77,489 local market-years. Organizational density is negatively associated with concentration, yet even populous nonprofit markets distribute revenue unevenly. Human Services markets contain a median of 45 organizations, while their median private-contribution concentration is equivalent to approximately seven equal-sized recipients. Government grants and program service revenue are generally more concentrated than private contributions, and leadership carries across streams only modestly. In the main models, private-contribution concentration is positively associated with subsequent net organizational growth, whereas grant and service-revenue concentration are negatively associated; estimates vary across specifications. These findings distinguish organizational counts from resource distribution within and across revenue streams.

title: Structural separation of adjacent photovoltaic arrays for area-based capacity attribution from high-resolution remote sensing imagery
Agentic predictive control for residential PV-battery systems: from natural-language scheduling requests to receding-horizon dispatch
Hydrogen-based green steel corridors: cost saving and emission reduction potentials of emerging trade routes
abstract: Deploying hydrogen-based direct-reduced iron (H 2 -DRI) technologies will be decisive to defossilize the global steel sector by replacing coal-based blast furnaces (BF) in conventional steelmaking. DRI can then either be directly fed into an electric-arc-furnace (EAF) and alternative electric smelting furnaces or transported as cold hot-briquetted iron (HBI) and a green commoditiy to a steel plant. The availability and expansion of low-cost renewable electricity and green hydrogen supply options is the essential and site-specific precondition to deploy H 2 -DRI plants that can be gradually switched from natural gas to hydrogen. However, near-zero emission steel made from H 2 -DRI needs to produced at competitive costs compared to fossil steel regulated under carbon emission pricing schemes. Based on revised green hydrogen cost forecasts in potentially low-cost countries like Australia or Oman, this study reveals the cost competitiveness of emerging green steel corridors built on international partnerships. With green HBI then exported to a representative EAF green steelmaking site, the analysis shows the potential cost savings of importing green HBI from renewable-rich countries when facing a future lack of affordable hydrogen supply options in leading steel countries like Germany or South Korea characterized by a high dependence on energy imports. Overall, low-emission crude steel based on 66 vol% H 2 -HBI imports achieves fossil cost parity in Germany in 2040 at increased carbon prices in the EU, while all 100% hydrogen-based steel scenarios inhere higher costs with a premium of 6%–13% over natural gas-based DRI-EAF crude steel at 828 € t −1 CS (with 0% scrap) at hydrogen costs ranging between 4.14 and 4.94 € kg −1 H 2 . In addition, a cradle-to-gate accounting of greenhouse gas emissions reveals that cost savings from HBI imports potentially come at the expense of up to 50% higher total emissions compared to an integrated H 2 -DRI-EAF plant running on iron ore pellet imports. All 100% H 2 -DRI-based scenarios yield an emission reduction between 42%–57% compared to a domestic benchmarked NG-DRI-EAF scenario at 1293 kg CO 2 (e) t −1 CS. The carbon footprint analysis further highlights the effect of upstream defossilization measures related to iron ore mining, pelletising and transport by rail and ship.

Human Mitochondrial HVRII as an Indicator of Island Groundwater Connectivity
abstract: This study explores the use of human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) as a potential tracer for anthropogenic inputs in confined groundwater systems, building on our previous application in urban watersheds. mtDNA represents one of the most robust sources of eukaryotic environmental DNA (eDNA) due to its multimembrane protection, high copy number per cell, and persistence in the environment, resulting in a valuable resource for both detection and when examining sequences, tracing. We investigated mtDNA transport in the groundwater of Lord Howe Island, a small shield volcano remnant and UNESCO World Heritage site, whose modest population and limited tourist load yield a tractable number of haplotypes. By targeting the hypervariable region II (HVRII) of the human mitochondrial genome, we examined the impact of local human inputs, including septic tanks, on local groundwater. Groundwater samples were collected from wells and small groundwater discharges, PCR-amplified, and analyzed via high-throughput sequencing, revealing unique haplotype frequencies that identified zones of impact. These findings were supported by Bacteroides 16S tracking, using human, bovine, and canine specific markers as well as bacterial counts and other water quality parameters. This approach demonstrates several advantages over more traditional source tracking markers, most importantly, which impacts are uniquely anthropogenic and their origin. Unlike artificial DNA tracers, mtDNA is naturally present in septic tank leach fields and is temporally unambiguous, like plant-based viral markers. Our work highlights mtDNA’s potential to help map anthropogenic inputs within groundwater, which is a tool that may be particularly valuable for island communities with limited wastewater infrastructure resources.
