ESG Data Governance for Sustainable Business: Ownership, Authority, and the Strategic Role of HR
abstract: The growing institutionalization of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting raises questions about how organizations allocate authority over ESG information. While existing research addresses reporting requirements and data governance structures, the organizational processes through which ESG data ownership emerges remain insufficiently theorized. This conceptual paper develops an integrated framework in which ESG data ownership is understood as the institutionally recognized allocation of governance authority over the definition, interpretation, validation, and use of ESG information. It identifies four interacting mechanisms through which this authority is formed: authority claiming, allocation of decision rights, interpretative alignment, and institutional stabilization. The framework distinguishes finance‐centered, sustainability‐centered, and matrix governance configurations as alternative outcomes of formation processes shaped by institutional and organizational conditions. Drawing on contrasting governance traditions in France and Germany, it highlights the context‐dependent nature of these arrangements. Particular attention is given to human resources (HR), whose expertise in producing and interpreting social ESG information does not necessarily translate into recognized decision‐making authority. By explaining how distributed functional expertise and competing authority claims are translated into institutionally recognized decision rights, the framework advances an understanding of how different governance configurations and positions of HR emerge.

title: From Disclosure to Capability: Sustainability Materiality as Strategic Adaptation Under Institutional Complexity
abstract: Sustainability materiality determines which environmental and social issues an organisation treats as significant enough to shape disclosure, governance and resource allocation. Research examines it predominantly as a property of reporting, leaving unexamined how firms build the capacity to make such determinations repeatedly under changing conditions. Integrating organisational paradox theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective, this study asks how that capacity develops under institutional complexity, drawing on interviews and corporate documents from a UK housebuilder reporting voluntarily. Five paradoxical tensions recurred and none were resolved, spanning early adoption, definitional ambiguity, stakeholder plurality, informational balance and supply chain data governance. Engaging them produced a strengthened sustainability function, cross‐functional routines, benchmarking and relational data governance. The paper defines sustainability materiality capability as a construct with interpretive, relational, infrastructural and governance dimensions, distinguishing the capacity that produces determinations from the determinations themselves, and extends both literatures to the privately owned firm reporting voluntarily.

title: When Climate Incentives Matter: CEO Compensation Design and Stock Market Responses to Climate Transition Risk in Europe
abstract: As climate transition risk becomes increasingly priced in capital markets, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate their preparedness for the low‐carbon transition. Climate‐linked CEO incentives have emerged as a prominent governance mechanism, yet their market relevance remains unclear. Using a sample of listed European firms from 2018 to 2022, we examine when climate‐linked CEO incentives are associated with stock market responses to climate transition shocks. We find that a greater economic weight of climate‐linked compensation is associated with more favorable market responses. This association varies with incentive design and context. Transition‐oriented KPIs exhibit the largest association, whereas process‐oriented KPIs also show a positive association. Broader environmental KPIs, by contrast, show no significant association, although this result may partly reflect their low prevalence in the sample. Moreover, the association is stronger when transition risk is more economically material, emerges under stronger internal climate governance, and is further strengthened by greater responsible capital ownership. These findings contribute to the literature by showing that the market relevance of climate‐linked executive compensation varies with incentive design, transition risk materiality, and the broader governance environment.

title: Management consultants – monsters or benign change agents? The case of the NSW transport asset holding entity
abstract: Purpose This study critically examines the role of private consultants in public-sector financial governance under New Public Management (NPM) and New Public Financial Management (NPFM). Focusing on the New South Wales Transport Asset Holding Entity (TAHE), the research investigates how consultancy expertise and accounting technologies were mobilised in the case study to construct a quasi-market entity that advanced short-term fiscal objectives while obscuring long-term financial realities and the public interest. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in political economy and public-interest accounting traditions, the study employs a multi-method, qualitative case study design. Informed by the theoretical lenses of consultocracy and consultology, the analysis triangulates legally vetted and publicly contested documents, including Auditor-General reports, parliamentary inquiries, financial disclosures and investigative journalism, to trace institutional decision-making and intra-firm knowledge practices. Findings The analysis demonstrates that consultants acted as powerful political-institutional actors. They shaped the structural and financial design of TAHE to classify capital funding as equity rather than as an expenditure. Crucially, distinct consultancy teams within a single Big Four firm produced contradictory asset valuations. Internal firm dynamics helped contain these contradictions, which included impression management, team segmentation and the disciplining of professional dissent. Together, they enabled the firm to suppress contradictory judgements, prioritising commercial and political imperatives over democratic accountability and public transparency. Originality/value This paper introduces consultology as a micro-analytic complement to consultocracy, showing how consultant power operates both institutionally and intra-firm through practices that stabilise contradictory expertise. The TAHE case reveals accounting classifications as political technologies that embed long-term fiscal obligations and accountability risks beyond effective oversight.

title: The Ethic of Decency and the Antecedents of Corporate Sufficiency
abstract: As the paradigm of perpetual economic growth is increasingly seen as incompatible with environmental and social sustainability, sufficiency has gained traction as an alternative organizing principle to align economic activity with socio-ecological well-being. This study advances understanding of why and how firms engage in sufficiency. We define corporate sufficiency as the practice of corporate self-restraint grounded in the imperative to operate within planetary boundaries, even at the risk of forgoing profits and growth. While prior scholarship has challenged profit maximization as a corporate guiding principle, less is known about why firms voluntarily practice self-restraint and how they enact sufficiency in an economic context geared toward growth. Through a qualitative analysis of 70 sufficiency-oriented firms, we identify three antecedents that either motivate or enable observed corporate sufficiency practices, namely responsibility, relationality, and excellence. We argue that these antecedents can be framed within the ethic of decency, which provides context-sensitive guidance for firms to deliberate on and enact self-restraint in production and consumption practices. Through the advancement of decency as an ethical framework for corporate sufficiency, this study extends and integrates sufficiency and business ethics scholarship. It challenges the instrumental logic that underpins the sustainable consumption discourse and proposes a normative framework for reconciling business conduct with the imperatives of planetary and human well-being.

title: Human Nature, Flourishing, and Virtue: Neo-Aristotelian Metaethics and Business Ethics
abstract: Neo-Aristotelian approaches in business ethics often focus on the way that various actions or practices within organizations contribute to or obstruct human flourishing. Despite this focus, very little research within business ethics has directly considered how flourishing grounds or justifies more specific claims about the obligations of business persons. We draw upon recent metaethical debates between Neo-Aristotelians concerning the notion of human nature and its role in providing a basis for ethical claims to shed light on the role of human flourishing in business ethics research. This debate is divided between “first-nature” naturalists, such as Foot, for whom nature serves as a normative standard for ethical judgment, and “secondnature” naturalists, such as McDowell and the early MacIntyre, who eschew appeals to nature, turning, instead, to goods and/or reasons for action embedded within practices and traditions. We review this debate and, in the process, categorize various neo-Aristotelian perspectives in business ethics insofar as they fall within either side of this divide. After this, we turn to MacIntyre’s later work, arguing that he provides a way of combining aspects of first and second-nature naturalism in a manner that is relevant to future research in business ethics.

title: The Digitalization–Fraud Paradox: Asymmetric Effects of Strategic Digital Orientation
abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping organizational governance, yet its ethical implications for corporate misconduct remain insufficiently understood. This study examines how strategic digital orientation (SDO), defined as a firm’s strategic commitment to developing and integrating digital capabilities, is associated with corporate fraud. Using 34,320 firm-year observations of Chinese listed firms from 2009 to 2022, we construct a multidimensional measure of SDO through textual analysis of Management Discussion and Analysis disclosures and measure corporate fraud using complementary regulatory databases. The results provide robust evidence of an asymmetric relationship between SDO and corporate fraud. Firms exhibiting relatively low to intermediate levels of SDO are associated with higher observed fraud risk, whereas the positive association weakens at higher levels of SDO. Moderation analyses show that internal control quality and innovation capability weaken the positive association between SDO and fraud, potentially by reducing governance misalignment associated with digital transformation. Mediation analyses reveal multiple competing governance mechanisms—audit quality, information asymmetry, technology intensity—with indirect effects that are statistically significant but economically modest. These findings are consistent with an asymmetric ethical risk framework in which technological opacity, accountability diffusion, and governance lag create ethical vulnerabilities that are partially offset by stronger monitoring and governance capabilities at higher levels of SDO. This research contributes to business ethics research by demonstrating how digital transformation reshapes accountability structures, redistributes moral responsibility, and generates asymmetric patterns of misconduct risk across firms exhibiting different levels of SDO.

title: Unleashing the Power of Constraints: Green Power Trading and Corporate Investment Efficiency
Strategic Discord or Coordination? Geopolitical Risk and Macroeconomic Policy Synchronization in Asia’s Leading Economies
Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
abstract: Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. Using interrupted time series analysis with and without control, we find that the passage of the Pendleton Act did, in fact, result in lower borrowing costs for the federal government of between 63 and 84 basis points depending on specification. Implications are discussed.

title: Born to Govern or to Extract? Party Types Across Administrative Levels in Colombia
abstract: Research on parties and corruption classifies them by ideology, while subnational studies set the party aside for the candidate. Indeed, organizational origin remains untested as a structured typology. I classify parties as traditional, personalistic, ethnic, rebel‐origin, or neo‐Pentecostal across three governmental levels. Operationalizing Attorney General prosecutorial records for 2011–2020, I build a composite corruption indicator for 1122 Colombian municipalities and estimate fixed effects, spatial, and regression discontinuity models. Rebel‐origin parties and citizen‐signature movements are associated with lower corruption, while traditional and personalistic types are indistinguishable. The ethnic category turns negative once parties whose origin and trajectory diverged are excluded, and tests of contested assignments strengthen the results. Voter turnout is positively associated with municipal corruption, a result that omitted variables do not account for. At the presidential level, however, party type loses significance. How a party was built, rather than its label, is therefore decisive for understanding municipal corruption.

title: Quantifying environmental-economic-performance balance in asphalt pavement designs: A service life-driven multi-criteria sustainability assessment framework
Long-term neurotoxic effects of early-life cobalt exposure on the zebrafish CNS: from larvae to adulthood
Characterizing multiple dimensions of climate hazards for conservation planning: a case study of estuaries in the Pacific Northwest
abstract: Incorporating the complexities of climate change into conservation planning can be challenging. Climate change is projected to change the mean and variability of temperature and precipitation, and change dynamics of extreme events of many climate variables globally. These changes will all have compounding effects on ecosystems worldwide, affecting species distributions, seasonal timings, and population dynamics. However, most recent climate-informed conservation planning frameworks only focus on changes in mean conditions, leaving out ecologically important information about seasonality and extreme events. Using a case study of estuaries in the Pacific Northwest, this research seeks to answer the question “How can the effects of climate change on estuaries best be modelled and described for practical use in ecological management?” To answer this question, we used downscaled climate projection data to estimate changes in the mean and variability of temperature and precipitation. Applying extreme value theory to these projection data, we also projected changes in the magnitude of extremes in temperature and precipitation for estuaries in the region. Using descriptive statistics and open source data, our results present a novel, holistic method of understanding climate risk, including estimating extreme events, highlighting a key research gap in conservation planning. These results also highlight that trends in the mean, variability, and magnitude of climate extremes are not consistent with each other, further underscoring the importance of considering multiple dimensions of climate change together. Despite uncertainty given by climate models, the methods presented here provide a reasonable approach to plan for conservation management in the face of climate uncertainty.

title: Why and where human-wildlife conflicts emerge: Explainable AI reveals species-specific drivers in the southern Western Ghats
Agro‐Diversity Pattern Along Slope and Disturbance Gradient: A Climate Resilience Approach for Food Security
abstract: Agro‐diversity in rainfed agriculture underpins resilient production systems, particularly in stressful environments like the Vindhyan highlands. This region, with its dry climate and undulating topography, supports a mix of traditional and modern crops suited to resource‐poor farmers. However, such highland agriculture is limited in distribution and needs to be expanded to eradicate poverty and address environmental issues. In this context, the aim of the present study was to explore crop diversity and composition (landraces and high‐yielding varieties [HYVs]) concerning disturbance and slope gradients. Three villages, categorized by disturbance index (high, medium, and low), were selected for this study. Agriculture in each village was further divided into high slope (> 22°), mid‐slope (10°–22°), and low slope (> 8°). Detailed surveys included 30 farmers in low‐disturbance (LD), 42 in medium‐disturbance (MD), and 60 in high‐disturbance (HD) areas. A total of 65 crop species were recorded, in which HD had 63 species, MD 59, and LD 49. Crop variety data revealed 116 landraces and 97 HYVs across the monsoon and winter seasons. In the case of crop variety composition, landraces dominated at LD and MD across slopes, while HYVs were prevalent at HD. Land cover and crop diversity indices varied significantly (p < 0.05) with disturbance and slope for both landraces and HYVs. Landrace diversity showed positive correlations with slope and soil rockiness but negative correlations with disturbance, soil depth, and soil moisture. Canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) explained 60.82% and 54.87% of the cumulative variance through the first two axes. These findings provide insights into crop diversity across slopes and disturbance gradients, supporting climate‐resilient strategies for future food security.

Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
abstract: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. Casual consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While selective consumers benefit from increased competition, casual consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: the equilibrium approaches full disclosure as the cost approaches zero or the mean valuation. When costs are high, further increases raise equilibrium informativeness and the welfare of selective consumers, while reducing the welfare of casual consumers.

title: Taxing Homeowners Who Can't or Won't Borrow
abstract: Using high-frequency administrative data covering millions of US homeowners, I document three novel facts about homeowner responses to property tax increases driven by rising home values. First, non-migrating homeowners cut consumption, exhibit financial distress, and do not borrow against their higher home values. Second, heterogeneity analysis shows that consumption responses do not vary by liquidity, consistent with savings target behavior. In contrast, distress responses are concentrated among liquidity-constrained homeowners. Many homeowners report being debt averse and therefore unwilling to borrow in order to avoid illiquidity and distress. Third, tax hikes induce migration—partly by displacing illiquid homeowners—but do not accelerate neighborhood change. A simple welfare framework reveals that the largest costs of property taxes arise from financial distress, suggesting welfare gains from policies that limit taxes for liquidity-constrained households.

title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
Keep calm and bank on: Bank run risks and the role of public communication
Trickle-down housing economics
The Costs and Benefits of Guest Worker Programs: Experimental Evidence from the India-UAE Migration Corridor,
abstract: We estimate the returns to temporary, legal migration using a randomized experiment with Indian applicants for construction jobs in the UAE. Individuals who migrate doubled their earnings. However, migrants paid substantial upfront costs to labor intermediaries and reported significant falls in well-being. We extrapolate linear marginal treatment effects for workers who declined the offer and find they would have similar pecuniary returns to migration but would experience larger drops in well-being. We estimate that accounting for the fall in well-being and the intermediary costs reduce the welfare gains of temporary migration to the UAE to one-half of the pecuniary gains alone.

The Bright and Dark Sides of CEO Personality in Corporate Sustainability: A Critical Review
abstract: Following PRISMA, we review 47 studies on CEO traits and sustainability using the Dark Triad, Positive Self‐regard, and institutional isomorphism frameworks. Narcissism is associated with CSR engagement and greenwashing; hubris with conditional green innovation; and overconfidence with mixed CSR outcomes and greater decoupling. Machiavellianism is linked to manipulation risks, while psychopathy is negatively associated with sustainability orientation. Core self‐evaluation and related attributes generally support stakeholder‐oriented engagement. Coercive, normative, and mimetic isomorphism help explain these relationships under different governance and financial conditions. The review distinguishes substantive engagement from symbolic compliance and identifies research priorities concerning endogeneity, personality measurement, and cross‐country differences.

title: Inflation, debt overhang and corporate investment
Equilibrium Leadership in Tax Competition: The Role of Capital–Labor Substitution/Complement
Adapting to the new abnormal: multinational corporations’ foreign subsidiary investment and country resilience to climate change
abstract: As climate change (CC) increasingly disrupts infrastructure, supply chains, labor availability, and public services, multinational corporations (MNCs) face growing uncertainty when selecting locations for foreign expansion. We examine whether host-country CC resilience has become an important determinant of international investment and how firm capabilities shape this relationship. Drawing on socio-ecological resilience theory and the resilience and turbulence framework, we analyze Global Fortune 500 firms investing across 155 countries between 2003 and 2017. We find that MNCs establish more wholly owned subsidiaries in countries with higher CC resilience, indicating that resilience is emerging as a strategic location-specific advantage. This relationship is stronger for firms with well-developed ESG capabilities and prior experience operating in resilient countries, but weaker for firms with greater financial slack. Our findings suggest that managers should incorporate CC resilience into location decisions alongside traditional economic and institutional criteria while considering their firms’ resource and capability profile to assess how effectively they can leverage host-country CC resilience. For policymakers, the results indicate that strengthening CC resilience can improve not only adaptation to CC but also national competitiveness in attracting MNC foreign direct investment. Overall, CC resilience is becoming a strategic determinant of where MNCs choose to invest.

title: Short-horizon capital in a bank-centered financial system: Japanese mutual fund launches relative to the U.S.
abstract: The median time from launch to peak assets under management (AUM) is nine months for Japanese active domestic equity mutual funds, versus 4.6 years for comparable U.S. funds. Japanese funds also grow much less from launch to peak, as strong initial inflows quickly give way to persistent outflows, while U.S. funds continue to attract net inflows for years. We link this compressed life cycle to Japan’s bank-centered, concentrated distribution system and front-loaded sales compensation. A larger launch size and higher sales load each predict earlier peak AUM in Japan, but not in the U.S.; within Japan, stronger distribution networks are associated with larger launches and earlier peaks, while longer pre-inception sales periods are associated with larger launch sizes and higher sales loads. The evidence shows that the same market-based financial product can follow different life cycles when embedded in different national systems of intermediation and compensation. Japan’s prolonged weak equity-market environment provides an additional context in which investors may reassess newly launched funds as realized performance becomes observable. Our findings suggest that incentives rewarding initial sales can mobilize capital rapidly without generating durable asset retention in an institutional environment such as Japan’s.

title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Wang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72322017]. Y. Li acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72132007]. Q. Zhang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 724B2024]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02206 .

title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. Zhang is partly supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) [Grant 72394361] and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Mathematical Foundations for Artificial Intelligence [2023B1212010001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01346 .

title: Learning from a Biased Sample
abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. RS is further supported by a NSF GRFP under grant DGE-1656518, a Stanford Data Science PhD Fellowship, and a Stanford Diversifying Academia Recruiting Excellence (DARE) Fellowship. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08073 .

title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: G. Feng acknowledges financial support from the Hong Kong Research Grants Council [Grant GRF11502023] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72203190]. G. Feng is partially supported by the InnoHK Initiative of the Innovation and Technology Commission of the Hong Kong SAR and the Laboratory for AI-Powered Financial Technologies. L. Jiang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72473027]. J. Li acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72473026]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03136 .

title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from disruptions such as pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, or cascading partner failures, and they can rapidly reconfigure whole-network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole-network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness-resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass preshock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness-resilience perspective opens for the study of network change. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19624 .

title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
abstract: We show that the canonical dynamic discrete-choice model of demand has built-in exclusion restrictions that overidentify the discount factor.

title: The unconscious relational binds of identity regulation: Social defenses and structuring fantasies
abstract: Why do workers cling to identities promoted by their work organizations, even when it entails suffering? We investigate this persistent grip of identity regulation on workers by bridging discursive and psychodynamic approaches. Drawing on the case of a Belgian healthcare organization and its implicit requirement for workers to see themselves as enthusiastic scouts, we show how unconscious relational mechanisms intertwine with organizational attempts at identity regulation. Our findings reveal how the requirement for enthusiasm strained workers who unconsciously managed it through a generational divide. Senior and junior workers adopted contrasting scout identities that allowed each group to cope in its own way while blaming the other for difficulties. Senior and junior workers further made sense of these contrasting identities by fantasizing about protecting others or being vulnerable. Through these unconscious mechanisms, workers came to claim scout identities that they could not reconsider because they were bound by defensive and fantasy dynamics. We conclude that these unconscious relational mechanisms recursively tighten the grip of identity regulation, reinforcing the attempts at regulation that initially triggered them. We argue that this is a form of self-defeating agency in which workers actively, if unconsciously, adopt regulated identities, thereby deepening their commitment and suffering.

title: How Do Employees Navigate Destructive Leadership Behaviour? A Focus on SMEs
abstract: Destructive leadership has detrimental effects on employee and organizational performance, yet we know little about how employees respond to such leadership behaviour, particularly in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs), where close interpersonal relationships and limited organizational support constrain employees’ responses. Drawing on Leader‐Member Exchange (LMX) theory, we examine the coping strategies employees adopt to navigate destructive leadership behaviour and the mechanisms that shape these strategies. We conducted 26 semi‐structured interviews with employees across diverse SMEs and job roles and analysed the data thematically. We identify three coping strategies: (i) adaptation, (ii) resistance and (iii) exit. Employees’ choice among these strategies depends on their assessment of their tolerance of personal and professional risks and their perceived power to influence or change their situation. These evaluations determine whether employees accommodate their leaders’ destructive behaviour, resist it or disengage entirely by leaving the organization. Our findings extend LMX theory by highlighting employees’ active role in evaluating their interactions and adapting their responses according to the associated risks and their power to influence or change their situation. The study also highlights the contextual dynamics of SMEs and offers insights for organizations seeking to recognize the effects of destructive leadership and support employees.

title: What Drives Business Performance Under Sustainability Pressures? Stakeholder Perspectives From the Portuguese Textile Industry
abstract: The growing sustainability transition is reshaping traditional manufacturing industries, requiring firms to reconcile environmental and social responsibilities with the need to remain competitive and financially viable. This challenge is particularly relevant in the textile industry, which faces increasing regulatory pressure, stakeholder scrutiny, and international competition. Against this background, this study examines how sustainability‐related investments and firm‐specific characteristics are related to business performance in the Portuguese textile industry between 2014 and 2024. Drawing on resource‐based view, agency theory, and stakeholder theory, we argue that the effects of sustainability‐related practices are not uniform but depend on the stakeholder perspective through which performance is assessed. Using an unbalanced panel of 1703 firms and applying the system generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator, business performance is evaluated through three complementary dimensions, such as operational efficiency (EBITDA margin), shareholder value creation (ROE), and economic sustainability (ROA). The results reveal substantial differences across performance dimensions. Environmental expenditure contributes positively to operational efficiency and shareholder returns, while its impact on economic sustainability is less evident. Social expenditure appears to strengthen managerial performance but generates limited short‐term benefits from shareholder and societal perspectives. In addition, liquidity, leverage, firm size, and workforce characteristics exert heterogeneous effects across stakeholder‐oriented performance measures. Overall, the findings highlight the existence of important trade‐offs between efficiency, profitability, and sustainability objectives. By demonstrating that the performance implications of sustainability‐related investments are stakeholder‐dependent rather than universal, this study contributes to the growing literature on corporate sustainability and performance. Furthermore, it provides new evidence on how firms operating in a traditional export‐oriented industry respond to sustainability pressures in a Mediterranean context.

title: Beyond the Circularity Illusion in Fast Fashion: A System Dynamics Evaluation of Circular Economy Strategies
abstract: In the last two decades, the rise of fast fashion, characterized by overproduction and short product lifecycles, has exacerbated the environmental impacts of the fashion sector at a global level. Driven by policy and market pressures, major fast fashion companies have started implementing circular economy ( CE ) initiatives, including recycling programs, reuse, and repair services, and the use of recycled materials. Even if such actions could be particularly relevant in fast fashion due to the sectors' high product volumes and extensive vertical integration, few studies focus specifically on evaluating in a holistic way all actions carried out by fast fashion companies. In detail, a comprehensive systemic analysis of the potential long‐term environmental benefits of CE strategies adoption in this sector is still lacking, as most studies focus on isolated actions or short‐term qualitative assessments. This study aims at addressing this gap by developing a system dynamics (SD) model to evaluate the long‐term environmental performance of CE strategies in fast fashion. The SD model captures the behavior of a fast fashion company under circular and linear scenarios, enabling comparative analysis and supporting decision‐making processes on a long‐term horizon. By integrating multiple CE interventions across the value chain, the study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of their environmental implications. Results suggest that implementing different CE actions in a structured and holistic way can contribute to reducing the environmental burden of fast fashion, although broader business model innovations are required to achieve more substantial and long‐lasting effects.

title: When Governance Unlocks Green Performance: Revisiting ESG Effectiveness in Resource‐Abundant Economies
abstract: As environmental, social, and governance (ESG) frameworks gain traction in global financial markets, questions persist about their true environmental effectiveness, especially in resource‐abundant economies where governance weaknesses prevail. This study revisits the ESG–environment nexus through the lens of institutional enrichment, asking whether governance quality can unlock the environmental potential of ESG systems. Using panel data for 20 extractive economies spanning 2000–2023, we employ cross‐sectionally augmented autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) and method of moments quantile regression (MMQR) techniques to capture both long‐run dynamics and distributional heterogeneity across carbon emissions, ecological footprint, and green innovation. The results reveal that ESG scores alone often correlate positively with environmental degradation, suggesting symbolic compliance rather than substantive sustainability. However, when interacted with governance quality—and particularly its squared term—ESG frameworks begin to exert a significant mitigating influence on emissions and ecological pressure while enhancing innovation performance. This demonstrates that institutional enrichment functions as a threshold mechanism, converting ESG disclosure into genuine environmental progress. The study reframes ESG not as a standalone sustainability signal but as a conditional financial governance instrument dependent on institutional strength. By linking corporate sustainability strategy with institutional capability, the research offers a governance‐based explanation for ESG heterogeneity and provides strategic insights for policymakers, investors, and firms seeking credible pathways toward green performance in resource‐dependent contexts.

title: Algorithmic Environmental Governance: Legitimacy Construction in AI‐Driven Sustainability
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational sustainability initiatives, creating governance and legitimacy challenges related to transparency, accountability, and trust. This study develops an exploratory process framework of algorithmic environmental governance to explain how organizations seek to construct and sustain legitimacy for AI‐driven sustainability initiatives. Drawing on institutional theory, we examine pragmatic, moral, and cognitive legitimacy using qualitative accounts from 12 senior organizational actors and complementary secondary documents, analyzed through a Gioia‐informed approach. The analysis identifies governance mechanisms—including transparency, accountability, data governance, and ethical policies—and the organizational practices through which participants perceive these mechanisms to support legitimacy and stakeholder acceptance. The resulting framework specifies theoretically proposed pathways from governance through organizational practices to legitimacy and sustainability‐oriented outcomes, including a recursive feedback relationship. Because the evidence is primarily cross‐sectional and reflects managerial accounts, these pathways and environmental effects are proposed rather than causally established. The study advances a context‐specific account of the institutional work involved in governing AI for environmental purposes.

title: Consumer perceived value formation in drone food delivery services: The moderating role of user experience
Enhancing brand experience and customer behaviour through brand love: An integrated analysis of AI-enabled luxury hospitality in Vietnam and Taiwan
Beyond Project Delivery: Value Co-Creation and Co-Destruction Through Stakeholder Interactions
Food well-being in hospitality, tourism and recreation: a systematic review and research agenda
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to synthesize the state of knowledge on food well-being (FWB) within hospitality, tourism and recreation (HTR) contexts through a systematic literature review (SLR). It examines key antecedents, experiential food consumption mechanisms and outcomes for both visitors and host communities, while identifying conceptual gaps in how FWB is theorized and applied in HTR research. Design/methodology/approach Following the structured SLR approach of and preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, this review systematically analyzes 635 journal articles, reviews, and book chapters published across 208 academic journals. Data were retrieved from Web of Science and ScienceDirect. An integrative bibliometric analysis was conducted using VOSviewer and the bibliometrix (R-package) to map intellectual structures, thematic clusters and research trajectories related to FWB in HTR settings. Findings The review reveals that FWB remains an emerging and under-conceptualized construct in HTR research, often embedded implicitly within studies on food tourism, gastronomy and culinary experiences. Existing research predominantly emphasizes hedonic and cultural dimensions of food experiences, with limited efforts to operationalize FWB as a distinct construct. Food experiences such as festivals and traditional gastronomy contribute not only to visitor satisfaction but also to individual well-being, community identity and rural tourism development. FWB further plays a transformative role in enhancing perceived value, engagement, loyalty and destination food identity. Originality/value This study offers one of the first comprehensive SLRs positioning FWB as a central construct in HTR research. It provides a foundation for future empirical work and practical guidance for destination managers, experience designers and policymakers seeking to foster well-being-centered food experiences aligned with community development and sustainability goals.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: High-tech vs. high-touch in hospitality: finding the balance of well-being for human assets
abstract: Purpose While the technology adoption literature focuses on customer outcomes and operational efficiency, the employee experience of navigating simultaneous high-tech and high-touch demands remains theoretically underdeveloped. To address this gap, this study aims to examine how the joint optimization of technical and social systems affects employee well-being, work quality of life and behavioral outcomes and propose critical questions, future research directions and theoretical and managerial implications. Design/methodology/approach Using socio-technical system theory as an analytical lens, this paper adopts a critical theory synthesis approach to examine the integration of high-tech and high-touch service delivery and its implications for employee well-being in the hospitality context. This study advances research by providing critical comparisons and considerations for well-being in a high-tech and high-touch environment. Findings The synthesis of the relevant literature suggests that technology should not be viewed merely as an external influence, but rather as an integral social component in the hospitality workforce. Technology is deeply intertwined with the industry’s high-touch service environment, making the balance between high-tech and high-touch a dynamic and continuously evolving relationship that subtly yet significantly shapes employee well-being. Research limitations/implications This study aims to spark critical thought and future research on the new nature of hospitality work being both high-tech and high-touch and how this expanded work demands affect already overworked hospitality employees. Originality/value This research outlines future research directions and actionable steps for practitioners to consider as they implement technology into human service-driven encounters. This paper also acknowledges the importance of employee well-being in future sustainable employment.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Back to the future: orchestrating dynamic capabilities for AI-enabled supply chain design
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted in supply chain (SC) design, but guidance on its adoption in the literature is fragmented and often overlooks empirical insights based on established digital technologies. As a result, cumulative theory building is hindered, and there is little clarity on recurring adoption issues and organizational challenges. This study explores how factors that affect the adoption of established digital technologies – such as the Internet of Things and radio-frequency identification – apply to the incorporation of AI into SC design from the orchestrator’s perspective. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a sequential mixed-methods approach. It begins with ten expert interviews to identify key reference technologies and core SC processes, which were then validated through a systematic review of 47 studies. Conditions for adoption were assessed using the technology–organization–environment and dynamic capabilities frameworks and applied to AI implementation in SCs. Findings We distill recurring AI adoption conditions into six dynamic implementation domains. We show that orchestrators address these through a recursive cycle of sensing, seizing and reconfiguring, in which reconfiguring resets the conditions sensed in the next iteration. This approach frames AI implementation as continuous capability renewal and foregrounds the intensified integration, data and coordination demands introduced by AI. Originality/value This research advances knowledge of AI adoption in SCs by grounding implementation in empirically accumulated lessons from established digital technologies instead of treating AI as an isolated phenomenon. Drawing on prior digitalization experiences with rich evidence of adoption clarifies AI integration in SC design.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: How effective are start-up grants for new businesses? Evidence from Romania
Change Begins With Us: Leveraging Cognition to Cultivate Meaning and Motivate Action
abstract: ROI | supply chain managementLet's get to the point.Society has long questioned its investment in higher education (Fawcett and Waller 2015), also known as the Academy.Today, those doubts are stronger than ever (Parker 2025).Consider this: global spending on higher education approaches $1 trillion each year. 1 We as scholars justify this investment by stressing the Academy's role: to discover and disseminate knowledge that makes the world a better place.Key stakeholders such as students, parents, corporations, and politicians increasingly challenge this value proposition.They ask, "Are we earning a reasonable return on our investment?"Consider the numbers: an actionable article-i.e., research that is relevant to managerial decision-making-costs more than $1.5 million (Martin 2012).As one pundit notes, "Many faculty articles… have little to no value to practicing managers" (Byrne 2014).A 2026 Gallup employer survey also found that only 22% strongly believe that "colleges are graduating students with the competencies MY business needs" (Gallup and Lumina Foundation 2026;Sugimori et al. 1977;Liker 2004).Considering the costs of what we do, and the perception that our discovery-and-dissemination efforts deliver limited value, the time has come to reflect on how we can level up society's ROI on higher-education investments.Our focus here is on improving the meaning and impact-i.e., the ROI-of supply chain research.Our goal: make actionable research a defining feature of SCM and the Journal of Business Logistics.1. Eliminate Waste.Lean defines waste as anything that consumes resources but adds no value for the end customer.Perhaps this is the lens through which skeptics conclude that academic research offers "little to no value" to society.How else should we perceive unread academic articles?Consuming resources without adding value undermines stakeholder confidence.Value creation isn't merely a matter of style; it is central to research that matters.If research does not enable effective action, regardless of how it performs on internally defined metrics such as citation counts, are we creating enough value to justify our constituents' investments?2. Respect People.Lean elevates respect for people because people are the only true source of creativity and the drivers of continuous improvement."Top" journals, however, tend to be formulaic.One result: Researchers, especially young scholars, focus on cracking the code rather than pursuing uniquely actionable research.They worry more about gaining other academics' respect than influencing practitioners.In a way, we act like old-school factory workers churning out "defective" products, underutilizing our scarcest resource: human creativity.To summarize, academic publishing too often promotes waste rather than creatively driving improved practice.It rewards research designs that are deeply rooted in existing theory and methodological detail rather than designs that are deeply rooted in real-world phenomena and address real-life challenges.One result: manuscripts can easily exceed 15,000 words yet say little that interests a nonacademic reader (Davison et al. 2024).Can we agree that we are operating below our potential?Others have called out the challenge (see Thomas et al. 2026).But the Academy changes slowly.The risk, as Jack Welch noted, is that when internal change is slower than external change, the end (Welch and Byrne 2001) Rittel and Weber is in sight.The Journal of Business Logistics is striving to pick up the pace, including through this To-the-Point special topic forum.Yet, we must do more to increase our ROI.

title: Deciphering the slow adoption of HR analytics: a comprehensive exploration of individual, social, and technological factors
abstract: The growing importance of analytics in management, including Human Resource Management, supports data-driven decisions and strategic objectives. Despite its benefits, HR professionals have been slow to adopt HR analytics. This study aims to identify factors that facilitate and hinder HR analytics adoption among HR professionals, with a focus on the moderating role of organizational culture. Using an integrated model that combines the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), this study examines factors influencing HR analytics readiness and their influence on adoption behavior The validation of model was accomplished through the employment of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), which was conducted using survey data from 305 HR professionals based in India. The findings show significant positive relationships between readiness for HR analytics and factors such as attitude, quantitative self-efficacy, peer influence, superior influence, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and tool trialability, while data availability was insignificant. Individual and social factors positively influence readiness, whereas organizational culture negatively moderates the relationship between readiness and the adoption of HR analytics. The findings emphasize the need for cultural reorientation to foster innovation and effectively implement HR analytics, offering valuable insights for managers, business leaders, and policymakers.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Shifting Gears: Government Subsidies and Innovation During Family Firm Succession
abstract: Government subsidies can support innovation, but how firms respond to them may change when decision authority within the firm changes. Drawing on resource dependence theory and socioemotional wealth theory, we argue that family firm succession may weaken the relationship between government subsidies and innovation input while strengthening their relationship with patent‐based innovation output. We analyze panel data on Chinese listed family firms from 2003 to 2021. The findings show that succession is associated with a weaker positive relationship between government subsidies and R&D investment but a stronger positive relationship between government subsidies and patent‐based innovation output. The strengthening of the subsidy–patent relationship is most pronounced after successors enter the firm but before they assume full authority, and reverses after the predecessor exits. The study advances our understanding of how succession changes the relationship between government subsidies and firm innovation.

title: Making sense of signals: the functional roles of third-party signals in entrepreneurial finance
Enacting organizational design under institutional plurality: a praxis perspective on entrepreneurship centers
abstract: Entrepreneurship centers have become prominent organizational units in higher education, providing student-focused support in entrepreneurial learning, early-stage venture development, and engagement with broader ecosystems. These centers operate under institutional plurality, where educational, venture-enabling, institutional, and ecosystem-facing expectations can generate organizational tensions around what centers have to prioritize, whom they should serve, how their contributions should be assessed, and how they should be designed. Drawing on an abductive multiple-case study of seven centers, this study examines how entrepreneurship centers configure and enact organizational design under institutional plurality. We develop a praxis perspective on organizational design that explains how centers navigate organizational tensions among interdependent design elements. We show that this occurs through recurring praxis mechanisms, including the reframing of the purpose of entrepreneurship, the differentiation and staging of activities through barrier lowering, funneling, and temporal sequencing, the structural bridging of centralized and faculty-embedded arrangements, the hybridization of academic and practitioner expertise, and the brokerage and orchestration of internal and external collaborations. Through these mechanisms, centers translate plural demands into connected organizational arrangements without fully resolving the underlying tensions. These findings show how entrepreneurship centers pursue organizational coherence under institutional plurality without relying on a stable logic of fit. Instead, actors enact and adjust interdependent design elements through situated praxis. By conceptualizing organizational design in entrepreneurship centers as an ongoing accomplishment, this study advances understanding of how these centers are organized under plural demands and offers broader implications for organizational design when organizational purpose is plural and negotiated.

title: A multilevel perspective on academic spin-off creation and growth in Europe
An entrepreneurial ecosystem in a small island developing state: when support organizations become entrepreneurial
abstract: Entrepreneurial support organizations (ESOs) are key actors in entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) emergence, yet little is known about how they operate in resource-deprived contexts. We conceptualize resource deprivation as the mutually reinforcing effects of unfavorable country-level conditions and EE nascency, which limit the availability of resources for entrepreneurship. Drawing on 28 semi-structured, in-person interviews across 25 ESOs in the Solomon Islands, we examine how ESOs navigate this dual liability of resource deprivation while resourcing entrepreneurs. We find that ESOs address the dual liability through building markets from within, empowering marginalized groups, and creating external linkages. ESOs move beyond conventional support roles to mobilize resources in response to local needs, often engaging nontraditional local actors, such as churches, and external actors, including overseas NGOs. While broadening the scope of support may help secure additional resources, it can also lead to a lack of focus in the nascent EE, which potentially creates new barriers in EE emergence. Moreover, ESOs become entrepreneurial in their efforts to secure external resources, which may create dependencies on actors outside the EE.

title: Alternative Data as Audit Risk Signals: Evidence from Online-Sales Data
journal_name: Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory

title: Data-driven capability and corporate cost stickiness: evidence from information processing, expectation revision, and governance transparency
abstract: Purpose Existing literature explains cost stickiness primarily through adjustment costs, managerial optimism, and agency conflicts, but overlooks the role of data-driven capability at the micro-foundational level. This study aims to investigate how a firm's data-driven capability reshapes asymmetric cost behaviour and to uncover its underlying micro-mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2013 to 2024, this study constructs a firm-level measure of data-driven capability via textual analysis. We employ empirical regressions to examine its effect on cost stickiness, supported by sensitivity checks and endogeneity corrections. We further conduct mechanism and heterogeneity tests, and examine the effect on administrative expense stickiness. Findings Data-driven capability is significantly associated with lower cost stickiness, a result robust to endogeneity corrections. Mechanism analyses provide suggestive evidence consistent with three channels: information processing, expectation formation, and governance transparency. The association is more pronounced in firms with higher business complexity and severe agency conflicts, and is also significantly associated with lower administrative expense stickiness. These findings uncover the micro-mechanisms through which data-driven capability influences cost adjustment behaviour. Originality/value This study is original in extending the cost stickiness literature by introducing data-driven capability as a novel micro-foundational determinant, moving beyond traditional cost and agency perspectives. By employing textual analysis to construct a firm-level measure, it provides a new methodological approach. The value of this research lies in uncovering the specific micro-mechanisms driving asymmetric cost behaviour and offering practical implications for digital-era cost management, helping managers understand how data resources optimise resource allocation during demand contractions.

title: Let's Get Loud: Vulnerable and Grandiose Narcissism and National Markets' Preference for Prominent Luxury Brands
abstract: Prior studies of individual consumers report that people high in vulnerable narcissism (VN), who depend on the approval of others, favor loud luxury brands, whereas people high in grandiose narcissism (GN), who seek admiration and distinction more than approval, favor them less. We ask whether the same contrast separates national markets. For 30 countries from 2021 to 2024, we measure a market's prominence preference, the slope of its calibrated Google Trends interest across up to 21 luxury brands on their measured logo prominence, and relate it to country means of VN and GN from more than 50,000 respondents. In spatial Durbin panel models with economic, demographic, and institutional controls, markets higher in VN preferred loud brands once GN was held constant ( b = 1.17, p = 0.043), and this association exceeded the one for GN (difference = 1.65, p = 0.046). The VN estimate was not significant at alternative respondent thresholds or in several other checks, and with 30 countries the design could detect only large effects. In exploratory analyses, the GN association was negative where income was evenly distributed and weaker where it was concentrated, and the VN association did not vary significantly with income concentration.

title: The effect of advertisements with people with disabilities (PWD) on brand evaluation: examining the moderating role of brand type
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how advertisements featuring people with disabilities (PWD) influence consumer responses. It tests a sequential process in which disability representation increases perceived warmth and perceived competence, thereby enhancing brand coolness, and examines whether the effects extend to brand evaluation. Design/methodology/approach Across four experiments, this study uses controlled experimental designs to test the effects of advertisements featuring PWD on brand coolness and brand evaluation. The studies examine a sequential process involving perceived warmth and perceived competence and assess how this process varies between luxury and non-luxury brands. Findings The results reveal that advertisements featuring PWD increase perceptions of brand warmth and competence, which sequentially enhance brand coolness and brand evaluation. However, this effect was stronger for non-luxury brands and attenuated for luxury brands, suggesting inclusive cues offer less incremental value when status is already established. Research limitations/implications This research focuses on visible physical disabilities and samples from the United States and the United Kingdom, which may limit generalizability. Future research should examine other disability types and cultural contexts. Practical implications The findings indicate that incorporating PWD in advertisements can enhance brand evaluations for non-luxury brands by activating warmth that reinforces competence. In contrast, for luxury brands, such cues do not necessarily translate into more favorable brand responses and therefore require careful alignment with existing brand schemas. Originality/value Departing from accounts that treat disability representation primarily as a moral or symbolic gesture, this study positions inclusive advertising as an input into consumer brand evaluation and integrates the Stereotype Content Model (SCM) and the Brands as Intentional Agents Framework (BIAF) to clarify a sequential mechanism through which disability representation shapes brand coolness via warmth and competence. It further identifies brand type as a critical boundary condition and shows how these effects extend to brand evaluation.

title: The call for signaling of expertise on social media: the case of food influencers
abstract: Purpose A tension exists between engagement-driven platform visibility and consumers’ need for credible dietary advice with direct health implications. This research aims to examine how expertise cues help consumers identify credible food influencer content and how qualified influencers can communicate expertise effectively in social media environments. Design/methodology/approach Across six studies, the authors combine secondary analysis of 397 Instagram recipe posts from 40 qualified and non-qualified food influencers with five experiments involving 1,977 participants: US adults recruited through MTurk (Ns = 231, 309 and 284) and US undergraduates (Ns = 601 and 552). The experiments manipulate source qualifications, message design, expertise-salience cues and measure individual differences in BMI and body-esteem, to examine effects on perceived expertise, health-related outcomes and social media engagement. Findings Consumers often do not distinguish clearly between qualified and non-qualified food influencers when expertise cues are absent. Secondary data analysis shows meaningful differences in the reliability of content produced by these sources. Across the studies, making expertise salient increases perceived expertise and improves both health-related and engagement outcomes. The authors further show that combining informational and motivational message elements strengthens the effect of qualifications on perceived expertise, and that body esteem shapes consumer responsiveness to expertise signals. Research limitations/implications The findings are based primarily on Instagram-related contexts and may not generalize fully to other platforms or audience groups. Future research should examine additional platforms and broader samples. Practical implications The findings offer practical guidance to qualified food influencers seeking to strengthen their “knowledge influencer” persona through strategic message design and expertise signaling, with implications for combating diet and nutrition misinformation. Originality/value This research refines source credibility theory by showing that expertise in influencer-mediated food communication is not always immediately visible or automatically persuasive. Instead, its effectiveness depends on how clearly it is signaled in message content and how consumers interpret those cues. The research therefore specifies the conditions under which expertise becomes credible and consequential in digital food contexts.

title: How nostalgia guides purchase intentions for art-infused products
abstract: Purpose This research aims to investigate how nostalgia influences consumer purchase intentions for art-infused products. Design/methodology/approach Three laboratory-based experiments were designed to test the key hypotheses. Studies 1, 2 and 3 used between-subjects designs with sample sizes of n = 284, 280 and 328, respectively. Findings Studies 1 and 2 examine low- and high-involvement product categories, respectively, revealing that inducing nostalgia significantly increases purchase intentions for art-infused products compared to a control condition. Study 3, focusing on a medium-involvement product, reveals that this effect is serially mediated by perceived abstractness, product meaningfulness and novelty. Research limitations/implications Future work can explore the role of other emotions, such as pride and serenity, in the context of art-infused product consumption decisions. Practical implications The findings have implications for how art-infused products can be effectively marketed. Originality/value Although prior work has examined the role of emotions such as “awe” in creative contexts (Hagtvedt, 2025), nostalgia’s impact on consumer responses to art-infused products has yet to be investigated.

title: Mergers and acquisitions in tourism and hospitality: Winner's curse and ideological divergence
Small N, High Stakes: Simulating Adverse Impact With Bayesian Logistic Regression Analysis and Permutation Tests
abstract: Organizations frequently evaluate adverse impact with rules of thumb and statistical tests that perform poorly when hiring cohorts are small, raising scientific concerns that have legal and ethical implications. To address these concerns, this study conducts Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests as two new approaches to conducting adverse impact analysis under small-sample conditions. Simulations were varied across a realistic range of effect sizes, selection rates, and group sample sizes. The performance of each method was evaluated in terms of Type I error rates and statistical power. Results indicated that both Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests are viable alternatives to traditional methods under small-sample conditions. Bayesian odds-ratio rules with noninformative or weakly informative priors in particular demonstrated higher power than frequentist methods at small sample sizes, although no method reached .80 power on average. Their Type I error rates sometimes exceeded the nominal .05 level but remained well below those of the 4/5ths rule. Implications and advantages of each method are discussed in detail.

title: A Double-Edged Sword? Creators’ Responses to AIGC Tagging on Digital Art-Sharing Platforms
Upholding Sufficiency-Ethical Practices: Insights from a Sufficiency-Oriented Community in Ecuador
abstract: The concept of sufficiency presents a compelling alternative to the dominant paradigm of unrestrained economic growth and resource exploitation, emphasizing the importance of achieving a balance between needs and wants to ensure well-being within planetary boundaries. With intensifying ecological and social pressures, sufficiency offers not only a theoretical critique of unlimited growth but also a practical framework for moving toward sustainable lifestyles. Prior research, while examining sufficiency through practices like goods repair and seasonal consumption, has inadequately addressed the ethical grounding of these practices, despite the fact that practices are the means by which ethical principles become visible. To address this gap, this study investigates how ethical virtues serve as organizing principles for sufficiency practices, drawing on social practice theory to bridge virtue ethics and sufficiency. Utilizing qualitative data obtained from an Ecuadorian non-profit organization, we develop a process model that explains how sufficiency-ethical practices are established, formalized, disseminated and upheld. This work extends the literature on the intersection of sufficiency and ethics by providing a comprehensive exploration of organizational virtues as organizing principles for sufficiency practices and by shedding light on the potential for fostering sufficiency-oriented communities that enhance resilience, justice, solidarity and environmental stewardship.

title: Corporate Employee Responsibility and Government Employment Subsidies: Analysis of More Talk Than Action
abstract: Can enterprises secure government subsidies by embellishing hard information? From the perspective of corporate employee responsibility, this study examines the impact of inconsistency between words and deeds in employee responsibility on the allocation of government fiscal employment subsidies. Empirical results demonstrate that more talk than action (MTTA) in corporate employee responsibility significantly reduces the level of government employment subsidies obtained by enterprises, with this effect being primarily driven by less action.
