Further analysis reveals that the government’s promotion of Internet‑plus‑government‑services effectively strengthens the supervision of corporate employee responsibility, thereby amplifying the inhibitory effect of MTTA on access to employment subsidies. This moderating effect is more pronounced in state-owned enterprise, firms operating in labor-intensive industries, and enterprises located in regions with low fiscal revenue. Additionally, MTTA in corporate employee responsibility also significantly restricts enterprises’ access to other types of government subsidies. The findings of this research provide empirical evidence and policy implications for standardizing corporate employment practices, advancing the digital transformation of government governance, and optimizing the institutional framework of Internet‑plus‑government‑services.

title: Trade Wars and Corporate Strategic Boundaries: Geopolitical Competition, Supply Chain Restructuring, and Diversification of Chinese Manufacturing Firms
abstract: Using the 2018 U.S. Section 301 tariffs as a quasi-natural experiment, this article examines how geopolitical trade conflict reshapes corporate diversification in a 2012–2024 panel of Chinese A-share manufacturing firms. Difference-in-differences estimates show that firms in the targeted industries significantly broaden their business portfolios relative to unaffected manufacturers. Two channels transmit the effect: reduced supply chain concentration and compressed expected returns on core businesses. The response is confined to non-state-owned enterprises and is strongest among moderately diversified firms. The article provides the first causal evidence linking a geopolitical trade shock to corporate diversification in an emerging market, with implications for supply chain and portfolio strategies under geoeconomic uncertainty.

title: Accounting Intelligence and Corporate Resource Allocation Efficiency: Evidence from the Low-Altitude Economy Industrial Chain
abstract: The low-altitude economy concentrates frictions that distort corporate investment: long horizons, rapid technological iteration, and tight coupling between upstream and downstream segments. Using a text-based index of accounting intelligence built from the annual reports of Chinese A-share firms in the low-altitude economy industrial chain from 2010 to 2024, we examine whether the intelligent transformation of accounting improves resource allocation. We find that accounting intelligence reduces investment inefficiency, and the result holds under an instrumental-variables strategy and a range of robustness checks. The effect operates through lower agency costs and more transparent disclosure of trading partners. It is concentrated among firms whose intelligent accounting is embedded in routine bookkeeping and shared-service processes rather than in decision-oriented vocabulary, suggesting that implementation, not the language of transformation, is what disciplines investment.

title: Education Policy in Multilevel Systems: Introducing the Index of Regional Powers in Education ( IRPE )
How Does implicit debt shape local governments’ low-carbon governance? A public value conflict perspective
abstract: Against the backdrop of accelerating green development and low-carbon transition, governments worldwide face challenges balancing economic development and low-carbon governance. Particularly when faced with fiscal pressure and public debt accumulation, local governments often confront public value dilemmas. This study examines how implicit debt affects local governments’ low-carbon governance efficiency via public value conflict, and further analyzes the effect of local leadership turnover frequency on this mechanism. Results show that implicit debt intensifies public value conflict in local low-carbon governance, thereby inhibiting low-carbon governance efficiency. Moreover, a higher frequency of local leadership turnover further strengthens this mechanism.

title: Beyond Anticipatory Governance: Defensive Steering for the Life Sciences in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Anticipatory governance attempts to manage emerging technologies by forecasting trajectories to mitigate future risks. However, it requires confidence in the direction of the technology and what that direction requires of us. Because biotechnological development is highly processual, decentralized, and dual-use-properties compounded by artificial intelligence-we argue that achieving the epistemic consensus required for anticipatory governance is inherently constrained. In turn, we introduce "defensive steering" as a necessary complementary framework. Instead of requiring policymakers to predict uncertain futures, defensive steering leans into the polycentricity of biotechnology governance and demands that actors across the biotechnology regime complex continuously steer the present technological landscape toward greater defense-dominance on the margin. Through market-shaping, subsidies, innovation, and regulations, actors can influence the timing, rate, properties, deployment, and diffusion of defensive tools. While legitimacy under polycentricity is contested, it is also collectively conferred. Ultimately, this framework offers a practical, real-time strategy to mitigate risks from emerging biotechnologies.

title: Association Between prenatal cannabis use and pregnancy loss: a population-based retrospective cohort study
abstract: Biological evidence suggests prenatal cannabis exposure may increase risks of miscarriage and stillbirth, but epidemiologic studies are limited by methodological weaknesses. Addressing these gaps, we evaluated associations between prenatal cannabis use and pregnancy loss in a population-based retrospective cohort. The study included 233,860 pregnancies (184,296 individuals) universally screened for substance use upon entry into prenatal care (~8-10 gestational weeks) between January 1, 2011 and September 30, 2019. Prenatal cannabis use was defined as any use (self-report or urine toxicology) and frequency (self-report). Miscarriage and stillbirth outcomes were obtained from electronic health records and California vital records. Cox proportional hazards models were conducted separately for miscarriage and stillbirth adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, maternal comorbidities, and maternal prenatal use of other non-cannabis substances. The cohort was 38.6% non-Hispanic White, with mean (SD) maternal age 30.6 (5.5) years; 6.6% screened positive for cannabis. Overall, 5.5% of pregnancies ended in miscarriage and 0.4% in stillbirth. Prenatal cannabis use (vs. none) was associated with a 13% increased risk of miscarriage occurring after entry into prenatal care (~8-10 weeks gestation; aHR: 1.13,95%CI: 1.03-1.22), rising to ~30% after excluding other substance use. Weekly (aHR: 1.32,95%CI: 1.07-1.63) and daily (aHR: 1.29,95% CI: 1.02-1.63) use (vs. no use) showed similar increases. No association was observed for stillbirth. These findings add to the growing body of evidence linking prenatal cannabis use with adverse pregnancy outcomes and may help inform clinical counseling, harm reduction strategies, and public health policies.

title: Comparing randomized trials
abstract: Disagreements between well-conducted randomized trials addressing the same causal question generate intense discussion of possible explanations and sometimes stir controversy. In this issue of the Journal, Virkud et al. (Am J Epidemiol. 2025; doi:10.1093/aje/kwaf202) compared two double-blind randomized trials of 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) for the prevention of recurrent preterm birth, considering differences in population characteristics as the leading explanation for the disagreement between the trials' marginal (population-averaged) results. In this commentary, we outline considerations for comparing randomized trials addressing the same causal question, including explanations beyond differences in population characteristics. We highlight parallels between comparing trials and benchmarking observational analyses against trials, and note that selection of between-study comparisons for interrogation may introduce statistical complications that should be considered alongside causal issues. We emphasize that formal between-study comparisons rest on long chains of causal and statistical assumptions, and that the interpretation of disagreements requires substantive knowledge to assess the plausibility of competing explanations. Technical details are presented in a companion report.

title: Interpreting Ambient Exposure Associations in Veteran Suicide and Overdose Mortality
Evaluating PII De-identification models for crash narratives: zero-shot benchmarking and a case study of fine-tuning and cross-jurisdictional transferability
Community environment has similar risks for subsequent maltreatment reports as risk factors: The impact of structural disadvantage on child protective service involvement
A Qualitative Study of Facilitators and Barriers to Care-experienced Children’s Wellbeing During the Transition to Secondary School
abstract: While school transitions can be challenging for all children, those with experience of maltreatment, including care-experienced children, face additional complexities linked to poorer wellbeing outcomes. This study explored the barriers and facilitators influencing UK care-experienced children’s wellbeing during the transition from primary to secondary school. Twenty-six care-experienced children and 25 caregivers from England and Wales participated through the ReThink Programme. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with both groups before and after the transition, one year apart, and analysed using a framework-based thematic approach. Three overarching themes were identified: children’s sense of belonging, relationships and emotional support; the extent to which systemic support met individual needs; and children’s personal resources, including coping strategies and self-perceptions. Findings highlight dynamic interactions between relational, systemic and individual factors shaping wellbeing for care-experienced children across this period. While some experiences mirror those of the general population, distinct challenges were identified requiring targeted policy and practice responses.

title: Shared decision-making and decisional self-efficacy in fertility preservation among male cancer patients: a cross-sectional study on the mediating role of social support
Policy advisory systems and democratic governance in Italy
abstract: Policy advisory systems (PASs) shape how governments organise and use expertise, yet their implications for democratic governance remain underexplored. This article examines how the governance of PASs influences democratic responsiveness and democratic accountability, asking how different organisational arrangements shape these core democratic dimensions. Focusing on the Italian PAS between 2020 and 2025, the article analyses how organisational analytical capacity mediates the relationship between democracy and technocracy. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of three governments, it discusses the consequences of the features and dynamics of the PAS (such as the creation of new advisory bodies, pluralisation, inclusiveness, adaptability, politicisation and elite circulation) on democratic governance. The findings show that these organisational arrangements can both enhance and constrain democratic responsiveness and accountability, depending on the institutional context and the inherited characteristics of the PAS. By linking PASs, policy analytical capacity and democratic governance, the article demonstrates how the governance of expertise shapes policy making and offers a framework for understanding when advisory systems strengthen or weaken democratic performance.

title: Interpersonal trust in the policy advisory process: a research agenda
abstract: Interpersonal trust is a key factor determining whether advice is taken into account in policy making, yet it has received little substantive attention in scholarship on policy advice and expert knowledge. Its role has only grown in importance amid accelerating democratic backsliding and the increased personalisation of politics in many jurisdictions. This article argues that policy scholarship can build on insights from other social science disciplines, which have a long-standing and rich tradition of researching trust, to develop a more purposeful and systematic approach to analysing interpersonal trust and its role in policy making. It sets out a research agenda for studying the phenomena that advances understanding of the informal dimensions of policy making, which have largely remained elusive. In doing so, it provides an analytical lens for examining policy making in settings characterised by weaker (or absent) democratic institutions, where interpersonal relationships may exert greater influence over policy decisions. Developing a stronger and more nuanced understanding of interpersonal trust is increasingly important given policy scholarship’s growing interest in non-democratic settings and the apparent erosion of democratic norms in many established democracies.

title: How municipalities organise policy implementation under weak enforcement
abstract: Municipalities in Spain are subject to legal transparency requirements that are weakly enforced. This article examines how municipalities organise implementation under weak enforcement: how arrangements change over time, who takes responsibility and what prompts them to change. Drawing on 51 interviews with officers in charge of transparency in municipalities of varying sizes and compliance levels, we trace how implementation has evolved since 2010. We find that municipalities typically assign transparency duties to existing staff and structures, rather than creating dedicated roles. Although legal enactment often initiates implementation, moves towards more specialised arrangements are associated with external incentives, such as evaluations or rankings, rather than with legal enactment alone. Administrative and technical staff tend to drive implementation, although political backing often supports organisational change. Our findings suggest that weak enforcement matters not only for whether municipalities comply, but also for how they organise and prioritise implementation, allocating attention and resources among competing demands.

title: Beyond Union Membership: Wage Formation and Collective Institutions
abstract: Using linked Norwegian employer‐employee register data for 2016–2023, we examine how union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage relate to wages. Union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage represent distinct dimensions of collective presence and should not be treated as conceptually equivalent. We find that union members earn more than non‐members irrespective of coverage, while the relationship between wages and union density depends on membership and coverage. Collective agreements are not associated with a uniform wage premium. However, covered firms have smaller white‐collar wage premia and a weaker relationship between wages and productivity for white‐collar workers.
journal_name: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: The Reversal of the Gender Gap in Automation: Evidence From the US Labor Market
abstract: This paper documents a reversal in the US gender gap in the probability of automation, 1976–2019. Women initially had higher automation probabilities than men, but the gap narrowed and reversed. The aggregate change occurs mainly within sectors, from clerical and retail sales to professional and technical occupations. The reversal is associated with education and occupational work‐hour structure. It is concentrated among newer cohorts: cohort‐specific gaps absorb most of the trend and attenuate as education, work‐hour structure, and social skills are added. These patterns are consistent with broad changes in women's occupational conditions but do not identify their causal mechanisms.
journal_name: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: From Mid-Level to Major Impact: Strengthening Women’s Leadership in Public Higher Education Institutions Through Strategic Human Resource Management for SDG Realization
abstract: Women remain underrepresented in higher education leadership despite sustained gender-equity efforts. This qualitative meta-synthesis examined how strategic human resource management (SHRM) supports women’s leadership in public higher education institutions by integrating evidence from 57 studies published between 2020 and 2025. Four themes were identified: SHRM as an enabler of women’s leadership; women’s leadership as an organizational capability; organizational and socio-cultural barriers; and strategic priorities for institutional action. The evidence indicates that women’s leadership is strengthened when equitable recruitment, leadership development, supportive organizational cultures, and accountability mechanisms operate as an integrated HR system. Persistent structural and socio-cultural barriers nevertheless continue to restrict advancement. Accordingly, this paper proposes an analytical framework linking SHRM, women’s leadership, SDG 4 (Quality Education), and SDG 5 (Gender Equality).

title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
abstract: Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. We also uncover that leaks become less—not more—likely when there is a negative expert assessment of a policy proposal (relative to a control group receiving no expert assessment). Our findings help elucidate the information‐sharing dilemmas faced by public administrators.

title: Unlocking lithium-ion battery state of health estimation via interpretable pseudo-linear parallel deep neural network
Nuclear energy powered hydrogen production for green metallurgy: Current status, coupling roadmaps, and techno-economic challenges
Scenario-adaptive Shapley allocation of multi-market benefits in renewable energy base-transmission systems through sparse interaction learning
System-level optimization of seawater-based water supply and cooling for large-scale green hydrogen and ammonia production under variable renewable operation
abstract: As green hydrogen and ammonia projects expand in arid coastal regions, coupled demands for process water (PW) and cooling water (CW) increasingly constrain cooling system (CS) selection and water supply infrastructure sizing. To address this research gap, a transferable methodology for designing and techno-economically evaluating cooling and water supply systems for large-scale seawater-based production is presented. It combines time-resolved renewable power and ammonia production modelling, CS performance models, water treatment plant (WTP) sizing, PW and CW storage simulation, and cost assessment. It is applied to the 1.5 GW Phase 1 Murchison Green Hydrogen Project in Western Australia as a case study, using hourly ERA5 climate data for 2015–2024. The investigated CS options include once-through seawater cooling (OTSC), dry cooling (DC), wet cooling towers (WCT), and adiabatic hybrid coolers (AHC). Storage-based optimization substantially reduced the required peak treatment capacities, lowering WTP capacity by 12.4% (to 273 m 3 /h) for PW and CW capacity by 20.6% (to 1,127 m 3 /h) for WCT, and 63.0% (to 636 m 3 /h) for AHC. These reductions translated directly into lower PW-related capital expenditure, operational expenditure, and levelized cost of water (−8.7%, −4.2%, and − 7.3%, respectively). On an integrated cost basis, WCT achieved the lowest levelized cost of cooling (5.96 USD/MWh th ), below DC (38.0%), AHC (44.7%), and OTSC (73.6%). A simplified cost-allocation sensitivity showed that neglecting water treatment and marine infrastructure requirements can alter the CS ranking. The analysis further indicated that CS and water supply make a non-negligible contribution to the total levelized cost of hydrogen, accounting for 2.0–7.4%.

title: Comparative multi-criteria assessment of hydrogen production pathways for nuclear microreactor deployment
An asymmetric multi-scale time-frequency fusion network with dynamic sparse experts and adaptive optimization for ultra-short-term load forecasting
Unlocking public EV charging flexibility for grid balancing: A year-long empirical assessment of unidirectional and bidirectional smart charging in Prague
abstract: The transition of imbalance settlement in the Continental Europe synchronous area to 15-minute market time units, together with rising shares of variable renewable generation, raises the operational value of sub-hourly demand-side flexibility. Electric vehicles at public charging stations are an attractive source, yet empirical estimates of the balancing value of public smart charging remain scarce. This paper quantifies the technical potential of aggregated public smart charging in Prague to absorb the 15-minute system imbalance of the Czech transmission system operator ČEPS, using a full year of real charging-session data: 286,492 sessions across 1051 charging points. An ex-post optimization on a session-level flexibility envelope evaluates four configurations: the unidirectional (V1G) and bidirectional (V2G) operating modes, each under two user-comfort scenarios in which the delivered energy is preserved exactly (S1) or relaxed to the greater of 80% of it or 30 kWh (S2). The fleet’s uncontrolled load is removed first, so the same energy is re-timed, not added. Public V1G absorbs 4.44% of the imbalance energy under S1 and 4.85% under S2; V2G absorbs 7.09% and 7.64%. Bidirectional operation increases the absorbed energy by more than half, whereas relaxing comfort adds only about half a percentage point, so the bidirectional-infrastructure axis carries far more value than the user-incentive axis. These figures are a best-case ceiling computed with hindsight, not an operational forecast; valued at Czech final settlement prices, the V2G potential is a gross avoided balancing cost of up to about EUR 480,000 per year.

title: Coordinating ecological and recreational functions in urban green infrastructure: A multilayer network approach across spatial scales
Winter is coming: unfolding frictions through a practice-based view of smart heating technology use
Auction cadence, Petrobras divestments and the institutional evolution of Brazil's oil sector (1995–2025)
abstract: This article examines Brazil's oil-sector transformation from 1995 to 2025, emphasising how changes in auction cadence – the frequency and timing of bidding rounds organised by the National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) – interacted with regulatory reforms, contractual regime shifts and Petrobras's asset strategy to shape investment, Local Content (LC) and fiscal outcomes. Using primary legal and institutional documents (laws, decrees, ANP bidding notices and results), Petrobras strategic plans and public time-series evidence on production, reserves, investments and government participations, the study traces three phases: early post-monopoly annual rounds that supported exploratory momentum; a pause and regulatory redesign around the pre-salt layer, a major offshore oil province, that altered incentives; and an accelerated sequence of rounds and open acreage offers (a continuous bidding modality) after 2016. Quantitative evidence shows Petrobras investment commitments fell from a 2012–2013 peak of roughly US$236 billion to about US$55 billion by 2021, while realised capital expenditure also contracted sharply after 2014. Offered LC rates in offshore exploration dropped from highs near 86% to around 18% in recent rounds. The analysis documents a negative synergistic association consistent with a mechanism whereby irregular auction cadence and state asset retrenchment may have jointly reduced conditions supporting domestic supplier demand. The analysis is descriptive and associational rather than causal. Policy recommendations include institutionalising a predictable auction calendar, reconfiguring LC instruments linked to finance and R&D (research and development), and measures to mitigate divestment impacts.

title: Carbon footprint of household electrical and electronic equipment consumption in the UK
abstract: The rapid growth in household electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) consumption presents significant environmental challenges globally, particularly regarding carbon emissions and waste management. However, existing studies tend to focus on a limited set of products or life-cycle stages, and there remains a lack of system-level assessments that employ dynamic and prospective life cycle assessment (LCA) methods to evaluate household EEE decarbonisation strategies. This study combines LCA with dynamic stock-flow modelling to estimate annual changes in product stocks, new-product inflows, reuse, waste product generation, recycling and disposal, and to first quantify the annual life-cycle carbon footprint of the UK household EEE system from 2010 to 2022. Exploratory prospective scenarios to 2030 with consideration of interventions such as increased reuse and acquisition avoidance through non-reuse mechanisms are then assessed. Results indicate that acquisition avoidance is the most effective intervention, reducing emissions by more than 10% compared to business-as-usual by 2030, while the increased-reuse scenario yields a 4% reduction. Across all scenarios, EEE energy consumption remains the dominant emissions driver, contributing over 70% of total emissions by 2030. While reuse reduces manufacturing-related emissions, prolonged use-stage emissions may offset these gains for energy-intensive appliances such as heaters and refrigerators. In contrast, low-energy products such as laptops and mobile phones offer greater carbon savings per unit reused. These findings highlight the need for systemic interventions that integrate acquisition avoidance, energy efficiency and targeted reuse to decarbonise the UK household EEE system effectively in the short to medium term.

title: Decarbonization pathways of China's vehicle fleet under diversified NEV substitution: An LCA perspective
A large language model-assisted framework for embodied carbon screening of buildings in data-constrained contexts
Nontargeted Metabolomics Reveal Multi-Pathway Disruption from BPA Exposure in the Freshwater Snail Planorbella pilsbryi
abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA) is used in the production of plastics and resins and is a well-established endocrine disruptor in humans and vertebrates; however, its effects on invertebrates are not understood. This study employed metabolomics to examine the biological effects of BPA exposure in the freshwater pulmonate snail Planorbella pilsbryi after a 28-d exposure at three concentrations (0.13, 3.7, and 479 μg/L). Using nontargeted liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS), we characterized the metabolomic profile of exposure to BPA in P. pilsbryi and identified perturbations to biological pathways. BPA exposure caused a significant increase in the abundance of lipids at all concentrations in whole-tissue homogenates, and numerous biological pathways were dysregulated by BPA, including pathways related to energy, metabolism, and digestion. BPA also decreased the abundance of methylated nucleobases, suggesting changes to DNA and RNA that may affect physiological function and gene expression. Overall, the present study revealed insights into the ways in which BPA affects freshwater pulmonate snails. The findings also serve as a framework for the use of metabolomics as a tool to investigate sublethal end points of effect in a nonmodel species. Additional research, such as targeted approaches oriented by the findings of this study, is needed to elucidate the effects of BPA in aquatic mollusks.

title: Abiotic Methane Production Driven by Hydrogen Peroxide Generated during Anoxic–Oxic Transitions in Coastal Sediments
abstract: Coastal ecosystems are recognized as substantial sources of atmospheric methane (CH4), which has traditionally been attributed to anaerobic methanogenesis by archaea. However, reactive oxygen species (ROS) are known to mediate abiotic CH4 production through iron-mediated Fenton-type chemistry. Whether tidal redox oscillations in coastal sediments generate ROS to drive this pathway naturally remains unknown. Here, we combined slurry incubation experiments under anoxic–oxic transitions with geochemical measurements and metatranscriptomic profiling to investigate hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-driven abiotic CH4 production in mangrove sediments. Upon O2 exposure, anoxically incubated active sediments rapidly produced H2O2 at rates of 9.3–100.7 mmol kgDW–1 h–1. The H2O2 was then consumed within hours, pointing to its role as a reactive intermediate. Concomitantly, O2 exposure significantly enhanced CH4 production in active sediments, with the maximum yields varying from 1.6 to 8.1 times those under continuous N2. Furthermore, inactivated sediments retained CH4 production under O2 exposure, and H2O2 quenching suppressed CH4 production in both active and inactivated sediments. This indicates that a substantial fraction of the CH4 produced upon oxygenation was H2O2-driven rather than of enzymatic origin. Metatranscriptomic analysis revealed that O2 exposure downregulated the transcription of methanogenesis-related genes, further indicating that O2 availability may inversely regulate the biogenic and abiotic contributions to CH4 production. These findings reveal a naturally occurring abiotic CH4 production pathway driven by H2O2 generation during tidal redox oscillations and sustained by abundant endogenous methyl donors, with implications for the global CH4 budget.
authors: Huub J. M. Op den Camp

title: Coordinating Charge Supply with Target-Reaction Utilization in Electrochemical Water Treatment
abstract: E lectrochemical water treatment offers controllable pollu- tant conversion with flexible operation and modular design.Advances in electrodes and reactors have expanded its capabilities.1 Yet greater electrode activity or charge input improves treatment only when reactant availability and interfacial conditions support productive utilization.As these conditions evolve, fixed electrical input can become inappropriate.Efficient treatment therefore requires joint design of charge supply and the conditions governing its utilization.Charge supply is specified by the applied current and its temporal profile, with cumulative charge given by its time integral.Target-reaction utilization capacity is the maximum charge-transfer rate that the intended transformation can productively accept at a given time and electrode location under specified reaction conditions.Stoichiometry defines charge requirements, whereas mass transfer, interfacial kinetics, and electrode surface availability constrain the productive rate.For a transport-limited direct reaction, this utilization capacity reduces to the limiting current:

title: Plastic Flows and Footprints in Norway’s Sea-Based Aquaculture Sector: A Material Flow Perspective
abstract: Marine plastic pollution is an increasing environmental concern, yet aquaculture’s contribution remains poorly quantified despite its rapid expansion and reliance on plastic infrastructure. Limited data on plastic stocks, flows, losses, and end-of-life (EOL) management constrain effective mitigation and circularity strategies. This study presents a system-wide assessment of plastic use and management in Norway’s sea-based Atlantic salmon aquaculture industry. A static Material Flow Analysis (MFA), informed by data from equipment manufacturers, suppliers, operators, and waste-management stakeholders, quantifies plastic stocks and flows across equipment deployment, use, repair, replacement, environmental losses, and end-of-life treatment. The results indicate annual marine plastic losses of approximately 2737 t, corresponding to 1.2–1.7 kg per tonne of salmon produced. Feed pipes, walkway components, and consumable ropes dominate leakage. Approximately 37,400 t of end-of-life plastics are collected annually, with 42% directed to incineration with energy recovery, 22% landfilled, and limited recovery through recycling. These findings highlight substantial opportunities to strengthen collection, recycling, and resource recovery. This first comprehensive national-scale assessment establishes a quantitative baseline for monitoring and policy development. It demonstrates MFA’s utility for identifying leakage hotspots and supporting Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and circular economy strategies to reduce plastic pollution from aquaculture.

title: Products of Indoor Ozone Chemistry Are Associated with Office Workers’ Negative Emotion
abstract: Numerous chemicals, emitted from humans, building materials, and cleaning agents, are present at high concentrations in modern energy-saving buildings with low air change rates (ACRs). Outdoor ozone entering indoors oxidizes these chemicals on surfaces and in the air to form more toxic compounds, collectively termed ozone reaction products (ORPs). In this study, 141 participants working in two open-plan offices within a commercial building were assessed for their work well-being daily for 21 consecutive workdays, while hundreds of chemicals in the office air were continuously measured. Among the well-being metrics assessed, negative emotion was most robustly associated with measures of the net ORP mixture, with an interquartile-range increase corresponding to a 0.054-point increase in negative emotion (95% CI: 0.032–0.076), against a mean score of 1.449 on a 1–5 scale. Associations were also observed for individual ORPs and persisted after adjustment for morning emotional state, copollutants, or other potential confounders in sensitivity analyses. In contrast, ozone, PM2.5, carbon dioxide, and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) showed weaker or no robust associations. As negative emotion is a sensitive indicator of early mental health risk, the finding underscores broader health implications of ORP exposures that are projected to increase as tropospheric ozone levels increase.

title: Pesticides and Tire-Derived Chemicals in Urban Stormwater Ponds: Spatiotemporal Dynamics, Co-Occurrence, and Implications for Environmental Monitoring
abstract: Urban stormwater contains complex mixtures of tire-derived chemicals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and other contaminants of emerging concern, yet traditional active monitoring of urban stormwater runoff is severely constrained by precipitation events, high sampling risks, and localized spatial biases. This study evaluates whether stormwater retention ponds serve as passive, spatial–temporal integrators of urban pesticides and tire-derived chemical fingerprints. A regional survey of 13 (sub)urban stormwater retention ponds and year-long, biweekly sampling of a subset of four ponds was combined to characterize the distribution, occurrence, spatial signatures, and temporal dynamics of urban pesticides, tire-derived chemicals, and metformin. Contaminant concentrations in the ponds were similar to those previously observed in stormwater runoff. Distinct temporal dynamics were observed among contaminant classes. Tire-derived chemicals displayed concentration peaks in early spring, whereas peak concentrations of pesticides were detected in early summer. Principal component analysis and Spearman correlations revealed that tire-derived chemicals and urban pesticides co-occurred spatially and temporally. Redundancy analysis and linear mixed-effects models indicated that the spatial distributions of contaminants can be partly explained by land use types within drainage areas. These findings successfully expand the conceptual framework of stormwater retention ponds beyond structural runoff management, establishing them as effective passive spatial–temporal integrators for tracing urban contaminants.

title: From Bulk Removal to Precision: The Next 60 Years of Water Treatment
Reconciliation through Integration: A Source-Level Bayesian Framework for Developing Measurement-Integrated Methane Inventories
abstract: Bottom-up (BU) inventories and top-down (TD) aerial measurements at midstream natural gas facilities frequently diverge, and this discrepancy remains a central challenge for methane accounting in the sector. Previous approaches typically reconcile this divergence by treating BU and TD data as independent estimates of a single true quantity to be adjusted toward agreement, rather than as evidence that each captures only part of a more complex underlying system. This complexity arises from methane emissions being strongly governed by equipment operational state and therefore instantaneous aerial “snapshots” translate poorly to annual inventories. We argue instead that BU and TD are complementary sources of evidence that should be integrated. We present a source-level Bayesian framework that constructs BU prior distributions for each emission source category and updates them with attributed aerial detections through an empirical data-augmentation procedure. The resulting posterior distributions were propagated through unit-level activity data and source-specific information via Monte Carlo simulation to produce annual estimates. Across 64 compressor stations, measurement-integrated annual estimates were 84% higher than the BU inventory, a difference driven almost entirely by compressor vents (rod packing and seal vents) and leakage through blowdown and isolation valves, which together accounted for 90% of the asset-level revision. The revision was heterogeneous across stations and source categories, emphasizing the importance of source-level, station-specific integration when developing an emissions inventory.

title: Uranium(VI) Removal from Water by Continuous-Flow Iron Electrocoagulation: Removal Pathways and Uranium Retention in Residual Solids
abstract: The removal of uranium(VI) from groundwater is important for both drinking water treatment and pump-and-treat remediation of contaminated aquifers. This study evaluated U(VI) removal by continuous flow-through iron electrocoagulation (EC) under realistic treatment conditions and environmentally relevant water chemistries. The effects of iron dose, pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), dissolved inorganic carbon, and Ca2+ were examined using EC followed by flocculation and sedimentation. Under oxic conditions, U(VI) was removed by adsorption to EC-generated Fe(III) oxides. Under anoxic conditions, U(VI) was removed via a two-step pathway of adsorption followed by reduction to less soluble U(IV) and U(V) species by mixed-valent iron solids (green rust and magnetite). Among the tested combinations of pH (6–8) and DO (oxic and anoxic), the best overall U(VI) removal performance was achieved under oxic pH 7 and anoxic pH 8 conditions. Both conditions gave effective (>90%) removal after 11 s of residence time in the EC reactor, followed by up to 10 min of post-EC treatment with a 10 mg/L Fe dose. Carbonate species and Ca2+ inhibited removal under both oxic and anoxic conditions by forming stable aqueous complexes with U(VI). EC achieved faster and greater U(VI) removal than with chemical coagulation or contact with preformed iron solids. The stability of U removed during anoxic EC was evaluated by exposing residual solids to air. After 24 h of air exposure, only ∼10% of U was released to water. The majority of immobilized U likely remained associated with magnetite. This study provides mechanistic insight into U(VI) removal, solid reactivity, and U stability during EC.

title: Climate Effect of Alternative Binders: Life Cycle Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Potential as a Carbon Sink
abstract: Substituting Portland cement (PC) with alternative binders offers a promising pathway to mitigate the climate impacts of the cement industry, one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize. While substantial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are generated during production, most alternative binders can sequester CO2 during their service life. This effect has been acknowledged from a technical perspective, yet its significant influences on the GHG footprint of alternative binders remain unresolved. In this study, we quantify the CO2 uptake of common alternative binders alongside their lifetime GHG emissions. We demonstrate that most binders can take up a larger amount of CO2 than PC during usage, due to a thermodynamically high uptake capacity or high uptake kinetics. The uptake reactions enable a dynamic CO2 loop, with 1–248% of the production emissions being recovered over a 100-year structure service life. However, when the slow reaction rate is considered, the associated climate benefits can be up to 71% lower than the theoretical apparent uptake value. Our results highlight the importance of combined CO2 uptake modeling in assessing the decarbonization potential of alternative binders, and provide a basis for justifying the capability of these binders for use as building carbon sinks.

Enhancing laccase stability, productivity, and reusability in biological pretreatment for biomass valorization
abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is a sustainable feedstock for second-generation biorefineries; however, its efficient conversion is hindered by biomass recalcitrance, primarily due to the presence of lignin. Among biological pretreatment approaches, laccase-mediated pretreatment has emerged as an environmentally friendly and selective strategy for lignin modification and removal. This review focuses on laccase-mediated biological pretreatment, with particular emphasis on improving enzyme stability, productivity, and operational reusability to enable efficient biomass valorization. Laccase-mediated pretreatment facilitates effective delignification while preserving carbohydrates, leading to reduced processing time, enhanced saccharification efficiency, and minimal formation of inhibitory by-products. Recent advances in enzyme immobilization techniques and recombinant expression systems have significantly improved laccase stability and operational performance, contributing to improved cost-effectiveness, as evidenced by techno-economic and life cycle assessment studies. Overall, laccase-mediated biological pretreatment represents a sustainable alternative to conventional pretreatment methods. Future research should prioritize the development of robust laccase variants and cost-effective immobilization strategies, particularly utilizing agro-industrial residues, and their integration into biorefinery frameworks to facilitate large-scale industrial application.

Not Learning from Others
abstract: We study social learning using experiments where two people independently learn relevant information and can share it to make accurate private decisions. Across three experiments, people are substantially less sensitive to information others discover than to equally-relevant information they discovered themselves. This holds when they must learn information from others through discussion; when the experimenter perfectly communicates the information; and even when participants observe others’ information with their own eyes. Our results therefore stem not from a failure to elicit information from others but a systematic tendency to underweight it relative to one’s own information. Our findings illustrate a powerful barrier to social learning that might underlie many documented cases of failure to learn from others.

title: The Economic Dynamics of City Structure: Evidence from Hiroshima’s Recovery
abstract: This paper examines the resilience of city structure to a large shock and its underlying economic mechanisms. We analyze the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, which was an exogenous shock that leveled the city center but not its periphery, by combining newly digitized data with a dynamic quantitative urban model. We first construct spatially granular data within Hiroshima and document the resilience: the city center recovered just about five years after being destroyed. Importantly, we also show that the recovery of the city center is not necessarily explained by its fundamental locational characteristics. We then develop a novel dynamic urban economics model that allows us to disentangle the mechanisms underlying the recovery. Our calibrated model finds that strong agglomeration forces, together with individuals’ expectations of the recovery, created a strong incentive to rebuild the city center quickly despite the catastrophic shock.

title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright
abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.

title: Fintech Expansion
abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)

title: CHILE
abstract: We introduce CHILE, an asset-pricing framework with asymmetric information, general utility functions, and arbitrary payoffs. It features a large economy (LE) with continuous-and-heterogeneous information (CHI). The defining feature of this information structure is that the total amount of information stays finite as the economy grows large. We use the framework to study how concentration—the presence of market participants of different sizes—affects market quality, namely liquidity and information efficiency. Greater concentration proves a double-edged sword: it raises liquidity but harms information efficiency. (JEL D01, D53, D82, E19, G12, G14)

title: Carbon home bias
abstract: We undertake a global analysis of institutional investor portfolios and find widespread underweighting of companies with higher carbon emissions, both in levels and intensities. This underweighting is largely driven by foreign companies with high carbon emissions, both at the intensive (tilting) and extensive (exclusion) margins. Domestic firms with high emissions are overweighted but by a smaller magnitude. These results reveal a bias for domestic companies with high carbon emissions. The carbon home bias is stronger in settings where institutions have tighter business connections, in countries with weaker social norms regarding climate crisis, and where the political environment is more polarized.

title: Trade Liberalisation and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in India
Selective Recommendation and Credible Exaggeration in Multidimensional Communication
abstract: A sender who wants a receiver to acquire items regardless of quality cannot communicate credibly about one item, but with several she can, by recommending weakly better items. We characterise a continuum of selective recommendation equilibria combining partial statements with full statements recommending everything. Recommendations in partial statements are always followed; those in full statements are followed probabilistically, leaving senders indifferent. Full statements remain credible despite recommending bad items—what we call credible exaggeration. In experiments, senders use partial statements selectively alongside full statements; receivers follow nearly all recommendations in partial statements and almost half in full statements, transmitting information.

Bank CEO turnover: The role of shareholders
abstract: This study examines whether the identity of the controlling shareholder affects chief executive officer (CEO) turnover in banking. Using a hand-collected panel covering all commercial banks in Poland from 1994 to 2024, we document substantial ownership-based differences in CEO turnover. Foreign-owned banks are generally less likely to replace CEOs than domestic private banks, and this association persists after controlling for profitability and bank risk. Severe short-term underperformance raises the likelihood of dismissal, but state-controlled banks, which exhibit higher CEO turnover overall, tie dismissal less closely to underperformance. CEOs’ own political and regulatory connections are unrelated to forced turnover, whereas the state-ownership differential in CEO turnover narrows before regular parliamentary elections and widens substantially afterward, consistent with political influence operating at the ownership level rather than through individual CEOs. Overall, we show that the identity of the controlling shareholder is associated with both the incidence and performance sensitivity of CEO turnover, and the main ownership patterns are robust across a variety of tests.

Dictator face can aid
abstract: This paper tests the hypothesis that donors rely on their impressions of dictators’ faces to assess their propensity to misuse foreign aid. It examines whether foreign aid is higher in countries ruled by competent-looking or trustworthy-looking dictators. We analyze the relationship between facial impressions and foreign aid on a sample of 274 dictators from 100 nondemocratic countries between 1975 and 2010. We find that the probability of receiving aid is sensitive to dictators’ facial competence, though the amount received is not. We observe that the effect of competence on aid operates primarily through bilateral aid. By contrast, we find no overall evidence that dictators’ facial trustworthiness affects aid. Furthermore, we observe that the impact of facial impressions has evolved over time: trustworthiness was more important to donors during the Cold War, while competence became the most salient trait in the post–Cold War era.

title: NORA-HANDY: Political capture and socio-ecological regime selection
abstract: Human–nature models with unequal access to resources can generate social collapse followed by ecological rebound, but they usually treat inequality as an exogenous parameter. We develop NORA-HANDY (Negotiated Orders and Regime Accessibility), an extension of the HANDY model in which the capture coefficient, the institutional weight of elite claims on common wealth, is generated by a bounded political-settlement process that combines threshold contestation with slower institutional constraint. We ask which institutional mechanisms select among survival, depressed persistence, and the collapse of the productive population (Type-L collapse). Two analytical results organize the answer. First, a single elite/commoner population ratio marks both the end of the positive material equilibrium branch and the onset of terminal commoner decline. Second, an exact invasion criterion determines whether a protected elite can grow within a commoner-dominated regime; it yields an explicit critical rate of downward status mobility and shows that, with equal class birth rates and impermeable classes, such a regime is always open to elite invasion. Both thresholds depend on politics only through the distribution of capture over time, and at a given mean capture temporal dispersion can only strengthen them. Numerical experiments show that deep but temporary rollback can block elite invasion that constant capture at the same mean allows; that, under one parameter set, different inherited elite populations lead to survival or to collapse; and that downward status mobility selects among collapse, a stable periodic low-inclusion regime, and commoner-only survival. Ecological rebound is therefore not in itself evidence of sustainability: across these regimes, the ecological stock is highest where the social outcome is worst.

Coming Clean on Hidden Ties: How Transparency in Related‐Party Transactions Shapes Business Group Internal Organization
abstract: This study demonstrates that transparency reforms trigger organizational restructuring within pyramidal business groups rather than simply eliminating opacity. Building on pyramidal ownership theory, we argue that enhanced disclosure alters the relative value of security benefits and diversion across hierarchical layers and jurisdictions. Exploiting the 2008 Brazilian reform of related‐party transaction disclosure as a natural experiment and leveraging a unique dataset covering both publicly traded and privately owned business groups, we show that increased transparency shapes the top layers of the pyramid to maximize security benefits. At the same time, to partially offset the loss of private benefits of control due to increased diversion costs, we find that groups increase the number of offshore affiliates to relocate diversion‐prone activities to jurisdictions with weaker disclosure regimes. These findings contribute to related literature by demonstrating that transparency reforms trigger organizational adaptation across both hierarchical and geographic dimensions.

title: Theory‐based foundations of Bayesian entrepreneurship
abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs can observe the same evidence yet reach different conclusions about an opportunity. We connect the theory‐based view with Bayesian Entrepreneurship by separating a qualitative theory of value creation—the mechanisms it admits, what it rules out, and where it applies—from the probabilistic beliefs needed to use it. The separation explains why actors disagree despite shared evidence, why different disagreements call for different experiments, and why an experiment can improve prediction without separating theories. It also distinguishes disagreement about an opportunity from differences in costs, constraints, or capabilities. When evidence is thin, a more focused theory can make acting worthwhile sooner without being more accurate. A worked theory card for Vanguard shows how to diagnose disagreement, and we outline tests of the resulting hypotheses. Managerial Summary Founders, investors, and mentors often read the same evidence differently because they hold different theories of how a venture will create value, not because one side lacks information. Before asking for “more traction,” they should state the founder's theory and its strongest rival, then locate the disagreement: whether a mechanism matters, how strong it is, which market conditions will arise, whether lessons transfer between settings, or how predictable results are. Each calls for a different test. When the parties share a forecast but differ in costs, contracts, or capabilities, the remedy is a change in terms or staging rather than another test. A worked example for Vanguard shows the method. Focused theories can justify acting sooner, but focus does not make them right.

Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification
abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods and the University of Michigan School of Information for financial support. They also gratefully acknowledge support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy (EXC 2126/2 – 390838866), and from the Center for Social and Economic Behavior at the University of Cologne. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08000 .

title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability
abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. When research indicates that differences in overconfidence are associated with other behaviors, beliefs, or evaluations, researchers should account for the possibility that differences in ability could provide a sufficient explanation. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by the UCLA Anderson Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05184 and https://researchbox.org/1597 .

title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy
abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01507 .

title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

title: Confident and Well‐Connected: The Interplay of Line Managers' HR Self‐Efficacy, Brokerage, and HRM Implementation
abstract: HRM implementation, defined as line managers' execution of core HRM tasks, has been identified as a key challenge in realizing the competitive advantages associated with HRM. Integrating social cognitive and social network theories, we investigate the joint effect of line managers' HR self‐efficacy (i.e., their confidence in their ability to effectively perform HRM‐related tasks) and their positions as brokers (i.e., their role as intermediaries between otherwise disconnected contacts) in HR advice networks on HRM implementation and establish a link to team performance. Multilevel analyses were conducted using multisource survey data from 88 line managers, their 325 subordinates, and 69 of the line managers' direct superiors across six Indonesian firms. The findings reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, with medium levels of self‐efficacy linked to more effective HRM implementation than either low or high levels. Moreover, line managers' positions as HR information brokers moderate the inverted U‐shaped relationship: The curve remains steeper at low levels of brokerage, but becomes shallower at high levels. Finally, HRM implementation mediates the joint effect of self‐efficacy and HR information brokerage on team performance. Taken together, these findings challenge the assumption of a linear relationship between HR self‐efficacy and HRM implementation, enrich understanding of the social foundations of line managers' HRM implementation, and contribute to broader discussions on the enablers and effects of HRM implementation.

title: Action-Oriented Narratives: How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

title: Platform Information Design and Competitive Price Targeting
abstract: We study platform information design, in which a platform provides information about individual consumers, enabling sellers to set targeted prices. Because targetable information partitions the market and might intensify seller competition, what information should be provided remains an empirical question. We collect novel microdata from Steam, the dominant PC video game platform, and use granular consumer purchase and usage data to estimate their heterogeneous demand for video games. We then develop an equilibrium targeted pricing model to simulate counterfactual outcomes under all possible information designs. We demonstrate that the profit-maximizing information design—which distinguishes heterogeneous consumer types while accounting for the design’s equilibrium impact—yields substantially higher profits compared to demand-based heuristics that ignore the equilibrium impact.
