title: Does following justice rules feel constraining or liberating for leaders? The moderating role of justice sensitivity
abstract: Some leaders feel drained after adhering to justice rules, whereas others experience justice rule adherence as restorative. Why does the same justice behavior have such divergent psychological consequences for the leaders who enact it? Drawing on self-discrepancy theory, we propose that perceived lack of control explains this divergence and that justice sensitivity determines which experience is more likely to emerge. Specifically, for leaders low in justice sensitivity, justice rule adherence increases perceived lack of control, leading to higher emotional exhaustion. For leaders high in justice sensitivity, justice rule adherence decreases perceived lack of control, thereby reducing emotional exhaustion. We tested our hypotheses in a scenario experiment (316 participants) and a daily experience sampling study (411 observations from 52 leaders). By demonstrating that justice rule adherence can have psychologically draining versus restorative consequences for leaders through perceived lack of control, this research advances a leader-centered, self-based perspective on organizational justice and offers new insights into when and why adhering to justice rules sustains rather than sacrifices leader well-being.

title: The effect of relative performance information on the performance of task novices
Artificial intelligence, new product development, and design: Towards a framework for artificial intelligence adoption in innovation research
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly central role in organizations’ digital transformation. There is growing scholarly interest in how AI supports innovation, that is, how activities and processes aimed at producing novel ideas, problem solutions or other outputs can be enabled by autonomous machines. This article focuses on the role of AI in new product development (NPD) and aims to develop theoretical insights into how AI is reshaping innovation processes. In a systematic review of 1,192 articles published in business and management journals between 1993 and 2024, we identified 67 relevant to AI, NPD, and design. Through a focus on design activities, choices and results, we analyse how AI has been adopted in NPD processes. We find that AI can help manage design complexity and relax traditional constraints, evidencing an alignment with theoretical frameworks centered on process and methodology; at the same time, current adoption of AI in NPD remains largely focused on the implementation and pursuit of measurable performance outcomes. By integrating our findings with existing innovation and AI literatures, we propose an integrative framework that builds on three pillars—strategic orientation, collaboration architecture, and value optimization—and sheds light on the role of governance as a meta‐level coordination mechanism.

title: Decoding transdisciplinary research practices in the global climate innovation system: A comparative review
abstract: We review and compare knowledge outputs from three different actors in the global innovation system for climate change: non‐profit organisations, consulting firms and academics from management and organisation studies (MOS). All three actors issue research publications that can inform how practitioners and policymakers make sense of, and respond to, the climate crisis. Using content analysis and bibliometric techniques with a corpus of more than 4.5 million words and 26 000 cited references, we systematically evaluate evidence of transdisciplinary practices in these texts. Compared to the knowledge outputs of MOS scholars, non‐profits’ and consultancies’ knowledge outputs consistently feature (1) more involvement of cross‐sector stakeholders in knowledge production, (2) more holistic issue conceptualisations, (3) more diverse knowledge foundations and (4) more transformation knowledge offered to a broader set of stakeholders. Moreover, academic management research is barely utilised by non‐profits and consultancies. Given the MOS community's ambitions for greater societal impact, these results ought to prompt reflection on prevailing scholarly practices within our field. We suggest that transdisciplinary practices are part of the epistemic norms that yield influence and foster collaboration within the global climate innovation system. At present, most MOS scholarship on climate action is at odds with these norms. We discuss two scenarios—MOS scholars as ‘preferred suppliers’ or as ‘coveted teammates’—to aid the uptake of our scholarship beyond our discipline and to fashion a more active role for us in shaping climate action.

title: The Policy‐Mix Paradox: How Green Credit and Carbon Trading Shape Green Innovation Commercialization Potential
abstract: Environmental regulation can induce green invention, yet whether those inventions retain commercialization potential remains uncertain. We examine this post‐invention boundary by studying how carbon emissions trading (CET) and green credit policy (GCP) shape the commercialization potential of firms' green inventions. Drawing on institutional complementarity theory, we argue that CET and GCP address sequential constraints: CET strengthens the incentive to invent, while GCP provides the financing capacity required to sustain development. Using an unbalanced panel of Chinese A‐share firms from 2011 to 2024, we measure commercialization potential through 5‐year forward citations to green patents. CET exposure is negatively associated with commercialization potential, whereas GCP exposure is positively associated with it. The interaction indicates that GCP attenuates the negative CET association. Mediation analysis shows that financing constraints and debt maturity transmit part of the interaction. These findings extend institutional complementarity theory and refine the Porter hypothesis: Regulatory effects depend on complementary financial institutions.

title: ESG Disclosure and Performance of Commercial Banks: Evidence From an Emerging Economy
abstract: This study examines the impact of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure on the financial performance of banks in an emerging market, and whether these effects differ between publicly and privately owned banks. We use panel data on 32 commercial banks (10 public and 22 private, 352 bank‐year observations) listed on India's National Stock Exchange (NSE) over 2012–2023. Two‐way fixed‐effects panel models regress return on equity (ROE), net interest margin (NIM) and Tobin's Q on the Bloomberg composite ESG disclosure score and its environmental, social and governance pillars, controlling for bank size, leverage, nonperforming assets and Tier‐1 capital. We then estimate pooled ESG‐pillar × ownership interaction models and a difference‐in‐differences (DiD) analysis of India's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) mandate. Composite ESG scores are positively associated with financial performance, but this relationship is driven primarily by environmental disclosure among privately owned banks, whereas public banks show negative associations across ESG dimensions, suggesting tensions between developmental mandates and market‐oriented ESG outcomes. The DiD analysis finds a preliminary association between BRSR‐linked exposure intensity and postmandate ROE that holds for private banks alone. The findings suggest that regulators should require pillar‐level rather than only composite ESG reporting, offer public sector banks differentiated compliance support rather than weaker reporting obligations, and monitor ESG‐disclosure outcomes separately by ownership type; bank managers and investors should likewise evaluate ESG disclosure pillar by pillar. This study contributes granular, ownership‐contingent evidence from an emerging‐market banking sector and a cautious examination of a major disclosure‐regulation mandate.

title: From Gender to Green: Women Leadership Index and Environmental Innovation
abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of the women leadership index (WLI) on environmental innovation. This study employs a sample of 1715 non‐financial firms across Asia‐Pacific, Europe, and the Middle East and Africa over the period 2016–2023, comprising 13,215 firm‐year observations. The analysis is conducted using fixed‐effects regression, complemented by robustness checks and endogeneity tests. The results indicate that the WLI has a positive and statistically significant effect on environmental innovation. Consistent with human capital theory and upper echelons theory, higher levels of education and broader experience enhance female directors' cognitive capacity, strategic orientation, risk management capabilities, and decision‐making quality. Accordingly, these attributes enable firms to implement environmental innovation practices more effectively. These findings suggest that the success of environmental innovation cannot be achieved through tokenistic female representation alone but requires the substantive capabilities of female directors. Accordingly, the recruitment and development of female board members should emphasize education, experience, and competencies that support environmental innovation. This study extends the innovation literature by positioning the WLI as a proxy for female directors' capabilities in driving environmental innovation. Accordingly, it shifts the focus from gender as mere representation to women's leadership as a source of innovation capability.

title: Socially Responsible Investment Indices and Geopolitical Risk: Quantile Time‐Frequency Connectedness and Conditional Performance
abstract: This study investigates the connectedness between socially responsible investment (SRI) indices and geopolitical risk (GPR) using a quantile time‐frequency dynamic connectedness framework. By conditioning on both market states and investment horizons, we document a state‐dependent transmission pattern: While GPR co‐moves with broader uncertainty, it acts predominantly as a net receiver of shocks at the median quantile. However, during extreme market conditions, GPR transitions to a dominant transmitter, generating persistent long‐term spillovers that intensify co‐movements and potentially reduce diversification benefits. We also identify heterogeneity across the selected SRI proxies. At the median quantile, broad ESG and Islamic screening proxies act as net transmitters, whereas clean energy, green bonds and green building indices act as net receivers. Furthermore, our conditional performance analysis reveals that clean energy and green building indices exhibit relatively stronger risk‐adjusted performance under elevated and extreme GPR regimes. An equal‐weighted SRI portfolio consistently delivers positive concurrent returns across all four geopolitical risk regimes and records its highest risk‐adjusted performance under the most restrictive condition. These findings suggest that investors and portfolio managers may benefit from incorporating both geopolitical risk conditions and investment horizons into SRI portfolio monitoring and allocation decisions, recognising the heterogeneous sensitivity of sustainable asset segments to geopolitical shocks.

title: Between promise and practice: Intelligent automation and workplace inclusion in hospitality HRM
Can gossip fuel hospitality employees' innovation? Exploring the paradoxical effects of negative workplace gossip
The tides of retention: A mixed methods understanding of push, pull, and mooring in maintenance service agreement renewals
Organizational resilience and sustainable purchase behavior: a multi-level analysis of employee–consumer engagement with environmental initiatives
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the mechanisms through which organizational resilience capabilities generate sustainable consumer behavior in service organizations, along with integrating organizational and consumer perspectives within a multi-level framework. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on multi-source and time-lagged data collected from 52 hotels, 847 employees, and 1,203 consumers, we tested a moderated sequential-mediation model. The model specifies organizational resilience as the antecedent, employee engagement and consumer engagement as sequential mediators, and sustainable purchase behavior as the outcome. Consumer green values, price sensitivity, and subjective norms are tested as moderators of the indirect pathways. Findings Organizational resilience influences sustainable purchase behavior through a sequential engagement cascade: resilience → Employee engagement → Consumer engagement → Sustainable behavior. This cross-level mechanism operates contingently on individual consumer characteristics. Specifically, consumer green values and subjective norms amplify the engagement cascade, while price sensitivity attenuates it. The findings demonstrate that organizational capabilities do not automatically translate into sustainability outcomes; rather, their effectiveness depends on psychological interpretation and behavioral expression within specific social contexts. Practical implications Service managers should recognize that resilience initiatives require intentional employee mobilization and engagement activation to generate consumer sustainability responses. Sustainability strategies should account for consumer heterogeneity, tailoring communications and value propositions to distinct consumer segments characterized by different value orientations, economic constraints, and social influences. Originality/value This research intends to advance service management theory by demonstrating how organizational capabilities operate through human-centered mechanisms and contingent on contextual factors. By bridging organizational behavior and consumer research, the study provides a more nuanced understanding of value co-creation in sustainability contexts and identifies critical intervention points for service organizations seeking to translate resilience into environmental impact.

title: Civic uncertainty for sale: prediction markets and corporate authority over democratic expectations
abstract: Prediction market platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi exercise corporate authority over democratic expectations by turning uncertain outcomes involving elections, policy and geopolitical events into objects of market governance. We urge business and society scholars to examine how this authority is organised and legitimised.

title: Does mandatory accounting disclosure of derivatives and hedging activities affect the cost of debt? Evidence from SFAS 161
abstract: This study examines whether mandatory disclosure of derivatives and hedging activities affects private debt contracting when lenders already possess private information about borrowers. Exploiting the adoption of SFAS 161, which mandates structured and disaggregated disclosures on derivative and hedging activities, we find that firms that increase their derivatives and hedging disclosures experience loan spreads that are 9.6 basis points lower than those of firms with little disclosure change. Cross-sectional evidence is consistent with improved comparability as the main mechanism for the effect. We also find that the reduction in loan spreads is larger for firms with more extensive pre-adoption disclosures, consistent with standardized reporting rather than new information driving the effect. Loan spreads also decline when industry peers increase disclosure, suggesting benchmarking externalities from comparable reporting. The effects are also stronger for firms with greater agency frictions, where voluntary disclosure is less reliable, and in syndicated and non-relationship loans, where borrower-specific private information is less informative. Additional analysis shows that pricing effects are concentrated in newly originated loans, whereas for existing loans, lenders relax covenant restrictiveness. Overall, our study shows that mandatory disclosure improves the comparability of complex financial information and influences debt contracting even in settings where lenders have access to private information.

title: Sharing brings caring? The double-edged impact of talking about customer mistreatment on proactive customer service performance
Mitigating cognitive dissonance in consumer decision-making: the role of marketer message sidedness and user-generated content valence
How and when leaders respond to team voice with silence and avoidance: Roles of leader team identification and identity threat
Interpreting Emotion in Digital Consumer Data: A Protocol for Analyzing Meaning–Affect Correspondence in Psychology and Marketing
abstract: Research on consumer emotion increasingly combines qualitative interpretation and computational sentiment analysis, yet guidance on how researchers should interpret the relationship between contextual meaning and computationally identified affect remains limited. Existing approaches frequently integrate these methods but offer less clarity when their outputs converge, partially diverge, or appear to conflict. We address this challenge through the Interpretive–Affective Analysis Protocol (IAAP), an interpretive–pragmatic protocol that establishes contextual meaning independently before introducing computational affect as a second analytical representation. IAAP comprises five stages: Meaning, Affect, Connection, Diagnosis and Adjudication, and Interpretation. Using a worked demonstration based on interview and online review data concerning public electric vehicle charging, we illustrate how researchers can diagnose relationships between meaning and affect, investigate apparent discrepancies, and develop defensible interpretations. IAAP is built on the proposition that meaning–affect correspondence constitutes an important object of inquiry. The protocol examines how the convergence, partial divergence, or strong divergence of meaning and affect can inform understanding of how marketplace experiences are appraised, communicated, and expressed in digital consumer data.

title: Mobilising sustainable consumption through mindful resonance
abstract: Purpose There has been a wealth of recent research examining the role of mindfulness in fostering sustainability. This paper aims to respond to criticisms of research to-date and calls for qualitative research, through an approach that examines consumer lived experiences of mindfulness and consumption. Mindfulness, rooted in Buddhist practices, promotes ethical behaviour and compassion, which are essential for sustainable consumption. However, the paper critiques existing definitions of mindfulness, primarily based on Kabat-Zinn’s present moment awareness, suggesting a need for a broader understanding. The authors examine how mindfulness does (not) foster sustainable consumption in clothing, drawing on Rosa’s (2019) resonance theory to conceptualise mindful resonance as a process through which altered attention may transform consumption relationships. Design/methodology/approach The authors address calls for qualitative research on mindfulness beyond dominant cross-sectional approaches. Drawing on a one-year, multi-method qualitative study with 19 mainstream clothing consumers with no prior mindfulness experience, the authors introduced a range of mindfulness practices to encourage reflection on consumption. Using dialogical analysis, the authors examined how consumption meanings and practices evolved over time. The findings show that mindful resonance develops gradually as consumers move from socially accelerated patterns of consumption towards more decelerated and sustainable forms of consumption. Findings The authors use the concept of “mindful resonance” to refer to the mobilisation of a consumer subjectivity which links inner mindfulness experiences with external consumption realities. This approach goes beyond sustainable attention and bridges the gap between self-interest and collective sustainability efforts, encouraging critical reflection on consumption behaviours. The authors argue that mindfulness does not inherently produce sustainable consumption. Mindful attention can create a pause that interrupts habitual consumption and enables consumers to become affected by consumption experiences. The authors conceptualise this as mindful resonance, unfolding through four modes: recognition, resetting, reinterpretation and redirection. These frame how consumers identify discrepancies between values and practices, interrupt accelerated consumption, reconsider consumption meanings and change practices. Sustainable consumption emerges when transformed relationships can be enacted within marketplace conditions. The findings highlight restraint and deceleration, suggesting sustainability can involve consuming less and differently. Research limitations/implications Positioning mindfulness within lived consumption contexts addresses limitations of quantitative, cross-sectional research. The authors conceptualise mindful resonance as a relational process, shifting attention from whether mindfulness produces sustainable behaviour towards, how attention may contribute to transformed subjectivities. Practical implications The authors argue that marketers and policymakers should move beyond interventions that optimise consumption towards opportunities for pause, restraint, repair, reuse and product use, while enabling deceleration. The paper emphasises that mindfulness should not be viewed as a mere instrumental technique to modify consumption but must be used to engage with personal and environmental impacts of consumption to reduce consumption. Originality/value The paper explores the pathway between mindfulness and sustainable consumption, addressing criticisms of existing research. It emphasises the need for qualitative studies to understand consumer experiences and the role of mindfulness in fostering sustainable behaviours. The authors reveal how as a consumer subjectivity mindfulness does(not) foster sustainable consumption. The authors advance mindful resonance as a subjectivity explaining how mindfulness may become relationally transformative. This reframes mindfulness from a behavioural solution, to a potential catalyst for sustainable consumption.

title: Words in motion: how dynamic linguistics undermines medical crowdfunding success
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how dynamic linguistics, referring to language that leads readers to mentally recreate the described movement, undermines medical crowdfunding performance, challenging the assumption that perceived dynamism enhances persuasive effectiveness across communication contexts. Design/methodology/approach Three studies are conducted using a multi-method approach. Study 1 analyzes field data from 106,428 medical crowdfunding campaigns on GoFundMe. Study 2 employs a controlled experiment to provide preliminary evidence for the empathy avoidance mechanism. Study 3 further examines the proposed mechanism through a moderated mediation approach by manipulating campaign category (medical vs non-medical). Findings Dynamic linguistics negatively affects medical crowdfunding performance because it prompts donors to experientially recreate the depicted suffering, triggering empathy avoidance. This downstream negative effect is weaker in non-medical campaigns, where suffering is less central. Research limitations/implications The findings extend dynamism research from the visual to the linguistic domain, identifying a boundary condition whereby the mental simulation that enhances persuasion in positive or neutral contexts becomes counterproductive when content involves human suffering. They also advance empathy avoidance research by identifying dynamic linguistics as a communication-level antecedent, complementing prior work focused on factors external to message content. Practical implications Crowdfunding platforms can integrate dynamic linguistics detection into their writing assistance tools to flag problematic phrasing in medical appeals. Campaign creators should exercise caution when using language that leads donors to vicariously recreate suffering in medical appeals. Originality/value This study challenges the well-established finding that perceived dynamism enhances persuasive effectiveness, showing that in medical crowdfunding dynamism evoked through language can backfire and reduce fundraising performance.

title: Lightning in a bottle: theorising spontaneity as improvisational practice
abstract: Purpose This study aims to theorise how spontaneity operates as skilled improvisational practice within consumption experiences, moving beyond its characterisation as mere absence of planning. Design/methodology/approach A 14-month ethnography of live grassroots stand-up comedy in Liverpool: participant observation at 28 shows, depth interviews with 10 comedian-audience members and informal interviews with 26 others. The lead researcher also performed stand-up. Analysis was iterative and hermeneutic. Findings Spontaneity operates through three interdependent dynamics: singularity (creating irreproducible encounters), sociality (building connections through collaborative navigation of unscripted situations) and speculation (engaging productive uncertainty that authenticates spontaneity). Rather than occurring naturally, spontaneity emerges through cultivated improvisational competence. Both performers and audiences perform essential labour in co-producing spontaneous moments, with genuine risk of failure constitutive of spontaneity’s credibility. Research limitations/implications Our focus on performer perspectives provides insight into producing spontaneity, though future research could examine how non-performing consumers navigate it differently. This study provides a framework for understanding how improvisational practice shapes consumption experiences across contexts requiring fluid response to unpredictable circumstances. Practical implications Practitioners cannot script spontaneity, but they can cultivate conditions for it to emerge. Training should develop improvisational competence, the capacity to respond fluidly to unscripted situations, rather than enforce rigid service scripts. Providers should recognise that consumers perform essential labour in co-producing spontaneous moments; creating space for audience contribution matters as much as performer skill. Experience designers should also consider that spontaneity privileges those comfortable with uncertainty, potentially excluding consumers who prefer predictable encounters. Originality/value Spontaneity is typically treated as the absence of planning, something that simply happens to an experience. This study shows the opposite: it is skilled labour, cultivated yet genuinely unrehearsed and co-produced, with audiences helping to make it rather than merely witnessing it. This study further shows that the risk of public failure is not a hazard to be managed but the very thing that authenticates the spontaneous moment. In doing so the authors answer calls to specify the theoretical architecture of consumption experience and extend work on experiential labour’s resistance to commodification.

title: Sustainability Mindsets in Corporate Sustainability Management: A Theoretical Exploration from the Mindset Theory of Action Phases
abstract: This paper explores sustainability mindsets, which have received increasing attention in the corporate sustainability management literature. Sustainability mindsets often appear as peripheral but necessary for successful corporate sustainability management. However, despite these references in the academic literature, the discussion lacks theoretical foundation. To analyze and advance the concept of both individual and organizational sustainability mindsets, the paper draws on Gollwitzer’s mindset theory of action phases as a theoretical perspective, in particular on goal setting and striving, implementation intentions as well as action control. The paper identifies the need to link organizational sustainability goals to individual goals of employees. It shows that implementation intentions (also called if–then plans) can be beneficial in corporate sustainability management but an important part is to establish a goal hierarchy when multiple goals exist, which is often the case in a multi-faceted sustainability strategy. A possible solution is to prioritize different goals for different teams based on their strengths. Furthermore, integrating sustainability into organizational and individual routines and creating a level of automaticity is an important element that corporate sustainability management can benefit from. A normative, processual framework is proposed, inspired by Gollwitzer’s mindset theory of action phases and what corporate sustainability management can learn from it. The conceptual paper contributes to the academic literature by attempting a definition of individual sustainability mindsets as well as an organizational sustainability mindset and how corporate sustainability management can support and subsequently benefit from the development of these mindsets.

title: The Risk Mitigation Effect of the Central Bank Communication on RMB Internationalization: Evidence from Listed Companies in China
abstract: This study examines the impact of central bank’s RMB internationalization communication on corporate foreign exchange risk from the perspective of expectations management. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2016 to 2023, we find that positive sentiment in RMB internationalization communication significantly reduces corporate foreign exchange risk. This effect primarily operates by fostering cross-border RMB usage, which serves as a substitute for geographic diversification in corporate risk management. The risk-mitigating effect is mainly observed for non-USD currency exposures, while USD exposure remains rigid. The effect is also moderated by corporate-level and external environmental factors. This study provides a novel economic perspective on how expectations management affects corporate foreign exchange risk and offers valuable insights for corporate foreign exchange risk management.

title: Between Security and Openness: Local Practice and Firm Cybersecurity Risk Under National Digital Security Governance
abstract: Local governments in China have moved to the center of digital security governance, yet how their uneven regulatory effort shapes risk inside firms remains largely unmeasured. We assemble a prefecture-level measure of cybersecurity governance intensity from the text of municipal policy documents and match it to Chinese A-share listed firms from 2014 to 2024 to examine its effect on firm-level cybersecurity risk, a construct we read from the language of corporate annual reports. Firms operating where local governance is more intensive carry lower cybersecurity risk, and the finding survives an instrumental-variables strategy that exploits governance in other cities of the same province, a battery of alternative measures and specifications, and a count-model treatment of the outcome. Stronger governance also raises firms’ AI capital and deepens their utilization of data elements, responses that, we argue, sharpen threat detection and shift protection from after-the-fact response toward prevention. The effect is more visible among state-owned and data-intensive firms, though we read the subsample contrasts descriptively. The results tie the macro supply of digital security governance to micro-level firm risk and identify local governance capacity as a modest but consistent institutional lever bearing on firm operational stability in emerging markets.

title: Importing Green Institutions: Firm-Level Exposure to Environmental Provisions in RTAs and Green Innovation in China
abstract: This paper examines how firms’ import-side exposure to environmental provisions in regional trade agreements (RTAs) relates to green innovation. We develop a firm-level measure, Green Institutional Density Exposure (GIDE), that maps the depth and enforceability of RTA environmental provisions onto firms’ import portfolios. Using Chinese listed manufacturing firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that higher GIDE is associated with greater and higher-quality green innovation. This association is stronger in industries with greater global value chain embeddedness and among firms with more complex imports, stronger green knowledge bases, and fewer financial constraints. It is also stronger when exposure originates from more central countries, but weaker in highly polluting industries. Evidence for policy-pilot environments is suggestive. Results are robust across alternative specifications, while shift-share IV estimates provide complementary but inconclusive evidence amid remaining endogeneity concerns. Overall, the findings indicate that the GIDE-green innovation association varies with firms’ conversion capacity and with source-country and firm-level conditions.

title: Predicting Corporate Financial Misconduct Risk from the Multidimensional Coupling of Financial and Textual Information
abstract: Annual reports contain both financial information and narrative disclosures, and inconsistencies between these signals may provide early warnings of corporate financial misconduct. Using Chinese A-share firms listed from 2015 to 2024, this study constructs measures of financial reporting distortion, textual distortion, and their coupling mismatch index. Conditional firm fixed-effects logit models show that financial reporting distortion, textual distortion, and their coupling mismatch are positively associated with subsequent financial misconduct risk. A one-standard-deviation increase in mismatch corresponds to an odds ratio of approximately 1.118 for subsequent financial misconduct. The mismatch index remains significant after controlling for the individual distortion measures, indicating additional explanatory power. Further analyses show that mismatch is associated with lower information disclosure quality, greater analyst forecast dispersion, more misconduct events, and larger regulatory penalties. The relationship between mismatch and misconduct risk exhibits a U-shaped pattern. By integrating structured financial signals and unstructured textual disclosures, this study demonstrates that cross-dimensional information divergence provides an incremental signal for identifying corporate financial misconduct and contributes to audit risk assessment and information governance.

title: Financial Literacy and Consumption Resilience Among Chinese Households
abstract: How closely does a household’s financial literacy track its ability to sustain consumption above a poverty threshold? We examine 5,618 Chinese households surveyed in 2019 and use their consumption in 2017 to estimate the conditional probability of exceeding a specified welfare threshold. At the benchmark of $1.90 per person per day, a one-standard-deviation difference in financial literacy corresponds to a one-percentage-point difference in this probability after adjustment for household characteristics and province fixed effects. The association persists when we use an additive literacy score, raise the threshold to $3.10, or exclude the four municipalities directly under the central government. Assets, business ownership, stated risk tolerance and spending on children’s education each correlate with literacy and resilience. These patterns suggest explanations worth testing with longitudinal data. Estimates are larger among households below the median income than among those above it. Shared local conditions and the timing of the survey limit causal interpretation.

title: Does Climate Policy Uncertainty Affect Environmental Rating Disagreement? Evidence from China
abstract: This study examines how Climate Policy Uncertainty (CPU) affects Environmental Rating Disagreement (ERD). Using a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2007 to 2023, together with text-based CPU indices and firm-level policy sensitivity, we document consistent evidence that CPU raises ERD. Mediation analysis shows that CPU is positively associated with firms’ green innovation and that green innovation is negatively associated with disagreement, but the implied indirect effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the direct effect of CPU is undiminished. The CPU-ERD association therefore appears to operate through the ambiguity of climate policy signals rather than through firms’ environmental investment. Cross-sectional analyses reveal that analyst coverage and media attention attenuate the impact of CPU, whereas provincial regulatory intensity and complexity strengthen it. In high-CPU environments, disagreement is amplified primarily among local rating agencies, reflecting their heightened sensitivity to domestic policy dynamics. These findings establish climate policy uncertainty as an important determinant of ESG rating inconsistency, with implications for investors, policymakers, and rating agencies.

title: A Hidden Treasure: The Impact of CEO Industry Expertise on Trade Credit
abstract: CEO industry expertise is a hidden treasure and may grant the firm more access to trade credit from suppliers. This study investigates the impact of CEOs with industry expertise on corporate trade credit. Using a sample from China, we find a positive correlation between CEO industry expertise and trade credit. These CEOs can improve the corporate information transparency, social trust, and strengthen bargaining power, thereby facilitating increased access to trade credit for their firms. Additionally, our cross-sectional analyses indicate that the positive effect of CEO industry expertise on trade credit is dominantfor CEOs hired from outside, firms in the early stage, and regions with immature financial markets. Overall, our study provides new evidence for firms to understand the role of CEO industry expertise as a hidden treasure of organizations in trade credit.

title: Inward FDI Deregulation and the Carbon Emissions of Manufacturing Enterprises: A Quasi-Natural Experimental Study
abstract: This study examines how inward FDI deregulation affects the carbon emissions of Chinese manufacturing enterprises, using the 2002 revision of the Catalog for the Guidance of Foreign Investment Industries as a quasi-natural experiment. Based on data on 73,124 enterprises from 1998 to 2009, we find that FDI deregulation significantly reduces enterprise carbon emission intensity through both a technology effect and a competitive pressure effect, without sacrificing output growth. A series of robustness checks, including Bartik instrumental-variable estimation, corroborate these findings. This study provides evidence on how FDI deregulation affects manufacturers’ sustainable development, with implications for carbon reductions through high-quality FDI.

title: Victimized and Unprepared: Financial Fraud Experience and Retirement Saving
abstract: As population aging and pension reform place greater responsibility for retirement security on individuals, understanding the barriers to adequate retirement saving has become increasingly important. Using nationally representative microdata from the China Aging Finance Survey for 2020–2023, we examine the relationship between financial fraud experience and two dimensions of retirement saving: participation and accumulated reserves. The results show that individuals with fraud experience are significantly less likely to participate in retirement saving and hold lower retirement reserves. Mechanism analyses provide evidence consistent with three pathways: reduced risk tolerance, greater financial exclusion, and distorted retirement-planning cognition. These adverse associations are particularly pronounced among rural residents, low-income households, individuals without basic pension coverage, and older respondents. The study extends the literature on life-cycle saving by highlighting how adverse financial experiences are associated with subsequent long-term financial engagement and retirement preparation. The findings underscore the importance of fraud prevention and consumer protection and, more broadly, suggest potential roles for accessible redress, targeted financial education, and broader pension protection in strengthening retirement resilience among financially vulnerable households.

title: Curbing Greenwashing in Emerging-Market Green Finance: A Government-Enterprise Evolutionary-Game Analysis
abstract: Against the global drive for sustainable development, greenwashing severely distorts the operation of green-bond markets. This article constructs a bounded-rationality two-party evolutionary-game model to explore strategic interactions between governments and enterprises on greenwashing regulation. We solve replicator dynamic equations and adopt Jacobian-matrix stability analysis to identify equilibrium states, followed by numerical simulations under three representative scenarios. The results show that the system yields three conditionally stable evolutionarily stable strategies: (relaxed supervision, greenwashing production), (strict supervision, greenwashing production), and (relaxed supervision, green production). Government penalties for greenwashing and social benefits generated by high-quality green projects significantly determine the system’s evolutionary direction and convergence speed. Higher social benefits of green projects facilitate convergence toward the ideal equilibrium where enterprises voluntarily implement genuine green production. Accordingly, we propose policy measures including optimized penalty design, improvement of returns for green projects, perfecting information-disclosure systems, and strengthening government-enterprise collaboration. This research provides theoretical references for mitigating greenwashing risks and promoting the sound development of emerging-market green-bond markets.

title: Exchange Rate Appreciation and Export Quality: The Role of Robots
abstract: This paper provides a novel channel between exchange rate appreciation and export quality upgrading through robot adoption. Using a difference-in-differences framework that utilizes China’s exchange rate regime reform in 2005, we investigate the effects of Renminbi appreciation on the export quality of Chinese firms. Our results show that exchange rate appreciation significantly improves export quality. The key driver of export quality upgrades is the increase in robot adoption by firms. Furthermore, we find that firms increase productivity and human capital in response to the exchange rate appreciation.

title: Can Cross-Border E-Commerce Improve Zombie-Firm Governance? Evidence from China’s Comprehensive Pilot Zones
abstract: This study explores the micro-level impacts and underlying mechanisms of cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) on zombie firms using panel data from China’s A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2024. The analysis employs a difference-in-differences methodology, leveraging the establishment of extensive China CBEC Comprehensive Pilot Zones as the differential treatment backdrop. Results indicate that CBEC significantly reduces the probability that a firm is classified as a zombie firm. In the “Panel B: Survival Effect Sample,” policy exposure is associated with recovery from zombie status among firms that remain in the listed-firm sample. In “Panel C: Persistence of zombie status before exit,” policy exposure is associated with a higher probability of remaining in zombie status before exit from the listed-firm sample. At the city level, greater pre-policy zombie-firm exposure is associated with a relatively larger increase in urban consumption expenditure and a relatively larger decline in energy consumption after policy implementation. This study provides practical evidence for emerging markets worldwide to address governance challenges associated with zombie firms.

title: ESG Rating Divergence, Financing Frictions, and Green Innovation in Emerging Markets: Evidence from China
abstract: ESG ratings from different providers often disagree about the same firm-year, leaving lenders and managers with conflicting signals about environmental quality. This study asks how that disagreement relates to corporate green innovation, to the cost and availability of external finance, and to a publicly verifiable alternative signal, using six commercial ESG ratings for Chinese A-share firms over 2011–2023. Three patterns emerge. First, higher divergence goes with fewer green invention patent applications, while utility-model filings do not move, so the association falls on the most substantive form of green patenting. Second, divergence goes with less bank borrowing and a higher cost of debt, and next-year debt cost carries a small but statistically distinguishable share, about 8%, of the invention association two years later. Third, among firms holding government green-manufacturing certification, the adverse invention slope is indistinguishable from zero. Together, the results are consistent with the view that the coherence of sustainability information, and not only its level, is relevant to how external capital reaches substantive green innovation in emerging markets. All estimates come from firm and year fixed-effects models and are associations rather than causal effects.

title: Economic Effects of Foreign Access to China’s Banking Sector
abstract: Foreign access is a key factor in high-level opening-up of China’s banking sector, and its economic effect evaluation is of great value in testing the effectiveness of foreign access. Based on estimated tax equivalents of foreign access barriers in the banking sector, this study employs the global simulation analysis of industry-level trade policy (GSIM) model to quantitatively simulate the economic effects of foreign access on China’s banking sector. Under the model’s assumptions, results reveal that foreign access in China’s banking sector is associated with increases in its domestic sales and exports, and decreases in imports. Admitting foreign investment in the banking sector is projected to yield higher producer and consumer welfare in China’s banking sector and improve net social welfare. We also find that foreign investment in China’s banking sector is estimated to raise employment in the sector and in manufacturing under the model’s fixed-coefficient production assumptions, and a smaller proportion of labor compensation indicates a greater employment effect in manufacturing. These simulation results are subject to the limitations of the partial equilibrium GSIM framework, including comparative statics and fixed-coefficient production assumptions, and should be interpreted as assumption-dependent scenario outcomes rather than validated quantitative forecasts. This study expands the research scope of the partial equilibrium model and provides a quantitative basis for prudently promoting foreign access in the banking sector.

title: Environmental Performance Feedback and Green Collaborative Innovation: The Role of AI Investment and Financial Slack
abstract: This study investigates how firms organize green collaborative innovation in response to environmental performance feedback. Drawing on the behavioral theory of the firm and because green innovation often requires knowledge distributed across organizational boundaries, we argue that firms may respond through collaborative expansion, reflected in breadth, or collaborative intensification, reflected in depth. Using data from Chinese A-share listed firms in heavily polluting industries from 2010 to 2023 and employing PPML estimation, we find that compared with firms performing at or above aspirations, below-aspiration firms exhibit greater collaborative breadth and depth. Among below-aspiration firms, however, a widening performance gap increases depth but not breadth, whereas a widening above-aspiration gap reduces both dimensions. Financial slack strengthens the effect of below-aspiration gaps on breadth, while AI investment weakens the negative effects of above-aspiration gaps on both dimensions. These findings extend performance-feedback theory by showing that feedback can alter firms’ involvement in joint innovation without necessarily changing partner scope. They also identify distinct resource and technological conditions that shape these responses. For policymakers, the results suggest improving environmental-performance comparability and providing targeted support for interorganizational green innovation.

title: “Vehicle–Battery Separation” and Supply Chain Resilience in Lithium-Battery Firms: Evidence from Battery-Swapping Business Model Innovation
abstract: Vehicle–battery separation enabled by battery-swapping business models may reshape demand, financing, and transaction structures along the lithium-battery value chain. Using Chinese listed-firm data from 2001 to 2025 and a triple-difference design, this study examines the effect of China’s 2021 battery-swapping pilot policy on lithium-battery firms’ supply chain resilience. The results show that the pilot significantly improves resilience, with gains concentrated in resistance capacity, recovery capacity, and government support. Mechanism analyses indicate enhanced sales stability, reduced financial constraints, and lower customer and supplier concentration. The findings reveal how business model innovation strengthens upstream supply chain resilience.

title: Constructing a New Food CPI Using Retail Scanner Data: An Alternative Data Perspective
abstract: Retail scanner data are well suited to timely consumer price measurement, yet their use in China remains limited. Using transaction prices and quantities from the China Ants Alliance, this study constructs a scanner-based Food Consumer Price Index (sFCPI) that captures food price dynamics in China’s modern chain supermarket channels. The analysis examines its consistency with the official Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Food CPI (FCPI), as well as its predictive value. The sFCPI exhibits strong growth-rate correlations with CPI and FCPI, at 0.821 and 0.796, respectively. Over a common 24-month out-of-sample period, incorporating the sFCPI reduces root mean squared error by 37.0–42.8% for CPI growth and 40.4–46.0% for FCPI growth across directly comparable models. Bootstrap inference provides the strongest evidence of forecasting gains for growth rates, particularly for FCPI, while statistically significant improvements in direction and magnitude forecasts are observed in selected specifications. The weekly index (sFCPIw) provides higher-frequency price information, and robustness checks broadly support the main growth-rate forecasting results. These findings support the use of retail scanner data as a complementary source for consumer price measurement and short-term inflation assessment in a large emerging market.

title: Product cannibalization, corporate restructuring, and innovation: A theory of how existing product lines affect firms’ innovation and commercialization incentives
Knowledge‐Based Industry Sectoral Regimes and Internal Labour Flexibility: The Visibility and Adjustment of Overtime During Systemic Disruption in the United Kingdom
abstract: Understanding how firms adjust labour input during economic disruptions requires attention not only to employment changes but also to the internal mechanisms through which work is reorganised. Although industrial relations research distinguishes between internal and external labour flexibility, less is known about how industry sectoral regimes are associated with observable differences in internal working‐time adjustment. This study examines whether manufacturing and knowledge‐intensive services (KIS) differ in their reliance on recorded paid overtime as an observable form of internal working‐time adjustment and whether this difference changes during systemic disruption. Using UK regional panel data from 2016 to 2025, we measure overtime dependence (OD) as the ratio of paid overtime hours to total paid hours. Fixed‐effects models with region and year effects examine sectoral differences, whereas dynamic specifications assess persistence in overtime utilisation. The analysis focuses on the 2020–2021 COVID‐19 period, with alternative periods used for robustness analysis. The results show that manufacturing exhibits substantially higher OD than KIS, but this difference narrows significantly during the 2020–2021 systemic disruption period, driven primarily by a sharper contraction in manufacturing OD. Alternative temporal specifications provide additional evidence on the timing and robustness of this change. Lower recorded paid overtime in KIS should not be interpreted as lower labour flexibility, because adjustment may occur through alternative mechanisms not observed in the present data. The study contributes to industrial relations research by conceptualising recorded paid overtime as an observable indicator of one internal working‐time adjustment margin rather than a comprehensive measure of labour flexibility.

title: Designing inclusive AI in public service delivery: experimental evidence on individual preferences for government chatbots
abstract: As governments deploy artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots in public services, inclusiveness has become a central concern, yet which design features shape preferences remains unclear. We conceptualize inclusiveness at the human–AI interface along three dimensions—cultural, functional, and cognitive. A conjoint experiment with 1,250 respondents in Guangdong, China, examines how these features shape willingness to use government chatbots. Results show that cognitive inclusiveness—explanatory outputs—consistently increases preference; cultural inclusiveness operates conditionally—chiefly when design reflects citizens’ linguistic identity; functional inclusiveness has modest effects. Shifting from organizational arrangements to citizen–state interactions, we contribute to research on AI governance, digital inclusion, and inclusive public service delivery.

title: Decoding AI sovereignty
Heterogeneous takeover-strategy effects in automated driving: The role of traffic scenarios and driver attitudes
Modeling over-height vehicle bridge strikes using random parameter negative binomial–Lindley models: a multi-region analysis
Modeling the injury severity of riders and pedestrians in crashes involving micromobility vehicles
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric micromobility vehicles (MMVs) in European cities has raised concerns about rider and pedestrian safety. Previous studies have largely analyzed the factors that influence the injury severity of cyclists. However, the determinants of injury severity in crashes involving e-bikes and electric personal mobility devices (e-PMDs), which are often faster and heavier than conventional bicycles, remain poorly understood. This study investigates the effects of the characteristics of the road, the environment, and the road users on the severity of crashes involving cyclists, e-cyclists and e-PMD riders. Police crash data were analyzed in Paris and Lyon between 2019 and 2023. The dataset was enriched with the characteristics of the built-environment extracted using GIS. Logistic regression models were then estimated for four crash types: crashes with motorized vehicles, crashes with other MMVs, crashes with pedestrians and single-vehicle crashes. The results show that the factors influencing injury severity differ significantly based on the crash type. In crashes with pedestrians, the latter are far more likely to be injured than riders. In crashes with pedestrians and crashes between MMVs, colliding with a male or a younger individual raises the probability of injury. In crashes with motorized vehicles, heavy second-party vehicles increase the fatality probability while the presence of cycle facilities reduces it. For single-vehicle crashes, slopes are associated with fatalities. These results support protected cycle facilities, the separation of MMVs from heavy vehicle traffic, and intersection designs adapted to MMVs.

title: Responding to child abuse and neglect in Norwegian schools: Responsibility and scope for action in light of children's lived experiences
abstract: This qualitative study explores how teachers and school nurses in Norwegian compulsory education (Grades 3–10) perceive their mandate and scope for action when responding to child abuse and neglect (CAN), including childhood exposure to intimate partner violence (CEIPV). Drawing on 17 individual interviews and three focus groups with 25 teachers and school nurses, analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, the study identified three themes: responsibility beyond expectations, caring under constraints, and unrecognized potential for care. The professionals' accounts were interpreted through a children's rights framework and contextualized through children's lived experiences reported in an earlier study from the same research project. The findings highlight professionals' strong sense of responsibility for supporting and protecting children exposed to CAN, the institutional and organizational constraints on their scope for action, and the potential for support at school. Contextualized through children's lived experiences, the findings draw attention to predictability, stable relationships, tailored support, participation, and academic engagement as important dimensions of children's everyday school life. Taken together, these perspectives suggest that the school's potential for support and protection lies not only in formal responses, but also in sustaining the relational, pedagogical, and social support available at school. Recognizing and supporting these relational, pedagogical, and social dimensions of school practice, alongside clear roles, relevant knowledge, collaboration, and organizational support, may strengthen the school's protective role for children exposed to CAN.

title: Childhood maltreatment and epigenetic age acceleration in adulthood: Moderation by obesity risk
Learning convex voltage constraints for transmission–distribution coordinated dispatch: A decoupled input convex neural network
A transferable framework for integrating shared socioeconomic pathways into hybrid urban growth models: Lessons from central Vietnam
abstract: Translating global Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) into locally grounded, spatially explicit urban scenarios remains a methodological challenge for urban futures research. This study develops a hybrid framework that combines participatory SSP downscaling, Random Forest-derived urban growth propensity, scenario specific spatial protection, and stochastic cellular automata simulation to examine alternative urban futures for Hue, Vietnam, to 2050. Locally contextualized SSP1–SSP3 assumptions were operationalized through alternative growth settings and protection of ecosystem-based adaptation opportunity areas, flood-prone land, and tourism areas. From a 2020 urban extent of 208.42 km², the mean simulated urban area reached 437.02 km² under SSP1, 487.37 km² under SSP2, and 564.81 km² under SSP3. High probability growth clusters were concentrated in coastal lowlands, peri-urban and industrial development zones, and western development corridors. Agricultural land accounted for the largest share of projected conversion, with combined cropland and rice losses increasing across the scenarios. Landscape analysis indicated increasing urban coalescence in the main simulations; however, a constant area sensitivity showed that part of this pattern resulted from differences in total urban growth quantity. Additional sensitivity experiments confirmed that scenario divergence reflected the combined influence of growth settings and spatial protection. The framework provides a transparent approach for linking locally contextualized SSP narratives with empirical growth patterns, spatial planning constraints, uncertainty, and comparative urban futures analysis.

title: Carbon emission quota allocation for China's power industry: Considering intergenerational and interprovincial responsibility
An effect of the few? Public acceptance gaps for hydrogen infrastructure in Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands
abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as relevant for the implementation of hydrogen infrastructure, yet existing research has focused mainly on average acceptance levels rather than on how acceptance gaps are distributed within the population. This study empirically examines the gap between national and community acceptance for electrolysers, pipelines, and underground hydrogen storage in Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands, using standardized quota-based online surveys (N = 3402). The results from inferential statistics show robust acceptance gaps across all three technologies, but no substantial differences in gap magnitude between them. Cross-national variation is statistically significant but small. At the individual level, more than half of respondents report identical national and community acceptance ratings, while positive gaps (defined as higher national acceptance than community acceptance) are substantially more common than negative gaps. A descriptive decomposition further shows that respondents meeting a predefined low-community-acceptance threshold account for a disproportionately large share of the aggregate gap. This subgroup is not only less accepting at community level, but also reports substantially lower national acceptance. The findings therefore show that average acceptance ratings alone provide an incomplete basis for interpreting the societal context of hydrogen infrastructure policy, because they may conceal where low acceptance is concentrated within the population. However, the results are to be interpreted with limitations, inter alia because only stated attitudes were measured, rather than actual behaviour.
