HRM practices positively moderate the relationship between cultural capability and perceived firm performance, indicating that stronger HRM practices make this relationship more favorable. These findings reveal a more complex capability–performance relationship than anticipated, suggesting that organizational capability development and deployment do not necessarily correspond with immediate performance gains and that their performance implications may depend on complementary organizational conditions.

title: Green Innovation Marathon: Research on the Impact of Resilient Leadership on Employees Green Sustainable Innovation in Chinese Manufacturing Firms
abstract: The current study examines the relationship between resilient leadership and employee green sustainable innovation of manufacturing firms in China. We also test green work authenticity as a mediator and leadership cultural distance, corporate environmental ethics as boundary conditions. After that, we explore the equivalent coupling mechanism that leads to high employee green sustainable innovation. Three studies are designed per the “causal confirmation‐action mechanism‐combination effect” logic. Results show: (1) Resilient leadership can be deconstructed into three sub‐dimensions. These positively affect employee green sustainable innovation. (2) The mediating role of green work authenticity is verified, which is moderated by leadership cultural distance and corporate environmental ethics. (3) There are three configuration modes to realize high employee green sustainable innovation. They are resilient leadership drive mode, psychological field drive mode, and environmental field drive mode. We broaden the research boundary of enterprise green sustainable innovation, and provide practical enlightenment for manufacturing firms to effectively guide employee green sustainable innovation.

title: The Complementary Role of Open Innovation and R&D: A Pathway to Eco‐Innovation
abstract: Why do firms with comparable levels of external knowledge sourcing achieve fundamentally different eco‐innovation outcomes? This study examines how green and non‐green R&D interact with inbound open innovation strategies to shape the intensity of eco‐innovation implementation. Although prior research has largely treated R&D as homogeneous, we distinguish between green and non‐green R&D and argue that each develops distinct, domain‐specific absorptive capacities. Drawing on absorptive capacity theory and the natural resource‐based view, we argue that green R&D builds domain‐specific absorptive capacity that enables firms to translate external knowledge into competitive environmental capabilities more effectively than non‐green R&D. Using merged data from 709 Irish firms, we employ negative binomial regression to test for complementarity and substitutability between internal R&D and different forms of external knowledge sourcing. Capital‐intensive investments in software act as strategic complements to internal R&D, with this complementary relationship being stronger for green R&D. Conversely, contracting out R&D substitutes for green R&D for particular eco‐innovation outcomes, potentially limiting the development of firm‐specific environmental capabilities. These findings demonstrate that strategic alignment between inbound open innovation and green R&D is critical to building sustained competitive advantage through eco‐innovation.

title: A Practice‐Based View of Circular Economy Practices in an Emerging Economy: A Multiple Case Study
abstract: Manufacturing organizations are facing increasing sustainability issues, including waste generation, greenhouse gas emissions, environmental degradation, employee health and safety risks, and excessive utilization of hazardous chemicals and non‐renewable resources. To address these issues, the circular economy (CE) is recognized as a sustainable business model. Though firms are increasingly adopting commonly available, imitable, and publicly known CE practices, there is a scarcity of research examining the adoption patterns and implementation diversity of these practices shaping sustainable performance in manufacturing firms. Accordingly, this study aims to investigate the operationalization of CE practices in the process manufacturing industry in Pakistan for achieving sustainable performance. Using a multiple case study approach, 19 semi‐structured interviews were conducted with corporate managers and senior executives in the textile, packaging, leather, and paint and coating industries in Pakistan. Building on the practice‐based view (PBV), this study highlighted various CE practices under the cleaner production, product stewardship, and digital practices in the critical process manufacturing sector. The findings provide fresh empirical insights into the CE literature by illustrating the adoption patterns, underlying reasons for heterogeneity in the implementation of CE practices, and sustainable performance. Overall, the findings can guide practitioners, researchers, and policymakers to understand the execution of CE practices for sustainable performance in the critical process industry.

title: Trust in Industrial Symbiosis: Dynamics, Determinants and a Conceptual Framework
abstract: Industrial symbiosis (IS) plays an important role in supporting circular economy transitions by enabling firms to exchange materials, energy, water and by‐products, thereby improving resource efficiency and reducing waste. Despite its environmental and economic benefits, IS adoption remains infrequent, with trust‐related barriers constraining implementation. Although existing research widely recognises the significance of trust, it offers fragmented explanations of how trust develops and is managed within IS ecosystems. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review that synthesises current knowledge on the conditions that facilitate trust development and the mechanisms by which organisations manage stakeholder perceptions of trustworthiness. Building on these findings, the study proposes a context‐specific definition of trust and develops a dynamic stakeholder trust management framework that conceptualises trust as a temporal and adaptive process requiring ongoing management. These contributions provide a foundation for understanding trust in IS networks and establish an agenda for future empirical research.

title: Green Supply Chain Practices and Firm Performance: Digital, Innovation, and Resilience Capability Architectures
abstract: Green Supply Chain Management Practices (GSCMP) are central to sustainable business strategy, yet their association with Firm Performance (FP) may depend on complementary organizational capabilities. Drawing on the Natural Resource‐Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study examines how GSCMP, Green Digital Transformation Capabilities (GDTC), Green Innovation (GI), and Firm Resilience (FR) are associated with FP within a capability architecture. Data from 247 Vietnamese firms, collected through a three‐wave, time‐separated survey, were analyzed using PLS‐SEM, artificial neural networks (ANNs), and fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). PLS‐SEM shows that GSCMP, GDTC, GI, and FR are all positively associated with FP. More importantly, GSCMP is associated with FP not only directly but also through significant indirect pathways via GDTC, GI, and FR, consistent with distinct capability pathways connecting green supply chain practices with performance. In turn, ANN indicates that GSCMP has the highest predictive importance, although differences among predictors are modest. fsQCA identifies four configurations sufficient for high FP, none of which requires every capability to be present. Together, the findings show that the performance relevance of green supply chain transformation is associated with differentiated capability pathways and alternative configurations rather than a single universal transformation pathway.

title: Biodiversity and Clean Energy Market Spillovers: Strategic Insights Into Tail Risk and Ecosystem Resilience
abstract: This study investigates dynamic higher‐order spillovers and co‐movements between biodiversity and clean energy markets. Employing a General Autoregressive Conditional Volatility Skewness Kurtosis (GARCHSK) framework combined with time‐varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP‐VAR) connectedness and wavelet coherence analysis, we examine return, volatility, skewness, and kurtosis spillovers across different time horizons. Our findings reveal strong moment‐dependent connectedness. S&P clean energy and electric vehicles act as net transmitters of return spillovers, whereas hydrogen emerges as the dominant transmitter of volatility spillovers. S&P clean energy is the principal transmitter of skewness spillovers, particularly to wind and solar markets, whereas hydrogen and electric vehicles dominate kurtosis transmission. Biodiversity consistently exhibits a net‐receiver position across all four moments, whereas wind markets are particularly exposed to higher‐order risk spillovers. Dynamic connectedness intensifies around major periods of market stress, including the COVID‐19 pandemic, the Russia–Ukraine war, and subsequent geopolitical tensions. Wavelet coherence further reveals time‐ and frequency‐dependent co‐movements, with particularly strong and persistent medium‐ and long‐term linkages between biodiversity and hydrogen and electric vehicle markets. These findings provide insights for investors and policymakers, highlighting the importance of incorporating biodiversity considerations into sustainable investment strategies and financial decision‐making to support resilient and environmentally aligned investment outcomes.

title: Supply chain analytics, supply chain mapping, and social and environmental sustainability: unveiling the role of participative decision-making
abstract: Purpose Although the functions of human resource (HR), supply chain (SC) and sustainability management are implicitly connected in the era of Industry 5.0, the existing literature often treats them as separate entities. Grounded in the contingent resource-based view, this study aims to explore the direct impact of participative decision-making (PDM) on SC analytics (SCA), SC mapping (SCMap) and sustainability, and the moderating effect of PDM. Design/methodology/approach Survey data collected from manufacturers in China were analysed to empirically test the proposed research model. Findings The findings demonstrate that PDM positively influences both SCA and SCMap, thereby contributing to improved social and environmental sustainability. Furthermore, the moderation analysis reveals that PDM plays a crucial role in strengthening the associations between SCA and environmental and social sustainability, as well as between SCMap and social sustainability. Originality/value The empirical findings contribute significantly to the literature on HR, SC and sustainability management by formulating and testing an integrated HR–SC capabilities–sustainability performance model, which also provides valuable managerial implications.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: When location matters more: regional institutions, firm age, and productivity
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the relationship between regional institutional quality and hospitality firms’ labor productivity and investigates whether this relationship varies with firm age. Design/methodology/approach This study analyzes 48,599 Italian hospitality firms observed from 2013 to 2019. Firm-level data are matched with an indicator of regional institutional quality and local-level information. An instrumental–variable approach is employed to address potential endogeneity. Findings Regional institutional quality is positively associated with labor productivity. However, this association weakens as firms mature. Average marginal effects show that institutional quality is especially beneficial for younger hospitality firms, suggesting that high-quality institutions may partially compensate for liability-of-newness constraints. Practical implications Regional institutional improvements may strengthen hospitality productivity, especially for younger firms. Policymakers should prioritize government effectiveness, regulatory quality, and voice and accountability, while young firms should leverage regional support networks to access resources and build legitimacy. Originality/value By integrating New Institutional Economics with the liability-of-newness perspective, this study advances a place-based view of hospitality firm productivity. It shifts attention from national to regional institutions by identifying regional institutional quality as an underexplored feature of place, while further showing that the institutional quality–productivity nexus is contingent on firm age.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: In country we fight: Sanction, institutional support, and innovation performance of targeted firms
abstract: As geopolitical tensions continue to escalate, sanctions are increasingly employed by political actors and impose substantial institutional constraints on targeted firms. Yet firms vary considerably in their responses, with some intensifying technological innovation while others do not. This study examines a salient but underexplored boundary condition, institutional support, that shapes the relationship between sanctions and targeted firms’ innovation performance. Specifically, it considers both formal institutional support provided by government actors and informal institutional support arising from societal expectations. Using the U.S. Entity List as the empirical context and a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2013 to 2022, the findings show that sanctioned firms are more likely to enhance their innovation performance when operating in sectors supported by industrial policy and when located in regions characterized by more pervasive nationalist sentiments. These findings offer valuable insights for research on international sanctions and innovation, while also highlighting the importance of nationalism in shaping firms’ responses to geopolitical tensions.

title: Family firms in small business and entrepreneurship research: A synthesis and future research agenda
abstract: This article introduces a Virtual Special Issue that brings together 11 articles on family business published in the International Small Business Journal between 2006 and 2025. Although these contributions have shaped how family involvement is understood in small business and entrepreneurship research, they have largely been published in isolation. We synthesise them around three arenas: the arena of identity, concerning who the entrepreneurial family is and becomes and how entrepreneurial identity and capabilities are reproduced across generations; the arena of governance, concerning how families navigate succession, authority, leadership transitions, and exit; and the arena of context, concerning how family firms are shaped by the social, institutional, cultural, and temporal environments in which they are embedded. Through an integrative framework, we argue that family businesses are not merely a governance variant of the small firm but a distinctive mode of organising entrepreneurship, in which paradox operates as a constitutive feature across all three arenas: the tensions between family and business logics, continuity and renewal, and control and autonomy are navigated rather than resolved. After reviewing the dominant methodological approaches in the corpus, we outline four directions for future research: the micro-processes of family entrepreneurship; the family as a multi-entity entrepreneurial ecosystem; family firms and societal grand challenges; and new family-level constructs and associated measures.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: Learning by supplying in global value chains: how downstream R&D spillovers shape supplier value capture
Climate change policy and climate risk disclosure: evidence from machine learning and textual analysis
abstract: Purpose This study examines how National Climate Change Policy (NCCP) influences firm-level climate risk disclosure (CRD). The study also investigates whether the policy affects transition- and physical-risk disclosure differently, and how analyst coverage, political connections and CSR intensity shape this relationship. Design/methodology/approach The study uses firm-year data for companies listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange from 2007 to 2022. CRD is measured using a hybrid computational linguistics framework that combines Word2Vec embeddings, semantic expansion and multi-stage expert validation to construct separate disclosure indices for transition and physical risk. The empirical analysis employs an exposure-based difference-in-differences design. Findings The results show that NCCP affects climate disclosure selectively rather than uniformly. The policy significantly increases physical-risk disclosure, whereas transition-risk disclosure declines in the baseline specification. Dynamic estimates support parallel trends and indicate that the effects emerge gradually. Further analysis shows that policy-relevant political connections are associated with stronger disclosure responses, while higher CSR intensity mitigates the decline in transition-risk disclosure and amplifies the increase in physical-risk disclosure. Analyst coverage provides suggestive evidence of an information-intermediary channel. Practical implications The findings suggest that climate policy alone may not be sufficient to ensure broad-based transparency in a weak-enforcement environment. Stricter mandatory rules, better institutional coordination and external monitoring may improve corporate climate transparency. Originality/value This study provides evidence from a climate-vulnerable emerging economy and introduces a validated text-based CRD measure that distinguishes transition-risk from physical-risk disclosure and shows that policy effects depend on political access, external monitoring and strategic capacity.

title: Board Interlocks and Corporate Risk Disclosures
abstract: Synopsis The research problem This study examined how board interlocks influence the content and quality of corporate risk disclosures in U.S. public firms. Although firms are mandated to report material risks in their annual reports, it remains unclear how they identify which risks to disclose and whether shared board members shape this process. The central question of this study is whether directors with multiple board memberships facilitate the transfer of risk information across firms, and whether such transfers enhance or undermine disclosure quality. Motivation Risk disclosure plays a critical role in investor decision-making and regulatory compliance but also poses proprietary and reputational risks. While prior literature emphasizes the role of board structure in disclosure practices, the impact of interlocking directorates—shared directors between firms—remains underexplored in the context of textual risk disclosures. The test hypotheses The first hypothesis tests whether firms disclose a higher number of similar risk factors when they are interlocked through a shared director. The second hypothesis tests whether the quality of a newly disclosed risk factor is associated with the disclosure of a similar risk by a linked firm. Target population This study investigated the Item 1A risk reports of U.S. public firms. Adopted methodology The study employed a stacked regression estimator, which generalizes two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (TWFEDID) by allowing for dynamic and heterogeneous treatment effects, OLS regressions, and textual analysis of archival data. Analyses We applied the Top2Vec topic modeling technique to identify and compare the contents of 45,205 Item 1A sections from nonfinancial U.S. public firms between 2006 and 2023. The stacked regression estimator model tested whether firms connected through shared directors disclose more risk factors on the same topics than similar, nonconnected firms. We assessed disclosure quality using specificity, length, and readability metrics. We estimated OLS regressions on risk factor-firm-year observations to evaluate whether the quality of newly disclosed risk factors is affected by prior disclosures from interlocked firms. Findings We found that interlocked firms simultaneously disclose more risk factors with the same topic, particularly when the shared director is an executive director. Further, the shared risk factors between interlocked firms are often less specific, shorter, and harder to read, indicating reduced disclosure quality. Our findings suggest that board interlocks generate imitation rather than insight, producing more boilerplate risk disclosures instead of informative knowledge spillovers.

title: ESG disclosure, paradoxical strategic orientations, and firm performance
Digital maturity, industry context, and firm outcomes: evidence from Thailand
Beyond firm boundaries: how supplier digital technology innovation builds corporate operational resilience
Systematic review of ethical branding: unveiling insights, epistemology, and future perspectives
abstract: Consumers expect brands to act with transparency, fairness, and responsibility. Yet ethical branding research remains fragmented, with inconsistent definitions and limited understanding of links between ethical commitments, branding practices, and consumer outcomes. This paper reviews 80 peer-reviewed articles published between 2002 and 2022 to identify future research directions. The review identifies seven definitions and two complementary perspectives: a process-focused view centred on ethical conduct and consumer-visible signals, and a state/system-focused view centred on organisational policies, governance routines, and verification practices. It identifies four core responsibility dimensions: environmental, social, economic, and health. Ethical branding is associated with consumer trust, loyalty, word of mouth, purchase intention, and willingness to pay, although relationships vary across contexts. Research gaps include limited development and measurement of health responsibility, inconsistent verification of ethical claims, and reliance on cross-sectional designs and stated intentions. The resulting research agenda connects what brands say with what they do.

title: Work design in digital platform labor: Development and validation of the Microworking Conditions Scale
abstract: In light of the rise of AI, microwork is becoming an increasingly important branch of the platform economy. This global labor market of individual workers who label data and moderate content supports the development of technological innovation. Little is known about their working conditions and how these conditions affect their well-being, however. This article presents three studies that outline the development of an integrative framework of working conditions in microwork, a complementary scale, and the validation of this scale. Based on current literature on microwork and guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Microworking Conditions Scale (MWCS) comprises 15 working conditions, nine adopted from existing frameworks (e.g., Work Autonomy) and six newly conceptualized (e.g., Availability Requirement). The measurement structure of the MWCS was confirmed by exploratory factor analyses ( n = 407) and confirmatory factor analysis ( n = 455). All 15 microworking conditions show convergent, discriminant, criterion, and predictive validity. The final scale consists of 45 items, three per microworking condition. The MWCS addresses the fragmented nature of the literature on microworking conditions and fills in gaps in the measurement of new working conditions emerging from microwork. The article further discusses the theoretical and practical implications, as well as directions for future research.

title: Skipped-generation child-rearing and the digital social integration of older adults: An empirical study in China
abstract: As the world enters the era of intelligence, the integration of the digital society has become increasingly crucial for the elderly to keep up with the pace of social development and avoid being marginalized. At present, there are still few studies exploring whether the act of intergenerational nurturing can facilitate better integration into the digital society. This study used grandparents who were raising grandchildren as the research participants. We first interviewed 18 such participants to construct a framework based on grounded theory. Then, we used a structural equation model to analyze the impact of living rearing and educational rearing on digital social integration through the methods of smart technologies use and digital social participation, and used an artificial neural network for showing variable importance. The results show that living rearing is positively associated with the breadth and depth of using smart technologies and promotes interpersonal interaction and digital social participation among all grandchildren age groups. Educational rearing significantly increases the digital social participation of people but as the grandchildren start formal education, the effect of educational rearing on digital social participation and methods of use is not significant. The depth of smart technology use shows a positive impact on digital social integration. The results expand the scope of research on the social integration of older adults and intergenerational relationships. The results also support policy intervention measures that combine family support with age-friendly technological design to bridge the digital divide and promote fair participation in digital society.

title: The structural alignment of virtual influencers and deepfake endorsers
abstract: Purpose This study aims to understand the effectiveness of virtual influencers versus deepfake endorsers in marketing. It investigates the cognitive processes shaping consumer responses to these digital endorsers. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the structural alignment theory, and across four studies using eye-tracking and experiments, the authors tested various factors, including eeriness, customer engagement, place identity and product manifestations. Findings Deepfake endorsers generally outperform virtual influencers in generating customer engagement and word-of-mouth. Virtual influencers are perceived as more eerie than deepfakes. Deepfakes are more effective in place-based contexts, but virtual influencers are more effective when endorsing NFTs compared to physical products. Research limitations/implications The paper contributes to the structural alignment theory to indicate that customers undergo a cognitive restructuring during the structural alignment process upon perceiving a digital endorser. Practical implications The findings help marketing managers guide the strategic selection of digital endorsers. Developing an endorser portfolio including both deepfake and virtual influencer endorsers is suggested. Matching specific endorsers with campaign target audiences, objectives and product types is recommended. Using different types of digital endorsers at various points in the customer journey can maximize engagement. Originality/value This study is among the first to compare different types of digital endorsers. It contributes to understanding digital endorser effectiveness by highlighting cognitive processes and boundary conditions shaping consumer responses and preferences.

title: In from the cold: intermediary strategies for sourcing from a stigmatized supply network after a geopolitical shift
abstract: Purpose As geopolitical shifts reshape global sourcing, firms increasingly reconsider suppliers in regions previously excluded by sanctions, boycotts and other geopolitical instruments. Such exclusions often leave a lasting stigma, and suppliers in these regions struggle to establish legitimacy as buyers discount their signals. This research examines how supply chain intermediaries undertake legitimation work to overcome suppliers' legitimacy deficits that otherwise deter reintegration. Design/methodology/approach We conduct a longitudinal multiple-case study in the Uzbekistan cotton–textile industry (2019–2026), a revelatory instance of reintegration after the lifting of a global boycott. The three cases are buyer–supplier relationships in this setting, each brokered by the same three intermediaries. We draw abductively on 46 interviews with buyers, suppliers and intermediaries, over 80 h of observations, and 2,231 pages of archival documents. Findings Uzbek suppliers face three legitimacy deficits: cognitive illegibility, pragmatic incompatibility and moral fragility. In response, intermediaries employ three strategies: (1) cognitive bridging to render suppliers comprehensible; (2) network grafting to make exchange workable; and (3) norm cascading to embed global standards into supplier practices so that compliance becomes credible and durable. Together, these strategies move suppliers from exclusion to accepted sourcing relationships with global buyers. Originality/value We extend supply chain geopolitics research to reintegration, showing how a previously excluded region re-enters global sourcing following a geopolitical shift. We theorize intermediated legitimation as the mechanism enabling this, with legitimation work shifting to the intermediary. Contrary to the sequence assumed in prior literature, cognitive legitimacy emerges as the gateway to pragmatic and moral legitimacy.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Refine more, explore less? How buyer–supplier inventor ties shape innovation search outcomes
abstract: Purpose Innovation in supply chains depends on technical coordination between buyers and suppliers, yet close coordination may constrain a firm's ability to search beyond established supplier interfaces. This study examines how inventor ties shape buyers' exploitative and exploratory innovation as distinct outcomes of innovation search. Inventor ties refer to overlaps in inventor identities across buyer and supplier patent records. We further examine whether these relationships vary with technological distance and supplier concentration. Design/methodology/approach We use a panel of 1,872 buyer–supplier dyad-year observations from Chinese A-share listed firms over the period 2007–2024 and estimate firm fixed-effects models. The analysis examines the relationships between inventor ties and two innovation outcomes within firms. It also tests the moderating effects of technological distance and supplier concentration. Findings Inventor ties are positively associated with exploitative innovation but negatively associated with exploratory innovation. Technological distance weakens the positive relationship with exploitative innovation and weakens the negative relationship with exploratory innovation. Supplier concentration strengthens both relationships because a concentrated supply base reduces the buyer's flexibility to redirect innovation across alternative supplier interfaces. Originality/value The study shows that inventor ties can facilitate interface-based refinement while also reinforcing innovation lock-in. It advances operations and supply chain management research by explaining how technical actors embedded in buyer–supplier interfaces shape firms' innovation portfolios, thereby linking supply chain coordination mechanisms to the exploration-exploitation trade-off.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Earnings Management of Oil & Gas Firms After the Russian Invasion of Ukraine
abstract: Political crises often lead to sharp increases in energy prices and, consequently, in the profits of oil and gas companies. However, exceptionally high profits may be perceived as unethical, creating reputational and legitimacy concerns that can influence firms’ financial reporting behavior. Yet, there is no evidence whether European oil & gas firms manage earnings after sudden political crises, and whether their responses differ across countries. Using a difference-in-differences design, this study documents that European oil & gas firms engaged in significant income-decreasing earnings management—through both accrual-based and real activities—following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. This effect is particularly pronounced in the third quarter of 2022 and the first quarter of 2023. We further find that (real) earnings management by oil & gas firms is more pronounced in countries that implemented windfall profit taxes and in institutional environments characterized by stronger democratic governance. At the firm level, the effect is concentrated among oil & gas firms with relatively low sustainability scores, which exhibit significantly greater income-decreasing earnings management than control firms. These findings suggest that earnings management decisions were driven not only by tax considerations but also by legitimacy and reputational concerns. This study contributes to the literature by providing cross-country evidence that exploits variation in taxation regimes and institutional settings, and by explicitly examining the role of legitimacy and reputational concerns in shaping corporate reporting behavior.

title: Toward AI leadership: A systematic literature review of leadership behaviors enacted by conversational agents in psychosocial interventions
abstract: This project is a systematic literature review that investigates how conversational agents (CAs; e.g., chatbots and virtual assistants) enact leadership-equivalent behaviors in psychosocial interventions, including therapy, counseling, and coaching. Advances in artificial intelligence have enabled these systems to move beyond process automation and engage in adaptive, relational, and motivational dialogue with users. As such, they increasingly perform functions that parallel those of human leaders, raising important theoretical and practical questions about the nature of leadership when enacted by nonhuman agents. The review has three main purposes. First, it examines which leadership behaviors are effectively exhibited by conversational agents, using Yukl et al.’s (2012) taxonomy of task-, relationship-, change-, and externally-oriented behaviors as an organizing framework. Second, it investigates the mechanisms through which these behaviors exert influence on users in psychosocial contexts, and identifies points of divergence from human-enacted leadership theory. Third, it distills methodological lessons from the existing evidence base, particularly regarding causal trustworthiness, intervention transparency, and replicability, to inform the design of future AI leadership research. The evidence base for this review draws primarily from rigorous experimental and longitudinal studies in medical and behavioral sciences, which provide a strong foundation for assessing agent-enacted influence. Synthesizing this literature, we aim to deliver: - An integrative behavioral framework that maps agent behaviors to leadership theory. - A research agenda outlining methodological standards and open questions for studying AI leadership. - Theoretical refinements that extend leadership theory to account for influence processes enacted by artificial agents. The expected outcome is a comprehensive and causally trustworthy assessment of how conversational agents perform leadership functions in psychosocial interventions, contributing both to leadership theory and to the responsible design of AI systems that increasingly shape workplace interactions.

title: When a woman reaches the top: CEO succession and organizational gender inequality
abstract: What changes within organizations when a woman becomes the leader? Prior research has characterized female leaders either as queen bees who distance themselves from other women or as agents of change who promote inclusion. Rather than adopting this binary characterization of leaders, we examine whether, and for whom, male-to-female leadership succession is followed by changes in inequality across organizational domains. Using longitudinal administrative data on 433 large Brazilian firms (2003–2017) and a staggered difference-in-differences design with doubly robust estimators, in which male-to-female CEO successions are compared with male-to-male successions, we trace subordinate women's outcomes in wages, vertical mobility, and turnover, overall and by wage quintile. The pattern is selective: the gender wage gap narrows among top earners from the fourth year after succession, whereas it remains unchanged, or widens slightly in a few years, in the middle of the wage distribution; we detect no consistent change in vertical mobility or turnover. We read this narrowing as an association: its causal interpretation holds only under the identifying assumptions and is fragile to modest departures from parallel trends. After male-to-female succession, subordinate women's outcomes neither uniformly improve nor systematically worsen; where a change is observable, it concerns pay and is concentrated among the highest-paid women. We offer several theoretically grounded post hoc interpretations of this pattern, which our data cannot distinguish, and argue that mapping where and for whom such changes occur is a necessary step before theorizing about the mechanisms through which female leadership relates to organizational inequality.

title: Credit Repair, Government Resource Access, and Innovation in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
abstract: We examine whether China’s 2019 credit-repair reform affects innovation among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Using NEEQ-listed firms from 2014 to 2023, we find that adversely recorded SMEs increase R&D investment following the 2019 credit-repair reform that standardized credit repair for administrative-penalty information. These firms also receive more subsidies and are more likely to obtain government procurement contracts, providing evidence consistent with the government-resource-access channel. The effect on R&D investment is stronger for smaller firms, firms with higher managerial shareholding, and firms in regions with more developed social credit systems and lower fiscal pressure, but weaker for more serious violations. We also find suggestive evidence of improved innovation efficiency.

title: Resisting Epistemic Injustice and Unresponsive Regulation: Testimonies From Unmarried Couples
abstract: Theoretical studies on responsive regulation and epistemic justice rarely examine how epistemic and regulatory dimensions operate together in administrative systems where citizens must (re‐)verify their eligibility for formally‐granted rights. In the case of Israel, despite extensive legal recognition of common‐law partnerships, unmarried couples face invasive verification demands and systematic credibility deficits that married couples bypass entirely. Epistemic injustice enables regulatory unresponsiveness by providing justification for fragmented bureaucracy and intrusive treatment, while unresponsive regulation actively reproduces epistemic injustice, positioning unmarried couples as less credible. Notwithstanding, rather than accepting marginalization, such couples resist by identifying alternative knowledge networks, documentation sources, and recognition frameworks. This article (i) demonstrates how epistemic injustice and regulatory unresponsiveness function as mutually constitutive forces in unmarried couples' lived experiences; (ii) theorizes unmarried couples' proactive epistemic resistance; and (iii) beyond the Israeli context, articulates design principles for more epistemically just responsive regulation that is grounded in participants' experiential and positional knowledge.

title: The Effects of Teacher Strikes on Compensation, Working Conditions, and Productivity
abstract: We document the nature of teacher strikes in the United States and examine how they affect compensation, working conditions, and productivity using an original dataset of 745 teacher strikes between 2007 and 2024. The vast majority (89%) of strikes are motivated by compensation, and just over half are motivated by working conditions. We examine the impact of strikes on both strike aims and student achievement in an event study framework. The average strike leads to a 6% ($7,629) increase in combined annual wages and benefits and a 0.5 student (3.2%) decline in pupil–teacher ratios after 5 years. We find little evidence of sizable impacts on student achievement, on average, up to 5 years poststrike. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that strikes did cause student achievement to increase in districts with lower relative expenditures per pupil and in states where teacher strikes are illegal, both contexts where strikes achieved larger gains in teacher compensation. Math achievement declines in the short‐term after atypically long strikes, likely due to lost instructional time.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Platform governance and elections in an era of democratic erosion
COVID-19 pandemic and productivity among epidemiologists: results from the 2021 Society for Epidemiologic Research Diversity & inclusion survey
Role of simulation-based analyses in self-controlled vaccine effectiveness studies
Longitudinal utility of the Berlin questionnaire to assess obstructive sleep apnea risk: a sequence analysis approach
Continuously controllable surrogate-risk scenario generation via behavior-prior modeling for safety-critical testing
Developing an LLM-assisted safety knowledge graph for the governance of unmanned aircraft systems: Integrating accident risks with regulatory requirements
From envy to harm: how evil eye beliefs amplify interpersonal hostility
abstract: Belief in the evil eye is widespread across many cultures and religious traditions, especially in highly competitive, zero-sum cultures where provoking malicious envy is perceived as dangerous. We investigate cultural evolutionary claims that evil eye beliefs build on common understandings of interpersonal envy, giving magical force to people's negative feelings about others' success. Across three studies using diverse North American university and online samples, we compare laypeople's beliefs about the evil eye and interpersonal envy. Studies 1–2 ( N = 1358) used an open-ended free-list task, in which believers described the likely sources, victims, and outcomes of the evil eye, whereas non-believers answered analogous questions about envy. Participants described similar themes across both concepts, including negative personality traits and personal achievement. However, the evil eye was associated with broader and more severe harm such as illnesses and bad luck. Study 3 ( N = 1187) replicates these findings using closed-ended questionnaires. Overall, the sources, victims, and outcomes of the evil eye were evaluated significantly more negatively than envy. These studies support cultural evolutionary theories that evil eye beliefs give supernatural force to interpersonal hostilities by broadening the scope of possible harm arising from feelings of malicious envy.

title: “My Life Has Been a Series of Moves”: Iranian Women’s Transnational Patriarchal Bargains
abstract: This article examines how Iranian women negotiate gendered expectations across the life course and across borders under shifting global, economic, and geopolitical conditions. I extend Deniz Kandiyoti’s concept of “patriarchal bargains” by introducing transnational patriarchal bargains to theorize how these negotiations unfold over time and across space. Drawing on 40 life history interviews with two cohorts of Muslim middle-class Iranian women—those who came of age under the Pahlavi monarchy (1925–1979) and those raised after the Islamic Revolution (1979)—who later migrated to Canada with precarious legal status, I show that migration is not a single life-changing event but part of ongoing gendered negotiations that begin long before departure. These negotiations span family, state, and transnational contexts and shift in response to changing structural conditions and intimate life events. The concept of transnational patriarchal bargains offers a framework for analyzing how migrant women navigate competing gender regimes while managing precarious pathways to settlement in the Global North.

title: Holding it Together: Maternal Coping After Counter-Radicalization Referrals
abstract: Drawing on a multi-sited ethnography conducted in Tunisia, Italy, and Québec, Canada, between 2015 and 2025, this article examines how 131 Muslim mothers navigate the aftermath of counter-radicalization interventions. The mothers’ narratives form part of a broader ethnographic corpus comprising interviews with other family members and prevention professionals. I argue that maternal endurance—holding it together—is not simply a form of emotional resilience but a mode of moral labor shaped by gendered and racialized surveillance. Through three interconnected practices— asl and denial (referring to moral rootedness, dignity, and face-work), faith (as both refuge and discipline), and the daughter-relay (an intergenerational economy of care)—the analysis shows how women sustain family life while absorbing the burdens of suspicion, responsibility, and scrutiny. Rather than conceptualizing coping as resistance, the article highlights the ordinary routines through which mothers care, pray, preserve dignity, and maintain relationships under pressure. By framing maternal endurance as gendered moral work, I demonstrate how security governance operates through the intimate sphere of care and how everyday practices of survival become central to the reproduction of family life under conditions of surveillance. Thus, the article contributes to feminist and postcolonial scholarship on motherhood, moral governance, and agency under constraint.

title: When Porn Becomes the Educator: A Mixed-Methods Study of Adolescent Pornography Consumption
Sexual Health and Intentions to Use Anabolic–Androgenic Steroids Among Boys and Men
Linking Women’s Equality With Government Integrity: Can Gender Budgeting Curb Corruption?
abstract: Policies addressing gender inequality have increasingly been linked to more ethical governance, as women tend to be disproportionately burdened by corruption compared to men. One such policy is gender budgeting, an innovative approach to resource allocation that considers the impact of government spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite the growing popularity worldwide, we know little about its effectiveness in curbing corruption. This study evaluates the impact of gender budgeting on grand (political) and petty (bureaucratic) corruption using difference‐in‐differences estimations across a panel of 136 countries from 1980 to 2023. The results reveal a significant reduction in petty corruption, as gender budgeting improves the impartiality of public bureaucracies. Heterogeneity analyses also indicate a decrease in grand corruption, but only in countries with adequate levels of budget transparency, oversight, and public participation. The study highlights the far‐reaching consequences of gender reforms for the quality of governance.

title: Why Do Special Districts File for Bankruptcy in the United States?
abstract: Special districts outnumber general‐purpose local governments in the U.S., yet their use of bankruptcy protection remains largely unexamined. This study explores why some districts file for bankruptcy while others do not. Using novel federal court data from 1982–2021, we document key characteristics of these filings. Nationwide analysis indicates that deficits, debt burdens, and administrative costs are positively associated with filing, while capital outlays and county economic strength are negatively associated. A case study of Nebraska, the state with the most such filings, shows how bankruptcy serves as a last resort, but a nontrivial one, for districts facing severe financial distress.

title: Consistency sorting of retired batteries using multidimensional health features derived from a simplified P2D model
Component-resolved voltage-loss monitoring of PEM water electrolyzers from routine operating data
Exploiting flexibility in workflow scheduling for coordinated operation of geo-distributed data center microgrids: A multi-agent reinforcement learning approach
Electric vehicles as mobile energy carriers: An activity-based agent-based model of residential PV origin energy flows and V2G
abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is turning transportation management into a coupled mobility and energy planning problem. Public EVCS deployment affects travel behavior, parking duration, and local electricity demand, while EV batteries may also provide flexible storage through vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operation. However, the extent to which EVs can redistribute residential photovoltaic (PV) energy depends not only on charging infrastructure but also on daily activity schedules, state-of-charge conditions, dwell times, and station-side constraints. This study develops an activity-based agent-based model to evaluate EVs as mobile carriers of residential PV-origin energy in an urban charging system. The model links home charging, activity-based travel, public charging, V2G discharge, stationary battery energy storage systems, and charging station feasibility constraints. The framework is applied to Eindhoven, the Netherlands. Results show that EVs can acquire substantial residential PV-origin energy through home charging, but consume only about 6% of it during daily travel. Most PV-origin energy remains stored in EV batteries when vehicles arrive at non-home locations, creating technical potential for redistribution. However, activity context is the dominant bottleneck limiting V2G opportunities, indicating that urban V2G potential is shaped less by infrastructure availability alone than by when and where eligible EVs are parked during daily routines.

title: When hydrogen is not fully flexible: Implications for sector-coupled energy models
A mechanism-guided Bayesian physics-informed neural network for unified battery state-of-health monitoring using field data
Pricing nature loss: An application to land-use change in Finland
abstract: We study the Pigouvian solution for biodiversity loss, a fee levied on nature loss from deforestation. Combining Finnish data on land-use changes and property price transactions with a biodiversity index, we quantify the economic and environmental impacts of a 'nature loss fee'. We examine five biodiversity-weighting approaches to fee structures and their effects across urban-rural categories and regions. We find that a uniform area-based fee on deforestation significantly reduces the loss of forest and biodiversity. An approach targeting biodiversity hotspots effectively preserves them at a relatively low cost, while a middle-ground policy based on a linearly weighted area-and-quality measure balances deforestation reduction and biodiversity preservation across regions. Comparing these fees to command-and-control policies, we find that nature loss fees achieve biodiversity preservation at significantly lower costs.

title: Exploring landscape preferences for greenways: A multi-source preference method based on social media and deep learning
Diagnosing the equity–feasibility dilemma in green space planning: A policy-grounded planning support framework for secondary cities
Building the collective layer: Regulatory pathways for energy communities in Costa Rica and Spain
abstract: Energy communities are increasingly promoted as instruments for decentralization, consumer participation, and local energy governance, yet their regulatory development remains uneven across jurisdictions. This study compares Costa Rica and Spain to examine how distinct electricity-sector architectures enable the transition from individual distributed energy resources (DERs) to collective energy participation. A structured regulatory analysis was conducted across 14 dimensions grouped into four blocks and assessed using an expert-based four-level ordinal maturity scale complemented by a qualitative transferability assessment. Costa Rica obtains an overall descriptive score of 1.57, compared with 2.57 for Spain. Costa Rica possesses a relatively developed formal basis for individual self-consumption, network access, general DER-related tariff treatment, and electric mobility. However, shared storage, generally applicable aggregation, and flexibility services remain insufficiently operationalized, while the largest gap concerns energy sharing, legal recognition of energy communities, governance, and multi-user settlement. Spain provides an operational but evolving benchmark for collective allocation and billing rather than a directly replicable model. Based on the comparative findings, the study proposes a three-phase sequence covering collective operation, governance and implementation capacity, and flexibility and system services, subject to further legal, tariff, institutional, and pilot validation.

title: Effects of fine-granular electricity procurement for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen production - a comparative analysis of production strategies
abstract: Renewable hydrogen is an integral part of managing the energy transition due to its potential to drive the decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors. However, the market uptake of renewable hydrogen produced via electrolysis is impeded by high costs and risks across the hydrogen value chain. Additionally, within the European Union (EU), strict regulatory requirements on renewable hydrogen affect the economic viability of electrolysis projects. In the transition phase towards a renewable hydrogen economy, expanding electrolyzer operations beyond renewable hydrogen production to include low-carbon hydrogen may increase economic performance and attract investment in electrolysis projects. In our study, we assess the economic impact of supplementing renewable hydrogen with low-carbon hydrogen production in compliance with the EU regulatory framework, utilizing fine-granular electricity procurement across five exemplary bidding zones (BZs). For BZs exhibiting high potential for grid-connected low-carbon hydrogen production, Levelized Cost of Hydrogen for a renewable hydrogen production strategy including non-oversized long-term PV-, wind- and hydropower Power Purchase Agreements may be reduced by up to 78.7 % through additional short-term low-carbon hydrogen production. However, significant variations in electricity generation across BZs result in numerous BZs not meeting the regulatory requirements, limiting the overall potential of electrolytic low-carbon hydrogen production. In less decarbonized BZs, establishing low-carbon hydrogen entails the risk of ongoing investments in natural gas infrastructure, counteracting the role of low-carbon hydrogen as a transitional solution. To advance the energy transition supported by hydrogen, we recommend that policymakers align hydrogen regulation with long-term decarbonization objectives by integrating financial subsidies for electrolytic low-carbon hydrogen.

title: A review on design of floating offshore wind farm control systems
abstract: Floating wind energy is growing rapidly, as it enables energy generation in deep water and avoids near-coastal development barriers. In floating offshore wind farms (FOWFs), inter-turbine aerodynamic interference known as the wake effect raises the levelized cost of energy (LCOE). Wind farm control (WFC) mitigates this effect by coordinating turbines at the farm level. Designing a WFC system, however, requires choosing a WFC strategy, model dependency, and communication topology, choices that jointly determine the feasibility and performance of the resulting system. To map the current research landscape and identify unexplored gaps, this paper presents a systematic review of current studies on WFC design for FOWFs across four dimensions: WFC strategy, model dependency, communication topology, and simulated environmental conditions. The analysis reveals that turbine repositioning is the most mature and highest-gain strategy, whereas wake mixing has yet to be demonstrated at large scale. Moreover, attention is uneven across objectives, with most studies concentrating on power maximization and load minimization, leaving power tracking largely untouched. Additionally, reviewed studies are either model-based or built on precomputed look-up tables designed only for ideal wind conditions, and 85\% adopt a centralized communication scheme. No study combines a model-free scheme with a noncentralized topology. Therefore, the field has not yet tested the architectures or the conditions most relevant to utility-scale deployment. Building on these findings, we summarize unique FOWF control challenges and recommend research directions toward feasible, effective WFC systems for commercial-scale floating wind.

title: Interpretable fuzzy XAI framework for multidimensional industrial energy and emissions assessment
Industrializing critical mineral recovery: Technologies, readiness, scale-up, and commercial deployment
abstract: Critical-mineral recovery from manufacturing scrap, end-of-life products, mine wastes, industrial residues, and mineral-rich aqueous streams can diversify supply while reducing waste disposal and dependence on primary extraction. However, translating high extraction efficiencies achieved in the laboratory into plant-wide recovery of specification-grade materials remains a major challenge. To address this gap, this structured review evaluates the industrial implementation of established and emerging recovery technologies by examining patent disclosures, pilot and demonstration activities, commercial projects, technology readiness, key performance indicators, and scale-up requirements. Mechanical, pyrometallurgical, and hydrometallurgical operations have reached commercial deployment in specific feed–process–product configurations, whereas the readiness of direct recycling, hydrogen processing, electrochemical recovery, biohydrometallurgy, advanced solvents, membranes, and supercritical-fluid processes remains application-dependent. Patent disclosures show intellectual-property activity in integrated process configurations involving feedstock classification, selective separation, reagent regeneration, controlled crystallization, and direct material reuse but do not independently demonstrate technical maturity or commercial operation. Industrial cases in battery recycling, direct lithium extraction, rare-earth magnet recovery, and electronic-waste refining show that deployment depends on integrating pretreatment, extraction, purification, environmental control, and product finishing. Relevant performance indicators include overall elemental recovery, product quality, throughput, process availability and specific energy, reagent, and water consumption. Reliable scale-up requires representative feed testing, continuous integrated pilot operation, recycle-loop closure, residue management, product qualification, and techno-economic and environmental evaluations based on measured operating data. The resulting framework distinguishes among levels of evidence and stages of implementation, from laboratory results, patent claims, and pilot validation to announced capacity, commissioning, and sustained commercial operation.

title: Hydrogen storage for sustainable transportation: Safety challenges, technological advances, and regulatory perspectives
Detection and control of trace organics readily permeating to reverse osmosis membranes in electronics‑grade ultrapure water production: A review
Mechanistic Interpretation of Machine Learning Model Explanations Depends on Data and Model Design: Evidence from Activated Carbon Filtration
abstract: Understanding the mechanisms governing complex environmental systems is a central challenge across environmental science and engineering. Where mechanistic understanding is incomplete, machine learning (ML) combined with explainable AI methods─particularly Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)─has been increasingly applied to environmental data sets, with the resulting explanations often interpreted as reflections of underlying process mechanisms. However, the extent to which SHAP explanations reflect true system behavior depends on the conditions under which the model was developed. Here, we systematically investigate how model class, data regime, and hyperparameter configuration as components of the learning environment affect the mechanistic consistency of SHAP-based explanations, using granular activated carbon (GAC) filtration for micropollutant removal from wastewater as a case study. We show that all three components impact explanations and their consistency with proven mechanisms. Model class can affect which feature interactions are captured; the characteristics of the training data─both distribution and lacking coverage of joint feature space regions─shape which relationships can be learned; and hyperparameter sensitivity differs substantially between model classes. These findings demonstrate that SHAP explanations cannot be interpreted independently of the learning environment, but we argue that they can still serve as a valuable tool for hypothesis generation in environmental ML applications.

title: Revisiting the Climate Benefits Provided by Wood through Future-Oriented Material and Energy Displacement
abstract: Displacement factors (DFs) quantify climate benefits of wood-based products relative to non-wood alternatives. Existing DFs are typically static whereas economy-wide decarbonization motivates a forward-looking assessment. Previous work focuses on semifinished materials and lacks harmonized, transparent modeling. This study provides an open-access, unit-process-based database of future-oriented DFs for 81 wood-product-material-variants across six end-use categories. It uses time-explicit life cycle assessment (LCA), which links processes to the technology landscape as they occur, under three decarbonization scenarios for 2020–2070. Wood-based products showed positive DFs in 2020, with weighted averages from near-zero for furniture to 1.04 kg C/kg C for chemicals and textiles, though lower than previous estimates. DFs declined over time for all products except chemicals, most steeply under climate-ambitious scenarios. Wood sustained the highest benefit in the least ambitious scenario. The decline was driven by faster decarbonization of non-wood products that contain proportionally more fossil-intensive components. Time-explicit LCA yielded lower DFs for long-lived products as end-of-life processes were assigned to more decarbonized future years, an effect not captured by conventional or prospective LCA. Energy-related DFs approached near-zero by 2070. The findings support redirecting wood flows from energy toward long-lived material applications and caution against harvest intensification justified on displacement arguments alone.

title: Laboratory and Field Investigation of Amines in Automotive Brake Wear Particles
abstract: Nonexhaust vehicle emissions (brake wear, tire wear, and road dust) now dominate particulate matter (PM) sources in urban environments as tailpipe emissions continue to decline. Among these, brake wear particles (BWPs) remain under-characterized, particularly their organic composition. This study investigates the formation and atmospheric relevance of amines released during the thermal degradation of phenolic resin, the primary binder in brake pads. Controlled brake dynamometer and phenolic-resin thermal degradation experiments were performed together with field measurements adjacent to two Southern California freeways (I-5, Santa Ana, and I-710, Long Beach). High-resolution mass spectrometry analysis revealed the prevalence of nitrogen-containing compounds across all data sets with dicyclohexylamine (C12H23N; DCHA) consistently detected in laboratory and ambient particles. DCHA concentrations in laboratory particles ranged from 0.08 to 1.6 ng/μg across brake pad types and resin conditions. DCHA was measured in air sampled onto filters at levels ranging from 2.1 ± 1.6 pg m–3 (Santa Ana) to 3.5 ± 1.7 pg m–3 (Long Beach). Ambient levels of DCHA correlated with near-road NO and brake-associated metals (Fe, Ba), suggesting a possible link between its emission and braking activity. These findings identify brake wear as a previously under-recognized source of DCHA and related organic nitrogen compounds, often associated primarily with tire wear emissions.

title: Mechanisms and Prediction of Microcystis Removal by Sediment Resuspension in Drinking-Water Reservoirs
abstract: Microcystis blooms threaten drinking-water quality, yet sustainable in situ controls are needed. A survey of 43 drinking-water reservoirs in eastern China and the Tibetan Plateau found moderate- to high-intensity blooms in 26% of the reservoirs. We evaluated sediment resuspension (SR) as a nature-based intervention. Experiments with ten sediments showed that Microcystis removal (35.0% ± 14.3%) coincided with declining dissolved Fe and Al. Experiments and scanning electron microscopy–energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM–EDS) identified Fe/Al-mediated flocculation and settling, rather than particles alone, as the primary short-term removal pathway. Sediment composition regulated reactive Fe/Al supply and utilization: maximum Fe+Al removal increased with active Fe+Al content (R2 = 0.88, p < 0.001), whereas flocculation effectiveness declined as the fine-particle fraction (<63 μm) increased (R2 = 0.67, p < 0.03). We developed a sediment-property-based model from these relationships. Across more than 30 reservoirs in eastern China, predicted Microcystis removal averaged (1.37 ± 1.97) × 108 cells L–1. In a Microcystis-dominated reservoir, predicted and field-fitted removal rates differed by 6%. Observations from five filamentous-cyanobacteria-dominated reservoirs suggested Fe/Al-related flocculation may also aid removal of other taxa. This study provides a mechanistic, predictive basis for evaluating SR in bloom management.

title: Using Street View and Remote Sensing Imagery to Estimate NO2 and PM2.5 Concentrations for the Continental US
abstract: Land use regression (LUR) models are widely used for estimating fine-scale ambient air quality. Street view and remote sensing imagery are emerging sources to measure built environment features which may enhance traditional LUR predictors and further improve model performance. In this study, we investigate using various combinations of street view and remote sensing derived features to develop national annual NO2 and PM2.5 machine learning models (2007–2020). Predictors in our models include: (1) Google Street View (GSV) imagery derived semantic features, (2) satellite-based aerosol estimates, and (3) Landsat-derived spectral indices and elevation. Full models combining all predictors achieved the best model performance, with random 10-fold cross validation R2 values of 0.92 for NO2 and 0.75 for PM2.5. Models incorporating GSV-derived features generally achieve enhanced model fit. Beyond conventional internal model evaluation, we examined how different predictors impact the spatial patterns of model prediction surfaces. GSV-informed models yielded a wider range of model estimates and better captured intraurban air pollution variability─a finding confirmed by external validation using independent mobile monitoring and calibrated PurpleAir measurements. Our results highlight the potential of street-view imagery to characterize fine-scale spatial gradients in air pollution and thus support more spatially resolved exposure assessment.

title: Complementary Mechanisms for Fe(II)-Mediated Nickel and Cobalt Release from Laterites
abstract: Nickel (Ni) and cobalt (Co) mining must increase as renewable energy generation and energy storage technologies expand. Most of the world’s Ni is found in laterite deposits, but the processing of these ores is costly, energy-intensive, and damaging to the environment. Here, we present a novel ferrous leaching approach that operates at ambient conditions (22 °C, pH 7.5) to recover Ni and Co from four lateritic domains from the Barnes Hill Deposit in Tasmania, Australia. Ni and Co K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) shows that most of the Ni is bound in iron (Fe) (oxyhydr)oxide and silicate phases, whereas Co is predominantly associated with manganese (Mn) oxide minerals. Under optimal leach conditions, up to 38% of Ni and approximately 100% of Co are recovered. XAS analysis on the leached samples shows that Co (and Mn) release occurs by Fe(II)-induced reductive dissolution of Mn oxides. In the case of Ni, 57Fe-isotope tracer results suggest Fe(II)-catalyzed mineral recrystallization is repartitioning solid-phase Ni to a more labile form, while Ni hosted in silicate phases such as serpentine can also be extracted with a mild acid wash. Our results demonstrate that ferrous leaching is highly effective at solubilizing Co (and Ni) and thus may be a viable strategy for processing Co-rich laterites as well as metal-bearing Mn oxides such as deep-sea nodules and crusts.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Methane Detection: From Continuous Monitoring to Verified Mitigation
abstract: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, responsible for roughly 30% of warming since preindustrial times. A small number of large point sources account for a disproportionate share of emissions, creating an opportunity for substantial reductions by targeting relatively few sites. Detection and attribution of large emissions at scale for notifying asset owners remains challenging. Here, we introduce MARS-S2L, a machine learning model that detects methane emissions in publicly available multispectral satellite imagery. Trained on a manually curated data set of over 80,000 images, the model provides high-resolution detections every 2 days, enabling facility-level attribution and identifying 78% of plumes with an 8% false-positive rate at 697 previously unseen sites. Deployed operationally, MARS-S2L has issued 2,776 notifications to stakeholders in 25 countries, enabling verified, permanent mitigation of six persistent emitters, including a superemitter in Algeria that had been releasing approximately 27,500 tonnes of methane annually for at least a decade and a previously unknown emitter in Libya first identified by MARS-S2L. These results demonstrate a scalable pathway from satellite detection to quantifiable methane mitigation.

title: When Selectivity Is Not Enough: Product-Centered Metrics for Environmental Separations
abstract: Nanofiltration (NF) has traditionally been evaluated through the lens of water production, utilizing water/solute selectivity as the primary performance metric. As NF increasingly targets selective solute fractionation for resource recovery, the focus has shifted toward solute/solute selectivity. However, relying solely on selectivity can be fundamentally misleading because it frequently misaligns with practical process objectives. Furthermore, evaluating materials strictly based on instantaneous selectivity can potentially obscure the true process-level viability. This Perspective redefines performance evaluation by establishing a unified, product-centered framework applicable across three distinct separation scenarios: recovering the permeate, the retentate, or both streams as valuable products. To this end, we introduce a new framework based on the recovery-retention diagram to evaluate generic binary separations. This framework demonstrates how separation outcomes are intrinsically governed by both membrane performance and feed composition, which can be captured by the separation trajectory. Ultimately, transitioning from a purely selectivity-based evaluation framework to a product-centered one bridges the critical gap between bench-scale material discovery and scalable process engineering.

title: Heatwaves Shift Ozone Formation toward Greater NOx Sensitivity through Enhanced VOC Availability and Radical Cycling
abstract: Heatwaves aggravate surface ozone (O3) pollution, yet their impacts on O3 formation sensitivity and precursor control effectiveness remain insufficiently resolved. We integrate reanalysis data, ground-based observations, satellite retrievals, meteorological normalization, and observation-based modeling to elucidate the effects of heatwaves on O3 concentrations, precursor availability, radical chemistry, and O3 formation sensitivity in an emission-intensive urban basin. Heatwave frequency, duration, and cumulative intensity during April–September increased by factors of 2.1–3.2 in 2015–2024 relative to 1975–2014. Heatwaves not only enhanced O3 formation but also reshaped O3 formation sensitivity by increasing BVOCs and AVOCs possibly associated with fuel evaporation and solvent use, elevating ROx levels, and strengthening the oxidation of NO by peroxy radicals. Observation-based modeling revealed a shift from VOC-limited toward transitional regimes in urban Chengdu during the more strongly heatwave-affected Augusts, while satellite diagnostics provided supporting evidence for changes toward greater NOx sensitivity in parts of the basin. Sensitivity simulations further demonstrated that O3 formation sensitivity to NOx increased systematically with rising temperature and that sufficient NOx reductions effectively weakened the temperature sensitivity of O3 formation in Chengdu. These results support climate-adaptive O3 mitigation combining routine VOC–NOx controls with stronger reductions in NOx and temperature-sensitive AVOC emissions during heatwaves.

title: Biomass-Derived Supramolecular Living Hydrogels for Adaptive Dye Wastewater Remediation
abstract: Dye wastewater from textile, leather, and paper industries poses a persistent threat to aquatic ecosystems owing to its chemical recalcitrance and potential toxicity. Microalgae provide a sustainable strategy for dye bioremediation through synergistic bioaccumulation and biodegradation. However, these microbes suffer from limited tolerance to the complex composition of dye wastewater and are difficult to recycle after treatment. Here, we report retrievable living microalgae-loaded polysaccharide hydrogel networks coated with tannic acid (MPH@TA) for efficient purification of wastewater containing diverse dyes. The flexible supramolecular networks containing Chlorella pyrenoidosa create a protective microenvironment that supports robust microalgal growth and efficient dye removal while reducing the leakage of microalgae. Notably, MPH@TA achieves removal efficiencies of 97.7% and 94.5% for 100 mg L–1 malachite green and reactive red, respectively, highlighting its implementation for both cationic and anionic dyes. The living MPH@TA system enables facile recyclability and effective treatment of complex real dye wastewater. Transcriptomic analysis shows that MPH@TA modulates the antioxidant defense, redox metabolism, and respiratory energy supply of microalgae, thereby enhancing microalgal tolerance and biotransformation of dye molecules. This work not only provides a simple yet efficient strategy for water purification but also advances insights into microbe–material hybrid interactions for engineered living materials.

title: Comparative life cycle assessment of virgin and recycled resin stretch film production: A cradle-to-gate approach
