A semantic knowledge graph for mapping composition and recoverability of end-of-life products
abstract: The European green and digital transitions depend on strategic and critical raw materials, whose supply faces significant disruption risks. Circular economy strategies, such as recycling from the urban mine, are essential to mitigate these risks. However, assessing the urban mine's potential is challenging due to product heterogeneity, poor traceability, variable material stocks and fragmented composition data lacking interoperability across hierarchical levels (product-component-material-element). To address these issues, we developed a product-centric waste stream composition knowledge graph together with its underlying ontology, enabling a structured and interoperable representation of composition data across hierarchical levels. The composition ontology was extended with the metal wheel of recycling to provide insights into recovery routes. Ontology alignment was achieved using ROBOT, an open-source library for automating ontology development, ensuring integration into existing semantic frameworks. Two cases were analyzed: baseline and query-optimized ontology. Our semantic-driven approach enables seamless navigation across composition levels, supports reasoning, and facilitates comprehensive assessments of material availability. We demonstrate semantic querying using SPARQL and introduce a natural language interface powered by a large language model (LLM). The resulting knowledge base is extendable, compatible with LLM-based applications, and supports urban mine evaluation and product design.

title: Advancing solar desalination through circular economy integration of recycled metal absorbers and thermal enhancers: A comprehensive Energy, Economic, and Environmental analysis
Is closing the loop always better? A comparative life cycle assessment of multilayer plastic beverage packaging
abstract: Plastic waste is a global environmental challenge. In the United States (US), about 90% of annually generated plastic waste is landfilled or incinerated, while less than 9% is recycled. Multilayer plastic films, widely used in food and consumer packaging and representing a substantial and growing fraction of plastic waste, are particularly difficult to mechanically recycle mostly due to their heterogeneous polymer composition and presence of residual organic contamination. Despite their prevalence, limited studies have assessed the end-of-life environmental impacts of these systems, and primary industrial data for large-scale recycling under current technologies remain scarce. This study presents a first-of-its-kind cradle-to-grave/cradle-to-cradle life cycle assessment (LCA) of multilayer plastic bags used in Bag-in-Box (BiB) beverage packaging systems, developed using primary data that reflect realistic industrial production and recycling conditions. Three end-of-life scenarios are evaluated: conventional waste management, open-loop mechanical recycling into stretch-wrap film and closed-loop mechanical recycling back into BiB bags. Across the examined impact categories, i.e., climate change, energy demand, and water use, virgin polymer production contributes more than 50% of total environmental burdens. Both recycling pathways reduced impacts relative to conventional waste management; however, open-loop recycling outperformed closed-loop recycling. This result arises from higher material recovery efficiency in open-loop processing, enabling greater displacement of virgin polymer. The advantage of open-loop recycling persists when scaling results to US-wide production and across sensitivity analyses of transportation, process and end-of-life parameters. These findings challenge the assumption that closed-loop recycling is preferable for complex plastics and highlight the need for rigorous, data-driven LCA to inform end-of-life strategies, policy development, and infrastructure investments.

Taxonomy of innovation terms applied for sustainability, with innovability as a candidate construct for constitutive innovation–sustainability integration
abstract: Eight partially overlapping terms describe the phenomenon of innovating in ways that serve sustainability: eco-innovation, green innovation, sustainability-oriented innovation, sustainability-driven innovation, sustainability-related innovation, innovation for sustainability, innovability, and corporate social responsibility combined with innovation and sustainability strategy. No study has mapped definitional patterns, inter-term relationships, and hierarchical structure across all eight terms simultaneously. This study addresses that gap through a Systematic Literature Review of 381 articles (2009–March 2026) from Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and EBSCOhost, with extraction using a dual-independent large language model (LLM)-agent architecture that achieved near-perfect inter-agent agreement (κ = 0.950). Three findings emerge. First, 82.7% of articles adopt prior definitions without modification, yet reproduce divergent rather than shared formulations. Second, 81.4% define their focal term in contrast to conventional innovation, revealing a predominantly negative collective identity. Third, 46 declarations of synonymy and 49 of non-synonymous relations between eco-innovation and green innovation coexist within the same corpus, journals, and period, leaving the relationship between the two most-cited terms (75.3% of the corpus) structurally unresolved. The study proposes a four-level hierarchical taxonomy ordering the eight terms by scope of sustainability integration, theoretical orientation, and definitional institutionalization, providing a structured decision framework for research and practice. Innovability is advanced as a candidate construct for the constitutive integration of innovation and sustainability at Level 1 — integrating those two domains, not the other terms. Given its small corpus (five articles), this placement is a theoretical proposition to be evaluated, not an established finding.

Decisive, supportive, or irrelevant? The shifting roles of macro-level drivers in the circular economy transition
abstract: Research on the circular economy (CE) transition has identified its macro-level drivers, yet has largely examined them in isolation. This paper addresses another dimension: not whether a factor is a driver, but how and when it is associated with circular performance. It argues that the role of macro-level conditions shifts with the performance dimension and with the accompanying conditions, so that, in a configurational rather than causal sense, the same condition may be decisive (core) in one configuration, merely supportive (peripheral) in another, and configurationally irrelevant (either present or absent) in a third. Applying fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to 26 EU member states, it examines how economic development, market-based and non-market-based environmental governance, income equality and green-transition attitudes combine across resource efficiency, system-level circularity and low material footprint. No condition plays the same role across all dimensions. For resource efficiency, economic development is decisive, while governance modes and green-transition attitudes are supportive. For a low material footprint, green-transition attitudes and, with weaker support, income equality are decisive in distinct configurations. For system-level circularity, market-based governance is decisive in the configurations with the highest coverage, including under policy-stringency measures only, while economic development is supportive. Environmental governance and economic development thus exchange roles between efficiency and circularity. The core patterns are largely robust to alternative measures, calibrations and temporal windows, although less so for circularity. By showing when each condition is decisive, supportive or irrelevant, the analysis suggests differentiating CE policies across performance dimensions and national profiles.

Explanation of the experimental procedure and evaluation methodology for reporting the performance of a standalone solar cooker
abstract: The methodology for reporting the performance of a segment parabolic concentrator solar cooker based on experimental testing data of two identical prototypes is presented. The two prototypes of this novel standalone solar cooker were tested under clear-sky conditions using a pot filled with 2.5 kg of water, shielded by a transparent glass enclosure to minimize heat losses via the greenhouse effect. The water load was successfully heated from a temperature close to the ambient to a final temperature of 95 °C in 45 min. An exponential fit was applied to the measured water temperature, enabling the derivation of performance curves data. A single experiment of testing at the same time the two identical prototypes was used to describe the experimental procedure in some detail. The preliminary results of a single test show that both prototypes produce comparable temporal load temperature evolutions and that the predicted time taken to the load change temperature from 20 °C to 100 °C, at standard conditions, is about 51 min. A set of data of several experimental tests of the two prototypes operated in the same way are also briefly reported. The differences in the predicted performance indicators, such as the standard specific cooking rate, are small when using the average data from all tests compared with the values predicted using data from the reference single experiment.

Impacts of human pressures on freshwater wetland soil microbial community composition and function
abstract: Microbial communities are key to nutrient and carbon cycling in wetlands. Wetlands are impacted by human perturbations including farming and roading infrastructure. Constructed treatment wetlands (CTWs) can be used to mimic the function of natural wetlands. A pilot study investigated the impacts of dairy farming and roading infrastructure on natural and CTWs. The topsoil or sediment (100 mm depth) under intensively grazed pasture (Farm-pasture), road verges (Road-verge), adjacent natural wetlands (Farm-natural; Road-natural) and CTWs (Farm-constructed; Road-constructed) and wetlands more isolated from human perturbations (Near-pristine) were collected. Soil chemistry parameters, microbial community composition using phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) analysis and microbial function using extracellular enzyme activities (EEA) were measured. There was evidence of soil nitrogen enrichment in Farm-natural and Road-natural wetlands. Near-pristine wetlands had greater absolute fungal PLFAs and there was a shift from Gram-negative bacteria prevalence in Near-pristine to Gram-positive bacteria prevalence in Farm and Road-verge treatments. Farm- and Road-natural wetlands exhibited greater ß-glucosaminidase and ß-glucosidase activities compared to Near-pristine inferring accelerated nitrogen and carbon cycling possibly in response to elevated soil nitrogen. Soil zinc and copper concentrations were elevated in Farm- and Road-natural wetlands above the Near-pristine wetlands, but there were no indications of effects of elevated trace elements on microbial community structure or function. Soil carbon and nitrogen were the predominant factors affecting microbial structure and function. There were significant differences between natural and constructed wetlands indicating they were different at the microbial scale.

Comprehensive utilization of dairy sludge: A review of biodiesel and nutrient recovery research
abstract: The properties of dairy sludge vary depending on the waste treatment processes used by each plant. Characterization of dairy sludge reveals that it primarily consists of organic compounds such as lipids, proteins, and lactose, as well as inorganic elements such as P, K, Ca, and Al. Previous studies have proposed various applications for sludge reuse. The most extensively discussed application is its use as a fertilizer, by focusing on the presence of N, K, and P. However, these studies often overlooked the organic compounds in the sludge. The second most explored application involves utilizing the lipids in dairy sludge for biodiesel production. However, these studies frequently ignored the residual sludge left after lipid recovery and the presence of inorganic elements. Another promising approach is sludge pyrolysis, which can produce minimal waste by generating valuable by-products such as biochar, bio-oil, and syngas. This review highlights how existing studies often focus on isolated components of dairy sludge while overlooking the broader implications. Furthermore, it identifies the missed opportunities in sludge reuse strategies. The review suggests that a more composition-aware approach could inform integrated reuse pathways that better align with circular economy principles and sustainable outcomes.

title: Parsimonious theorizing
abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs act on theories of value, and the theory‐based view favors simplicity. Yet a theory can be too thin to guide action or too heavy to carry, and simplicity cannot tell which. We model a theory as bundles linking attempted actions, uncertain implementation states, and external conditions to a focal outcome, and make its structure a choice variable. Parsimony then calls for optimal rather than minimal complexity: structure whose contribution to the value of acting justifies its carrying cost. Under the model's assumptions, optimal complexity rises with value at stake, representational capacity, and domain knowledge, and falls with bundle overlap. Theories also change. The entrepreneur's theory shapes her awareness, so some bundles are worth carrying for what they open, while commitments make revision path dependent. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need to explain a future that does not yet exist: what they will try, what must work, and why customers, partners, or investors should care. We show how to weigh the value of linked actions, their possible results, and outside conditions against the effort of understanding, communicating, and testing them. More detail is worthwhile when the potential payoff is greater, the entrepreneur knows the business better, or the team can handle complexity; overlapping ideas add less. As evidence accumulates, the theory may need to expand, shrink, or be rebuilt. Some ideas are worth keeping because they reveal new possibilities. Earlier investments can make changes costly, so a failed test may call for reshaping the idea rather than abandoning it.

title: How Climate Policy Uncertainty Influences Corporate Environmental Violation: A Moral Disengagement Perspective
abstract: Growing climate risks, resulting from frequent extreme weather disasters, prompt governments to strengthen climate governance. However, the rapid evolution of climate policies has heightened policy uncertainty, posing challenges for firms' environmental compliance. Drawing on moral disengagement theory, we argue that climate policy uncertainty (CPU) creates moral ambiguity and interpretive latitude, thereby fostering corporate moral disengagement and increasing environmental violation (EV). Using data on Chinese listed firms in 2011–2023, we find that CPU is positively associated with EV. Peer firms' EV reinforces focal firms' moral disengagement and amplifies the CPU‐EV relationship, whereas local government environmental attention mitigates the main relationship. Mechanism analysis suggests that moral disengagement is a cognitive channel linking CPU to EV. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the CPU‐EV relationship is more pronounced among state‐owned firms and firms in regions with weaker Confucian culture and lower climate vulnerability. Our study offers novel insights into how CPU shapes firms' environmental misconduct and its underlying cognitive mechanism.

Shifts in Bacteria–DOM Interactions Accompany Changes in Methane Emissions with Weakening Glacial Influence in Proglacial Lakes
abstract: Proglacial lakes formed by glacial retreat are increasing in number and may feed back on climate change if they contribute to aquatic greenhouse gas emissions. However, this potential feedback depends on how microbial processing of dissolved organic matter (DOM) responds to climate change-related processes, such as weakening glacial influence, and on the potential consequences of these responses for methane (CH4) emissions. We investigated nine proglacial lakes on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau to characterize bacterial communities and DOM pools along a gradient of weakening glacial influence, and to assess how shifts in bacteria–DOM interactions are associated with CH4 emissions. We found that bacterial community assembly and DOM assembly were decoupled, with different responses to the same environmental pressures. With weakening glacial influence, the DOM pool in proglacial lakes may increasingly comprise relatively recalcitrant DOM components. Meanwhile, DOM production or transformation may become less dependent on specific bacteria–DOM interactions, while DOM degradation becomes increasingly specialized. Together, these shifts could favor the accumulation of substrates for methanogenesis and were associated with changes in methanogenic community composition and reduced potential resource competition between methanogens and bacteria, which may contribute to higher CH4 emissions from proglacial lakes. These findings reveal associations between weakening glacial influence and shifts in microbial carbon processing, providing new insights into potential climate feedbacks from expanding proglacial lakes.

Modelling integrated rewilding and fire management strategies to enhance long-term carbon dynamics under climate change
abstract: Leveraging vegetation to remove atmospheric CO 2 is key to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Rewilding may enhance carbon (C) stocks through vegetation growth. However, increased vegetation connectivity may boost fire activity and associated emissions, potentially offsetting C gains. We used the landscape dynamics model REMAINS to simulate fire, vegetation, and land-cover dynamics over 40 years (2018-2058) across four 500-km 2 landscapes in the Italian Alps, a region affected by land abandonment and increasing fire hazard. Land cover and vegetation age were mapped using Corine-Land-Cover and historical aerial photographs. Fire behaviour was calibrated using national fire data and FWI projections under RCP4.5. C stocks and fire emissions were estimated from simulation outputs and 161 field plots. We compared Strict Rewilding (SR), prioritizing protected areas without considering fire hazard, with Fire-Smart Rewilding (FSR), targeting low-flammability areas, under alternative fire-management scenarios including suppression, prevention, and Integrated Fire Management. Compared with SR, FSR showed context-dependent effects, being beneficial only in landscapes with high fire activity, where it reduced burned area by up to 30.6% and increased net C change by up to 0.161 tC ha −1 yr −1 (226.9%). When combined with fire-management, FSR benefits extended across additional landscapes and increased further, reducing burned area by up to 47.6% and increasing net C change by up to 0.299 tC ha −1 yr −1 (420.8%) relative to business-as-usual. Prevention-based scenarios performed best, while suppression-only strategies were less effective or counterproductive. Rewilding can enhance long-term C dynamics if spatial allocation accounts for flammability and is integrated with effective fire-management.

From conidial production to soil amendment: Integrated reuse of rice-based substrates from Metarhizium robertsii and Trichoderma asperellum
abstract: Rice is a major solid substrate for fungal biocontrol conidial production, yet the downstream use of the residual matrix remains underexplored. We evaluated an integrated strategy linking successive conidial production cycles by Metarhizium robertsii and Trichoderma asperellum with an agricultural assessment of the final spent fungal substrates (SFS). Conidial yields, time-normalised productivity, colony-forming capacity and direct germination were determined. Maximum conidial yields reached 4.00 × 10 9 and 4.20 × 10 9 conidia per gram of dry substrate (con/gds) for M. robertsii and T. asperellum , respectively; direct germination remained above 92% across cycles. Across successive reuse cycles, cumulative conidial yields reached 6.98 × 10 9 and 6.25 × 10 9 con/gds for M. robertsii and T. asperellum , respectively, corresponding to 2.97 and 1.49 times their respective first-cycle yields. These results demonstrate the additional productive potential of the original rice matrix even before subsequent evaluation as a soil amendment. SFS from each fungus was incorporated into soil at different doses in a 60-day greenhouse pot experiment using tomato plants; 1% SFS from M. robertsii cycles (M1%) significantly increased tomato stem diameter relative to unamended soil, whereas SFS from T. asperellum at 0.1% (T0.1%) increased stem length and leaf number. In the preliminary assessment, T. asperellum -derived SFS at 10% (w/w) arrested tomato seedling growth and was accompanied by extensive fungal overgrowth. This integrated strategy extends productive rice recycling to the assessment of the final residual fraction as a soil amendment. The findings guide future mechanistic and application studies.

AI innovation spillovers of focal firms and the construction of sustainable supply chains: Evidence from suppliers’ ESG performance
abstract: In the context of increasingly extended ESG governance responsibilities across global supply chains, it is essential to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to inter-organizational environmental governance. Using data from Chinese A-share listed firms spanning 2009 to 2022, this study considers these listed companies as focal firms within supply chain networks and examines the relationship between the AI innovation of focal firms and the ESG performance of their supplier firms. Focal firms' AI innovation is positively associated with suppliers' ESG performance, although the preferred baseline estimate is imprecise. Moderation analysis reveals that green innovation linkages, advance payment arrangements, and strategic coordination notably strengthen this positive relationship. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the spillover effect is more pronounced when focal firms and suppliers are located in the same province, engage in higher-level data asset sharing, and when suppliers have stronger capabilities in environmental information disclosure. A direct comparison does not establish a statistically significant difference between the upstream and downstream AI-ESG associations, with the transmission effect moderated by the supply chain structure and inter-firm differences in ESG capability endowments. This paper offers practical implications for focal firms to effectively exercise leadership roles and facilitate the construction of sustainable supply chains.

An engineered cohesion system reduces errors in aged mammalian eggs
abstract: In humans, female fertility declines rapidly from approximately 35 years onward owing to a steep increase in eggs in which chromosomes have split prematurely or that harbor an incorrect number of chromosomes (aneuploid eggs). A leading cause of age-related aneuploidy in eggs is the premature separation of sister chromatids (PSSC), which is caused by a loss of cohesin from chromosomes. In this study, we created an artificial cohesion system that reduces PSSC in aged mouse eggs. We further engineered a separase-cleavable sequence into the system, allowing for its scheduled deactivation during anaphase. We demonstrated that the artificial cohesion system could be adapted to tether human chromosomes, providing a proof of principle for the future development of approaches to reduce PSSC in eggs from women of advanced reproductive age.

Millisecond-scale imaging of fragmented earthquake rupture by near-source fiber-optic sensing
abstract: Small earthquakes [i.e., those of magnitude (M) <3] are commonly modeled as simple circular ruptures, leaving the fine-scale spatial attributes of rupture dynamics unresolved. We used near-source distributed acoustic sensing to image the millisecond-scale rupture of an M 2 earthquake within a swarm sequence in California’s Brawley Seismic Zone. Inverting fiber-derived apparent source time functions revealed two distinct rupture episodes separated by 42 milliseconds, reflecting rupture arrest followed by dynamic renucleation. Analysis of a 3-hour sequence showed adjacent, largely nonoverlapping fault patches activated in succession, forming complementary slip partitioning. These fragmented failure patterns within the M 2 rupture and its sequence limited rupture growth, consistent with the absence of a dominant mainshock. Microearthquakes, which are now accessible by fiber-optic sensing, provide direct constraints on fault mechanics across scales bridging laboratory experiments and large earthquakes.

title: Rough fracture zone as a gateway to the 2025 M w 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake
abstract: Rough fault segments typically terminate giant earthquakes but are rarely reported to foster them. However, rupture characteristics of the 2025 moment magnitude (M w) 8.8 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake are consistent with initiation in a rough zone. Its early rupture was sluggish, lasting ~50 seconds with limited slip but strong, scattered high-frequency radiation. Rupture then propagated southward into a smoother segment, producing >20 meters slip with less intense high-frequency radiation. Using also the rupture characteristics of four M w 7+ foreshocks and aftershocks, we reveal variably sized seismic patches within the rough zone. We interpret these behaviors as manifestations of stress or frictional heterogeneities on the rough segment that favor localized failures yet can foster a giant rupture when spatially connected to a smooth, locked neighboring segment, a scenario previously underrecognized and meriting consideration in seismic hazard assessments.

title: Abrupt surface water decline during 2023–2024 record warming
abstract: Global warming is expected to accelerate the hydrological cycle, yet its impact on terrestrial water availability is uncertain. Using assimilated streamflow observations from 150 major basins and satellite data for over 1.2 million water bodies, we show a global-scale synchronized decline of streamflow and surface water storage during the 2023–2024 record-warm period, the largest reduction since 1991. South America accounted for 70.4 ± 4.2% of the global streamflow decline. This abrupt depletion was driven by compound ocean–atmosphere forcing, in which concurrent El Niño and tropical North Atlantic warming triggered large-scale atmospheric subsidence, moisture divergence, and amplified drought. These findings reveal that extreme warming can induce abrupt water losses even in humid regions, underscoring a critical vulnerability of global hydrology and water security.

title: Rebuilding science’s social contract with the public
abstract: Much has been written about how the social contract between science and society in the United States is in crisis. According to its terms, research will yield broad economic, health, and security benefits to the very public that funds it. But this relationship depends on public trust in science, its systems, and the scientists themselves, and therein lies the problem. Beyond making discoveries and publishing results, scientists shape their own culture, and that is where some changes may be the key to rebuilding public trust.

title: A tryptophan cation radical determines radical transfer kinetics and catalytic rate in a ribonucleotide reductase
abstract: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) is the sole enzyme responsible for de novo deoxynucleotide synthesis for DNA replication and repair. In the Escherichia coli class Ia RNR, a radical must traverse 32 angstroms along a pathway composed of amino acids spanning β and α subunits to complete each turnover. By incorporating unnatural amino acids to alter reduction potentials of pathway tyrosine residues, we (i) perturb the rates of radical transfer and show that they match the rates of deoxynucleotide production and (ii) directly observe a tryptophan cation radical (W 48 + •) as a kinetically competent pathway intermediate. Together, these results establish that radical transfer through W 48 in α 2 β 2 is the rate-limiting process, which controls the enzymatic activity of E. coli RNR.

title: Integrating established and emerging tools to assess wildlife condition from the ground, up
abstract: Metabolic energy links individual physiology to population-level dynamics, making wildlife body condition a cornerstone of conservation science. Emerging technologies, including unoccupied aircraft systems, make remote assessment of animal condition possible at unprecedented scales, and physiologically grounded validation is essential for strong inference. Here we examine the strengths and challenges of traditional and remote methods, using a comparative perspective that emphasizes both lipid and lean mass dynamics in evaluating wildlife health. We provide a framework that integrates complementary approaches to assess wildlife condition across diverse systems, matching emerging methods with the required physiological resolution, species characteristics, and temporal and spatial scales, while enhancing research ethics. Expanding capacity to track wildlife energetics from individuals to populations requires novel approaches and is vital for conservation in a changing world.

title: Priming of AGO2 by type I interferons balances inflammation and antiviral immunity
abstract: Argonaute-2 (AGO2)–mediated RNA silencing contributes to antiviral defenses in plants and insects and may contribute to mammalian immunity, too. However, it is unknown whether AGO2 is modified upon infection or inflammation in mammals. We identified that the ubiquitin ligase RING-finger protein 126 (RNF126) interacts with and ubiquitinates AGO2 to enhance its small interfering RNA or microRNA loading. Using data from cells in vitro and mouse tissues, we propose that RNF126 is induced by type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling and promotes the ability of AGO2 to silence proinflammatory genes and inhibit viral replication. Lipid nanoparticle delivery of RNF126 mRNA to mice inhibited inflammation and viral replication. These findings identify cross-talk of IFN-based immune signaling and AGO2-mediated RNA silencing and suggest that the RNF126-AGO2 axis helps to balance inflammatory and antiviral immune protection.

title: Counter-ion confinement reverses ion selectivity in subnanometer channels
abstract: Ion transport in nano- and subnanometer channels is central to processes such as ion separation, energy conversion and storage, and nanofluidics. Conventionally, positively charged nanochannels favor anion transport and vice versa. We report that cationic covalent organic framework membranes with sub–one-nanometer channels exhibit selective cation transport. This reversal in selectivity arises from a counter-ion confinement effect, which inverts the electrostatic environment inside the channel wall and creates a secondary confinement region. The counter-ion confinement mechanism concomitantly suppresses coexisting ion competition in mixed-salt systems, enabling membranes to retain high selectivity under practical separation conditions. Our findings provide a design strategy for creating adaptive and highly selective membranes for precise ion transport and separation.

title: Binding kinetics enable tumor-selective MAPK and growth suppression by a Type 1 RAF inhibitor
abstract: Targeting the RAS/MAPK pathway has long been constrained by dose-limiting toxicity in normal tissues at doses required for durable tumor control. Although Type 1.5 RAF inhibitors improved selectivity in BRAF(V600X)-monomer tumors, a comparable strategy for RAF dimer-driven cancers, including those with RAS mutations, has been lacking. We describe ELV-3111, a potent Type 1 RAF inhibitor that inhibits RAF dimers and exploits binding kinetics for tumor selectivity. ELV-3111 primes RAF in normal tissues, and its rapid dissociation during drug clearance generates drug-free RAF dimers that paradoxically activate MAPK signaling. RAS-mutant tumors are spared, where RAF is already primed. Combined with a MEK inhibitor, ELV-3111 restored normal tissue signaling while deepening tumor pathway inhibition, producing regressions across RAS- and BRAF-mutant experimental models. Thus, inhibitor dissociation kinetics provide a generalizable source of therapeutic index.

title: AI-based digital pathology defines spatial border ecosystems in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: The invasive tumor border in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is currently poorly understood. We integrated digital pathology and spatial multi-omics to define border ecosystems in TNBC. AI-based digital pathology identified five border ecosystems, three associated with prognosis. Spatial multi-omics analyses further resolved the spatial niche, molecular mechanisms and clinical relevance of these ecosystems. Immune-infiltrated borders contain a triadic immune niche associated with favorable prognosis and immunotherapy sensitivity. Tumor–stroma borders harbor a MIF + fibroblast exclusion niche that blocks immune infiltration and suppresses T cells function, predicting poor prognosis. Tumor–adipose borders, featured an FLT1 + endothelial niche, promote hypoxia, vascular leakage, and tumor dissemination. Targeting this niche inhibits tumor progression. Collectively, these findings establish a spatial resource that might enable border-directed therapeutic strategies in TNBC.

title: Mechanisms of nucleosome disruption shape epigenetic inheritance pathway choice
abstract: Maintaining cell identity requires duplicating the genome and epigenome during S phase. As DNA is copied, histones extracted from parental nucleosomes are transferred to nascent strands, which preserves the position of epigenetic marks. How the replisome coordinates these processes is unclear. Using reconstitution with purified yeast proteins, kinetic measurements, structural biology, mass spectrometry and genomics, we examined nucleosome-replisome encounter and histone transfer. Parental nucleosomes can be unwrapped ahead of the fork by the MCM helicase, aided by FACT and Ctf4, or by Tof1. Nucleosomal DNA unwrapping by MCM creates a FACT binding site, helping strip histones off DNA. Ctf4 enhances FACT-stimulated histone extraction, retains parental histones and hands them to Tof1, en route to lagging-strand redeposition. Thus, extraction via Ctf4 commits histones to lagging-strand transfer.

Juking the Stats: Policing, Misreporting, and Policy Evaluation
abstract: We analyze a game-theoretic model of crime and crime reporting to study the quality of crime statistics. An offender potentially engages in illicit behavior; an enforcer chooses effort and how to report outcomes. Because of signaling concerns, the enforcer may misreport. We show that multiple equilibria can exist and characterize when crime is under- or overreported. Increasing the enforcer’s costs of data manipulation can backfire, increasing misreporting in crime statistics. When calculating treatment effects of parameter changes, the effect on reported statistics will not equal the effect on true statistics, and the true effect can be under- or overestimated.

title: Firms’ Perceived Cost of Capital
abstract: We analyze firms’ perceptions of their cost of capital using hand-collected data. The perceived cost of capital is associated with the allocation of capital across firms. In a model with inefficient financial markets, firms can maximize their current market value by setting their perceived cost of capital equal to the expected returns on their debt and equity. In the data, little variation in firms’ perceived cost of capital can be justified by variation in expected returns, suggesting that firms do not follow this market-value maximization benchmark. Alternatively, firms may aim to maximize their “fair value” corrected for financial market inefficiencies. In the data, a fair-value benchmark (based on the CAPM) can justify half the variation in the perceived cost of capital. However, most of the variation can be justified by the beliefs of financial analysts about expected returns. Using a quantitative model, we find that the observed distortions in the perceived cost of capital can substantially impact capital allocation and thereby reduce aggregate productivity.

title: Improving VAT compliance by switching who remits the tax: Evidence from construction firms
abstract: Many countries use a reverse charge mechanism (RC) in the value added tax (VAT) system to combat tax evasion in specific high-risk sectors. The RC shifts the liability to remit VAT from the seller to the buyer. We study the adoption of RC in the construction sector in Finland in 2011 using tax return data on the universe of Finnish firms. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that reported net VAT liabilities in the construction sector increased by 5%. Furthermore, we find that the adoption of RC increases reported payroll taxes and income tax withholding, suggesting spillovers from VAT enforcement to other tax bases. Changing the remittance policy decreased VAT evasion among small subcontractors that provide services for large firms. Taken together, our results and conceptual framework show that shifting remittance liability can reduce tax evasion even in a VAT system in which the paper trail mechanism already deters it, provided that downstream firms are relatively compliant.

title: Predicting the effects of a large-scale cash transfer: Financial frictions, occupational choice, and local labor markets
Comment on “Scaling up agricultural insurance” by Jeremy Majerovitz and Heitor S. Pellegrina
A Signal-Extraction Theory of Inflation Pass-Through
abstract: I develop a theory of state-dependent signal extraction in price setting. Firms infer how much sectoral price movements reflect persistent aggregate or transitory sector-specific disturbances. When inflation is low relative to sectoral variation, sticky-price firms discount competitor movements because following transitory movements risks leaving them mispriced. As inflation rises relative to sectoral noise, firms increasingly attribute these movements to aggregate shocks and sticky firms respond more strongly. UK micro-price data support these predictions: below approximately 1.9% sectoral inflation, sticky firms respond less to competitors than flexible firms; above it, the gap closes. This convergence generates state-dependent aggregate inflation dynamics.

title: Offsets from the periphery: World-system position and voluntary carbon credit issuance
abstract: This paper examines whether voluntary carbon offsets reproduce patterns of Ecologically Unequal Exchange. Moving beyond a simplistic Global North–South dichotomy, I analyze whether the intensity of offset generation is systematically associated with a country’s structural position in the world-system, independent of its regional geography. Using a cross-sectional dataset of 100 nations, I regress carbon credit intensity (credits per GDP) on a novel continuous World-Systems Index. Crucially, ordinary least squares models with continent fixed effects are employed to distinguish structural variation from broad regional heterogeneity. The results reveal a robust and significant negative gradient ( p < 0.001 ): Peripheral states exhibit disproportionately higher issuance intensity than core states. This pattern holds within continental regions, indicating that the pattern is not solely attributable to continental location. These findings suggest that voluntary carbon offsets may reproduce existing global environmental inequalities by appropriating the sink capacity of peripheral regions.

When Algorithms Meet Shariah: Mapping the Knowledge Landscape of Artificial Intelligence in Islamic Finance
abstract: The research aims to consolidate and synthesize the fragmented literature concerning artificial intelligence (AI) in Islamic finance. In addition, the paper lays out a roadmap for future studies by identifying key antecedents, decisions, and outcomes associated with the adoption of AI in Islamic finance. The study used bibliometric analysis and a systematic literature review from 64 research studies related to the application of AI in Islamic finance. The review followed the PRISMA protocol to identify and screen articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The selected studies were analyzed according to the theory‐context‐method (TCM) and antecedent‐decision‐outcome (ADO) framework, further exploring the integrated framework for future research. The review identifies a fragmented but rapidly evolving knowledge base dominated by Islamic banking, governance, and AI‐enabled financial services. By integrating the TCM and ADO frameworks, the study develops a holistic AI adoption ecosystem and four stakeholder‐centric (i.e., financial institutions, Regulatory authorities, customers, and Society) research frameworks that explain how strategic drivers, governance capabilities, customer experiences, and social innovations collectively shape responsible AI adoption and value creation in Islamic finance. The proposed frameworks support financial institutions, regulators, and technology providers in designing responsible AI strategies.

title: Mapping the Research Landscape of Energy Poverty and Transport Poverty: A Bibliometric Analysis and Critical Synthesis
abstract: Energy poverty and transport poverty are recognized as interconnected forms of socioeconomic disadvantage. However, they have largely evolved as distinct research fields and remain only partially integrated at the theoretical, measurement, and policy levels. This study maps and critically synthesizes the development of these two bodies of literature and their emerging intersection, with particular attention to the mechanisms underlying dual energy–mobility vulnerability. Using data from the Web of Science, we develop three bibliometric corpora comprising 856 studies on energy poverty, 653 studies on transport poverty, and 35 publications explicitly examining their intersection. We combine performance analysis, journal and author co‐citation networks, keyword co‐occurrence analysis, thematic evolution, and a critical assessment of measurement approaches to examine the development of these fields, identify areas of convergence, and highlight persistent conceptual and methodological gaps. The results indicate that the two fields have followed distinct intellectual trajectories, while becoming increasingly interconnected. Energy poverty research is structured around affordability, vulnerability, housing energy efficiency, health, and energy justice. Transport poverty research is organized around accessibility, mobility disadvantage, spatial inequality, and social exclusion. Although the cross‐domain literature remains limited and relatively recent, it increasingly focuses on shared mechanisms, including household budget constraints, affordability, accessibility, spatial vulnerability, infrastructure provision, and concerns related to just transitions. Measurement represents a key area of divergence between the two fields. Energy poverty research has benefited from more established expenditure‐based, consensual, and multidimensional indicators, whereas transport poverty continues to face challenges in defining normative thresholds for necessary mobility and travel. The evidence points to the need to move beyond treating energy and transport deprivation as separate sectoral challenges and toward an integrated framework of dual energy–mobility vulnerability. This perspective can provide a comprehensive understanding of how overlapping forms of deprivation are produced and distributed across households and places. It is particularly relevant for assessing the distributional implications of decarbonization, transport electrification, and broader low‐carbon transitions, where interventions in one domain may either reinforce or reduce vulnerabilities in the other.

title: Antitrust Law and Market Power in the Digital Economy: A Survey of Theory, Evidence, and Policy Design
abstract: Digital platforms generate substantial gains from matching, scale, and innovation, yet may sustain market power through mechanisms overlooked by conventional price analysis. This survey links each mechanism to observable implications, claim‐specific evidence, and remedy design. It covers multisided pricing, network effects, defaults and switching costs, data‐enabled learning, attention allocation, ecosystem leverage, acquisitions, and algorithmic pricing. A dated structured narrative protocol yields 100 traceable records and a 22‐study core empirical subset. Evidence is strongest for discrete policy or product changes. It is weaker when a theory of harm relies on an unobserved innovation counterfactual or an asserted data advantage. Policy should therefore match the intervention to the demonstrated mechanism. Effective design requires a defined target, measurable compliance, privacy and security safeguards, and revision rules. The proposed framework evaluates targetability, monitorability, reversibility, and error costs. It also identifies designs that can convert regulatory implementation into credible evidence on contestability, quality, innovation, and distribution.

title: Green Shipping and the Economic Incidence of Maritime Carbon Pricing
abstract: Maritime carbon pricing assigns compliance obligations to shipping companies, but its economic burden extends through freight markets, traded goods, and public budgets. This structured literature survey brings together 90 sources. It distinguishes direct maritime studies from adjacent transport research, general incidence analysis, and contextual evidence. The synthesis links compliance costs, freight prices, delivered prices, trade adjustment, and net welfare. Freight pass‐through varies with capacity, competition, bargaining power, contracts, and the adjustment horizon. Downstream effects depend on freight shares, inventories, sourcing alternatives and firms' capacity to absorb costs. Remote and trade‐dependent economies face greater exposure when substitution and finance are limited. Revenue recycling changes net burdens through transfers, while technology support also changes earlier compliance costs. Study comparisons identify differences in policy coverage, price definitions, shipping segments, and model assumptions. They do not establish a common maritime pass‐through coefficient. The literature provides a conditional account of burden shifting and explains why legal payments, gross economic costs, and welfare after revenue use must be evaluated separately.

title: From Maritime Vocational Education to Seafaring Careers Through Human Capital Formation and Labor Market Adjustment in Shipping's Green Transition
abstract: Shipping decarbonization changes the tasks, hazards, and career returns associated with seagoing work. This survey integrates maritime education and employment research with economics on vocational education, firm training, occupational licensing, and job matching. The Green Seafaring Human‐Capital Pipeline connects enrollment and school formation with qualifying sea service, certification, vessel assignment, promotion, retention, and shore transitions. It distinguishes certificates from usable labor supply and statutory sea time from experience with a particular fuel or system. The reviewed studies document assessment problems, restricted access to sea service, organizational barriers to energy efficiency, and several influences on retention. Their designs range from institutional analysis and qualitative cases to cross‐sectional surveys. Causal evidence on maritime training returns remains limited. A study‐level comparison and a matrix of apparently conflicting findings show how results depend on outcomes, institutions, and observation periods. The analytical framework specifies waiting, competing exits, and the conditions under which a later capacity constraint limits an upstream expansion. It yields three testable propositions about capacity, credential use, and certification delay. The policy synthesis separates existing legal obligations from transferable economic mechanisms and instruments that require evaluation.

title: A quantile count regression analysis of precision agriculture technology adoption intensity
abstract: Understanding technology adoption processes is crucial for agricultural policy and research, yet most studies rely on mean-based models that may obscure distributional differences. This study investigates precision agriculture technology adoption intensity using survey data collected between December 2024 and January 2025 from 342 German farmers. Adoption intensity is measured as the number of technologies used from a portfolio of 32 technologies and analysed by quantile count regression alongside negative binomial regression. Results reveal that risk attitude shows stable associations with across all quantiles, while farm succession exhibits increasing associations. Results demonstrate limitations of mean-based approaches and provide insights for stakeholders.

title: Old habits die hard: chairmen’s collectivist cultural orientation and firm innovation in China
abstract: Historical rice farming has shaped enduring collectivist cultures and contemporary behavioural norms. Using a sample of Chinese listed firms that disclose their chairmen’s birthplace during 2009–2019, we find that firms led by chairmen from regions with stronger collectivist cultures exhibit significantly lower innovation performance. This negative association remains robust to a battery of diagnostic tests addressing potential institutional confounders. Mechanism analyses suggest that collectivist chairmen suppress innovation by limiting the use of decentralised knowledge, reducing tolerance for risk and innovation failure, and fostering free-rider behaviour among employees. Moreover, the adverse effect of chairman collectivism is more pronounced among private firms, family-owned businesses, and companies whose chairmen experienced secondary collectivist socialisation. This cultural effect is stronger for exploratory than exploitative innovation. Overall, our findings underscore the long shadow of agricultural legacies in shaping corporate innovation through deep-rooted cultural values, highlighting the broader influence of informal institutions on managerial strategies.

title: Site Aggregation in Recreational Demand Modeling with an Application to the Impact of Sediments Runoffs in Coastal Waters
Age at Migration and Health Shock Resilience
abstract: Using comprehensive data on the Swedish population, we document that massive age-specific immigrant-native hospitalization gaps during the COVID-19 pandemic were strongly related to host-country exposure during childhood. Exploiting variation between siblings, we test and systematically rule out several potential explanations for the role of host-country exposure: it is not attributable to (i) shared family characteristics (e.g., genetics), (ii) birthplace-specific factors, (iii) known pre-existing medical risk factors, (iv) social or economic segregation, or (v) differences in vaccination behavior.

title: The WIC Cliff: Parental Mental Health Impacts From Benefit Transitions
abstract: This study examines whether the abrupt withdrawal of benefits from the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) affects caregivers' psychological well-being. Using nationally representative data from the National Health Interview Survey (2005-2014) and WIC's strict age-based eligibility cutoffs, we implement sharp and fuzzy regression discontinuity designs at 12 and 60 months of child age. We find that caregivers experience significant increases in depressive symptoms, anxiety, and psychological distress when their child turns one and formula support ends. At age five, when all WIC benefits cease, average effects are smaller and concentrated in anxiety. For families lacking access to Head Start, distress levels increase significantly, whereas those participating in Head Start exhibit reduced reactions. The findings emphasize that sudden cutbacks in safety-net programs can lead to significant psychological burdens on low-income caregivers, highlighting the importance of gradual benefit reductions and program alignment to safeguard family welfare.

title: Macroscopic market making
abstract: We propose a macroscopic market making model à la Avellaneda–Stoikov, using continuous processes for orders instead of discrete point processes. The model intends to bridge the gap between market making and optimal execution problems, while shedding light on the influence of order flows on the optimal strategies. We illustrate our model through three problems. The study provides a comprehensive analysis from Markovian to non-Markovian noises and from affine to nonlinear intensity functions, encompassing both bounded and unbounded coefficients. Mathematically, the contribution lies in the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control, guaranteed by the well-posedness of the classical solution to the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and the (non-)Lipschitz forward-backward stochastic differential equation. Finally, the model’s applications to price impact and optimal execution are discussed.

title: Optimal consumption and investment under relative performance criteria with Epstein–Zin utility
Optimal consumption and portfolio rules with dynamic adjustment of consumption bounds
abstract: We develop a comprehensive model of optimal consumption and investment choice over an infinite horizon. The framework incorporates costly adjustable spending bounds, with utility depending on actual consumption as well as current and future minimum allowable consumption levels. Higher minimum levels provide security but entail adjustment costs, leading to a non-trivial trade-off. The problem is transformed into an optimal switching problem through its conversion to a dual problem. The optimal switching problem is analytically characterised as a two-dimensional double obstacle problem. Our explicit solutions yield empirically consistent consumption patterns and U-shaped portfolio choices, indicating investors’ loss aversion to changes in consumption.

title: The economics of working environments: evidence from linked survey and register data
abstract: We use a large-scale survey from Denmark to construct firm-level measures of the working environment that capture its physical, psychological, and social dimensions. First, to validate these measures, we show that firms with better working environments perform better in unannounced workplace inspections conducted by a government agency. Second, using register data, we show that firms with better working environments have longer employee tenure, and that their employees are less likely to be hospitalized or experience work-related accidents. Finally, firms with better working environments have higher labor productivity and, ultimately, greater profitability. Collectively, our findings suggest that improving firms’ working environments can benefit both employees and shareholders.

Programmable Repayment: Risk-Sharing and Enforcement Through the Payment Platform
abstract: Payment platforms increasingly offer merchants loans with programmable repayment, deducting a share of merchants’ platform sales toward repayment. The contract transfers part of merchants’ cash-flow risk to the lender and automates collection, but merchants partly control which sales the platform processes. This puts risk-sharing in tension with enforcement. At a major Indian payment platform, merchants accept offers more often when sales are volatile or outside debts are overdue. After disbursal, borrowers’ platform sales fall 12 percent relative to matched controls. Declines are larger among high-volatility merchants and on second loans, so the deduction base shrinks with borrower risk and experience. These larger declines come without detectably greater outside arrears. Declines are smaller where cash is scarce, consistent with diversion. The lender nevertheless earns 9.6 percent annually before costs, above the 6.5 percent Treasury-bill yield. High-volatility merchants generate comparable loan returns, stay longer on the platform, and contribute more rental revenue.
