title: External Enablement Across Types of Environmental Change: Experimental Evidence on Onset Variance Effects
abstract: A growing research stream applies the external enablement framework (EEF) to capture how macroenvironmental changes benefit entrepreneurial pursuits. To refine and nuance the EEF’s guidance of future research in this domain, we examine the provisionally suggested structural relationships among its constructs. Combining between-subjects experiments and think-aloud protocols, we show that variance in the characteristics of macroenvironmental changes—specifically, their gradual versus radical onset—influences expectations of enablement and does so similarly across types of change. Our results also uncover relationships between macroenvironmental changes and agents beyond what the EEF explicates. We discuss implications for future research on macroenvironmental impact on business.

title: Echoes of Discord: The Effects of Global Conflicts and Disputes on Entrepreneurship
abstract: Mixed-nationality founding teams bring together heterogeneous, hard-to-replicate bundles of human capital and country-specific ties through their cross-national networks, providing a distinctive foundation for building successful ventures. Yet these connections may be vulnerable to nonmarket shocks. This study examines whether geopolitical conflicts and disputes between the countries of origin of immigrant founders affect the formation of new ventures. Leveraging data on the founders of start-ups established in Great Britain and global information on conflicts and disputes, I find that such tensions reduce the likelihood that nationals of hostile countries cofound firms together. The evidence is more consistent with social mechanisms and, particularly, the erosion of interpersonal relationships than with diminished access to cross-country resources or the loss of entrepreneurial opportunities. Start-ups of both low and high quality are affected, including in sectors that depend heavily on skilled human capital, such as high-tech and business services. The negative effect is substantially attenuated for nationality pairs that are heavily colocated across local areas and for founders with prior social exposure to individuals from the opposing nationality, indicating that interpersonal ties can buffer against geopolitical shocks. Conflicts do not affect the exit of existing firms, and the decline in mixed-nationality entrepreneurship is not offset by alternative team configurations such as solo ventures or those formed with conationals, natives, or individuals from third-party countries. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Funding: I gratefully acknowledge funding from the Institute for Leadership and Social Impact at Georgia Institute of Technology. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04559 .

title: Inferential Theory for Pricing Errors with Latent Factors and Firm Characteristics
abstract: We study factor models that combine latent factors with firm characteristics and propose a new framework for modeling, estimating, and inferring pricing errors. Following Zhang (2024), our approach decomposes mispricing into two distinct components: inside alpha, explained by firm characteristics but orthogonal to factor exposures, and outside alpha, orthogonal to both factors and characteristics. Our model generalizes those developed recently such as Kelly et al. (2019) and Zhang (2024), resolving issues of orthogonality, basis dependence, and unit sensitivity. Methodologically, we develop estimators grounded in low-rank methods with explicit debiasing, providing closed-form solutions and a rigorous inferential theory that accommodates a growing number of characteristics and relaxes standard assumptions on sample dimensions. Empirically, using U.S. stock returns from 2000 to 2019, we document strong evidence of both inside and outside alphas, with the former showing industry-level comovements and the latter reflecting idiosyncratic shocks beyond firm fundamentals. Our framework thus unifies statistical and characteristic-based approaches to factor modeling, offering both theoretical advances and new insights into the structure of pricing errors. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant DMS-2052955]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04971 .

title: Correcting the Unobserved Textual Confounding Factors in Regression by BERT and Partially Linear Regression
abstract: In the last decade, there has been a surge of text-mining applications in the information systems literature. In these applications, researchers typically construct independent variables from documents by various text-mining techniques. The most prominent example could be using online review sentiments to investigate online word-of-mouth issues. Typically, most documents contain information richer than the independent variable, and researchers may construct control variables from the same documents to alleviate endogeneity issues. However, researchers need to manually craft these variables, and this process may not guarantee that all the important confounding factors are extracted and included in the regression model with a correct functional form. If useful textual information is overlooked and a valid identification strategy is not available, the omitted variable bias may occur. To solve this challenge, we propose a novel model that utilizes text embedding based on the state-of-the-art neural network language model (i.e., bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)) to automatically create a new control variable vector for controlling latent confounding factors in the absence of a valid identification strategy. Moreover, our approach can be considered a semiparametric approach in that our model contains a linear term of the key independent variable and an unknown functional term of the textual control variables. Our approach extends the semiparametric framework, double machine learning, by introducing a novel Neyman-orthogonal loss function in an integrated deep neural network to minimize the estimation bias. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of controlling textual control variables by text embedding and improving the estimation performance by the novel loss function. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04758 .

title: Reducing Risk Through Trade Credit: Theory and Evidence from Dual-Channel Suppliers
abstract: Trade credit is traditionally viewed as increasing supplier risk, because delayed payments expose suppliers to buyer uncertainties. Using a stylized game-theoretic model, we show that this conventional wisdom can be overturned when a supplier is dual channel: operating a direct channel that sells to end customers in addition to an indirect channel that sells to an industry peer who serves the same market. Compared with zero trade credit provision where the supplier requires cash on delivery (COD), we observe empirically that high trade credit provision can lead to lower risk for the dual-channel supplier. We propose a possible mechanism for this risk mitigation effect—pooling: When the market overlap between the supplier and its peer buyer is sufficiently high, the random split of the overlapping market creates negative association between the supplier’s direct channel sales and the buyer’s trade credit payment. Trade credit does not always mitigate risk for dual-channel suppliers. If the supplier’s debt level is high, our theory predicts that trade credit exacerbates risk. We find empirical evidence consistent with our theoretical predictions using data on U.S. manufacturing firms that sell to their industry peers. The positive association between trade credit provision and bankruptcy risk is dampened or even reversed once a supplier begins selling to peer firms. This risk mitigation effect is stronger among suppliers with lower leverage and greater market overlap with their buyers. For highly financially constrained suppliers, trade credit provision is associated with an increase in bankruptcy risk after the supplier becomes dual channel. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03142 .

title: Embedded in Two Worlds: How Incumbents’ Brokerage Affects Adaptation When Old and New Supply Networks Coexist
abstract: The development of new technology architectures often opens up new markets within an existing industry. Incumbents face the decision of whether to enter the new technology market and how to do so. As incumbents attempt to enter the new market, they can become embedded in two buyer-supplier networks, one for the old and the other for new technologies. We argue that brokers have an advantage in this process because they have developed capabilities to integrate suppliers of new technology components or develop unique component combinations for the new technology products. In a study of the U.S. automotive industry between 2012 and 2022, we find that brokerage in the old technology network is positively associated with successful entry into the new technology (i.e., number and performance of new technology models). Surprisingly, brokerage in the old technology network had a stronger positive impact than brokerage in the new technology network on incumbents’ entry into the new technology market for electric vehicles.

title: Democratic Organizing and Contemporary Managerial Talent Markets: Internal Promotion or External Hiring?
abstract: We develop and empirically examine a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between democratic organizing and firms’ propensity to staff management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. Conventionally, the advantages of promoting through internal labor markets (ILM) have rested on the assumption that workers value intra-firm careers and anticipate remaining with the same employer for a longer term. These advantages may prove harder to attain in contemporary labor markets, given that declining tenure and workers’ growing preference for inter-firm careers possibly reduce the information advantage of ILM and undermine internal candidate retention. We propose that firms with more democratic organizing are less susceptible to these ILM challenges, enjoy higher benefits from recruiting internally and are thus more likely to fill management positions through internal promotion. Using longitudinal employer-employee linked data for Danish firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that firms with worker board representation (WBR), one form of more democratic organizing, are more likely than firms without WBR to fill management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. This association is stronger where (i) worker representatives have broader intra-firm experience and are more likely to possess promotion-relevant information; (ii) more managers and professionals have peers serving as worker representatives on the board. These results are consistent with a higher economic viability of internal promotion in firms with more democratic organizing, and largely inconsistent with the conventional account of powerful workers distorting firms’ hiring choices. Interviews with worker directors and human resource professionals illustrate the proposed mechanisms.

title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring
abstract: We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.

title: Editorial data
Public Sentiment and Share Repurchases
Territory‐as‐pedagogy: Learning with the Territorial Imaginaries of Rural and Indigenous Students in Management Education
abstract: Business schools are being asked to prepare managers for a climate‐altered world, and that debate has centered largely on what curricula contain, paying less attention to territory as an epistemic and pedagogical category, or to the students whose territorial knowledge sits outside dominant models. Drawing on an interpretive study with rural and Indigenous scholarship students at a private Mexican university, in which participant‐produced drawings were read alongside interviews and social‐cartography workshops, we ask how the territorial imaginaries of students from rural and Indigenous communities might inform more epistemically just curricula in business schools. We read the drawings as expressing five recurring territorial imaginaries that cohere into four themes and compose a relational territorial imaginary. Consequently, we advance the concept of territory‐as‐pedagogy, an account of territory as a co‐teacher that supplies the terms of economic and ethical reasoning rather than serving as a backdrop. We contend that territory‐as‐pedagogy makes ecological limits and obligation visible because students reason from relations and ties they hold to land, water, crops and kin, which a module added to a curriculum would struggle to reproduce. We propose it as a context‐specific resource for educators, stating a limit of place‐based pedagogy and contributing to decolonial and Indigenous management scholarship.

title: Moral Licensing Revisited: CSR and Cybersecurity‐related Disclosure After COP21
abstract: Using a sample of U.S. S&P 100 firms, we examine the relationship between firms’ CSR and cybersecurity‐related disclosure, exploiting the 2015 Paris Climate Conference (COP21) as an institutional shock in a difference‐in‐differences design. We find that, prior to COP21, firms’ aggregated environmental and social (E&S) profiles, and environmental (E) profiles are negatively but not significantly associated with cybersecurity‐related disclosure, whereas social (S) profiles exhibit a significantly negative association. Drawing on moral licensing theory, we argue that firm leaders who perceive their firms as having accumulated sufficient moral capital through CSR engagement may feel less compelled to respond proactively to emerging stakeholder expectations in non‐traditional responsibility domains such as cybersecurity. Following COP21, however, firms with stronger aggregated E&S, E, and S profiles increase their cybersecurity‐related disclosure. We interpret COP21 as an institutional inflection point that intensified scrutiny and strengthened evaluative standards surrounding corporate sustainability, thereby diminishing the protective value of previously accrued moral credentials. Under heightened accountability, firm leaders appear more inclined to reaffirm a responsible organizational identity through greater transparency and responsiveness to stakeholder information demands. Overall, our evidence suggests that greater cybersecurity‐related disclosure may help firms signal their commitment to cybersecurity and reinforce their socially legitimate identity.

title: Beyond the Greenium: A Behavioural Approach to Green Bond Investment Intentions in an Emerging Market
abstract: Green bonds, whose proceeds are reserved for environmental projects, are now a principal channel for private climate capital. India's sovereign green bonds go undersubscribed because institutional buyers will not accept a lower return for the label. Retail savings are the obvious alternative, yet household demand is almost unexamined. To address this, we test a dual‐pathway model on 453 aware but noninvested Indian retail investors surveyed in 2024–2025, in which biospheric values and knowledge reach intention partly through attitude. Partial least squares estimation supports the mediated structure, explaining 75.2% of the variance in intention (40.4 method‐adjusted). A rational‐financial route (0.388) and a normative‐environmental route (0.348) carry indistinguishable weight. Mediation roughly doubles the influence of knowledge and biospheric values relative to direct‐effects estimates. Green investment bias shows no relationship with attitude once biospheric values are in the model. Knowledge emerges as the priority for intervention, ranking highest in importance and lowest in current performance. The findings describe stated intention, not actual investment behaviour.

title: Assessing the Informational Value of Sustainable Packaging Under Information Overload: A Decision‐Support Perspective
abstract: Packaging plays a strategic role in sustainability communication under information overload conditions, yet the informational value of sustainable packaging is rarely assessed from a decision‐orientated perspective. This study proposes and empirically tests a decision‐support framework that integrates expert‐defined sustainability ideals with consumer perception gaps under uncertainty. Using fermented dairy products as an empirical context, the research combines focus group evaluations, semantic differential scales and intuitionistic fuzzy modelling to examine how sustainable packaging information is processed in real‐world decision settings. The results indicate that the informational value does not stem from the volume of sustainability‐related messages, but rather from their coherence, hierarchical organisation and alignment with functional and visual decision heuristics. Functional attributes, such as ease of use and ergonomics, show the strongest alignment with expert expectations, whereas sustainability cues generate informational value only when embedded in concrete usage contexts and supported by clear visual signals. The proposed framework offers strategic guidance for sustainable packaging design and sustainability communication under constrained consumer attention.

title: Rethinking justice theory for service recovery in the era of agentic AI
abstract: Purpose As hospitality firms increasingly aspire to deploy agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems capable of autonomous decision-making, service failures involving such systems give rise to responsibility indeterminacy. This paper aims to revisit justice theory to develop a collaborative justice governance framework for understanding and managing service recovery following agentic AI failures. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper critically reviews the service recovery and justice literature to examine how responsibility has been attributed in service failures and how distributive, procedural and interactional justice are operationalised in traditional service recovery and challenged by agentic AI. Building on these insights, each justice dimension is reframed to demonstrate how hospitality firms, frontline employees and customers collectively enact fair recovery. Findings This paper reconceptualises distributive, procedural and interactional justice as a collaborative governance process enacted through complementary stakeholder contributions. Hospitality organisations establish the organisational conditions that enable fair recovery, frontline employees translate these conditions into adaptive recovery practices and customers actively contribute to shaping recovery processes, and outcomes. Practical implications The framework provides actionable guidance for redesigning hospitality service recovery in preparation for agentic AI failures. It demonstrates that fair recovery depends not only on organisational responsibility but also on building collaborative recovery capabilities that enable hospitality organisations, frontline employees and customers to jointly restore fairness. Social implications This paper highlights the societal implications of responsibility indeterminacy for accountability and fair treatment in AI-mediated services, emphasising the need for governance arrangements that enable affected individuals to seek redress, challenge harmful outcomes and participate in recovery when agentic AI failures cannot be fully explained or attributed. Originality/value This paper extends justice theory introducing collaborative justice governance as a new theoretical framework explaining how hospitality organisations, frontline employees and customers collectively enact fairness under responsibility indeterminacy.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: How ESG content drives social media engagement: Insights from business-to-business firms
Rethinking healthcare professional well-being: a service ecosystem perspective on moral tensions in care delivery
abstract: Purpose This conceptual paper adopts a service ecosystem perspective to examine how healthcare professional well-being (HPW) is shaped through the negotiation of competing demands in service interactions. It introduces a moral lens to explain how these tensions carry implications for what is considered right and appropriate in practice across micro, meso, and macro levels within healthcare service ecosystems. Design/methodology/approach Using theory synthesis and adaptation, this paper integrates insights from multiple disciplines to map fragmented research on morality and HPW. It adapts existing perspectives on HPW to develop a multi-level, service-integrated framework that explains how the ongoing negotiation of moral tensions in care delivery shapes how HPW is sustained and eroded within service ecosystems. Findings The framework positions moral injury and moral resilience as interconnected, evolving processes shaped through ongoing negotiation of moral tensions within healthcare service ecosystems. It outlines four interlinked research directions, each with research questions and theoretical framing to guide future study. Research limitations/implications The paper provides a forward-looking agenda with research questions, theoretical lenses, and methodologies, offering conceptual and methodological scaffolding. Practical implications Managers and policymakers can support HPW by fostering collective reflection, psychological safety, and flexible policies that allow learning and adaptation within healthcare service ecosystems. Social implications It urges scholars and practitioners to view HPW as a moral domain where integrity, care, and moral sustainability are co-created. Originality/value This work advances service research by reframing HPW as a fundamentally moral phenomenon shaped within healthcare service ecosystems rather than as an individual state. The multi-level, service-integrated framework offers new theoretical insights into how HPW emerges through the negotiation of moral tensions embedded in care delivery, giving rise to divergent trajectories towards moral injury or moral resilience.

Building socially responsible global brand identity with AI and sustainability strategy
abstract: Purpose This research is an attempt to systematically review the current body of literature about strategic use of artificial intelligence and sustainability orientation to build a responsible global identity. Design/methodology/approach To conduct a systematic review and present a qualitative synthesis of literature, this research uses a multi-faceted four-stage PRISMA protocol that includes identification, screening, eligibility and inclusion. Findings Our analysis of academic knowledge reveals that available brand strategy literature mainly considers the consumer perspective and does not include the perspective of the global community of stakeholders. To address this gap, this study integrates sustainability orientation and AI strategy with governance, brand resilience and standardization–adaptation theory to explain how organizations can build socially responsible global brand identities. In doing so, the study provides a novel framework for balancing global consistency and local relevance in increasingly transparent and digitally connected markets. Originality/value This research offers a comprehensive analysis of theoretical, methodological and empirical knowledge to find answers to the research questions raised by the current context of sustainability consciousness and new age of artificial technologies.

title: Charting new paths: understanding trajectories of intercultural competence transfer from the university to the workplace
abstract: Intercultural competence (IC) has become increasingly important for employees working in culturally diverse organizations. While higher education institutions invest substantial resources in developing students’ IC, relatively little is known about how IC in university education is transferred into professional practice during the early stages of graduates’ careers. Existing transfer of training research has largely explained transfer either through individual characteristics or through organizational factors. Drawing on 30 qualitative interviews with graduates of international business programs, this study examines how graduates negotiate the opportunities and constraints presented by their workplaces as they attempt to apply their IC. We identify three distinct transfer trajectories, steady growth, disrupted, and explorative, which illustrate the dynamic, nonlinear, and individualized nature of IC transfer in professional contexts. Across these trajectories, transfer emerges as a negotiated process shaped by the interaction between individual agency and organizational conditions. We further identify three connected mechanisms shaping these trajectories: recognition of opportunities to apply IC, internal feedback from prior transfer attempts, and perceived status in intercultural interactions. By introducing a trajectory-based perspective, the study demonstrates a more nuanced understanding of how the transfer of IC is sustained, interrupted, or generalized across early careers.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Can training and development enhance both economic and ESG performance? A cross-institutional analysis of European firms
abstract: Amid growing stakeholder pressure for both economic performance and sustainability, understanding how training and development (T&D) influences these dual objectives has become relevant for modern companies. This study examines the impact of T&D on both economic and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance, considering the moderating role of institutional context. Using data from 2,394 European public listed companies across 27 countries between 2005 and 2024, the findings reveal a nuanced relationship between T&D and performance. While the impact of T&D on economic performance is mixed, depending on the type and design of initiatives, its effect on ESG performance is consistently positive, indicating that T&D contributes to sustainability objectives. Institutional context plays a moderating role, with firms in continental and liberal models benefiting most from T&D. This study advances the literature by integrating contextual variables and dual performance metrics, while also offering practical insights for managers, who should design context-specific T&D strategies to align with both economic and sustainability goals, enhancing long-term organisational success.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: From office corridors to digital feeds: how hybrid work reconfigures social media use in talent management
abstract: Hybrid and remote work have transformed how organizations manage talent, shifting developmental and relational HR practices from physical spaces to digital and social-media-enabled environments. Yet research still concentrates mainly on social media for recruitment and employer branding, offering limited insight into its role in ongoing talent management processes such as feedback, recognition, learning, and internal mobility. Drawing on McFarland and Ployhart’s (Citation2015) view of social media as an organizational context, this multi-case qualitative study examines how hybrid and remote organizations incorporate social media platforms into recognition, feedback, development, and internal mobility practices, and how employees and managers experience the resulting visibility and boundary tensions. Using 48 semi-structured interviews, digital ethnography, and document analysis across four knowledge-intensive firms, the study employs abductive thematic analysis, triangulating interview accounts with platform observation and organizational documents to develop within- and cross-case insights. Findings identify three organizational configurations through which social media becomes embedded in hybrid talent management – ‘connective glue’, ‘shadow HR’, and ‘soft surveillance’ - and show that employees’ positions along a joint visibility–boundary continuum, spanning arbitrage-to-dumping and porous-blending-to-hard-shell strategies, shape their perceived access to recognition, fairness, and development opportunities. The study’s principal contribution is this continuum model, which explains why the same platform affordances produce divergent perceived consequences for different employees in hybrid settings, extending contextual theories of social media into the ongoing, relational work of talent management. Because the qualitative design captures participants’ sensemaking rather than objective career outcomes, the findings are presented as perceived consequences for recognition, fairness, and development access rather than demonstrated effects on promotion, retention, or performance. The study offers talent management and employee relations research an empirically grounded, parsimonious typology, along with practical guidance for governing social media use in ways that are more inclusive and development-oriented in distributed work contexts.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Cognitive demands of flexible work and role stressors: Daily and weekly links with strain and positive adaptation
abstract: Cognitive demands of flexible work have been conceptualized as challenge demands that may both stimulate and strain individuals; however, insights on when either outcome prevails remain scarce. In this paper, we integrate the challenge–hindrance stressor framework with action regulation theory to test how daily and weekly demands for structuring of work tasks (DSWTs) and for coordinating with others (DCWOs) interact with role stressors at work to influence strain‐related outcomes (impaired detachment and exhaustion) and positive adaptation‐related outcomes (work engagement and cognitive flexibility). To test our theorizing, we conducted two independent diary studies—a 10‐day study (N = 92; n = 585) and a 10‐week study (N = 78; n = 476)—using multilevel path modelling with Bayesian estimation. Findings indicate DCWOs, but not DSWTs, were associated with higher daily and weekly exhaustion, lower weekly detachment and higher weekly cognitive flexibility. Moderation analyses further showed weekly role ambiguity amplified the positive associations of DCWOs with both exhaustion and cognitive flexibility. These findings suggest coordination demands in flexible work may involve strain‐related costs as well as positive adaptive gains, particularly when employees face high role ambiguity at work.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: “Not your accountant’s classroom”: everyday resistance and decolonising neoliberalism in UK accounting education
abstract: This study examines how accounting students and recent graduates in UK universities experience, negotiate, and at times resist the neoliberal and postcolonial logics shaping accounting education. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative design, it analyses semi-structured interviews with 21 participants across five UK universities and uses an integrated framework combining decolonial theory, audit culture critique, dialogic pedagogy, and everyday resistance. The findings are organised around three themes: constrained student agency within curricula shaped by assessment pressures and professional hierarchies; ethical unease and value dissonance generated by a curriculum organised around technical competence and employability; and a hidden curriculum through which belonging, legitimacy, and epistemic recognition are unevenly distributed. Resistance rarely appeared as open confrontation, emerging instead through peer learning networks, informal dialogue, reframing of assignments, and other small acts of curricular negotiation. The study shows that accounting education is a contested pedagogic space and argues for more dialogic, plural, and ethically responsive approaches to curriculum design, teaching, and student participation. In doing so, it foregrounds students’ negotiations of legitimacy, belonging, and critique, and informs debates on pedagogy, inclusion, and curricular transformation.

title: Internationalising accounting and finance education under conditional globalisation
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how accounting and finance education acquires international value within a conditionally globalised environment, and how professional recognition relates to universities' epistemic and public-interest legitimacy. Design/methodology/approach The paper develops a conceptual framework through an integrative discussion of accounting and finance education, internationalisation, signalling, legitimacy and professions research. Australian educational arrangements and published research illustrate the institutional relationships. Findings International value depends on interdependent relationships among university legitimacy, professional recognition, regulatory credibility, employer reputation, mobility opportunities and public-interest formation. Their importance varies by audience, discipline and jurisdiction. Professional recognition can amplify educational credibility when it complements knowledge formation; its dominance can weaken legitimacy when it displaces critical inquiry. Four propositions specify these relationships and their boundaries. Originality/value The paper conceptualises international accounting and finance education as reputational infrastructure. It connects conditional cross-border value with the productive tension between professional legibility and universities' responsibilities as custodians, critics and producers of knowledge, while distinguishing the disciplines' recognition pathways.

title: Being Together: Sense of Belonging and Virtual Item Purchases in Multiplayer Online Battle Arenas
abstract: Multiplayer online battle arenas (MOBAs) combine intensive coordination with team compositions that may vary across matches. This study examines the associations between players' sense of belonging to their team, Informational Susceptibility to Interpersonal Influence, Normative Susceptibility to Interpersonal Influence, and two self‐reported virtual item (VI) purchase behaviors: VI purchase for the Player's Avatar and VI Purchase for Teammates. The model integrates the frameworks of sense of virtual community and consumer susceptibility to interpersonal influence. Cross‐sectional survey data from 892 League of Legends players are analyzed using covariance‐based structural equation modeling (CB‐SEM) as the primary approach, complemented by PLS‐SEM and logistic regressions. SEM results indicate that sense of belonging is positively associated with both susceptibility dimensions and both purchase outcomes. Both susceptibility dimensions are positively associated with VI purchase for the Player's Avatar, whereas their associations with VI Purchase for Teammates are not statistically significant. Complementary logistic regressions also identify positive associations between belonging and both purchase outcomes, but indicate that conclusions regarding interpersonal susceptibility are sensitive to model specification. These findings suggest potential differences across purchase targets that warrant cautious interpretation, while highlighting the consistent association of belonging with both purchases across specifications. The study also informs publishers' efforts to design and test community features tailored to avatar‐oriented and teammate‐oriented purchases in settings where team composition may vary.

Maintaining Effort Amid Shared Adversity: How Hyperinflation Alters the Motivational Influence of Economic Hardship
abstract: Research suggests employees generally respond to economic hardship by exerting less effort and performing more poorly at work. We argue that economic hardship can facilitate the salience of socially valued role expectations and thereby help maintain work effort when it occurs during societally shared economic adversity, specifically hyperinflation. We first test hypotheses in Turkish healthcare organizations over nine weeks of skyrocketing inflation (Study 1). There was a positive but non‐significant effect of worsened economic hardship on increased work effort. We also found a significant interaction effect indicating that employees with high perspective taking responded to intensified economic hardship by increasing their effort, which was linked to higher job performance. Studies 2 and 3 experimentally manipulated worsening economic hardship and hyperinflation. Worsened (vs. unchanged) economic hardship did not reduce work effort, directly (Study 2) or indirectly through self‐transcendence (Study 3), in the hyperinflation condition, but it hampered effort in the no hyperinflation condition. Additionally, higher perspective taking enabled individuals to maintain their self‐transcendence (Study 3) and work effort (Study 2) in responding to worsened economic hardships amid hyperinflation, whereas it exacerbated the unfavorable effect of economic hardship in the no hyperinflation condition. We discuss theoretical implications for work motivation amid shared economic adversity, practical implications, our model's validity boundaries, and potential future directions.

title: Leader non-work-related personal resources: Literature review and integrative framework
abstract: Leaders' effectiveness depends not only on skills and motivation but also on personal resources that sustain energy and well-being beyond work. Yet research on leaders' non-work-related personal resources (NWPR) remains scattered across leadership, occupational health, and recovery literatures. To address this fragmentation, we combine topic modeling with integrative synthesis to conduct the first systematic review dedicated to leader NWPR. We analyze 312 articles and synthesize NWPR topics within a Context–Mechanisms–Outcomes framework. Findings show that the intellectual structure of leader NWPR research is highly fragmented, spanning eight theoretical domains. These diverse literatures converge in viewing leaders' recovery and well-being outside work as indispensable for sustaining effective leadership. Our integrative framework goes beyond descriptive synthesis by specifying how leadership contexts may activate or constrain NWPR mechanisms across time and levels. The framework positions leadership as a contextual amplifier: because leaders occupy roles of sustained visibility, accountability, and relational influence, their restored or depleted resource states may be enacted through interaction and may cascade to followers, teams, and organizations. It identifies three temporally nested mechanism pathways: daily depletion–replenishment, cumulative resource gain–loss dynamics, and cross-domain transfer with relational amplification. Through these pathways, off-job resources may shape leader well-being, leadership behavior, and multilevel outcomes. We also assess the causal trustworthiness of links between the framework's categories. Our synthesis provides a coherent foundation, propositions, and a research agenda for understanding how leaders' off-job personal resources may support well-being, ethical behavior, and enduring performance.

title: Hiring talent in technologically advanced countries: The paradox of springboarding for firms from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes
abstract: Research Summary Anecdotes suggest that multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes often leapfrog to technological leadership by recruiting talent in advanced host countries. Yet whether—and how—such a strategy works remains unclear. Using data on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the United States and interviews with skilled inventors, we uncover a paradox in the springboard‐via‐hiring logic: externally, weak home‐country IPR reputation deters skilled inventors from joining, limiting recruitment; internally, even when talent is hired, home‐country‐imprinted IPR routines constrain post‐hire learning, yielding incremental improvements. These effects are mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to host‐country patent infringement litigation. Our research suggests that springboard‐via‐hiring is institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. These findings offer implications for technology policy and MNEs' strategy amid geopolitical tension. Managerial Summary Can multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes leapfrog by hiring technical talent in advanced economies? Evidence on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the US high‐technology sector suggests: weaker home‐country IPR reputations make it harder to attract skilled inventors; even after hiring, home‐imprinted IPR routines can constrain recruits' knowledge transfer, often steering outcomes toward incremental improvements. These home‐country constraints are, however, mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to US patent infringement litigation. The springboard‐via‐hiring strategy is thus institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. We accordingly offer advice on technology policy and global R&D strategies for host‐country governments and MNEs amid geopolitical tension.

Skill certifications and migrant labor market integration: Experimental evidence from Colombia
abstract: This paper studies whether government-issued skill certification improves labor market integration when workers skills are hard to verify. We evaluate a randomized offer of access to an occupation-specific certification program in Colombia to locals and migrants, two groups with different ex ante signaling capacity. The program certifies existing skills rather than providing training. Among locals, the offer increases employment by reducing inactivity and raises hours worked. The effects persist unevenly over time and are robust to attrition bounds and alternative outcome measures. Among migrants, estimates are less precise and provide no evidence of effects in employment, hours, or wages. The results show that a common skill certification generates different patterns of labor market adjustment among locals and migrants.

FDI spillovers in history: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China's cotton spinning industry
abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo) to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. In order to capture the important role of distance in facilitating such spillovers we geo-localised the plants. Our results provide clear evidence for positive spillovers from Zaikabo to local Chinese mills, which go hand-in-hand with an upgrade in production technology towards greater use of capital. Spillovers are very localised, being strongest within a radius of up to 10 km around the Zaikabo and particularly strong for mills in Shanghai. Exploiting information on the workforce composition of the Japanese affiliates, we find suggestive evidence of a skilled-labour channel: spillovers tend to be larger from Zaikabo employing higher shares of skilled labour. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Our paper is the first to document FDI productivity spillovers in a historical context and to characterise the channels through which they operate.

abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between price dispersion and inflation, shedding light on one major source of the cost of high inflation. By analyzing novel product-level web-scraped data from over 60,000 restaurants and supermarkets across 18 countries facing high and low inflation periods, I uncover new evidence of a significant positive correlation between inflation and price dispersion. My findings reveal that average annualized inflation, ranging between 0 and 20 percentage points across countries within a condensed time frame, is significantly associated with higher price dispersion in both the restaurant and the supermarket sectors. The estimates indicate that the marginal effect of suboptimal inflation on product-level distortions is positive, economically significant in all inflation environments and heterogeneous across sectors. Cross-sectionally, I find that as annualized inflation rises from 0% to 10% inefficient price dispersion is about 46% higher for supermarkets and 73% higher for restaurants. Lastly, the relationship between inflation and price dispersion does not flatten much at higher inflation, so that the marginal cost of additional inflation does not vanish as inflation rises – a pattern standard menu-cost models do not generate. This indicates a sustained impact of inflation on price dispersion, implying that accommodating higher inflation levels incurs substantial welfare costs.

Spillover effects of foreign currency loans: The role of the bank lending channel
abstract: Local currency borrowers are statistically significantly affected by exchange rate fluctuations due to the bank lending chan‐ nel. Using microdata on borrowers from Hungary, this study examines the spillover effects of foreign currency loans on local currency borrowers following an unexpected appreciation of the Swiss franc (CHF) in January 2015. CHF corporate loans are considered unhedged since the majority of the borrowers did not have income in CHF. Our analysis indicates that banks holding a larger portion of unhedged CHF corporate loans reduced their lending in local currency corporate loans after the shock. This relationship is robust across both extensive (loans terminated by a given bank and no new loans at a bank or banks different from the account holder bank or banks) and intensive (no new loans at its current bank or banks) margins. Further investigation into the mechanisms reveals that banks with more unhedged CHF corporate loans experience an increase in non‐performing CHF loans post‐shock, reducing their capital adequacy. Furthermore, the evidence in our paper suggests that reductions in banks’ local currency lending due to exchange rate shocks adversely affect the investment activity of small firms and increase their likelihood of default.

title: Global production networks and imperfect competition
abstract: How do global production networks and market structure interact to shape the welfare effects of trade and competition policy? We develop a model with two-sided firm heterogeneity, matching frictions, and imperfect supplier competition. More productive buyers match with more suppliers, inducing tougher competition among them, lower input costs, and higher profits. Entry upstream thus benefits primarily high-productivity buyers, while lower trade or matching costs favor mid-productivity buyers. Reduced-form evidence confirms that larger French and Chilean firms import higher quantities at lower prices as more Chinese suppliers enter, and that suppliers charge diversified buyers lower markups. We estimate the model by adapting recent methods for combinatorial, discrete-choice problems. Counterfactuals reveal that the interaction of endogenous networks and markups significantly amplifies the gains from policies that facilitate supplier entry or firm matching, as well as from modern trade agreements that combine trade cost cuts with such policies.

abstract: This paper focuses on finite-player incomplete information games where players may hold mutually inconsistent beliefs without a common prior. We introduce absolute continuity of beliefs, extending the classical notion of absolute continuity of information in Milgrom and Weber (1985), and prove that Bayesian equilibria exist in a broad class of games, including those with discontinuous payoffs. Examples illustrate the scope and implications of our findings.

abstract: We define and study obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition of the set of agents. It encompasses strategy-proofness as a special case when the partition is the coarsest one and obvious strategy-proofness when the partition is the finest. For any partition, it falls between these two extremes. We establish two general properties of this new notion and apply it to the simple anonymous voting problem with two alternatives and strict preferences.

abstract: We study the adjudication of water rights in international rivers. We characterize allocation rules that formalize focal principles to deal with water disputes in a basic model. Central to our analysis is a family of geometric rules that implement concatenated transfers downstream. They can be seen as formalizing Limited Territorial Sovereignty, as suggested in the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. We apply our rules to the case of the Nile River, with a long history of disputes between downstream and upstream nations

abstract: This study aims to understand efficient network formation and optimal defensive resource distribution in the presence of an intelligent attacker. We present a two-player dynamic framework in which the Defender and the Attacker compete in a network formation and defence game with heterogeneous vertices’ values. Such a model allows for studying the trade-off between network efficiency and security. Contrary to the literature, we find that a centrally protected star network does not yield the maximum payoff for the defending side in most circumstances, even being the most secure network formation. Additionally, it reveals a new type of network that often arises in an equilibrium of the games with limited defensive resources—a maxi-core network.

Risk, time, and diet quality: Evidence from a general population survey
abstract: This paper explores the relationships between overall diet quality and attitudes toward risk and time using a general population survey. We combine a food frequency questionnaire and a choice-based preference module to elicit individual risk and time preferences. The online questionnaire was administered to a socioeconomic panel representative of the French population. We show that risk and time preferences are associated with individual heterogeneity in key aspects of diet quality, a result that holds across a wide range of robustness checks. Using a hierarchical Bayes framework, we jointly estimate individual risk aversion and impatience parameters and show that associations hold for both model-free and structural estimates of risk and time preferences. We further show that these associations account for a substantial share of the heterogeneity in dietary outcomes beyond sociodemographic controls. Risk and time preferences contribute to both the income-diet-quality and education-diet-quality gradients, but in opposite directions, resulting in a limited net contribution to explaining socioeconomic inequalities in diet quality.

In sickness and in health insurance: Gender in household benefit plan choice
abstract: I document that households in the United States are more likely to choose health plans offered by the husband's employer than the wife's. This gap may reflect gender disparities in employment status, plan quality, or an inherent gender effect. Using a novel identification strategy that holds employment status and plan quality fixed, I find that the gender effect increases the probability of selecting the husband's plan by 6.3 percentage points.

title: Recent minimum wage policy and its impacts on birth outcomes
abstract: After a pause in statutory minimum wage increases during the Great Recession, several states increased their minimum wages, including increases as large as 60% over just a few years. Using a triple difference-in-differences framework and data on the universe of births from 2010 to 2019, this study investigates how recent minimum wage hikes affected birth outcomes. We first document sizeable negative impacts of minimum wage policy on the labor supply and economic well-being of females aged 16-44. We then document small adverse effects on birth outcomes, estimating that minimum wage increases led to lower birthweight, fewer normal birthweight births, and more small for gestational age births. These findings generally contrast with an earlier literature relying primarily on much smaller minimum wage increases which showed more evidence of positive impacts on birth outcomes.

title: Beyond targeting women: Intrahousehold contexts and the effectiveness of food vouchers
abstract: Many transfer programs target women based on evidence that mothers are more likely than fathers to allocate resources toward child welfare. However, findings on gendered impacts remain mixed-likely because parental knowledge, preferences, and household decision-making roles differ across contexts. In this study, we experimentally vary the intrahousehold informational context itself through a randomized controlled trial in rural Ethiopia. Specifically, employing a factorial design, we cross-randomize two key dimensions: (1) which parent receives nutrition behavior change communication (BCC) - neither, mother only, or both; and (2) which parent receives a household food voucher - mother or father. We find that, pooled across settings in which fathers do not receive BCC, vouchers assigned to mothers generate larger improvements in child-feeding practices than vouchers assigned to fathers. The largest effects occur when mothers receive both BCC and the voucher. This maternal advantage attenuates and is no longer detectable when fathers also receive BCC. We provide suggestive evidence that when mothers have both a knowledge advantage and control over resources, they are better able to mobilize greater intrahousehold support. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for intrahousehold contexts, not just recipient gender, when designing nutrition interventions.

title: Patient sorting and downstream spending: evidence from an information disclosure program
abstract: Choosing a physician who can deliver high-quality care at a reasonable cost can improve health outcomes and reduce spending on healthcare. I study a disclosure program that classifies physicians based on quality and cost. I use a regression discontinuity design and find that physicians who score higher on both quality and cost effectiveness see 38% more new patients, and that younger patients are more responsive than older patients. Evaluating claims of patients who switch physicians following physician exit, I find that middle-aged patients experience larger reductions in spending than younger patients when switching to higher-quality, lower-cost physicians.

title: Labor unions and deaths of despair: Evidence from right-to-work laws
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between union membership and deaths of despair. Using state-level variation in the timing of the adoption of right-to-work laws as a natural experiment, I show that right-to-work laws are associated with a decline in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair. Two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates suggest that the adoption of a right-to-work law is associated with a 2.6 percentage point reduction in union membership and an increase in deaths of despair mortality of 13 additional persons per 100,000, implying there are approximately 7.5 additional deaths of despair for every 1,000 workers who lose union membership. An analysis of mechanisms suggests the increase in mortality is largely driven by increased opioid usage and a concomitant increase in overdose deaths. I support the TWFE results with estimates from two alternative estimators robust to concerns about treatment effect heterogeneity and variation in treatment timing. Estimates from the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) estimator and the Borusyak et al. (2024) estimator support the TWFE findings: right-to-work laws reduce union membership and increase deaths of despair.

title: Subsidies for innovative technology adoption: Experimental evidence on malaria in Burkina Faso
abstract: We evaluated both the demand for and impact of a prevention tool against malaria that requires repeated purchase and overcomes the limits of mosquito bed nets. We used a randomized experiment to examine the effects of subsidies for a mosquito repellent ointment that protects against mosquito bites and malaria on product use and malaria cases in Burkina Faso. Around 3100 households were randomly allocated to one of the three experimental groups defined by level of subsidy: 0, 50 or 100%. Subsidies strongly and significantly increase the probability of acquiring a jar of mosquito repellent ointment and using it regularly during the rainy season. We find no substitution with bed nets, but a strong effect on the use of mosquito coils. The treatment effects on usage are heterogeneous, including more positive outcomes for young children as reported by their caregiver. The impact on use continues even after the end of the subsidy, with effects on demand and willingness to pay elicited through a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak approach eight months after the end of the intervention. Our intervention induces a significant reduction in declared malaria occurrence during the rainy season, but no effect at the very end of the rainy season when blood tests were taken. The seemingly discrepancy will be partly explained by timing and sample size.

title: The effect of online sales bans on e-cigarette use
The adverse effects of weight reports in schools
abstract: Using rich survey data for England, we investigate whether providing parents with information about the weight status of their children reduces children's weight and improves health behaviors, or whether it has adverse effects. We exploit the timing of survey interview compared to the timing of sending out weight reports to parents in a difference-in-differences framework. Our analysis does not reveal the intended effects on body weight or health behaviors. Instead, we find adverse effects for children with overweight that are concentrated in disadvantaged families and driven by increases in breakfast skipping and feeling tired and unhappy at school.

title: Do Higher-Cost Settings Deliver Better Outcomes? Post-Acute Care Efficiency in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities and Home Health Agencies
abstract: Determining the value of different post-acute care settings for clinically similar patients is important for providers and payers. This study examines the causal effect of post-acute care (PAC) setting on Medicare spending and short-term patient outcomes among beneficiaries discharged from hospitals following treatment for stroke or congestive heart failure (CHF). Using 2013-2017 Medicare claims data, we implement an instrumental variable strategy that exploits daily variation in skilled nursing facility (SNF) bed occupancy at the hospital service area level to estimate the local average treatment effect of SNF versus home health agency (HHA) care. Our findings reveal no significant differences, on average, in 30-day mortality or rehospitalization rates between SNF and HHA care among stroke and CHF patients. However, the 95% confidence intervals do not exclude clinically meaningful reductions in 30-day mortality. Meanwhile, SNF care is associated with approximately $4700 more in Medicare spending per PAC episode. The spending gap is larger in markets with more constrained SNF capacity, particularly in states with Certificate of Need regulations, rural areas, and low-income neighborhoods. However, we do not detect statistically significant differences in short-term health outcomes across these markets on average, suggesting that supply constraints may amplify the spending implications of SNF use while the relationship between PAC setting and short-term clinical outcomes remains uncertain. These findings highlight the importance of aligning PAC discharge decisions with both clinical needs and local capacity considerations, particularly under value-based payment models.

title: Visual vs. Textual communication: Impact on firms’ inflation expectations and central bank credibility
abstract: We causally identify how firms’ inflation expectations and their trust in the central bank respond to information with the same relevant content presented through different formats. Simple text and visual communication effectively influence inflation expectations, while complex text messaging fails to yield similar effects. Firms exposed to visual representations of information adjust their expectations significantly more than those receiving equivalent information in text form. Notably, the effect of visual content is particularly strong but short-lived. Complex text messages may undermine the credibility of the central bank. These results suggest a scope for tailoring communication to better align firms’ inflation expectations with inflation targets while preserving the credibility of the monetary authority. title: Is bitcoin a hedge against central banking? Evidence from AI-driven monetary policy expectations
abstract: This study investigates the transmission of monetary policy narratives to Bitcoin prices, distinguishing policy expectations from realized policy implementation. We introduce a weekly Monetary Policy Expectations (MPE) index derived from the Large Language Model (LLM)-based classification of 118,000+ market messages, providing a granular measure of hawkish and dovish monetary policy discourse. We demonstrate that changes in the MPE index provide evidence of significant linear predictive information for Bitcoin returns at short-to-medium horizons, with significant Granger causality at multiple lags. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) further identifies nonlinear and regime-dependent relationships between monetary-policy expectations and Bitcoin returns, indicating that Bitcoin functions as a sensitive barometer of central bank signaling. In particular, hawkish monetary-policy narratives are associated with negative price responses that are not accounted for by contemporaneous Federal Funds Rate adjustments. These findings highlight Bitcoin's structural sensitivity to global monetary discourse, establishing LLM-derived monetary-policy sentiment as a high-frequency measure of central-bank communication and as an informative leading macroeconomic indicator for the digital asset landscape.

title: Forecasting the price of carbon with macroeconomic and financial variables
abstract: We tackle the issue of producing point, sign, and density forecasts for the monthly real price of carbon in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). We show that Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (BVAR) models augmented with factors based on macroeconomic and financial variables yield improvements in point and density forecasting performance, with the largest point-forecast gains emerging at intermediate and longer horizons. In particular, the one-factor BVAR model provides lowest values at six and nine months ahead, while the baseline BVAR performs best at the one-year horizon. By contrast, a large BVAR including all predictors individually does not improve point forecast accuracy, supporting the use of parsimonious model specifications. Simple forecast pooling delivers modest gains from medium horizons onward, but does not mitigate the time variation in relative forecast performance. We also provide a qualitative comparison of model-based forecasts with survey expectations and forecasts released by data providers, which further highlights that relative forecast performance varies over time. Moreover, we consider verified emissions and show that stochastic volatility improves point forecasts, with reductions of about 6.5 to 7.1% at the one-year horizon. Lastly, we use model-based forecasts to construct market monitoring tools that track demand and price pressure in the EU ETS.

“Made in heaven, matched by parents”: Can arranged marriage restrict labour market autonomy and participation of women?
abstract: Female labour force participation in India has stagnated despite gains in other aspects. Do Indian women prefer to stay out of labour market voluntarily or do social norms prevent their participation? We identify parental involvement in partner choice during marriage as an important bottleneck. We first find that women who had some degree of involvement in partner choice enjoy significantly more autonomy in post-marriage labour market choices than those whose marriages were arranged solely by parents. We use a marriage tradition instrument to estimate causal effects. Since autonomy and participation affect each other, next, we estimate simultaneous equations for autonomy and participation for only rural women. We use parental involvement in marriage and district-level share of drought-affected villages as two exogenous variables the former for autonomy and the latter for participation. We find that autonomy significantly increases participation. We further explain the mechanism through a theoretical model. To distinguish between autonomy and participation; we introduce a new household delegation game. Combining value-at-risk and expected-shortfall forecasts via the model confidence set
abstract: To comply with increasingly stringent international standards in risk management and regulation, several approaches have been developed in the literature for forecasting tail-risk measures such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). However, the accuracy of these measures can be significantly affected by multiple sources of uncertainty, including model misspecification, data limitations and estimation procedures. To address these challenges and enhance the predictive performance of individual models, this study introduces novel forecast combination strategies based on the Model Confidence Set (MCS) methodology. Specifically, a strictly consistent joint VaR-ES loss function is employed to identify the best-performing models, which constitute the Set of Superior Models (SSM). Subsequently, the VaR and ES forecasts of the models included in the SSM are combined using various weighting schemes. An empirical analysis based on nine stock market indices at the 2.5\% and 1\% risk levels provides evidence that the proposed combined predictors are a robust alternative for forecasting tail-risk measures, successfully passing standard backtests and consistently entering the SSM of the MCS.

title: Identifying good forecasters via adaptive cognitive tests
abstract: Assessing forecasting performance is a time intensive activity, often requiring months or years before we know whether or not the reported forecasts were accurate. Cognitive tests can be quickly administered and are predictive of forecasting performance, but it is unclear which and how many tests are optimal. In this study, we develop adaptive cognitive tests that optimize the selection and efficiency of cognitive tests to assess forecasters of different skill levels. The tests are based on item response models and the adaptive testing procedures commonly used in educational testing. We show how the procedures can select highly informative cognitive tests from a larger battery of tests, thereby reducing the time taken to administer the tests. We use a second, independent dataset to show that the selected tests yield scores that are highly related to out-of-sample forecasting performance. The approach enables real-time, adaptive testing, providing immediate insights into forecasting talent in practical contexts.

Modeling uncertainty in the covariance matrix for probabilistic forecast reconciliation
abstract: In minimum trace (MinT) forecast reconciliation, the covariance matrix of the base forecast errors plays a crucial role. Typically, this matrix is estimated and then treated as known. This can lead to an underestimation of the variance of the predictive distribution. To address the problem, we propose a Bayesian reconciliation model that accounts for uncertainty in the estimation of the covariance matrix. By adopting an Inverse-Wishart prior and assuming Gaussian residuals, the reconciled predictive distribution follows a multivariate t-distribution, obtained in closed form, rather than a multivariate Gaussian distribution. We evaluate our method on three tourism-related datasets, including a new publicly available dataset. Empirical results show that our approach consistently improves prediction intervals compared to MinT reconciliation.

Predicting inflation with recurrent neural networks
abstract: This paper applies a recurrent neural network, the LSTM, to forecast inflation. This is an appealing model for time series as it processes each time step sequentially and explicitly learns dynamic dependencies. The paper also explores the dimension reduction capability of the model to uncover economically-meaningful factors that can explain the inflation process. Results from an exercise with US data indicate that the estimated neural nets present competitive, but not outstanding, performance against common benchmarks (including other machine learning models). The LSTM in particular is found to perform well at long horizons and during periods of heightened macroeconomic uncertainty. Interestingly, LSTM-implied factors present high correlation with business cycle indicators, informing on the usefulness of such signals as inflation predictors. The paper also sheds light on the impact of network initialization and architecture on forecast performance.

title: Assessing the conditional calibration of interval forecasts using decompositions of the interval score
abstract: Forecasts for uncertain future events should be probabilistic. Probabilistic forecasts are commonly issued as prediction intervals, which provide a measure of uncertainty in the unknown outcome whilst being easier to understand and communicate than full predictive distributions. The calibration of a $(1 - \alpha)$-level prediction interval can be assessed by checking whether the probability that the outcome falls within the interval is equal to $1 - \alpha$. However, such coverage checks are typically unconditional and therefore relatively weak. Although this is well known, there is a lack of methods to assess the conditional calibration of interval forecasts. In this work, we demonstrate how this can be achieved via decompositions of the well-known interval (or Winkler) score. We study notions of calibration for interval forecasts and then introduce a decomposition of the interval score based on isotonic distributional regression. This decomposition exhibits many desirable properties, both in theory and in practice, which allows users to accurately assess the conditional calibration of interval forecasts. This is illustrated on simulated data and in three applications to benchmark regression datasets.

Directional-shift Dirichlet ARMA models for compositional time series with structural break intervention
abstract: Compositional time series frequently exhibit structural breaks due to external shocks, policy changes, or market disruptions. Standard methods either ignore such breaks or handle them through fixed effects that cannot extrapolate beyond the sample, or step-function dummies that impose instantaneous adjustment. We develop a Bayesian Dirichlet ARMA model augmented with a directional-shift intervention mechanism that captures structural breaks through three interpretable parameters: a direction vector specifying which components gain or lose share, an amplitude controlling redistribution magnitude, and a logistic gate governing transition timing and speed. The model preserves compositional constraints by construction, maintains DARMA dynamics for short-run dependence, and produces coherent probabilistic forecasts through and after structural breaks. The intervention trajectory corresponds to geodesic motion on the simplex and is invariant to the choice of ILR basis. A simulation study with 400 fits across 8 scenarios shows near-zero amplitude bias and nominal 80\% credible interval coverage when the shift direction is correctly identified (77.5\% of cases); supplementary studies confirm robustness across extreme transition speeds and non-monotone DGPs. Two empirical applications to COVID-era Airbnb data characterize performance relative to simpler alternatives. Where the break is monotone and ongoing, the intervention model achieves near-nominal calibration (79.6\%) while the fixed effect substantially under-covers (66.1\%). Where post-break dynamics are non-monotone, both models are acceptably calibrated and the fixed effect outperforms on point accuracy. The intervention model's advantages are thus specific to settings with roughly monotone structural transitions.

title: A conditional probability hierarchy for stochastic choice
abstract: We introduce point conditional probability spaces (PCPSs) as primitive building blocks for stochastic choice. This concept goes back to R\'enyi (1955), who proposed conditional probability spaces (CPSs) as a basis for probability theory. Luce (1959) noted the connection between CPSs and stochastic choice, and Cerreia-Vioglio et al. (2021) have developed the connection further. A PCPS is a CPS each of whose component probability measures concentrates on a singleton selection. We build a four-level PCPS-based hierarchy of families of stochastic choice rules. Level 1 consists of PCPSs, Level 2 is made up of finitely additive"conditionally consistent"mixtures of PCPSs, Level 3 comprises all finitely additive probabilistic mixtures of PCPSs, and Level 4 consists of all finitely additive signed probabilistic mixtures of PCPSs. We construct our hierarchy at a general measure-theoretic level that encompasses infinite choice sets. We also connect each level of our hierarchy to well-known axioms for stochastic choice, namely, the Weak Axiom of Stochastic Revealed Preference, Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives, and no Dutch book. We establish the relationship between total orders and PCPSs and demonstrate a sense in which PCPSs can be a more parsimonious representation of choice.

title: A note on the foundations of Grether’s α–β rule
The trade-off between minimal instability and larger improvements over deferred acceptance
abstract: The celebrated Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance mechanism (EADA) improves the efficiency of the DA algorithm via consented priority violations. Notwithstanding its many merits, we show that EADA can improve only two students when an alternative mechanism that Pareto-dominates DA could benefit all but one student. This shortfall in the number of students improved is not exclusive of EADA but extends to all setwise minimally unstable mechanisms, i.e. those that generate a set of blocking pairs that is never a strict superset of that of another mechanism. The incompatibility between number of students improved and minimal instability disappears when blocking pairs are compared cardinally rather than by set inclusion. In some problems, EADA can be doubly dominated: improving fewer students while generating more blocking pairs.

abstract: I consider a neoclassical growth model with a constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) utility function and derive a global closed form approximation that is arbitrarily precise as the discount rate $\rho$ is close to the population growth rate $n$. However, there still may be uncertainty over which version the buyer will get. title: On deterministic optimal mechanisms in a two-item setting for distributions with nondecreasing density
abstract: Consider the problem of designing a revenue-optimal auction mechanism when two heterogeneous items are sold to a single buyer having independent valuations over the items. The distributions of the buyer's valuation for the items are assumed to have densities that are positive, nondecreasing, and continuously differentiable on their support sets $[c_i,c_i+b_i]$ in the positive axis. I prove that the optimal mechanism is deterministic if at least one of the minimum valuations (i.e., either $c_1$ or $c_2$) is sufficiently high. I provide a method to calculate the threshold of $(c_1,c_2)$ beyond which the optimal mechanism is deterministic. I also provide a sufficient condition on the distributions of buyer's valuations for which the individual sale mechanism is optimal. I show that when $c_1$ is low and $c_2$ is high, it is optimal for the seller to sell item $2$ at the minimum valuation $c_2$, thus effectively reducing the problem to finding the optimal mechanism in the one-dimensional setting only for item $1$. I conjecture with promising preliminary results that this result can be extended to the three-item setting. Specifically, I conjecture that when $c_1$ and $c_2$ are low but $c_3$ is high, it is optimal for the seller to sell item $3$ at the minimum valuation $c_3$, thus effectively reducing the problem to finding the optimal mechanism in the two-dimensional setting for items $1$ and $2$.
